### **ORGANISATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT**

The OECD is a unique forum where the governments of 38 democracies work together to address the economic, social and environmental challenges of globalisation. The OECD is also at the forefront of efforts to understand and to help governments respond to new developments and concerns, such as corporate governance, the information economy and the challenges of an ageing population. The Organisation provides a setting where governments can compare policy experiences, seek answers to common problems, identify good practice and work to co-ordinate domestic and international policies.

The OECD member countries are: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and the United States. The European Commission takes part in the work of the OECD.

OECD Publishing disseminates widely the results of the Organisation's statistics gathering and research on economic, social and environmental issues, as well as the conventions, guidelines and standards agreed by its members.

#### **NUCLEAR ENERGY AGENCY**

The OECD Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) was established on 1 February 1958. Current NEA membership consists of 34 countries: Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia (suspended), the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and the United States. The European Commission and the International Atomic Energy Agency also take part in the work of the Agency.

The mission of the NEA is:

- to assist its member countries in maintaining and further developing, through international co-operation, the scientific, technological and legal bases required for a safe, environmentally friendly and economical use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes;
- to provide authoritative assessments and to forge common understandings on key issues, as input to government decisions on nuclear energy policy and to broader OECD policy analyses in areas such as energy and sustainable development.

Specific areas of competence of the NEA include the safety and regulation of nuclear activities, radioactive waste management and decommissioning, radiological protection, nuclear science, economic and technical analyses of the nuclear fuel cycle, nuclear law and liability, and public information. The NEA Data Bank provides nuclear data and computer program services for participating countries.

This document, as well as any data and map included herein, are without prejudice to the status of or sovereignty over any territory, to the delimitation of international frontiers and boundaries and to the name of any territory, city or area.

### **COMMITTEE ON THE SAFETY OF NUCLEAR INSTALLATIONS (CSNI)**

The Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations (CSNI) addresses Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) programmes and activities that support maintaining and advancing the scientific and technical knowledge base of the safety of nuclear installations.

The Committee constitutes a forum for the exchange of technical information and for collaboration between organisations, which can contribute, from their respective backgrounds in research, development and engineering, to its activities. It has regard to the exchange of information between member countries and safety R&D programmes of various sizes in order to keep all member countries involved in and abreast of developments in technical safety matters.

The Committee reviews the state of knowledge on important topics of nuclear safety science and techniques and of safety assessments, and ensures that operating experience is appropriately accounted for in its activities. It initiates and conducts programmes identified by these reviews and assessments in order to confirm safety, overcome discrepancies, develop improvements and reach consensus on technical issues of common interest. It promotes the co-ordination of work in different member countries that serve to maintain and enhance competence in nuclear safety matters, including the establishment of joint undertakings (e.g. joint research and data projects), and assists in the feedback of the results to participating organisations. The Committee ensures that valuable end-products of the technical reviews and analyses are provided to members in a timely manner, and made publicly available when appropriate, to support broader nuclear safety.

The Committee focuses primarily on the safety aspects of existing power reactors, other nuclear installations and new power reactors; it also considers the safety implications of scientific and technical developments of future reactor technologies and designs. Further, the scope for the Committee includes human and organisational research activities and technical developments that affect nuclear safety.

### *Foreword*

The Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) Working Group on Integrity and Ageing of Components and Structures (WGIAGE) aims to advance understanding of the integrity of structures, systems and components (SSC) under design and beyond design basis loads; to provide guidance in choosing the optimal ways of dealing with challenges to operating advanced and innovative nuclear power plants, including small modular reactors (SMRs); and to make use of an integrated approach to design, safety and plant life management.

This report seeks to improve the understanding and knowledge of activities which need to be performed to extend the operating time of nuclear power plants of the most common designs beyond 60 years (in most countries, this isfrom 60 to 80 years). The report provides a collection and analysis of available information and identifies areas that are properly addressed and those that need enhancements in knowledge and technology for safe longterm operation (LTO) beyond 60 years.

All figures and tables that do not list a source were created for the report and list the source as "NEA data", with the appropriate year.

Work on the report was initiated in October 2022 with the Nuclear Research and Consultancy Group's (NRG) task "LTO Beyond 60 Years", as part of the NRG PIONIER research project (2021-2024). In January 2023, it was decided to transfer the project to the NEA under the Working Group on Integrity and Ageing of Components and Structures (WGIAGE). A committee activity planning sheet (CAPS) was developed and approved by the WGIAGE and the NEA Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations (CSNI) in March to June 2023. Descriptive sections of the report (1-5) were finalised in August 2024 and conclusions including proposals for dispositioning developed and were agreed upon in December 2024. The report was submitted to the WGIAGE and presented in March 2025. The CSNI approved the report in June 2025.

This document was approved by the NEA Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations at its 77th session on 2-3 June 2025 (NEA/SEN/SIN(2025)1, not publicly available).

### *Executive summary*

### <span id="page-21-0"></span>**Background**

Although the original operational time frame of nuclear power plants, as defined by the licence term, the original plant design, and relevant standards or national regulations, is typically 30-40 years, it is possible for many nuclear power plants to operate beyond this time frame, provided that nuclear specialists demonstrate through analysis, testing and ageing management that such long-term operation (LTO) is safe. The number of countries giving high priority to continuing the operation of nuclear power plants beyond the time frame originally anticipated has steadily increased. Currently, more than 30% of all units already exceed 40 years of operation. An increasing number of operators are seeking to operate beyond 60 years, with the first licence to operate beyond this time span approved in the United States.

Electricity prices have been increasing in most developed countries, with wholesale prices rising by 100% to 500% from 2016 to 2021, depending on the region and country. Energy price increases and the European Union's response to a 2021 surge in wholesale energy prices were further exacerbated by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In this context, some European countries reconsidered their plans to phase out nuclear energy, encouraging them to opt for LTO, including beyond 60 years, while other European countries accelerated their new build programmes. It therefore became necessary to document the current knowledge base for LTO beyond 60 years and the areas where knowledge, research or innovation should be enhanced.

### **Objective of the work**

This report is the result of a collaborative task that aims to provide an overview of the status of knowledge regarding LTO of nuclear power plants, and to determine the gaps in knowledge and technology which need to be addressed to enable safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years. The report identifies the gaps to be addressed in a timely fashion and through well-focused programmes that avoid duplication of efforts.

First, this report identifies what is known about the technical and non-technical challenges and safety requirements that are relevant for LTO beyond 60 years, incorporating both laboratory and operational experience knowledge. Second, existing gaps in current knowledge are assessed to identify areas that could be enhanced. The final part of the report recommends actions to mitigate the existing gaps and to address the areas that could be enhanced. It is up to each organisation to decide what recommendations to implement and how, depending on their specific circumstances (e.g. periodic component replacement at prescribed intervals may be just as relevant as launching research to better understand ageing progression and the remaining lifespan of the component).

The study is focused mainly on pressurised-water reactors (PWRs), including VVERs (Russian designed PWRs), are they are the most common reactors, but also considers other major designs like boiling-water reactors (BWRs) and pressurised-heavy-water reactors (PHWRs). This task was performed in co-operation with several international nuclear organisations (including the International Atomic Energy Agency and the World Nuclear Association), utilities operating nuclear power plants, regulatory authorities, research institutes and technical support organisations (TSOs).

### **Results and their significance**

The main objective of this report is to identify areas for enhancement (AFEs) which need attention to support safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years. It should be noted that no technical issue of a generic nature linked to the effects of ageing was identified as critical and liable to involve systematic shutdown of nuclear power plants after 60 years of operation. The AFEs to be addressed in the frame of research activities aim at improving the knowledge of ageing phenomena and the performance of engineering methodologies for safe LTO beyond 60 years.

In addition to the AFEs, some important areas properly addressed (APAs) are also identified. The main objective of identifying APAs is to provide the technical audience with information and advice on what is available, documented and can be used as a knowledge basis for assessment, justification and preparation for safe LTO beyond 60 years. APAs refer to previous sections of this report and to relevant reference documentation. The list of APAs should not be seen as an exhaustive list of all areas/topics which are properly addressed for LTO beyond 60 years in all countries operating nuclear power plants as there are many other properly addressed areas/topics which can be specific to a given country or nuclear power plant.

Proposals for dispositioning, which are a part of each AFE, should provide a description of the suitable solutions for dispositioning of the identified AFEs to support nuclear power plant operation beyond 60 years. They can include:

- further R&D projects to fully characterise and manage ageing effects;
- new/enhanced testing, monitoring, inspection, diagnostic or repair methods;
- training on ageing management and LTO preparation;
- development of codes, standards, procedures and methodologies;
- other solutions (e.g. extended collaborative network for obsolescence/supply chain issues).

### **Main conclusions and recommendations**

While the main objective of this report is to identify AFEs which need to be resolved to ensure safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years, 16 APAs were also identified. After discussion among the task team members, it was decided that the following three APAs are of the highest importance:

- IAEA guidance for LTO beyond 60 years (Conclusion number A2.3-01).
- Sharing operating experience feedback and proven practices in ageing management (Conclusion number A2.3-02).
- Approaches to LTO justification (Conclusion number A2.5-01).

This report identifies 68 AFEs. After discussion among the task team members, it was decided that the following 15 AFEs are of the highest importance:

- Enhancement of equipment qualification programme (Conclusion number E2.3- 03).
- Clarity of regulatory authority expectations (Conclusion number: E2.5-01).
- Supply chain strategic management and long-term planning (Conclusion number E3.4-01).

- Knowledge and competence management and its important role in LTO (Conclusion number E3.5-02).
- Use of master curve direct fracture toughness technology (Conclusion number E4.2-02).
- Advanced mechanical assessment methods local versus global approach to brittle fracture assessment (Conclusion number E4.2-03).
- IASCC (irradiation-assisted stress corrosion cracking) behaviour in LWR environments: Data and models for LTO beyond 60 years (Conclusion number E4.3-01).
- Irradiation embrittlement of stainless steel (SS) and SS welds of reactor pressure vessel internals (RPVIs) (Conclusion number E4.3-02).
- Repair of highly irradiated materials of RPVIs (Conclusion number E4.3-04).
- Harmonisation of the numerous approaches for environmentally assisted fatigue (EAF) existing in parallel (Conclusion number E4.5-01).
- NDE (non-destructive evaluation) methods for selective leaching of buried and underground piping (Conclusion number E4.6-03).
- Fluence impact on concrete biological shield (Conclusion number E4.7-03).
- NDE methods for steel liner embedded in concrete (Conclusion number E4.7-08).
- Condition monitoring techniques for low-voltage cables (Conclusion number E4.8- 01).
- Obsolescence management of instrumentation and control (I&C) systems (Conclusion number E4.9-01).

### **1. Introduction**

### <span id="page-24-1"></span><span id="page-24-0"></span>**1.1. Background**

Safety is always the prime consideration in the operation of nuclear power plants and requires regular upgrades to the plants to ensure it is maintained. This is becoming all the more important as the average age of active nuclear power plants is rising and more countries are looking to extend the operation of nuclear power plants beyond the time frame originally anticipated (typically 30–40 years). Currently, more than 30% of all units already exceed 40 years of operation, and operators are increasingly seeking to extend licences beyond 60 years, with nuclear power plants in the United States being the first to receive approval to operate for 80 years.

Furthermore, it is estimated that by 2035, 50% of current light water reactor (LWR) plants will have been operating for at least 60 years, according to the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) COP 27 Portal[1](#page-24-3) .

The renewed interest in the long-term operation of nuclear power plants comes in the context of higher costs for electricity, whose wholesale prices increased by 100% to 500% from 2016 to 2021, depending on the region and country [1] and remained volatile thereafter due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022[2](#page-25-1) (source: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat). After the invasion, the European Commission and European Union countries started to work on a plan to make Europe independent from Russian fossil fuels before 2030.

This situation led some European countries (e.g. Belgium) to reassess their plans to phase out nuclear energy. As a result, interest grew in LTO, including beyond 60 years (e.g. the Netherlands), and in speeding up new build projects (e.g. in Czechia, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania). As of March 2023, the Belgian government had reconsidered its decision to phase out nuclear energy and allowed two of Belgium's nuclear reactors to operate beyond 2025. Germany, meanwhile, extended operation of its last units only by several months, to the spring of 2023, and phased out all nuclear units. There has also been no official indication from Spain's government about changes in its nuclear phase-out law.

With interest increasing in pursuing LTO beyond 60 years, it became clear that it was necessary to document the current knowledge base and the areas that might need enhancements in knowledge, research or innovation. From a technical and safety perspective, LTO beyond 60 years will require many activities, including evaluating designs against the latest codes and standards, addressing new physical and non-physical (obsolescence) age-related issues, conducting environmental impact assessments, and examining human resources and knowledge transfer issues.

### <span id="page-25-0"></span>**1.2. Objectives and scope**

This report is based upon a survey of the status of knowledge regarding LTO of nuclear power plants and seeks to determine the gaps in knowledge and technology that need to be addressed through focused programmes to enable safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years.

It aims to identify what is known regarding nuclear power plant component failure/degradation mechanisms, incorporating both laboratory and operational experience knowledge in a status report. Then the existing gaps in the current knowledge state are assessed to identify possible "areas of enhancement". The report ends with recommended actions to mitigate the "existing gaps" and to address the areas of enhancement. It is up to each organisation to decide, depending on the specific circumstances, whether and how to implement the recommended actions.

The work is focused mainly on pressurised-water reactors (PWRs), including water-water energetic reactors (VVERs, the Russian designed PWRs), as they are the most common design. However, the study also considers other major designs like boiling-water reactors (BWRs) and pressurised-heavy-water reactors (PHWRs). This task was performed in cooperation with other international nuclear organisations, utilities operating nuclear power plants, regulatory authorities, research institutes and technical support organisations (TSOs).

### <span id="page-26-0"></span>**1.3. Procedure**

The work on the report was initiated in October 2022 with the Nuclear Research and Consultancy Group's (NRG) task "LTO Beyond 60 Years", as part of the NRG PIONIER research project (2021-2024). A survey to identify available sources of information was performed and co-operation with external contributors was agreed in November 2022. The structure of the report, the intended content of the individual sections, the project schedule and the draft introductory sections were outlined in December 2022. Inputs from external contributors were incorporated by NRG in the first half of 2023.

In January 2023, it was decided to transfer the project to the NEA under the Working Group on Integrity and Ageing of Components and Structures (WGIAGE), which is part of the Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations (CSNI). A committee activity planning sheet (CAPS) was developed and approved by the NEA WGIAGE and the CSNI in March to June 2023. An NEA task team under the co-ordination of the NRG was established in June 2023. A technical survey questionnaire was developed and the responses and other inputs were incorporated into the report by February 2024.

The task team meeting was hosted by NRG in Petten, Netherlands in February 2024 to discuss the status of the interim report and agree on next steps. The interim report was presented to the NEA WGIAGE in March 2024.

The descriptive sections of the report (1-5) were reviewed and finalised in April to August 2024 and conclusions, including proposals for dispositioning, were developed and agreed upon in June to December 2024.

The knowledge and information collected, analysed and assessed in the report as well as the conclusions and recommendations will be disseminated internationally to improve the understanding of activities that will need to be performed, and that require enhancements, to extend the operating time of nuclear power plants of the most common designs beyond 60 years of operation.

### <span id="page-26-1"></span>**1.4. Organisation of the report**

Section 1, "Introduction", is followed by Section 2, "LTO perspectives and regulatory background", which provides discussion on the benefits of safe LTO, LTO perspectives in individual countries as well as on the status and applicability of national and international regulations and standards for LTO beyond 60 years.

Section 3, "Non-technical challenges for safe LTO of nuclear power plants", provides a brief description of non-technical challenges for safe LTO such as economic, political and environmental aspects, supply chain issues, human resources, knowledge and competence management issues.

Section 4, "Technical challenges important for LTO beyond 60 years", is a core section, providing analysis of the status of knowledge for key nuclear power plants structures, systems, and components (SSCs). It contains sub-sections on SSC descriptions, physical ageing, inspection and diagnostic methods, repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions, and potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years for each key SSC.

Section 5, "Safety requirements important for LTO beyond 60 years", discusses the availability of original design basis documentation, the development of codes, standards and regulations, and technological obsolescence issues.

Section 6, "Conclusions for nuclear power plant operation beyond 60 years", provides, based on inputs from previous sections, descriptions of "areas properly addressed" (APAs)
