### **2. LTO perspectives and regulatory background**

### <span id="page-28-1"></span><span id="page-28-0"></span>**2.1. Benefits of safe LTO of the existing nuclear power plants**

If the world is to achieve energy security and reach net zero carbon emissions, it is necessary to expand the amount of low-carbon energy sources, which can include replacing coal with nuclear energy, keeping the current nuclear power plants in service and building new nuclear energy capacity. Many countries are planning to keep the currently operational nuclear power plants in service until new energy options become commercially viable (e.g. small modular reactors, generation III fission reactors or fusion reactors). However, most current nuclear power plants have been in service for over 30 years and more than 30% already for over 40 year[s3](#page-28-2) .

For countries looking to use nuclear energy, LTO of currently operating nuclear power plants can be important to maintain capacity until new commercial LWRs are in place, followed potentially by commercial advanced reactors and small modular reactors. This means at least three additional decades of operation for the existing fleet.

Operating nuclear power plants are subject to continuous improvement, often governed by periodic safety reviews (PSR) every ten years, leading to the implementation of substantial safety enhancements and alternative solutions to keep them "as safe as a new build". Safe LTO of the existing fleet of nuclear power plants offers a key step in the transition to modern low-carbon energy production sources, whether nuclear or non-nuclear.

While the safe LTO of nuclear power plants has many challenges, it also has many benefits, including:

- economics: feasibility studies show that investment in safe LTO is one of the more profitable ways to produce low-carbon energy;
- environmental impact: nuclear energy is a key low-carbon energy sources in the current energy mix;
- energy security: LTO can help ensure independence from imported sources of energy like gas, oil and coal.

Additional advantages of safe LTO are related to broader perspectives and developments, such as the construction and operation of future nuclear energy production sources to reduce carbon emissions. They include:

- employment: continuous operation of nuclear power plants helps to maintain and stabilise significant numbers of highly qualified jobs in the region and country;
- retaining knowledge: highly specialised knowledge and expertise must be retained in the industry (the term "industry" is used in a meaning "nuclear industry" throughout the report), region and country to create the preconditions for future new builds;
- the involvement of local industry: the capabilities and capacity of local industry is maintained to support the operation, maintenance and other aspects of safe operation of existing nuclear power plants and will be ready to support the construction and operation of future new builds;

<span id="page-28-2"></span><sup>3</sup> IAEA (2024), PRIS - Reactor Information System, [www.iaea.org/PRIS.](http://www.iaea.org/PRIS)

• the transition to low-carbon energy: LTO of existing nuclear power plants will help keep carbon emissions low until other sustainable low-carbon energy sources are developed.

To enable LTO of the European nuclear power plant fleet beyond 60 years, the Sustainable Nuclear Energy Technology Platform (SNETP) combines the synergies that exist for industrial supply chains and human competences across dozens of European TSOs to support joint research, development and innovation to solve technical issues. The US Department of Energy has initiated the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Programme (LWRSP), with the main objective of enabling LTO of the existing nuclear power plants and the focus areas related to plant modernisation, materials research and risk-informed system analysis.

As nuclear energy gains momentum, nuclear experts, scientists and researchers are being asked to collaborate and find solutions to operate nuclear installations much longer than designed, beyond 60 years, with no increase in risk for safety and an increased return on investment, until other energy options become economically viable and scalable.

### <span id="page-29-0"></span>**2.2. Current LTO perspectives**

As of November 2024, thirty-one (31) countries and economies operated nuclear power plants worldwide. Twenty-eight countries and economies operated nuclear power plants with PWR reactors (Armenia, Belarus, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, China, Czechia, Finland, France, Hungary, India, Iran, Japan, Korea, the Netherlands, Pakistan, Russia, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Chinese Taipei, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States). Some of them also operated other types of reactors. Only four countries operated exclusively reactors of other designs than PWR (Argentina, Canada, Mexico and Romania)[.4](#page-29-1)

PWR reactors are also the most common design of units under construction. As of November 2024, new units with PWR reactors were in construction in eleven (11) countries already operating PWR reactors – Brazil, China, France, India, Iran, Korea, Russia, the Slovak Republic, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom – but also in three countries operating no PWR reactors yet – Bangladesh, Egypt and Turkey. Only a few reactors that are not PWRs (fast breeder reactors (FBR), PHWRs) are currently in construction in China, India and Russia.[5](#page-29-2)

Current operational targets differ among countries operating nuclear power plants and are influenced by domestic politics. This leads to unstable (or even missing) long-term national strategies for the exploitation of nuclear energy for electricity and heat production.

The situation regarding LTO beyond 60 years is relatively clear in the United States, where several licences were given to nuclear power plants to operate up to 80 years.

The nuclear power plants in Latin America, South Africa and Asia are more recent and currently working on LTO up to 60 years. In East Asia, a shift in public opinion in favour of nuclear energy and a constant rise in demand for electricity have led to changes in policy, with Japan and Korea dropping plans to phase out nuclear energy in favour of LTO of nuclear power plants. In Japan, which has a relatively older fleet, current regulations allow nuclear power plants to operate up to a maximum of 60 years. China continues in its

<span id="page-29-1"></span><sup>4</sup> IAEA (2024), PRIS - Reactor Information System, [www.iaea.org/PRIS.](http://www.iaea.org/PRIS)

<span id="page-29-2"></span><sup>5</sup> Ibid.

strategy to build dozens of nuclear units in upcoming decades and, because its fleet is young, there is not much need to consider LTO beyond 60 years.

The interest in operating nuclear power plants beyond 60 years has risen rapidly in Europe, particularly due to the rise in energy prices caused by the phasing out of some nuclear power plants and the invasion of Ukraine by Russia.

The government of Germany approved a law with a plan to gradually phase out all nuclear power units by 2022. This plan was delayed to 2023 due to the energy crisis but the last three PWR units were phased out in the spring of 2023.

The government of Belgium decided to phase out all seven PWR units in the country by 2025. The single Belgian operator, Electrabel, obtained the licence for LTO from 40 to 50 years for Doel 1 and 2 and for Tihange 1. The licences were valid until 2024 for Doel 1 and until 2025 for Doel 2 and Tihange 1. In 2023, the Belgian government decided to allow LTO of Doel 4 and Tihange 3 from 40 to 50 years, which means until 2035, but Doel 3 and Tihange 2 were permanently shut down after 40 years of operation in 2023. This meant that Belgium would lose approximately 4 000 MWs by 2025, which represents more than 35% of its consumption.

In 2019, the government of Spain announced the phasing out of three units by 2030 and of the last four units by 2035. Several operators in Spain currently operate six PWR units and one BWR unit. If the current phase-out plan comes into effect, all PWR units in Spain will be phased out before they reach 50 years of operation. Nevertheless, Spanish operators are considering the possibility of operating longer. In February 2025, the Spanish Congress approved a proposal calling for the government to implement a series of measures that would reverse the country's decision to phase out nuclear power.

A strong earthquake followed by a tsunami in Japan in March 2011 led to an accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, with cores melting in three reactors. After this accident, most reactors in Japan were suspended from operation, and safety measures are being implemented which should improve the robustness of the design to withstand extreme external events. The licensing process of Japanese nuclear power plants to comply with new regulatory requirements is still in progress. As of February 2025, 12 PWR units had restarted and four other PWR units had submitted applications and were waiting for the decision of the regulatory authority. The first two BWR plants (Shimane 2 and Onagawa 2) resumed operations towards the end of 2024 and nine other BWR units submitted applications. From the perspective of LTO or operation beyond the original design lifetime of 40 years, regulations in Japan were changed in March 2023. Under the new rules, Japan will abolish the current 60-year operating limit for reactors and introduce a new system in which additional operating extensions can be granted every ten years after 30 years of service, with no maximum limit specified.[6](#page-30-0)

In general, the length of the initial licensing term falls into three main categories: 10 years, 30 years and 40 years, as some countries base their licensing term on the design life of their reactor types in operation. For instance, PWRs and BWRs traditionally have a design life of 40 years, and VVERs and PHWRs traditionally have a design life of 30 years. In contrast, other countries base their relicensing term on the PSR process every ten years, specifying that authorisations are only valid for ten-year terms.

<span id="page-30-0"></span><sup>6</sup> NUCNET (2023), "Japan / Cabinet Approves Law To Allow Reactor Operation Beyond 60 Years", [www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-](http://www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-2023) [2023.](http://www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-2023)

In the case of VVER 440 reactors with a design lifetime of 30 years, operators have extended the operational lifetime from 30 to 50 years (Hungary, Finland), or from 30 to 45 years followed by an extension from 45 to 60 years (Russia, Ukraine). Some countries have even decided to extend the operational time span directly from 30 to 60 years (Bulgaria, Slovakia). Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant in Finland originally extended its licence from 30 to 50 years (Unit 1 to 2027 and Unit 2 to 2030). In February 2023, the operating licences of both Loviisa units were extended until 2050, which means up to 73 years for Unit 1 and 70 years for Unit 2[7](#page-31-0) . Similarly, Paks Nuclear Power Plant in Hungary extended the licence of all four units from 30 to 50 years and is considering a licence extension to 70 years. Other countries using VVER designs have extended the operating permissions by ten years in connection with successful PSRs (Armenia, Czechia).

Some other countries, considering the age of their units, have not decided how they will proceed with LTO (Belarus, Iran, India, Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates).

All the countries operating nuclear power plants use either a PSR approach, a licensing renewal approach (discussed below) or combinations thereof to justify LTO. Officially, they all consider 60 years of operation as a maximum time frame. Only the United States has already formalised rules for licences beyond 60 years.

Beyond PWRs, the design lifetime of the Canadian deuterium uranium (CANDU) units was originally 210 000 effective full power hours (EFPH), equivalent to 30 years of operation at 80% capacity factor, the initial operating term, limited by the testing capabilities in late 1970s. The first CANDU units, when approaching this limit, entered the retubing and refurbishment outage, replacing the fuel channels and feeders on the primary circuit, to gain another 30 years of safe operation. But a decade later, many utilities used extensive research & development (R&D) results in terms of improved fuel channel prediction models, updated the thermo-hydraulic model of the aged installation, or enhanced methodologies for critical heat flux calculation, proving that the fuel channels can be safely operated far beyond the initial limit, to 245 000 EFPH, or even 300 000 EFPH, equivalent to 30-35 calendar years. Although the fuel channels can be replaced every 30-37 years, for the rest of major components ageing effects still need to be controlled and mitigated if operation beyond 60 years is to be contemplated.

Even though 60 years of operation is officially considered a maximum operational time frame in most countries, many countries have initiated technical steps towards LTO beyond 60 years in recent years. These countries include, for example, Czechia, Finland, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden.

A description of the regulatory licensing requirements in most of the countries operating nuclear power plants was documented in Table 2.1 of the NEA report *Legal Frameworks for Long-Term Operation of Nuclear Power Reactors* [2], first published in 2019, with a second edition released in 2025.

The report summarises the answers to a survey questionnaire regarding the number of licence extensions permitted by the regulatory framework. As of 2019, the conclusion was that most countries have no limit on the number of licence extensions if the plant fulfils its safety compliance, based on PSR or other equivalent safety assessment. Out of the 20 countries that responded to this questionnaire, only four countries so far do not specifically allow for LTO beyond 60 years, namely:

1. Belgium, which allows ten years beyond the original 40-year operating term;

<span id="page-31-0"></span><sup>7</sup> Fortum (2025), Lifetime extension of the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant[, www.fortum.com/energy](http://www.fortum.com/energy-production/nuclear-power/plants/loviisa/lifetime-extension-loviisa-nuclear-power-plant)[production/nuclear-power/plants/loviisa/lifetime-extension-loviisa-nuclear-power-plant.](http://www.fortum.com/energy-production/nuclear-power/plants/loviisa/lifetime-extension-loviisa-nuclear-power-plant)

- 2. Hungary, which allows one extension of 20 years beyond the original operating term of 30 years;
- 3. Japan, which allows one extension of 20 years beyond the original operating term of 40 years;
- 4. Slovenia, which allows two extensions of ten years beyond the 40-year operating term.

Other countries, like Argentina, Canada, the Netherlands and Spain, can decide on a caseby-case basis to operate beyond 60 years, depending on the safety assessment and the economics in the feasibility study.

### <span id="page-32-0"></span>**2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years**

To assist its member states in effectively managing the effects of ageing and preparing for safe LTO, the IAEA has developed a comprehensive set of safety standards and other publications in the last decade. It consists of safety requirements, safety guides and lowerlevel publications such as safety reports, technical reports and TECDOCs.

The most relevant safety standards are, on the level of safety requirements, the Specific Safety Requirements No. SSR-2/2 (Rev.1) [3] and, on the level of safety guides, the Specific Safety Guide No. SSG-48 on "Ageing Management and Development of a Programme for Long Term Operation of Nuclear Power Plants" [4] and the Specific Safety Guide No. SSG-25 on "Periodic Safety Review for Nuclear Power Plants" [5]. High-level IAEA safety standards provide requirements and recommended ways to address the requirements (in safety guides). Other IAEA publications (e.g. safety reports) provide good practices and examples of how safety standards can be implemented. Safety standards are applicable for the whole period of nuclear power plant operation and thus do not distinguish between LTO beyond 30 or 40 years of operation and LTO beyond 60 years of operation.

IAEA publications other than Safety Standards may distinguish between LTO up to 60 years and beyond 60 years. For example, the IAEA International Generic Ageing Lessons Learned (IGALL) programme incorporated ageing management programmes (AMPs), time-limited ageing analysis (TLAAs) and ageing management review (AMR) lines which were used in the United States for LTO from 40 to 60 years [6] already in the first version of the IGALL safety report. IGALL also comprises the experience of several other member states in the Safety Report No. 82 (Rev. 2) on "Ageing Management for Nuclear Power Plants: International Generic Ageing Lessons Learned (IGALL)" [7] and the associated IGALL database. Nevertheless, the work is ongoing to fully incorporate NUREG 2191 US Generic Ageing Lessons Learned – Subsequent Licensing Renewal (GALL-SLR) [8] updates into IGALL AMPs, TLAAs and AMR lines and the practices from other member states.

The IAEA has developed Specific Safety Guide No. 48 [4] and a set of supporting safety reports SRS-82 [7], SRS-106 [9], SRS-109 [10], SRS-121 [11], SSG-69 [12] and other technical documents with the primary objective to support member states in ageing management and preparation for safe LTO. Nevertheless, the PSR consists of a systematic and comprehensive process to review the continued validity of the plant's licensing basis, cumulative impact of latest national and international standards, evolving regulatory requirements, plant ageing, OPEX and technological developments. PSR has been used by many operating organisations and regulatory bodies as a suitable licensing tool for the justification of the licence application for LTO.

The scope and use of PSR in support of LTO justification varies among IAEA member states; however, the most important principle when defining the strategy for LTO, is that operational practices shall meet national regulations and should follow international guidelines, as applicable [5]. Therefore, the operating organisations and regulatory bodies requested the IAEA's assistance in clarifying the use of PSR to support decision making for LTO. As a consequence, the IAEA has conducted a thorough assessment of the plants' PSR processes in several member states (as part of Safety Aspect of Long Term Operation [SALTO] peer reviews) in order to identify weaknesses, good practices and synergies between PSR and LTO preparation activities, and has developed a safety report on good practices with the use of PSR in support of LTO justification to complement the safety guides on PSR [5] and ageing management and LTO [4].

In this regard, the Safety Report Series No. 121 [11] provides a common basis and criteria for using PSR results in support of justification of LTO, good practices regarding LTO and PSR programmes at the plant, and it improves understanding of IAEA safety standards on PSR, ageing management and LTO. If PSR is to be used to support LTO safety assessment:

- The intent of the PSR is not to provide recommendations for the activities performed during LTO of a nuclear power plant. However, a PSR and its findings can be used to support the decision-making process for LTO or licence renewal.
- The scope of the review of the safety factors should be adapted to determine the feasibility of LTO. For example, the scope of the safety factor relating to ageing should be expanded to include an evaluation of TLAAs and assessments of ageing effects. In the review, increased importance should be given to degradation mechanisms and AMPs.
- PSR should take into account the entire intended period of LTO, which is typically 20 years (if not specified differently in the national regulations), as opposed to the typical period of PSR foresight of ten years.
- The key result from a PSR, which is in addition to LTO justification based on SSG-48 [4], is the review of design aspects and a global assessment of the overall review results. That part of PSR outcomes recommends a set of safety improvements, prioritised based on their safety significance and the associated risk and proposes an integrated implementation plan of the reasonable and practicable safety improvements (including physical modifications) to ensure a safe LTO.

The IAEA Safety Report Series No. 109 [10] on "Regulatory Oversight of Ageing Management and Long Term Operation Programme of Nuclear Power Plants" describes the regulatory approaches and practices followed in the member states for both methodologies: LTO licensing using PSR and an approach not or not directly using PSR. The document does not address nor exclude the option beyond 60 years. From a regulatory perspective, the PSR process is inherently applicable to license additional LTO periods. There is also no limitation from a regulatory point of view when a separate licensing act is applied.

The IAEA safety standards have been adopted by member states worldwide as a proven practice in a comprehensive and systematic safety assessment. As the IAEA safety standards are applicable for the whole period of nuclear power plant operation (including LTO beyond 60 years of operation), the IAEA safety standards can also be used to license the plants' operation beyond 60 years. The methodologies for AMR, TLAAs, AMPs and PSR safety assessment are systematic and comprehensive enough also for operation beyond 60 years. Some further updates or adjustments could be necessary at lower-level publications, for example to fully incorporate US GALL-SLR into the IGALL database (AMPs, TLAAs and AMR lines), which is expected to be completed by 2025.

<span id="page-34-0"></span>The United States is probably the most advanced country in the process of licensing nuclear power plants beyond their initial 40-year operating period, as US regulations allow licences to be extended (renewed) for 20-year terms, with no limit to the number of extensions. Most of the operating reactors in the United States have had their licences extended from 40 to 60 years, and several plants are requesting a second extension of their licence from 60 to 80 years of operation, termed "subsequent licence renewal" (SLR). SLR applications for 22 reactor units (including 14 PWRs) have already been submitted to the US regulatory authorities. And as of January 2025, 6 PWR reactors and 3 BWR reactors had received licences for 80 years of operation. The Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) has reported that more than 90% of the 80 surveyed reactor units have applied for, or intend to apply for, 80 years of operation [reference: Nuclear Energy Institute, "The Future of Nuclear Power– 2023 Baseline Survey"].

In accordance with the US Atomic Energy Act, carried out by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the US Department of Energy, legislation for the licensing of nuclear power plants in the United States includes provisions allowing for:

- plants to be licensed to operate for up to 40 years;
- licence renewal;
- no restrictions on the number of renewals (operation reach 80 or even 100 years).

Title 10 of the *Code of Federal Regulations* (CFR) Part 54 – Requirements for Renewal of Operating Licenses for Nuclear Power Plants [13], requires licensees to:

- identify the long-lived, passive structures and components within the scope of the regulation;
- demonstrate that the effects of ageing for in-scope structures and components will be adequately managed, such as with an AMP;
- evaluate TLAAs (time-based ageing calculations in the current licence that must be re-evaluated for the extended operating term).

Other aspects of the original licence are not reconsidered, but are required to be maintained. The US NRC License Renewal Safety Principles are based on maintaining a plant's current licensing basis (CLB) in the "same manner" and the "same extent" during the renewal term as in the first 40 years of operation [14]. The CLB model relies on compliance with other US NRC regulations that address component degradation, such as the Maintenance Rule [15], Equipment Qualification Rule [16] and required use of codes and standards (e.g. American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) in-service inspection (ISI) [17]), which need to be implemented in both the initial and extended licence periods (and which are not always in place in other countries). An AMP may start as early as ten years in advance of the period of extended operation (PEO), and they are subject to US NRC inspections for compliance with the commitments made for LTO, before entering the new licence term.

The US NRC possesses an extensive body of inspectors (on-site residents and teams that are based out of four regional offices), which is a characteristic of countries with large fleets of reactors but not always available in countries with a small fleet of nuclear power plants. This licensing model is based on a compliance check for regulations and additional requirements associated with generic (industry-wide) safety issues (as communicated in Generic Letters, US NRC orders, etc.). These are complemented by site-specific safety

issue resolution (e.g. performance assessment of inspection findings, materials ageing issues specific to the plant).

Ten CFR Part 54 is used for all renewal periods, with no additional requirements for SLR. The model for the SLR is like the first licence renewal, based on the following guidance documents:

- 1. *Standard Review Plan for Review of Subsequent License Renewal Applications for Nuclear Power Plants* (SRP-SLR), NUREG-2192 [18], which provides guidance to US NRC technical reviewers to ensure quality and consistent reviews of renewal applications. It is similar to NUREG-1800, Rev. 2, for initial renewal [19];
  - provides guidance for US NRC review of scoping and screening, AMR, and TLAAs [18], [19], [8];
  - is amended through the Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) process (SLR-ISG), based on operating experience or lessons learned from renewal application reviews. ISGs are incorporated in the next major revision of the SRP. Five SLR-ISGs were issued after the initial issuance of the SRP-SLR, and they became effective once they were issued.
- 2. *Generic Aging Lessons Learned for Subsequent License Renewal (GALL-SLR) Report* NUREG-2191 [8], which provides a generic technical evaluation for an adequate ageing management approach. It is similar to NUREG-1801, Rev. 2 [6], for initial renewal:
  - provides assessments for the AMR, including identification of materials, environments and ageing effects that require management;
  - identifies acceptable AMPs;
  - is amended by SLR-ISGs.

NUREG-2191 [8] and NUREG-2192 [18] provide generic guidance to address ageing issues based on existing plant programmes and additional activities to augment those programs for LTO. The guidance is updated periodically, based on industry operating experience as well as research and testing. NEI 17-01 [20] is industry guidance that provides power plants an acceptable approach to implement the requirements of the licence renewal rule and to use the US NRC guidance, as it applies to subsequent licence renewal.

In addition, the US NRC reviews of renewal applications include a historical check of maintenance and performance monitoring data (including internal and external OPEX) to ensure that the proposed AMPs adequately address site-specific ageing issues. Also, the US NRC reviews the applicant's final safety analysis report (FSAR) updates, which describe the new ageing management activities. The licence renewal process is based on plant commitments to implement the AMPs and US NRC inspections of plant implementation of AMPs, all of which require a strong regulatory body that is well-staffed with knowledgeable personnel. The US NRC also has a hearing process for any person who believes they would be adversely affected by a licence renewal.

The experience of US utilities with SLR has shown certain benefits in terms of time and resources spent, when compared with the first relicensing effort. These benefits result from the fact that:

• systematic methodologies and comprehensive safety assessments are used for scoping, screening and AMR, which are already documented;

- the identification of TLAAs may require only updates for revalidation from the first licence renewal;
- databases for sharing ageing-related OPEX are already in effect for data collection and further assessment;
- AMPs are in effect that mostly only need to be updated or complemented, building on prior efforts and analyses as opposed to performing those activities again from the beginning.

When developing the guidance and performing the first safety assessments for licence renewal, the US NRC and the industry have developed a comprehensive, but also economically efficient, model that proves to be viable for LTO. It relies on the advantages gained in terms of time and resources saved for SLR from 60 to 80 years of operation when applying the same methodologies and having the processes and the know-how required for the licence renewal justification already in place.

To conclude, the US NRC regulatory framework is currently the most advanced in terms of conducting the evaluation of the relicensing applications to operate nuclear power plants in the United States from 60 up to 80 years, and the US NRC has taken concrete steps to further improve the specific SLR guidance documents, based on the feedback from SLR application reviews. The same model could be used for licence periods of 80 to 100 years, if needed, as there is no limit in the US NRC current legislation on the number of renewals.

### <span id="page-36-0"></span>**2.5. Typical national regulatory frameworks to support LTO beyond 60 years**

Although each country and each reactor technology may have its particular needs and LTO justification methods, most countries rely mainly on IAEA safety standards as described in the previous section and many of them also use the US NRC approach as a reference. The IAEA safety standards developed for supporting ageing management and LTO, such as [3] and [4], are to a large extent consistent with the US NRC's regulatory framework as well as the safety reports mentioned in the previous section. On the contrary, PSR [5] is used in all countries but the United States. Also, PSR with a deeper focus on ageing aspects and LTO in support of LTO justification is used in many countries.

The various national approaches can be grouped into two main categories:

- The PSR-based approach where PSR is used as a main licensing tool for LTO. PSR for LTO is typically more rigorous, with a greater focus on ageing aspects, and covers the whole intended period of LTO. The PSR process is adapted for the LTO safety review in line with SSG-48 [4], which means mainly a larger scope of SSCs, revalidation of TLAAs, AMR for all in-scope SSCs, review of plant programmes and AMPs. This approach is typically used in countries with unlimited or continuing licences. The operating permit is typically extended after successful PSR for an additional ten years.
- The licence renewal-based approach, which is used in countries with a limited licence, for 30 or 40 years, and typically allows 20 years of licence extension. This approach relies primarily on IAEA safety standards developed for LTO, such as [3] and [4], and in many countries also on the US NRC approach as a proven practice. PSR is also used in these countries but has more of a supporting role in the justification of safe LTO.

Both approaches can also be successfully used for LTO beyond 60 years.

### *2.5.1. Examples of the PSR-based approach*

The approach of France is a typical example of a PSR-based approach. France relies primarily on the PSR approach but the IAEA's ageing and LTO related publications, such as SSG-48 [4] and the IGALL safety report [7], are also taken into account. The continued operation of a nuclear power reactor beyond 40 years is subject to the conduct of a PSR every ten years, which contains two parts:

- 1. The first part includes an evaluation of the condition and conformity of the facility to the applicable rules, incorporating an AMR. These verifications can include checks on the initial design studies as well as field inspections of equipment not covered by maintenance programmes or tests conducted every ten years. Any deviations detected during these investigations must be restored to conformity within a time frame commensurate with their potential consequences.
- 2. The second part is a safety reassessment, which aims to improve the level of safety considering the experience acquired during operation, changing knowledge, the requirements applicable to newer facilities and international best practices. Following these reassessments, the licensee is required to identify the modifications it intends to implement to improve safety.

In Korea, PSR is used for regular safety checks every ten years within the framework of a limited licence term of 30 or 40 years. For the last PSR term leading to LTO, an "intensified safety review" process is followed, focused on ageing management and critical component life assessments, as prerequisites to obtaining an operating licence extension beyond the original term of a nuclear power unit licence.

In Spain, the Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear (CSN), the regulatory body, issued the legally binding instruction establishing the requirements for the ageing management based on US regulations (10 CFR 54) [13]. The PSR is performed every ten years, in line with SSG-25 [5], and the lessons learnt after the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant accident and the European Union Nuclear Safety Directive 2014/87/Euratom [21], following the Stress Tests. As such, although the PSR is performed every ten years based on the IAEA safety guide, for the licence renewal the safety assessment is conducted in accordance with the US NRC model of an integrated plant assessment (IPA) and 10 CFR Part 54, "Requirements for renewal of operating licenses for nuclear power plants" [13].

Another example is Japan. The initial regulatory framework before the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant accident (FKDA) required nuclear operators to perform ageing management technical evaluation (AMTE) of SSCs starting from 30 years of operation and every ten years subsequently. Following the FKDA, regulatory requirements were drastically revised and were backfit to all nuclear power plants immediately. The operational period was limited to only one extension of up to 20 years after 40 years, upon approval by the regulatory body. To obtain the approval for the PEO (beyond the original term of 40 years), the licensees are required to:

- perform AMTE at the 40th year;
- perform special inspections, which can start five years prior to the application;
- implement long-term maintenance policies.

From the perspective of LTO or operation beyond the original design lifetime of 40 years, regulations in Japan were changed again in June 2025. Under the new rules, the period of operation will be determined by the Electricity Business Act. The operation period remains 60 years in principle, but some exemptions, such as the duration of reactor outage due to the backfitting, could be allowed. Independently of setting the operating period, the regulatory body set the rules for LTO, adopting a PSR-based approach in which additional operating extensions can be granted every ten years after 30 years of service, with no maximum limit specified[8](#page-38-0) . The licensees are required to submit long-term facility management plans after the intensive review of their ageing management. Special inspection prior to the 40th year remains, and additional inspection will be required if a plant exceeds 60 years of operation. Plant safety analysis will be confirmed by the current safety improvement assessment notification. This system is a merging of a safety analysis report (SAR) and a PSR, requiring safety assessments and a stress test every five years, and assessments of other safety factors every ten years. This system is also being reviewed in response to the increase in the number of restarted plants and the potential for LTO.

For other countries with an unlimited operational licence, continuous operation is typically regulated by an operational permit, usually for ten years, conditioned by periodic or continuous assessment and fulfilment of regulatory body requirements. The most important conditions are typically: the conduct of PSR [5] and compliance with other relevant IAEA Safety Standards such as [3] and [4]. This applies to countries like Belgium, Czechia, Sweden and Switzerland.

In Switzerland, for example, a PSR must be performed every ten years, whereby an assessment for LTO must be included in all PSRs after introducing the LTO period (40 years of operation). In the current regulatory framework, there is no general difference between periods beyond 60 years or more compared to the approach for beyond 40 years. The LTO assessment focuses primarily on the difficult to replace main components, especially the primary circuit (PWR) or the nuclear steam generation system (BWR), including the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) and internals and the steel, as well as the concrete containment. A backfitting concept and a plant life management concept must be submitted to maintain or increase the general safety level. The PSR and LTO assessment is based on national regulatory guidelines (ENSI-A03 [22], ENSI-B01 [23]) that reflect among others the IAEA standards [3] to [5].

Details on the IAEA model applied in the above-mentioned countries can be found in Chapter 3 of the NEA report *Legal Frameworks for Long-Term Operation of Nuclear Power Reactors* [2].

### *2.5.2. Examples for licence renewal-based approach*

The licence renewal-based approach is typically used in countries with a limited initial licence period of 30 or 40 years, mostly for PWRs and BWRs. An important aspect is that the practically proven US legislation and licence renewal applications are publicly accessible in English. If a country's regulatory framework for extended operation is not prescriptive, the utilities may choose to follow a proven practice and generally recognised model, like the US NRC model. The US model with original operational licence of 40 years and then an extension to 60 years, based on a licence renewal process, is applied with various modifications and conditions in many countries, for example in Brazil, China, Hungary, Mexico, Slovenia and South Africa. This allows using the detailed US NRC regulations and examples of similar US plants for benchmarking purposes. An important difference is that all these countries (except for Mexico) also use PSR with a ten-year periodicity and typically with a special focus on ageing aspects and considering the whole period of LTO in case of PSR in support of LTO justification.

<span id="page-38-0"></span><sup>8</sup> NUCNET (2023), "Japan / Cabinet Approves Law To Allow Reactor Operation Beyond 60 Years", [www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-](http://www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-2023) [2023.](http://www.nucnet.org/news/cabinet-approves-law-to-allow-reactor-operation-beyond-60-years-3-4-2023)

For example, in 2018 the nuclear safety authority in Brazil issued the "Regulatory Requirements for Long Term Operation for Nuclear Power Plants" - NT-007 [24], asking the licensee to perform a PSR in accordance with IAEA SSG-25 [5], before the normal IPA, in accordance with US NRC LRA model, "to ensure that any safety improvements required for LTO will be addressed as part of the preparation for LTO."

Nevertheless, out of the countries listed above, so far only Hungary considers officially an extension beyond 50 years of operation. But since they followed the US NRC model for LTO beyond 40 and this is used in the United States for the subsequent licence renewal, it can be expected that the US NRC approach will be used also for LTO beyond 60 years. Details on the US NRC model applied in the above-mentioned countries can be found in Chapter 3 of the NEA report *Legal Frameworks for Long-Term Operation of Nuclear Power Reactors* [2].

### <span id="page-39-0"></span>**2.6. Conclusions on regulatory framework and licensing process**

Based on the description of the regulatory frameworks of the IAEA, the US NRC and regulatory bodies from other countries provided in the above sub-sections, the following conclusions can be drawn:

- 1. The IAEA has developed a set of safety standards to support member states in their preparation for safe LTO. High-level Safety Standards provide requirements (in the safety requirement series) and recommended ways to address requirements (in the safety guides series). Safety standards are applicable for the entire period of nuclear power plant operation and thus do not distinguish between LTO beyond 30 or 40 years of operation and LTO beyond 50 or 60 years of operation. Other IAEA publications (e.g. safety reports) provide good practices and examples of how safety standards can be implemented.
- 2. Regarding national regulatory frameworks, the US NRC regulatory framework is the most mature in terms of specific regulations and practical experience with conducting the safety evaluation and licensing renewal to allow safe operation of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years. The general approach and methodology for licensing renewal from 60 to 80 years is the same as for the licensing renewal from 40 to 60 years, with only minor updates.
- 3. Although each country and each reactor technology may have its particular needs and LTO justification methods, almost all countries rely mainly on IAEA safety standards and many of them also use the US NRC approach as a reference. The various national approaches can be grouped into two main categories:
  - i. the PSR-based approach typically used in countries with unlimited or continuing licences;
  - ii. the licence renewal-based approach typically used in countries with a limited licence, typically for 30 or 40 years and typically allowing additional 20 years of licence extension.
- 4. International safety standards and national regulations provide general requirements for ageing management and LTO. Detailed requirements for specific SSCs are typically defined in specific codes and standards or technical specifications.
- 5. Many countries operating nuclear power plants facing LTO, or already operating nuclear power plants in LTO, have developed a set of national regulations for preparation for a safe LTO. They typically rely on IAEA safety standards and sometimes also on the US NRC regulatory framework as a practical reference.

<span id="page-40-0"></span>To better describe the potential challenges for safe LTO of existing fleet of nuclear power plants (including causes of permanent shutdown of nuclear power plants), this section uses examples of all major nuclear power plant designs in order to more thoroughly analyse potential threats relevant to nuclear power plants in the future. Nuclear power plants are currently facing the following challenges which can become a reason for, or contribute to, their permanent phasing out:

- 1. Technical challenges:
  - a. accidents or serious failures;
  - b. attainment of design lifetime;
- 2. Safety requirements.
- 3. Other challenges:
  - c. economic aspects;
  - d. political decisions;
  - e. environmental aspects;
  - f. supply chain issues;
  - g. human resources, knowledge and competence management.

The technical challenges for safe LTO beyond 60 years are described in detail in Section 4 and the challenges connected with increasing safety requirements are described in detail in Section 5.

Other challenges for safe LTO beyond 60 years are discussed in Section 3 to provide a comprehensive overview of challenges for safe LTO of existing nuclear power plants. They are discussed only on a general level and are not the subject of detail analysis. There is also no intention to develop any APAs or AFEs for economic aspects, political decisions and environmental aspects as it is outside the scope of this report.

### <span id="page-40-1"></span>**3.1. Economic aspects**

In the early years of the peaceful utilisation of nuclear energy, many prototype units of small electric output were phased out as they became unprofitable. Reactors of various early designs were phased out particularly in countries developing their own reactors, such as Canada, Czechia, France, Germany, Japan, Russia, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States. Except for early design units, several standard series units have been recently phased out due to changes in the energy market including the increased competitiveness of other energy sources (e.g. shale gas production in the Canada and United States), subsidies for renewable energy and increased taxes on nuclear energy production in Europe (i.e. units in Sweden, as discussed earlier).

### <span id="page-40-2"></span>**3.2. Political decisions**

Major nuclear accidents have historically been followed by political decisions affecting the nuclear sector. After the Chernobyl accident in 1986, all nuclear units in Italy were phased out. Germany decided on a gradual phaseout of all nuclear units until 2022 after the Fukushima Daiichi accident in 2011.

Sweden permanently shut down two BWR units of the Barseback Nuclear Power Plant built not far from the Danish capital Copenhagen in 2005 and 2010, respectively. After the reunification of Germany in 1990, Germany decided to phase out all Russian designed VVERs in East Germany. As a part of EU access agreements, several eastern European countries had to permanently shut down units of older Russian designs such as VVER 230 (Jaslovske Bohunice Units 1 and 2 in the Slovak Republic and Kozloduy Units 1-4 in Bulgaria) and RBMK (Units 1 and 2 at Ignalina, Lithuania).

Certain post-Fukushima Daiichi requirements and associated uncertainty in returns on investments led to the permanent shutdown of the BWR Muhleberg Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland.

Political aspects can have a significant impact on future investments and the operation of nuclear power plants. In March 2015, the Court of Justice of the European Union decided that tax from the utilisation of nuclear fuel or tax from spent nuclear fuel are compatible with the European Constitution. This legalised the introduction of special taxes and fees on nuclear power plants (e.g. tax from utilisation of nuclear fuel in Germany, tax from installed nuclear capacity in Sweden), an increase of existing fees, changes in insurance conditions, etc. Political decisions also impacted the profitability of potential LTO with increased taxes and increased payments for decommissioning and radioactive waste processing. Political decisions are in many cases the result of public opinion. From this perspective, an open and transparent public approach is of paramount importance for the prolonged operation of nuclear power plants.

### <span id="page-41-0"></span>**3.3. Environmental aspects**

The environment can in some cases play an important role in decision making connected with LTO of some nuclear power plants. Global warming, changing environmental conditions, population and demographic development can have major impacts on the feasibility of LTO. Decisions to phase out nuclear power plant or to not allow LTO for environmental reasons are typically closely related to political decisions, but the primary reason can be environmental.

Environmental aspects and their impact on LTO for nuclear power plants can be seen from two perspectives:

- 1. the impact of nuclear power plant LTO on the environment; and
- 2. the impact of a changing environment on LTO of nuclear power plants.

### *3.3.1. Impact of nuclear power plant LTO on environment*

The impact of nuclear power plant LTO on the environment is usually assessed within the scope of an environmental impact assessment (EIA). An EIA is a standard part of the preparation and approval process for the construction of new nuclear power plants, but also part of the approval of LTO projects in most of the countries operating nuclear power plants.

For example, in the United States, the EIA has a similar importance to the demonstration of the integrated safety assessment and is performed in parallel with the safety assessment according to national regulations. There are typically only minor differences between EIA for LTO from 40 to 60 years and 60 to 80 years. There are different values of input parameters for assessments like duration of operation, amount and quality of radioactive waste, volume of discharges, etc. Additionally, the US NRC issued a new version of its Generic Environmental Impact Statement[9](#page-42-0) for licence renewal to address 60 to 80 years, including additional evaluations related to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change.

For European countries, an EIA is required based on European jurisprudence (LTO Nuclear Power Plant D1/2; ECLI:EU:C:2019:622) [25], as part of the nuclear power plant licensing process for LTO. The EIA has to comply with the EU's Environmental Impact Assessment directive (2011/92/EU, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU [26]).

Each EU member state has its own national procedure for performing an EIA evaluation. For example, the Netherlands' commission for environmental assessment advises, as an independent committee, the national regulatory authority on the content of EIA-reports.

### *3.3.2. Impact of changing environment on LTO of nuclear power plants*

The potential impact of environmental changes on decision making connected with LTO of nuclear power plants can be related to:

- cooling water temperatures or flow rate changes not ensuring enough cooling capacity;
- extreme weather conditions like wind, flooding, snow (more information on SSCs assessment to cope with extreme weather could be found in IAEA-TECDOC-1818 [27]);
- demographic development in the exclusion zone of nuclear sites;
- modification of the microclimate in the proximity of nuclear sites;
- changes in public opinion against nuclear energy related to environmental issues.

Many nuclear power plants use cooling water from surrounding rivers or lakes, either in open circuit (without cooling towers) or in closed circuit (with cooling towers). Some areas have been experiencing a significant decrease in average or minimum water flow or an increase in water temperatures. This can lead to operation restrictions and ultimately to permanent shutdown or prevention of LTO. This issue is being closely investigated in several countries in connection with LTO from 60 to 80 years.

Another environmental factor is fast demographic development in some areas. In Canada, eight CANDU reactors have been commissioned at the Pickering Nuclear Power Plant site since 1971, at that time approximately 30 km from Toronto's city centre. Fast city growth in recent decades means the city boundaries are now 5 km from the plant. More urban development towards the plant is expected, leading to a decision to permanently shut down all units at the end of their original design lifetime and to not go for LTO. Nevertheless, in January 2025, the Ontario government approved Ontario Power Generation's (OPG) plan to proceed with refurbishment of Pickering Units 5-8 which would allow an additional 30 years of operation.

<span id="page-42-0"></span><sup>9</sup> US NRC (n.d.), "Generic Environmental Impact Statement for License Renewal of Nuclear Plants", Documents NUREG–1437, Revision 2, US NRC, Washington, [www.nrc.gov/reading](http://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/staff/sr1437/index)[rm/doc-collections/nuregs/staff/sr1437/index.](http://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/staff/sr1437/index)

### <span id="page-43-0"></span>**3.4. Supply chain issues**

Over the decades, the nuclear sector has experienced significant changes in its market situation. In the 1970s and 1980s, the vast majority of new nuclear power plants was designed, manufactured and constructed in developed countries like the Canada, European countries, Korea, Japan and the United States. After the Chernobyl accident in 1986, very few new nuclear power plants were built in these countries. Construction of new nuclear power plants continued only in some countries like China, India, Pakistan and Russia, but has gradually moved also to new, originally non-nuclear countries like Bangladesh, Belarus and Turkey. This change in the location of nuclear power plant construction was followed by a move in manufacturing to these new markets. Designing capabilities and capacities have also been moving towards the new markets.

Therefore, many traditional suppliers in developed countries operating nuclear power plants since the 1970s and 1980s lost their internal market, or saw it significantly reduced. Some suppliers decided to leave the nuclear energy market as the volume of sales became unattractive and perspectives for investments in new builds were diminishing.

This has a significant impact on the availability of spare parts and components, as well as on the maintenance and inspection services for the nuclear power plants from the 1970s and 1980s that are now facing LTO decisions. The supply chain issues also include technological obsolescence, which is the unavailability of spare parts or maintenance services.

The importance of ensuring a functional supply chain is understood in many countries operating nuclear power plants and considering LTO. Except for systematic proactive technological obsolescence management as described in [4], other solutions are considered or implemented in many countries, including long-term contracts with suppliers, cooperation among utilities, and commercial grade dedication.

While short-term supply chain disruptions like geopolitical events, natural disasters, global pandemics, mergers and acquisition or a loss of key personnel or documentation can impact any operational facility's supply chain, nuclear power plants in LTO face additional, unique challenges. Over time, these plants begin to experience gradual issues such as equipment obsolescence and the disappearance of original equipment manufacturers from the market. These ageing facilities may struggle to find spare parts and services for maintenance as they are no longer produced or provided. This highlights the critical need for strategic planning and investment in technology upgrades, supply chain partnerships, business continuity management in the supply chain, supplier relationship management and the cultivation of a skilled workforce capable of navigating these evolving complexities. Some nuclear operators have begun to require key suppliers to maintain business continuity management systems according to ISO 22 301:2019 [28], as a part of their integrated management systems. Such management systems go above and beyond nuclear quality management systems in the areas of knowledge management and maintenance of business operations in the case of disruptions.

The phaseout and shutdown policies of some countries has strongly affected supply options further afield. For example, some German-designed reactors continue towards LTO even though the Nuclear Safety Standards Commission (KTA) standard for supplier quality assurance (KTA 1 401 [29]) will no longer be reviewed or revised and suppliers are no longer seeking requalification. For those remaining German-designed reactors, this will mean a disruption to their legacy supply chain quality management. This situation leads to degradation of the supply chains of the still-operating reactors, which may require design changes, reverse engineering or expanded use of acceptance processes for commercialgrade products.

On the other hand, the resurgence in nuclear power plant construction in some countries and the increasing interest in small modular reactors (SMRs) worldwide presents an opportunity to revitalise the global nuclear supply chain. The anticipated demand for these new generation reactors necessitates a robust and diversified supply chain capable of delivering high-quality components on time and within budget. The growing market, with its positive outlook and forecast, could stimulate the emergence of new suppliers, fostering innovation and competitive pricing. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of the SMR business case, such as their smaller scale and potential for serial production, could lead to standardisation of components and more streamlined manufacturing processes. This new era could result in a resurgence of nuclear supply chains from which legacy nuclear power plants in LTO would certainly benefit.

As indicated within the WNA's *World Nuclear Supply Chain Outlook* [30], there is an expected turning point towards the 2030s, where the number of nuclear refurbishments for LTO will be increasing.

A revitalised nuclear supply chain could bring with it a better integration of contemporary issues in the legacy supply chains of nuclear power plants in LTO. These issues include corporate decision-making factors such as environmental, social and governance (ESG), circular economy, and sustainable manufacturing. Modern supply chains geared to nuclear new build may also bring with them a spillover of modern technologies to legacy supply chains such as deeper integration of Industry 4.0 principles, digital twin technology, additive manufacturing and artificial intelligence.

In 2020, two important reports from the European Commission JRC and Nucleareurope (then FORATOM) recognised that the nuclear industry faces challenges due to the discontinuation of products by original equipment manufacturers and stringent global requirements that discourage new entrants[10](#page-44-0). To mitigate these issues, the European nuclear industry could utilise modern, high-quality products from well-established suppliers in other industries that meet or exceed the quality of original item[s11](#page-44-1).

This approach of using high-quality industrial-grade items in safety-critical applications, known as commercial grade dedication (CGD), has been successfully applied in countries like Belgium, Canada, Korea, Spain, Slovenia and the United States. Several ongoing projects in Europe, such as in Czechia, Finland and Sweden, aim to replicate this approach. The key principles are empowering utilities and licensees to establish the suitability of these items for safety-critical applications and leveraging existing supply chain projects and international CGD experience to promote high-quality industrial-grade items with a harmonised approach. In 2022, Nucleareurope published a joint utility guideline about Commercial Grade Dedication[12](#page-44-2) and, in 2023, the IAEA published TECDOC-2 034 on Suitability Evaluation of Commercial-grade Products for Use in Nuclear Power Plant

Safety Systems [31]. Both publications outline approaches and good practices for increasing supply options for nuclear power plants in LTO.

### *3.4.1. Regulation, codes and standards*

Changes in the domestic regulatory landscapes pose challenges but also opportunities for nuclear power plants operating beyond 60 years. As rules change, legacy nuclear power plants sometimes struggle with costly and complex efforts to reach compliance, while maintaining their historical licensing basis. Regulators and standards development organisations (SDOs) play a role in ensuring that LTO beyond 60 years is not made effectively impossible due to these constraints. For the supply chain, there are positive developments where efforts to harmonise and standardise over time are progressing. The international quality management standard for suppliers of products and services important to nuclear safety (ISO 19 443:2018 [32]) is becoming more widely accepted is expected by nuclear power plant end-users for their supply chains. Such developments can help to create a strong, broad nuclear supply chain base which serves nuclear power plants in all lifecycle phases, including to the benefit of those operating more than 60 years.

### *3.4.2. Environmental, social and governance (ESG)*

As ageing nuclear installations continue to operate, they will be increasingly subject to the impacts of evolving ESG developments within the supply chain. One example of these challenges comes in the form of regulations concerning per- and polyfluoroalkylsubstances (PFAS). PFAS, a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals commonly used across various industries, are under scrutiny due to their potential environmental and health hazards. Proposals to ban or significantly limit their use pose a potential challenge to the nuclear industry, as these chemicals are used in many aspects of nuclear power plant operation, from coolant systems to protective clothing. As such, ESG developments in the supply chain could trigger obsolescence issues, as substances, components or even practices deemed non-compliant with new regulations may need to be phased out. Comprehensive obsolescence management strategies are required that not only consider technological advancements but also account for evolving societal and environmental standards.

### *3.4.3. Supply chains for refurbishment and retrofitting*

Major equipment replacement and the refurbishment of integral components of LTO beyond 60 years rely on a limited supply chain that involves specialised resources such as high-capacity cranes, advanced robotics and a skilled workforce. As nuclear power plants operate beyond 60 years, the need for these resources becomes increasingly critical to ensure safe and economical operations. However, the availability of such resources is constrained due to the niche nature of the nuclear industry, and the necessary investments in equipment, training and workforce development are considerable. The supply chain for these resources requires strategic management and long-term planning to ensure their availability when required. This involves fostering partnerships with suppliers, investing in training and development to build a skilled workforce, and promoting research and development into advanced robotics and other technologies relevant to equipment replacement and refurbishment. This way, a sustainable and resilient supply chain can be maintained to support the extended LTO of nuclear power plants.

### Recommendations:

- Establish collaborative industry-wide forecasting and foresight of LTO refurbishment needs.
- Invest in modern technologies and upgrade programmes.

- Leverage the resurgence of the nuclear industry/nuclear supply chain.
- Adopt proven, high-quality industrial products.

### *3.4.4. Conclusions on supply chain*

The importance of ensuring a functional supply chain is understood in many countries operating nuclear power plants and considering LTO. Unfortunately, many traditional suppliers have lost their internal market completely or seen it significantly reduced and decided to leave the nuclear market as the volume of sales dropped or prospective investments became unattractive.

The supply chain requires strategic management and long-term planning to ensure its availability. This involves fostering partnerships with suppliers, investing in training and development to build a skilled workforce, and promoting research and development. This way, a sustainable and resilient supply chain can be maintained to support the extended LTO beyond 60 years of nuclear power plants.

### <span id="page-46-0"></span>**3.5. Human resources, knowledge and competence management**

Besides the challenges described above, the topics of importance to LTO of nuclear power plants include the availability of qualified human resources in the long-term, the ability to retain knowledge and to transfer it to new generations at nuclear power plants, and competence management.

The IAEA establishes standards which are published in the IAEA Safety Standards Series. The publications in the series are categorised as Safety Fundamentals, Safety Requirements, and Safety Guides.

Regarding the responsibilities of licensees, the IAEA sets ten fundamental principles for safety in its Fundamental Safety Principles (SF-1)[13.](#page-46-1) The most relevant principles for this topic are:

- Principle 1: Responsibility for safety. "The prime responsibility for safety must rest with the person or organisation responsible for facilities and activities that give rise to radiation risks."
  - ‒ "The licensee retains the prime responsibility for safety throughout the lifetime of facilities and activities, and this responsibility cannot be delegated. Other groups, such as designers, manufacturers and constructors, employers, contractors, and consignors and carriers, also have legal, professional, or functional responsibilities with regard to safety."
  - ‒ The licensee is responsible for: "Establishing and maintaining the necessary competences;"
- Principle 3: Leadership and management for safety. "Effective leadership and management for safety must be established and sustained in organisations concerned with, and facilities and activities that give rise to, radiation risks."

To fulfil its responsibilities, a licensee must identify the competences necessary for the safe operation throughout the lifetime of the plant, recruit the staff needed to perform the necessary tasks, and develop and maintain the competence of the staff. Planning for LTO,

<span id="page-46-1"></span><sup>13</sup> IAEA (2006), *Fundamental Safety Principles*, Safety Fundamentals No. SF-1, IAEA, Vienna.

a licensee should plan for maintaining and developing the organisation and its competency over time and according to current and coming challenges.

### *3.5.1. Human resources*

Most operators consider LTO as a strategic programme that encompasses and advances all areas of activity in plant operations, including strategic human resources management (HRM), which involves aligning HR policies and practices with the organisation's longterm goals and objectives.

One of the major challenges in carrying out LTO programmes is the essential requirement for human expertise, skills and knowledge. Nuclear power plants have an operational lifespan of several decades, which can be extended beyond 60 years under specific conditions, often extending beyond the working lifetime of nuclear engineers involved in the design, construction and operation of the nuclear power plant. Many employees who contributed during the design and construction phases of the existing nuclear power plants have already retired or will do so soon. A similar situation exists in the R&D and regulatory sectors.

The existence of well-prepared staff, long-term HR strategies, workforce and staffing plans, talent pipelines established in collaboration with educational organisations (secondary schools and universities), fully functional talent management, and succession planning programmes are fundamental prerequisites for the successful implementation of the LTO programme in accordance with safety standards.

Many operators face the challenge of an insufficient nuclear workforce and a lack of interest in the sector by the younger generations. Considering the provisional lifespan of the nuclear facilities in LTO, this requires a pragmatic approach and co-ordinated initiatives from all stakeholders to attract the next generation of technical talents to the nuclear community. Co-ordinated measures executed by governments, industry, academia and R&D organisations will be crucial to avoid the lack of human resources and to maintain the supply of qualified and competent employees for the justified LTO period. This is necessary to ensure the flow of new recruits in a sustainable and long-term plan.

Regarding the HR policy and strategy to support LTO, the IAEA provides basic requirements in its safety standards SSR-2/2 (Rev.1) [3] and GSR Part 2 [33]. The most relevant requirements are:

- 1. GSR Part 2–Requirement 10: Management of processes and activities [33], "Processes and activities shall be developed and shall be effectively managed to achieve the organisation's goals without compromising safety.";
- 2. SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1)-Requirement 4: Staffing of the operating organisation [3], "The operating organisation shall be staffed with competent managers and sufficient qualified personnel for the safe operation of the plant.".

There are still areas that require improvement in the establishment and implementation of LTO staffing policies, objectives, and associated human resources strategies. This concern is identified in subsection Chapter 3.5.4 "Observations and Findings", of the present report.

### *3.5.2. Competence management*

The ability of the operating organisation to fulfil its responsibilities and objectives largely depends on the competence of its staff. Investing in the skills and knowledge of employees benefits each individual and secures the future of the organisation. This is especially important when it comes to LTO programmes. It is important to systematically assess competence needs in both the short and long term, and provide training and other competence development measures while continuously improving this aspect of the management system.

Senior management within the operational organisation must establish a vision and policy for competence management, leading to the formulation of goals, strategies and delivery plans. The competence policy serves as the primary means for senior management to communicate their commitment, expectations, and strategies for achieving the organisation's staff competence objectives.

When implementing LTO programmes, special consideration should be given to the generational transfer of personnel and knowledge, and the associated need for wellestablished competence management processes, including developing the competency model, assessing competencies, analysing gaps, and supporting competency development. Inadequate implementation of these may result in a lower level of organisational readiness for LTO programmes.

SALTO missions conducted over the last decade have also identified several deficiencies in this area, which, when combined or correlated with other risks, must be considered. These findings and concerns are indicated later, in Section 3.5.4 of this report, entitled "Observations and findings".

Regarding competence management for LTO and processes for recruitment, training and qualification of personnel involved in LTO, the most relevant requirements in IAEA safety standards are:

- 1. GSR Part 2–Requirement 9: Provision of resources [33], Senior management shall determine the competences and resources necessary to carry out the activities of the organiszation safely and shall provide them;
- 2. SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1)–Requirement 3: Structure and functions of the operating organisation [3], The structure of the operating organisation and the functions, roles and responsibilities of its personnel shall be established and documented;
- 3. SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1)–Requirement 4: Staffing of the operating organisation [3], The operating organisation shall be staffed with competent managers and sufficient qualified personnel for the safe operation of the plant;
- 4. SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1)–Requirement 7: Qualification and training of personnel [3], The operating organisation shall ensure that all activities that may affect safety are performed by suitably qualified and competent persons.

These findings and concerns are retained later, in Section 3.5.4 of this report, "Observations and findings".

### *3.5.3. Knowledge management*

There is a permanent need to select, recruit and train skilled and knowledgeable nuclear personnel, allowing them to gain experience by working with skilled colleagues for a sufficient period of time to transfer the knowledge and understanding of the organisation. There are several effective knowledge management tools supporting the knowledge transfer (on the job training, succession programmes, communities of practice, etc.). The expansion of nuclear energy in the 20th century attracted many young professionals, a significant part of whom are now nearing retirement. If numerous existing nuclear power plants are to extend their operating lifetimes (LTO), a new generation of engineers will be required to take their place. The adequacy of human resources, both in numbers and in competency, is a concern that utilities and governments must consider when contemplating long-term nuclear operations.

Like the construction of new nuclear power plants, lifetime extensions offer an opportunity to attract highly qualified personnel to the nuclear power sector. Although recruiting enough talent may pose challenges, especially when many nuclear power plants are expected to close in a few years, the potential for these plants to operate for many more years should make the nuclear industry a more appealing option for young scientists and engineers. However, this can only become a reality if decision makers ensure that there are sufficient facilities and student slots available in universities and other educational institutions to cultivate a pool of individuals with nuclear-related skills and knowledge.

On the other hand, the organisations shall continuously assess the potential loss of undocumented/critical knowledge related to attrition and plan appropriate measures to retain and transfer the knowledge for the LTO period. To protect their significant investments in personnel, the operators need to provide incentives aimed at retaining key people which will allow overlapping periods between the experienced workers and new recruits. This approach could be instrumental to accelerate the acquisition of technical capabilities by a new employee and help to transfer critical and unique knowledge, thus shortening the competence development time for the newcomers.

Based on the observations from SALTO reviews performed by the IAEA, maintaining competence in the organisations of the nuclear industry and nuclear regulatory bodies will soon become one of the most serious issues. The loss of workers who have the knowledge important for operation and safety is a clear challenge for the safe and reliable operation of nuclear facilities.

Fully implemented knowledge management (KM), deeply embedded, and integrated into the organisational management system, should encompass the entire plant life cycle. The primary advantages and benefits of KM become most apparent during the implementation of LTO programmes, specifically during the transfer of personnel and knowledge from one generation of nuclear experts to the next.

Knowledge management in LTO is based on the principle that all three components: people, process, and technology should work in harmony, and need not focus only on human resources, but also on compatible information systems and processes in a long-term perspective.

During the LTO period, special focus should be placed on non-physical ageing of SSCs, i.e. the process of their becoming out of date (obsolete) owing to the availability and evolution of knowledge and technology, and the associated changes in equipment and/or requirements, codes and standards.

The establishment of a nuclear knowledge management (NKM) programme and its implementation within a nuclear facility ensures that a nuclear power plant can be operated for a long period of time as a highly reliable, efficient, and safe installation. There is an obvious risk that, in the absence of knowledge transfer plans, core knowledge may be lost between different phases of the life of a nuclear facility for various reasons if not properly codified and/or transferred in advance.

Regarding knowledge management and knowledge transfer for LTO, the most relevant requirements in IAEA safety standards are:

- 1. GSR Part 2–Requirement 8: Documentation of the management system [33], "The management system shall be documented. The documentation of the management system shall be controlled, usable, readable, clearly identified and readily available at the point of use";
- 2. GSR Part 2–Requirement 9: Provision of resources [33], "The knowledge and the information of the organisation shall be managed as a resource";

- 3. GSR Part 2–Requirement 13: Measurement, assessment and improvement of the management system [33], "The effectiveness of the management system shall be measured, assessed and improved to enhance safety performance, including minimising the occurrence of problems relating to safety";
- 4. SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1)–Requirement 24: Feedback of operating experience [3], "The operating organisation shall establish an operating experience programme to learn from events at the plant and events in the nuclear industry and other industries worldwide."

### *3.5.4. Observations and findings*

Besides the safety requirements, the IAEA also provides a comprehensive set of safety guides, SSG-48 [4], SSG-25 [5], GS-G-3.1 [34], SSG-74 [35], SSG-50 [36], SSG-75 [37], SSG-72 [38], which provide recommended ways of fulfilling the safety requirements. Nevertheless, results of SALTO missions, published in the *SALTO Missions Highlights* from 2018 to 2022 [39] show some frequent issues in this area; some examples being:

- HR policy and strategy to support LTO not being adequately or fully developed (eight out of 11 reviewed nuclear power plants);
- competence management not being adequately or fully implemented (5/11);
- KM or knowledge transfer processes for LTO not being adequately or fully implemented (7/11).

Some examples of observations from SALTO reviews performed by the IAEA between 2015-2018 [36] and 2018-2022 [37]:

- HR policy and strategy being inadequate for the LTO period;
- the plant's HR policy and strategy being incomplete for LTO;
- the HR policy and strategy not being effectively implemented to support all future human resources-related challenges for LTO;
- LTO staffing policy, objectives and associated strategies for HR not being fully established and implemented;
- the plant not having finalised the process for ensuring plant personnel knowledge and competences related to ageing management activities;
- the plant having insufficient information technology to manage information and records to support the organisational objectives, strategies and needs for LTO with regards to HR development;
- the process for securing all competences required for safe LTO being incomplete;
- KM not being fully effective to support LTO;
- the plant not having an integrated and systematic programme for managing critical knowledge for LTO;
- KM implementation being incomplete to support LTO;

Similar observations have arisen during the Knowledge Management Assist Visits conducted in member states over the past years (IAEA TECDOC-1880 [40]) in the domains of HR and KM, for the work processes specifically oriented to NKM NG-T-6.10 [41]:
