Source: STP164720220064 [103]

EPRI is conducting multiple programmes investigating the potential thermal ageing of low alloy steel concern. The first effort was a literature review of all available data documented in MRP-438. Following that effort, EPRI documented the available margin to RPV P-T limits from a thermally aged pressuriser, which is the highest temperature component in the primary RCS. Westinghouse and Combustion Engineering NSSS plants are documented in MRP-463; B&W plants are included in MRP-474. The current ongoing effort is to test thermally aged pressuriser TPZR material harvested from a US plant that is undergoing decommissioning. The effort began in late 2022, with a final report expected before the end of 2024. The results from this testing effort, once compared to the analytical results, will inform future research in this area.

The VVER reactors (V-440/213 and V-1000/320) also contain samples for thermal ageing at hot leg temperatures (290°C for VVER 440 and 320°C for VVER 1000) as part of the RPV surveillance specimen program. Based on former experimental work performed in the 1980s with accelerated ageing (holding times at 350°C up to 10 000h), it was stated that VVER RPV steels are relatively stable against thermal ageing. Results of VVER-1 000 thermal ageing surveillance specimens testing obtained since 2009 exhibited, however, significant ageing of weld metal at temperatures between 310 and 320°C depending on time, Ni, Mo contents and Тk0. The shift of the critical temperature T<sup>k</sup> was not related to a strengthening effect. The maximum holding time reached 208 896 h [104]. Results for base metal and HAZ surveillance specimens did not show any systematic trend of strength or Tk for ageing times up to 170 000 h. Former assumptions of a significant shift of Tk during a transitional period are considered as an effect of scatter and sampling locations [105]. However, there is still room for improvement of existing analytical models of thermal ageing. A thermal embrittlement surveillance programme for material of primary circuity has been introduced since 2012 at the VVER 440 Bohunice Nuclear Power Plant and Mochovce Nuclear Power Plant for the materials of the RPV, primary circuit main circulation piping and SG shell. Details can be found in the Paper "Thermal ageing monitoring of primary circuit components at nuclear power plants in the Slovak Republic", IAEA-CN-194-012 [106]).

Ukrainian VVER-1 000 data for thermal ageing show that transition temperature (TT) shifts due to thermal ageing are obtained only from the fact that the initial TT and aged TT data are random variables, which are characterised by the scatter band [107]. The same results were obtained in Russia [108].

Thus, thermal ageing has been shown to be practically absent. That is why the Ukrainian standard for assessment of RPV embrittlement SOU NAEK 087:2023 "Methodology for determining the radiation embrittlement of RPV metal using the surveillance test data" [109], regulates as of 2023 the TT shift due to thermal ageing as zero.

### *4.2.2.3 Direct fracture toughness methodologies*

Beside the indirect RTNDT concept, the direct master curve approach, based on fracture mechanics tests, may also be used for a deterministic RPV safety assessment. The master curve approach was intensively investigated in the past and is now applied worldwide by using the reference temperature T0 [110].

In the United States, the master curve approach is used to monitor FT in RPVs as a complement to the existing regulatory surveillance programme to demonstrate the conservatism of the regulatory approach. The results of surveillance capsule testing are used for reactor vessel embrittlement projections to determine the increase in the reference transition temperature (RTNDT) which is used to index the reference FT curves for KIc and KIa as specified in the applicable national regulation. The embrittlement projections from the surveillance data are also used to demonstrate that the reactor vessel retains adequate FT to prevent ductile failure, usually through comparison to a regulatory requirement on the Charpy USE.

In 2010, the researchers in the international community identified irradiation effects and the FT master curve as a subject for continued research (see EDMA Vol 3 [44], Sect.6.6 Gap No. P-AS 04), especially due to:

- specimen size, especially regarding the pre-cracked Charpy specimen;
- shape of the master curve at high levels of embrittlement;
- dynamic loading (including crack-arrest);
- effects of intergranular fracture.

In the United States, direct FT methodologies were developed in 2021 as an alternative to Charpy V-notch methods for assessment of neutron embrittlement. The US PWROG submitted a direct FT methodology in topical report PWROG-18 068-NP [111]. This report describes the method for implementing direct FT testing in the structural analyses for the RPV and includes all the relevant limits for the RPV during the service life and is currently under review by the US NRC.

In addition, ASME Code Case N-830-1 [112] has been approved by the ASME Code, for use in Appendices A and G analyses, which provides a suite of toughness models based on the master curve T0, but it has not yet been included in US NRC Regulatory Guide 1.147, Inservice Inspection Code Case Acceptability, ASME Section XI, Division 1 [113]. These direct FT-based methodologies are not necessary to license plants for operation from 6080 years. However, these methodologies can be used to reduce unnecessary conservatism in analyses related to neutron embrittlement, such as pressurised thermal shock and pressure-temperature operating limits. A future revision to Code Case N-830, to Revision 2, will add applicability to Appendix E.

In some other countries the master curve approach was incorporated into the national regulation in the form of a reference temperature RTT0 based on the testing procedure ASTM-Standard E1 921 and the ASME Code Cases (formerly based on the Code Cases N-629 ASME XI und N-631 in ASME III, nowadays on N-830-1 [112]), e.g. in the guideline on ageing management of Switzerland ENSI B01/d [114] and the nuclear standard code KTA 3 203 of Germany [115]. In Czechia and in Finland, surveillance specimens are regularly tested for T0 and it is recommended to use the master curve approach for RPV lifetime re-assessment in the future. Size correction and different margins must be applied [116].

Currently, the US NRC is following an effort to develop a draft code case that would incorporate methodologies for accounting for embrittlement of RPV low-alloy steels into the ASME Code, Section XI. Code Case N-914 (MRP-462, Revision 1 [draft]) would allow for the use of an irradiated or unirradiated reference temperature, based on either Charpy V-Notch based (RTNDT) or direct FT (T0) – based (T0, RTT0). With respect to the toughness metric at the neutron fluence of interest, Code Case N-914 would allow use of either a Charpy V-notch based or direct FT (To, RTT0) as well. The code case offers an embrittlement shift model based on ASTM E900-15, or other embrittlement shift model, provided certain criteria are met. The EPRI technical team is currently reviewing and addressing comments on the draft Code Case by the Working Group Operating Plant Criteria (WGOPC) membership.

### *4.2.2.4 Stress corrosion cracking and long-term integrity of dissimilar welds*

The design and the welding techniques for DMWs of BWR, PWR and VVER nuclear power plants are similar, because ferritic steel (carbon or low-alloy steel) and stainless steel (high-alloy steel) are used as base materials. DMWs can occur as butt welds between piping components. They are also used to attach penetrations to pressure boundary components, e.g. joining reactor vessel head penetrations into the reactor vessel head. Because of the differences in materials across the weld and the differences in chemical composition that can occur in the deposited metal, DMWs can be susceptible to degradation modes that do not occur in similar metal welds.

DMWs in western type PWRs and BWRs, which include nickel base alloy filler metals, have been found to be prone to a form of SCC, known as inter-granular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC), often referred to as primary water stress corrosion cracking (PWSCC). Nickel base alloys (base and welding materials) are sensitive to environmentally assisted corrosion (EAF), as SCC occurs also in parts made of base metal alloy A600.

Depending on their location, the base and welding material (stainless steel or nickel base alloy), different degradation mechanisms must be considered as relevant for DMWs [117]:

- stress corrosion cracking of all types: intergranular (IGSCC), transgranular (TGSCC), interdendritic (IDSCC) (BWR, PWR);
- fatigue/low cycle and EAF (PWR);
- thermal ageing (safe ends of vessels) (PWR);
- thermal fatigue (safe ends of vessels, if the main coolant line [MCL] is austenitic) (PWR);

• boric acid corrosion (BAC) of the ferritic part of the DMW from the outside (PWR).

The ageing effects can be detected, monitored and trended, and predictions for future development can be done for all the above, except for thermal ageing, which is assessed based on destructive testing, to identify material properties at a certain moment in time. Currently there are no specific rules or standards regarding DMW; they are treated in the same way as similar metal joints and their mechanical properties are assumed to be equivalent to the material with the guaranteed mechanical properties of the materials used in welding, approach which leads to very conservative assumptions (IGALL AMP 163 [117]).

For long-term integrity of DMW, the following issues need to be considered as part of the evaluation of whether the operating time can be extended to 80 years (EMDA vol. 3, section 8.3 [44]):

- update of SCC disposition lines for Alloy 182 for BWR with normal and hydrogen water chemistry (NWC and HWC), since most recent data are above the current curves (e.g., BWRVIP-59 [118]). Recent SCC disposition lines exist for PWR and Alloy 182/82 (MRP-420R1 [119]) and Alloy 82 (BWRVIP-358 [120]), H-P Seifert, PSI;
- effect of long-term thermal ageing on the susceptibility of Alloy 182 and 82 weld metals to SCC;
- effect of long-term thermal ageing on the susceptibility of Alloy 152 and 52 weld metals to SCC;
- effect of alloying elements and the compounds formed during heat treatment on the susceptibility of LASs to SCC under BWR conditions;
- validity of the crack growth data for LAS and in the SCC disposition curves;
- crack behaviour at the fusion line between Ni alloy weld metal and LAS;
- effect of neutron irradiation on the susceptibility of LAS to SCC.

These issues are confirmed by EPRI MRP-386 "Recommended Factors of Improvement for Evaluating PWSCC Growth Rates of Thick-Wall Alloy 690 Materials and Alloy 52, 152, and Variants Welds" [121], showing that Alloy 690 and its weld Alloys 52 and 152 are much less susceptible to cracking than Alloy 600 and its weld alloys in PWR plants.

Research activities are aimed now at gaining a better understanding of the degradation mechanisms, developing qualified degradation assessment methods, and verifying models and analyses. Over the time, there were seven European research projects directly related to the assessment of DMW degradation and integrity, but only the last 3 are focused more on LTO:

- DISWEC Evaluation of Techniques for Assessing Corrosion Cracking in Dissimilar Metal Welds;
- BIMET Structural Integrity of Bi-Metallic Components;
- ADIMEW Assessment of Aged Piping Dissimilar Metal Weld integrity;
- NESC-III Project organised by the Network for Evaluating Structural Components (NESC) to extend the results obtained in the BIMET and ADIMEW projects;

- STYLE Structural integrity for lifetime management of non RPV components, developing simplified engineering assessment methods, deterministic and probabilistic, to qualify leak before break (LBB) procedures for lifetime management and integrity of reactor coolant pressure boundary components in European nuclear power plants [\(https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/249648/reporting/](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/249648/reporting), 2014) [122];
- MULTIMETAL Structural performance of multi-metallic components, aimed to develop a procedure for measuring FT in DMWs. The work will also include an assessment of LBB behaviour. This will be the technical basis towards the development of harmonised European codes and standards for multi-metal components, currently not available ([123];
- ATLAS+ Advanced Structural Integrity Assessment Tools for Safe LTO, quantifying inherent safety margins introduced by the conservative approaches used during design and dictated by codes and standards employed through-out the life of the plant. ATLAS+ will support LTO by using more advanced and realistic scientific methods to assess the integrity of piping, after carrying out large scale tests using original piping materials [124].

However, the effect of cold work remains an open issue, which has been tackled through the MEACTOS research project with the objective of mitigating environmental cracking of the nickel base alloy welds by optimising surface processing. The MEACTOS project, completed in February 2022, produced technically relevant information on mitigation of environmentally assisted cracking (EAC) initiation, to be incorporated into guidelines for modern surface machining and treatment techniques, as documented in [125].

The VVER reactors are made of low-alloy steel 15CH2MFA (VVER 440) and 15CH2NMFA (VVER 1000). The nozzles are made of low-alloy steel 22K. As the MCLs of the VVER 440 reactors are made of austenitic steel, there are safe ends with DMWs connected to the RPV nozzles. Yet in VVER 1000 reactors the nozzles are connected with similar metal welds to the MCLs made of low alloy steel with internal cladding. All DMWs in VVER reactors were welded with austenitic filler materials, i.e. nickel base alloy was not used.

While PWRs designed by Westinghouse and Framatome have austenitic MCLs and hence large DMW connected to the RPV nozzles, PWRs from some other designers like Siemens and Combustion Engineering have MCLs made of low alloy steel and hence similar metal welds at this location. There is a dissimilar weld between the first austenitic cladding layer and the RPV material. As the RPV of many other PWR designs, the RPV of VVER reactors have a two-layer cladding. The first layer of austenitic cladding has a higher chromium and nickel content to adjust for dilution effects with the base metal. It is covered by the second layer of austenitic cladding and is not in contact with the medium.

There are, however, some RPVs with single layer cladding that might be prone to SCC, in particular in contact with BWR NWC.

### *4.2.2.5 Environmentally assisted fatigue*

The environment can significantly influence fatigue crack initiation. EAF, or "corrosion fatigue", must be considered when dealing with components in the LWR environment. Three sources of fatigue are significant to the PWR RPV: system cycling, thermal cycling and flow induced vibration (IAEA –TECDOC-1 556 [50], Sections 4.4, 5.4, 6.3 and 8.2.4).

As for BWR RPV, EPRI has identified the available values of CUFen which is the cumulative usage factor (CUF) adjusted to account for the effects of the reactor water environment on component fatigue life, based on the 60-year licence renewal applications submitted in the report BWRVIP-343 issued in 2022 [126]. The results from collecting available CUFen results of limiting BWR locations applicable to extended operations beyond the original licensed period are compiled into a spreadsheet database, containing data from both US- BWRs and non-US BWR reactors.

High-cycle fatigue (HCF) is not considered to be an issue unless an attachment to the vessel is moving relative to the RPV, creating oscillating stresses (often the case with main coolant pumps). Another possibility is when thermal stresses are constantly changing due to mixing, as has been experienced in BWR feed-water nozzles. Also, thermal striping, again near the nozzles at the BWR safe ends, can result in potential high cycle fatigue (HCF). In general, HCF is not considered to be an issue for extended operation of RPV, as shown in EMDA vol. 3, sect.5 [44]: "For the RPV, fatigue is generally not considered to be a significant issue except for the replaceable closure flange studs and potentially in the nozzle regions where safety injection water is introduced into the RPV".

Low cycle fatigue may occur at high-stress intensity locations of the vessel nozzle region due to the general operating transients of the plant. But, the redesign of safe end/thermal sleeve configurations and feed-water spargers (for HCF), coupled with changes in operating procedures (for low cycle fatigue), have been effective to date, as no further occurrences of nozzle fatigue cracking have been reported for PWRs or BWRs.

The relationship between laboratory environmental fatigue testing and the actual operating conditions is the topic of an important and ongoing debate. Environmental fatigue effects measured in the laboratory have demonstrated that fatigue resistance in a water environment is lower than that in air. The relatively simple methods currently available for application of laboratory environmental effects appear to be overly conservative and do not address the complex, three dimensional geometries that occur in actual plant components and nonlinear, time-dependent stress loadings.

Plants currently address most environmental fatigue issues through stress-based monitoring and cycle counting, which can involve detailed reassessment of the cyclic loadings and associated stresses that are occurring at the nozzle connections. In other cases, refined stress analyses that more accurately reflect the actual stresses at the areas of concern have been performed. In most cases, fatigue issues can be resolved by using these approaches for current extended (60-year) operating life, as well as for an additional 20 years of operation.

Some multiple component locations could potentially exceed a calculated CUF of 1.0 when environmental effects are included. Thus, there is a need to develop an improved understanding of environmental fatigue effects, especially through modelling and testing of real components under realistic strain-rate loadings and in the proper plant chemistry ranges. One important aspect worth mentioning is related to the potential changes of the chemistry in the primary circuit. For example, there is an ongoing discussion whether potassium hydroxide (KOH) could be an alternative to lithium hydroxide (LiOH) for pH control in the primary system of PWRs. If this would be considered in the future, fatigue testing in this type of environment could become important. On this topic, H-P Seifert (PSI, Switzerland) considers that: "From a corrosion point of view, very little difference is expected for SCC and EAF between LiOH and KOH at the same pH at temperature. A few tests with spot check characters might be sufficient." [127]. For some RPV of VVER designs, there are welded joints with incomplete penetrations (e.g. weld of distribution ring to the austenitic cladding of the RPV itself, weld of austenitic cladding to the CRDM nozzle). These are potentially high-risk areas, as it is difficult to computationally assess fatigue development, and the required service life of 60+ years is currently not proven. To

In some countries with VVER reactors, national regulations require environmental fatigue assessment (e.g. NTD AME in Czechia). The austenitic steels used in VVER reactors are niobium stabilised grades that behave differently in contact with the primary environment than the typical unstabilised grades used in most PWR (except Siemens reactors that also used stabilised grades). Specific environmental fatigue curves and experimentally verified fatigue crack growth rates should be used to ensure safe LTO operation for 80 years with respect to EAF and flaw tolerance. A national programme has been initiated in Czechia to assess the environmental effects on the fatigue life of selected austenitic steels used for austenitic lining of VVER reactors and VVER internals steels with respect to the LTO 60+ requirements.

The standard surveillance programme for VVER RPV also contains low cycle fatigue (LCF) specimens. LCF testing is intended for determination of the LCF curve for the thermal aged and irradiated RPV materials followed by the RPV lifetime assessment using fatigue calculations. In the late 1980s early 1990s it was evidenced that LCF curve slightly increases due to irradiation and does not change due to thermal ageing. Therefore, after that, LCF testing has not been performed and LCF specimens are stored in the laboratories or remain in the reactor awaiting future implementation of new testing methods such as sub-sized, miniature, small punch, etc.

Fatigue calculations shows that fatigue is not a limiting factor for RPV lifetime over reasonable time periods, including LTO 60+.

### *4.2.2.6 Boric acid corrosion*

BAC itself is not an ageing mechanism as it leads to significant damage in the form of wastage only in case of leakage of primary PWR coolant onto low allow or carbon steel components. Therefore, it is important to avoid any primary coolant leakage and to ensure adequate monitoring to detect any leakage of boric acid containing coolant before it leads to significant damage. This general approach is independent of the age of the reactor, yet the likelihood of leakage may increase with age depending on the measures taken against other degradation mechanisms leading to leakage like SCC.

The rate of BAC wastage of the low alloy steel is dependent upon the temperature of the boric acid and the concentration of the boric acid. BAC due to leaking reactor coolant has resulted in wastage of the low alloy steels of the RPV flanges, top closure heads, and RPV studs at a rate of approximately 25 mm/year (MRP-308 [128]). Once a boric acid leak is detected, the wastage level of the given ferritic steel component must be determined. If the component's design thickness is marginal following detection of boric acid attack, an analytical evaluation is required to assess component's "fitness for service", but if the wasted component design thickness is violated, refurbishment by welding may be required (IAEA TECDOC-1 556, Section 6.6 [50]).

OPEX accumulated since 1999 has shown that PWSCC of Alloy 600 vessel penetrations, safe-ends and DMW and the associated BAC of low alloy vessel heads are safety significant ageing mechanisms, as well as economic concerns for Western design RPVs. A comprehensive description of the operational experience is presented in S.S. Hwang's article "Review of PWSCC and mitigation management strategies of Alloy 600 materials of PWRs" [129], concluding that:

• most Alloy 600 nozzles/penetrations and their welds are affected by the PWSCC;

- water chemistry measures are the zinc addition and optimised hydrogen operation;
- NDE techniques development is required to allow early detection of cracking and minimise Alloy 600 nozzles damage.

Following the Davis-Besse and Bugey incidents, EPRI conducted numerous experimental tests and performed PWR reactor vessel top and bottom head safety assessments to quantify the probability that unacceptable wastage affecting structural integrity would result, inspected interval and inspection sensitivity. Based on the experimental data, it was concluded that: "Current inspection requirements (N-729-2 for top heads, and N-722-1 for bottom heads) are still considered to be conservative and adequate to ensure nuclear safety for the BAC concern associated with PWSCC of top and bottom head nozzles" (EPRI MRP-308 [128]).

In 2018, EPRI Materials Degradation Matrix, rev. 4 [130], summarised the conclusions for RPV material susceptibility to BAC beyond 60 years of service: "Boric acid corrosion is relatively well understood. No additional R&D is needed at this time." However, if the AMP cannot control sufficiently BAC, nor modern surface machining and treatment techniques cannot ensure DMW long-term integrity, the ultimate solution is the replacement of RPV head and switching from Alloy 600 CRDM penetration nozzles to Alloy 690 (described later in Section 4.2.4 of this report).

Based on the experience from the current operation, contamination of the outer surface of the VVER RPV with the primary circuit medium due to leakage of the surrounding technology cannot be excluded. The outer surface of the VVER RPV (low alloy steel) is susceptible to corrosion by boric acid. The corrosion rate during exposure was experimentally measured. The necessary remedial measures to reduce surface degradation and to ensure the required service life were determined. These activities are being implemented as part of the AMP. No additional R&D is needed currently.

Based on the Ukrainian experience there have never been observed BAC on the RPV lower part. However, such degradation occurred very rarely for reactor studs and for the reactor upper head outer surface due to leakages through reactor upper head flanges of control rods, temperature and neutron monitoring.

### *4.2.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

ISI via NDE aiming at detecting and sizing potential indications in the core shell and the welded joints are performed by ultrasonic testing (UT). The entirety of the core shell of each RPV of the French fleet is inspected every 10 years using an automated ISI machine called MIS (25 mm depth of base metal under cladding are inspected). Similar machines are used in other countries, even if not used for underclad cracks.

### *4.2.3.1 Hydrogen flakes in Tihange 2 and Doel 3 RPV wall*

More information is available in MRP-367, Revision 1 [131] and MRP-431 [132].

### *4.2.3.2 Dissimilar metal welds diagnostics*

The type of inspection strategy used for Ni-Alloy 82/182 weld SCC strongly affects the reliability of tackling uncertainties of the depth sizing of axially oriented cracks. Consideration should be focused particularly on the choice of methods complementing the component weld structure and geometries (i.e. implementing inner diameter ultrasonic testing + eddy current testing [ECT]). The results of UT of Ni-Alloy A82/A182 welds for stress corrosion cracks include uncertainties regarding the actual depth of indication. There are significant uncertainties when comparing the result of the cracks depth before and after the repair (see IAEA TECDOC-1 852 Dissimilar Metal Weld Inspection, Monitoring and Repair Approaches, Section 4.4 [133]).

### *4.2.3.3 Current status of inspection and diagnostic methods*

ISI techniques (ultrasonic examination, UT) are well developed for RPVs. There are some accessibility issues for UT of some BWR RPV welds. The risk of incomplete UT coverage on these welds has been addressed by PFM analyses developed by industry (EPRI-BWRVIP [134] ) that have been accepted by the US NRC. EPRI-BWRVIP also published a report approved by an US NRC safety evaluation justifying reduced in-service examinations of BWR RPV nozzle to vessel inner radii [135].

For mechanical properties, the US industry is working on direct fracture mechanics methodologies to supplement or replace Charpy V-notch testing of specimens irradiated in materials surveillance programmes.

In Europe, research work to improve NDE system effectiveness for inspection of degraded materials through the NOMAD Project has been concluded, with the objective to develop, demonstrate and validate an NDE tool for the local and volumetric characterisation of the embrittlement in operational RPVs. The results from NOMAD delivered information complementary to the destructive tests of surveillance samples, which are currently assumed to represent the whole component and do not consider possible local material variations. For a list of publications see [www.nomad-horizon2020.eu](https://www.nomad-horizon2020.eu/)[14](#page-84-0).

In Ukraine, typically one RPV every four years is subjected to a periodical ISI, which includes: visual control, liquid penetrant inspection, magnetic particle inspection, ultrasonic inspection and eddy current inspection (depending on importance of controlling zone). At that, beltline core welds are subjected to ultrasonic inspection in 100% of their volumes and cladding on beltline welds and cladding on reactor coolant nozzle region are subjected to eddy-current inspection in 100% of their volumes as well.

### *4.2.3.4 Extension of RPV ISI interval from 10 to 20 Years*

The PWROG developed a technical basis report, WCAP-16 168-NP-A, Revision 3 [136], that justifies an extension of the ISI requirements for the RPV in ASME Code, Section XI, Categories B-A (closure head, reactor vessel welds) and B-D welds (inlet/ outlet nozzles to-vessel welds) from the standard ten-year inspection interval to 20 years. Most of the US PWRs have implemented these alternate requirements via approved licence amendment requests to the US NRC. As an example, Exelon submitted a licence amendment request [137] which was followed subsequently by a US NRC safety evaluation report (SER) [138]. The analysis requires assessment of past ISI results, calculation of through wall cracking frequency, and commitments for future ISI inspection dates.

<span id="page-84-0"></span><sup>14</sup> NOMAD (n.d.), Non-destructive Evaluation (NDE) System for the Inspection of Operation-Induced Material Degradation in Nuclear Power Plants, [www.nomad-horizon2020.eu.](https://www.nomad-horizon2020.eu/)

### *4.2.4. Repair, refurbishment, mitigation and replacement solutions*

### *4.2.4.1 Attenuation of embrittlement and PTS loading*

RPV lower part is considered not to be replaceable: This makes RPV a major determinant of the lifetime of nuclear power plants.

There are different methods to reduce neutron flux onto the RPV wall by special shielding fuel assemblies. These are used in many reactors, especially those of older vintage and those foreseen for LTO. These methods are:

- low leakage fuel management placing fuel assemblies with high burnup at the periphery of the core (low neutron flux);
- introduction of fuel assemblies at the periphery with some or all rods filled with fuel of lower enrichment or solid rods made of steel or rods filled with absorber material.

Depending on what part of the RPV needs shielding (base metal or weld) there are different configurations to consider. So, all these special rods may contain the shielding material at their full length or only part of their length. These special shielding fuel assemblies may be placed only at the hot spots of the vessel (main axis (at 0°) or at 45° depending on the core configuration) or all around the core, see e.g. [139], [140]. The situation in some countries is described in more detail below.

A mitigation strategy is applied in France to reduce the irradiation damage of the RPV shell, such as:

- low leakage fuel management (low neutron flux);
- progressive introduction of Hafnium rod absorbers, starting from the oldest nuclear power plants (900 MWe). The hafnium rods are positioned on the periphery of the core facing the areas of the vessel most exposed to neutron fluence.

For a few RPVs, the mitigation could be complemented by a decrease of the thermal stresses in case of safety injection thanks to a continuous heating of pressure and temperature relief tank water, which enables to increase the margin to fast fracture study.

As reported in the national assessment report (NAR) of Finland, Section 5.1.4 [141], to mitigate

> the most important degradation mechanism of Loviisa RPVs – the irradiation embrittlement of the RPV core area and its weld - progressing much faster than expected, immediate design modifications of the active core had to be implemented in the early years of operation, such as:

- Core reduction by replacing the outmost fuel elements with dummy fuel elements of stainless steel (SS), flux reduction 83%;
- Introducing a new fuel loading pattern to achieve a low leakage core design, flux reduction 18%.

Besides core design modifications for normal operation, the following actions and plant modifications have been implemented to reduce the risk of brittle fracture of the RPV during accident or transient conditions:

- Temperature increase of emergency core cooling water;
- Decrease of head and flow rate of high-pressure injection pumps;

- Introduction of a signal from high primary system pressure to stop the high pressure pumps;
- Modification of protection signals associated with occurrence of potential steam line break;
- Thermal annealing of Loviisa 1 RPV core area weld".

In Sweden, at Ringhals 3 and 4, several modifications of shielding assemblies were introduced, containing three rows of stainless-steel rods at the outermost periphery of the core and low enriched fuel in the other rods or even shielding assemblies with different axial zoning. In the axially bottom part, where the weld is located, the shielding assemblies have a zone where all rods are SS rods, instead of fuel rods, while in the axially upper part the rods contain low enriched fuel [139].

Low leakage core configuration is standard in Switzerland and was introduced in the 1980s. The usage of shielding rod assemblies is an option, which is currently under evaluation to further support LTO beyond 60 years. Another alternative to reduce the flux could be the installation of shielding between core and RPV wall. An example was the Korean reactor KORI-1 which used Tantalum pads. Both methods seem to be combinable. The sooner such shielding is implemented, the greater its effectiveness.

Temperature increase of emergency core cooling water is also applied in one instance in Switzerland.

### *4.2.4.2 Annealing – experience from VVER*

Neutron irradiation embrittlement can also be mitigated by thermal annealing of the reactor vessel.

Annealing of 15 VVER-440 RPVs in Armenia, Bulgaria, Finland, the Slovak Republic, the Russian Federation and Ukraine was carried out successfully. There are seven VVER-440 RPVs still in operation after annealing, with plans to close another one in the next few years.

Annealing is a historically well mastered technology for VVER-440 RPVs with proven performance, and the regeneration of material properties will typically allow for a service life extension of 15 to 30 years, depending on the current condition of the vessel material and the method of operation. The base and weld metal of these vessels do not contain nickel as an alloying element and the annealing is carried out for 100 h at nominally 475°C [77], [79].

The OPEX in recovery of VVER-1 000 reactor vessel core welds and base metal mechanical properties by thermal annealing consists of the pilot recovery annealing of Unit 1 of the Balakovo plant, carried out in 2018 with a similar technology as previously applied to VVER-440 reactor vessels, but only for core welds (IGALL AMP 162 PWR Reactor Pressure Vessel [142]). The base and weld metal of VVER-1 000 vessels contain nickel as an alloying element; the core weld of the RPV of Balakovo-1 even has a very high nickel content leading to different irradiation embrittlement mechanisms compared to VVER 440 materials. The annealing temperature was chosen to be 565±15 C to recover the embrittlement [143].

Finland's experience regarding the original surveillance programme and the new surveillance programme for Loviisa 1 RPV after the heat treatment are detailed in the NAR, section 5.1.3 [141], issued by the national regulatory authority STUK. The report shows that:

"After the heat treatment of the core weld seam in 1996, new surveillance specimens were installed in the Loviisa 1 RPV (VVER-440). This surveillance programme is limited only to monitoring the weld material. The programme consists of two thermal annealing and three irradiation cycles. The length of irradiation cycles equals to three operating cycles, and the entire programme lasts 9 years. The material for the programme has been acquired from the RPV manufacturer and is representative for Loviisa 1 core area weld. Based on the results of the new surveillance programme it has been demonstrated that "the margin to brittle facture of RPV weld 4 can be considered acceptable even after 50 years of operation".

However, embrittlement mechanisms in Western and Russian-type RPV steels are somewhat different, because the main factor in the former steels is copper (US NRC Reg. Guide 1.99 Revision 2 [62]), while it is phosphorus in the VVER-440 steels (Russian Standard PNAE G-7-002-86)." And if for VVER-440 there is consistent OPEX on the topic, as mentioned in EMDA vol. 3, Section 6.4 'Thermal annealing and irradiation [44]', a fair amount of data exists for annealing of US nuclear power plants RPV steels, but not for re-irradiation.

Details on the techniques of thermal annealing process (wet and dry) are described in IAEA NP-T-3.11, Section 5.8.1 [78] and general guidance for in-service annealing may be found in ASTM Standard E509-86, Edition 2021 [144], which contains general procedures for conducting an in-service thermal anneal of a reactor vessel to demonstrate the effectiveness and degree of recovery, providing also direction for a post-anneal vessel radiation surveillance programme. It should be assessed, though, if the latest guidelines are comprehensive enough for the complete characterisation of the annealed microstructural changes for the safe operation beyond 60 years of annealed RPV.

### *4.2.4.3 PWR SCC mitigation and repair strategies for RPV penetration nozzles*

According to the paper "Review of PWSCC and mitigation management strategies of Alloy 600 materials of PWRs" [129], the recommended strategy to manage PWSCC of Alloy 600 RPV CRDM penetration nozzles is summarised in Figure 4.7.

<span id="page-88-0"></span>**Figure 4.7. Management strategies for PWSCC of Alloy 600 penetration nozzle**

Source: Journal of Nuclear Materials [129]

There might be an issue with nickel alloy welds in bottom penetrations or inlet nozzles which might be remedially repaired if leakage occurs. Outlet nozzles have been repaired and the whole circumference has been replaced by weld inlay as a contingency.

Significant effort is required also for the preparation, approval and implementation of a DMW repair and a well–designed repair plan is crucial for the success of implementing a weld repair to mitigate SCCs. At the very least, a DMW repair plan should include (as referred to in IAEA TECDOC-1 852 [133], Section 4.4):

- designing the weld repair;
- reviewing the codes, standards and regulatory requirements;
- selecting the process for repair/mitigation (welding or not welding process);
- performing a safety analysis;
- following the design change process;
- revising documents (procedure, drawings, ISI programme and others); and
- developing the welding process and execution.

The most important lessons learnt, and recommendations obtained from several international studies on DMW, with different NDE techniques and procedures, show that:

• defect orientation has an influence on detection performance (circumferential defect show a greater likelihood of detection than axial defect, as function of depth);

- defect orientation does not influence depth sizing performance based on depth sizing by root mean square error (RMSE) results for large bore and small bore nozzles;
- procedures that include ECT performed better at length sizing than procedures that do not include ECT, particularly for axial defect;
- phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) performance is better than conventional UT performance for small bore nozzles as measured by probability of detection (POD) and depth sizing by RMSE;
- PAUT performance is marginally better than UT performance for large bore nozzles as measured by POD and depth sizing by RMSE;
- mitigation might have influence to cost due to longer inspection interval.

### *4.2.4.4 BWR SCC (IASCC, IGSCC) attenuation methods*

The mitigation methods available for SCC attenuation in BWR reactors are presented in detail in IAEA-TECDOC-1 470 BWR pressure vessels, Chapter 7 [51] and IAEA-NP-T- 3.13, Chapter (Please add this a new reference), for example:

- via water chemistry control:
  - ‒ coolant chemistry control;
  - ‒ noble metal chemical application (NMCA) and hydrogen water chemistry;
  - ‒ deposition of noble metals by plasma spray and hydrogen water chemistry;
- via surface treatment:
  - ‒ shot peening/water jet peening/ laser peening (already applied underwater remotely to core shrouds in Japan);
- via heat treatment solution annealing of Type 304 stainless steel, which is a wellestablished method for eliminating sensitisation, thereby reducing SCC susceptibility;
- via mechanical stress improvement process (MSIP) on RPV nozzles [145];
- via weld overlay on RPV nozzles [145].

The qualification requirements for stress improvement processes, including peening, do vary greatly on existing code rules and regulatory environment (IAEA-TECDOC-1 852 [133], Section 4.1.7).

### *4.2.4.5 Weldability of Irradiated Materials*

Weld repair techniques are not qualified for RPV LAS with fluence greater than 1x1017 n/cm2 . However, this is a low priority issue because it is unlikely that weld repair of RPV LAS would be needed due to little in-service degradation. Most detected flaws have been non-surface breaking and can be accepted for continued service by analysis.

### *4.2.4.6 Experience with RPV head replacement*

According to France's national assessment report (NAR) on topical peer review (TPR) for ageing, Section 5.4.1.7 [146] "The discovery of PWSCC on an RPV closure head adapter of the Bugey reactor No. 3 in 1991 was the first instance of a leakage caused by PWSCC in the world. The longitudinal cracks were propagated from inside the penetration and leakages have also been found by visual inspection in the reactor vessel heads in reactors in Japan and the United States. Some leakages were produced from the crack in the J-weld which propagated to the outer surface of the head penetration. The cracks were caused by PWSCC with high residual stress by the J-weld".

In 1994, the decision was made in France to replace all vessel heads of 900 MW(e) and 1 300 MW(e) units with closure heads equipped with adapters made from nickel alloy 600. The replacement closure heads are equipped with adapters made from nickel alloy 690. Subsequently, replacement of vessel heads started in Japan and the United States. More details about the strategies for PWRs reactor vessel head replacement (RVHR) can be found in IAEA NP-T3.2, Section 5 and Appendix 2 for a list of RVHRs [147]. As the list of RVHR from the origin 1993 until 2005 is quite long, there are numerous lessons learnt and improved strategies that emerged over the time.

Framatome has developed a technology, "Framatome's Integrated Head Assembly (IHA)", that replaces existing components above the reactor vessel closure head and enables the entire component to be removed during a refuelling outage in fewer steps. The IHA is customised to serve the unique requirements of each plant in the United States and internationally — Combustion Engineering, Westinghouse and B&W designs.

A typical IHA can reduce polar crane use by a factor of ten. The design replaces the existing components above the reactor vessel closure head (RVCH) to enable the entire RVCH to be removed during a refuelling outage, in fewer steps than the current design requires. Thus, it reduces critical path time, maintenance costs and manpower by combining the RVCH and most of its supporting systems into a single removable unit. The IHA's main features enable RVHR to be completed in 26 days, during refuelling outage: www.framatome.com/solutions-portfolio/docs/default-source/default-documentlibrary/product-sheets/a0146-p-us-g-en-232-06-20 iha.pdf?Status=Master&sfvrsn=421d133d\_2[.15](#page-90-0)

### *4.2.4.7 Swiss experience with replacement of RPV heads and repair of nozzle welds*

In the BWR Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant, fifteen RPV feedwater nozzle welds DMW have been recently enhanced by MSIP. One weld DMW on a feedwater nozzle with an indication was repaired by applying full structural weld overlay repair (FSWOL).

For the CRDM and in-core monitoring housing penetrations, a roll repair method was prepared by Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant for the case of potential leakages in the seal welds.

In the PWRs of Beznau Nuclear Power Plant, the RPV closure heads were successfully replaced in 2015. This eliminated SCC susceptible nickel base alloys 600 or 182/82. Further, it excludes the occurrence of the CRDM thermal sleeve wear issue, observed at some French and Westinghouse type reactors, especially with a so-called "T-cold" design. The Beznau replacement heads use a design without thermal sleeves.

### *4.2.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

Since the RPV is the key component in terms of safety and extended plant life, and is considered irreplaceable, its structural integrity must be demonstrated without compromise.

As of October 2022, the state of the art of research in relation with RPV capability for LTO beyond 60 years was summarised for each specific type of reactor in the EPRI IMT, considered the baseline for the status report.

For PWRs, there are 61 open R&D gaps identified in PWR IMT EPRI Report 3 002 018 255 (MRP-205, Rev. 4) [89] compared to 73 open corresponding technical gaps in the previous version of the IMT, and some priorities were adjusted as a result of changed industry perspectives. An additional nine new gaps were identified based on OPEX and related to the need to incorporate previously out-of-range-effects that are now recognised to be feasible due to extreme seismic events.

The majority of the high priority gaps are assessment gaps (e.g. assessment of environmental effects on fatigue resistance, PWSCC characterisation, thermal and irradiation combined effects, IASCC characterisation, flow induced vibration and wear) with a significantly lower number of inspection and examination gaps (e.g. NDE for CASS material), and fewer mitigation and repair and replacement gaps.

For BWRs the key remaining gaps include the assessment of SCC crack growth, management of highly irradiated components, and effective implementation of waterchemistry-based SCC mitigation technologies. Although there are some open RPV integrity-related regulatory issues, the remaining ageing management commitments that must be fulfilled (e.g. BWR ISP capsule testing and evaluation) and opportunities for further optimisation of RPV integrity management methods, the latest IMT results for BWRs do not include any key active/open technical R&D gaps related to RPV integrity (BWR IMT EPRI Report 3 002 018 319 BWRVIP-167 [48]).

For VVERs, the key findings in VVER IMT EPRI Report 3 002 021 033 (MRP-471) [49] include 37 open R&D gaps identified based on comparison with the gaps identified in the PWR IMT (MRP-205, Rev. 4 [89]). The majority of the high priority gaps are assessment gaps (e.g. reactor AMP during LTO period, IASCC characterisation, void swelling of SSs, fluence impact on SS mechanical properties, environmental effects on fatigue resistance) with a significantly lower number of inspection and examination gaps, which is like the PWR IMT results. Overall, the distribution of R&D gaps for VVERs reflects the perspective that mechanisms of degradation in VVERs are relatively well understood. The key remaining gaps relate to the ability to evaluate the extend of degradation and to predict the ability to continue operations without extraordinary actions which are the subject of ongoing research.

### *4.2.5.1 Open technical issues and conclusions*

As of November 2024, EPRI has not identified any significant gaps or challenges that would preclude a US or international PWR from operating to 60 or 80 years of total operation from an RPV integrity standpoint based on EPRI assessments performed consistent with US licence renewal methodologies and standards. Existing R&D, mandatory regulatory documents and related ageing management guidance is adequate to address LTO.

The US NRC has not identified any gaps related to ageing management of RPVs that generically preclude renewing plant operating licences for 60-80 years of operation. The US NRC sees a need for confirmatory research in:

- a. This issue is mitigated by gathering RPV surveillance data to adjust predictions of embrittlement made using the current US NRC guidance in RG 1.99, Rev. 2 [62]. The proposed US NRC rulemaking, if approved, would ensure more timely withdrawal and testing of surveillance capsules to ensure the necessary RPV embrittlement data is available in a timely manner to support 80 calendar years of operation. Due to the existing material surveillance programmes, this issue is not considered to impact safer operation of plants. This issue is expected to apply to only a few highfluence PWRs, since most plants will not reach fluences of 6x1019 n/cm2 or greater, particularly at the 1/4T location that is used in the calculation of P-T limits.
- b. If the plan for removing the full-size compact tension (CT) surveillance specimens cannot be adapted to cover the maximum fluence of the RPV during the operational lifetime is not an option (i.e. not enough specimens available in the reactor), the use of miniaturised CT specimens should be enforced. The miniaturised CT specimens can be reconstituted from subsized specimen machined from tested specimens should be re-introduced for continued irradiation. The preferred size of broken Charpy specimens should be (e.g. 0.16T or 0.18T-CT) to allow machining.
- c. Or, if the expected remaining lifetime and the lead factor does allow it, new specimens from RPV archive material could be an alternative. After withdrawal of all the surveillance capsules, continued dosimetry of the RPV must be assured. In any of the above cases, a systematic use of the master curve methodology is recommended.
- d. Also, generation of low-flux high fluence data relevant for European Integrated surveillance programmes should be established in Europe, similar to EPRI Co-ordinated Reactor Vessel Surveillance Programme (CRVSP) (MRP-326/rev.1) [69], PWR Supplemental Surveillance Programme (PSSP) Capsule Fabrication Report (MRP-412) [70] in the United States.
- 2. Use of methodologies that could reduce over-conservatism in evaluating RPV FT is a common goal both for North American and European power plants facing LTO beyond 60 years, such as:
  - a. Approval of direct FT-based methodologies to supplement or replace Charpy-V notch (CVN) based approaches.
  - b. The direct usage of master curve data for establishing an T0 based embrittlement trend curve and as alternative to the ASME KIc-Curve, which seems to be a reasonable option. The latter has already been implemented as an ASME code case (N-830), while the former is still in progress.
  - c. Approval to consider the Warm Pre-Stress (WPS) effect. In several investigations it was shown that the FT at low temperature is increased by a previous high loading ("pre-stress") of a crack at higher temperature, i.e. in the ductile regime. The amount of toughness increase depends on the load path. The inclusion of the WPS effect in RPV assessments can reduce over-conservatism and enable more accurate evaluations of the

safety margins against limiting conditions, which may occur at PTS events [94].

- 3. To secure the LTO beyond 60 years for French reactors, in addition to the mitigation strategy on nuclear power plant management presented in Subsection 4.3.4 (involving three physical levers), several methodological levers are under development or evaluation to reduce the conservatism of the fast fracture analysis:
  - a. Toughness evaluation using the internationally used master curve method, which allows the determination of a toughness indexing parameter (T0) from a limited number of toughness tests (with specimens from the PVISP) and the derivation of a toughness curve as a function of temperature, as an average curve or as the desired fractile (e.g. the 5% fractile with statistically 5% of the data below this curve), instead of the current RTNDT approach;
  - b. Local approach of fracture using Beremin model, which is based on stress instead of K. It can represent loading history, local plasticity effects at crack tips (constraint effects, such as the in case of small defects) and scale effects;
  - c. Approval of consideration of the WPS effect (see Section 4.2.5.1). The inclusion of the WPS effect in RPV assessments can reduce conservatism and enable more accurate evaluations of the safety margins against limiting conditions, which may occur at PTS events [94];
  - d. Other methodological levers that are to be investigated in the longer term, such as:
    - o Two parameters approach of fracture mechanics (J, Q). This global approach is another way to represent the effects of local plasticity at the crack tip;
    - o PFM approach;
    - o Crack arrest phenomenon and associated criterion.
- 4. Re-irradiation behaviour of post-irradiation annealed RPV steels to use RPV annealing as a mitigation strategy for LTO beyond 60 years for certain RPVs that experience high embrittlement (e.g. RPVs with high Ni and Mn).

Thermal annealing, successfully performed for numerous VVER reactors, has never been applied for western type reactors. But in the past, there was a Code Case, N-557-1, "In-Place Dry Annealing of a PWR Nuclear Reactor Vessel", available. The applicability was limited up to the 1995 edition and it was never endorsed by the US NRC. The Code Case has been annulled on 05/13/2020, with the expectation, that the Code Case will never be applied. But due to the changed economic conditions, a re-evaluation of this Code Case could be an option.

In fact, annealing is already considered a possible option for some VVER-1 000 reactors by including additional surveillance samples. It should be noted that annealing technology has been well employed previously for VVER-440 reactor vessels but has yet to be applied for VVER-1 000 reactors on a commercial basis. To achieve this, further research is needed on the effectiveness of annealing and re-irradiation of post-irradiation annealed RPV steels. The technical readiness level of this technology should be increased to be able to apply this in practice for VVER-1 000 reactors.

5. Extension of the existing surveillance specimens' programme for VVER. For a VVER RPV, where the assessment of resistance to fast fracture due to temperature and neutron embrittlement is performed according to VERLIFE procedures [148] or national codes and regulations based on this procedure, it is necessary to extend existing surveillance specimen programmes. According to VERLIFE procedures [148] it is possible to extrapolate experimental embrittlement curves by about 10% relative to the experimentally attained fluence value. As the neutron irradiation spectrum of surveillance specimens should correspond to the neutron irradiation spectrum during operation and because the lead factor should not be too high to avoid any flux effect, the opportunities to accomplish this task are limited. It is suitable to use reconstitution technology for manufacturing of the specimen, to use material harvested from decommissioned RPVs, and where necessary, to use replacement material. Extension of the current surveillance programmes should be carried out as soon as possible, including monitoring of the fluence of the RPV material.

Due to the lack of remaining surveillance specimens for RPV LTO 60+ justification of the sub-sized and miniature specimen testing methods (such as CT0.16T) needs to be developed. These specimens or even two full-size specimens can be produced from broken halves of the tested SS and put to reactor for reirradiation.

5. Effect of thermal ageing on long-term irradiated RPV materials (Ni low alloy steels) and DMW.

Out of the possible ageing degradation mechanisms considered for DMW, thermal ageing and its effect of embrittlement, due to loss of FT, still needs to be understood and addressed. Short-range and long-range ordering that results in hardening, localisation of plastic deformation and build-up of internal stresses due to lattice contraction in case of constraints, increasing SCC susceptibility and decreasing fracture resistance during LTO, should be investigated.

6. Improving a non-destructive methodology to reliably identify SCC in DMWs.

A non-destructive methodology to reliably identify weld repair spots would be desirable. Such repair spots at the inner surface often act as a starting point and cause of SCC because of their disadvantageous residual stress profiles. While in general, weld repairs at the RPV should have been documented, they sometimes were not, at older reactors.

The reliable detection of SCC cracks in DMW is still challenging. The interpretation of the UT results should be assisted by artificial intelligence (AI) or ML technology.

7. FT and strength data of RPV materials after long-time exposure to operating temperatures.

Irradiation embrittlement and high nickel and manganese levels in welds cause a large transition temperature shift. Mitigating actions might be to use shield fuel assemblies at the core periphery as early as possible during the lifetime of the RPV, or to anneal the weld.

This is a general comment regarding shielding of the belt line region as well as the extended beltline region. The surveillance specimens are subjected to a certain flux; if the parts of the RPV that experience a high fluence have a low flux that differs significantly from the surveillance specimens, this might be a concern. The socalled lead factor can reach up to 30-50. It is commonly known that flux is a factor in the materials' response to irradiation. This area is of concern and must be further investigated.

8. Fatigue evaluation of welds with incomplete penetration (in VVERs) based on cyclic stress - strain curves of the RPV materials.

The usual fatigue life assessment method (linear elastic) is difficult to apply, and the other approach (elastic plastic) is more suitable. To ensure the required service life with respect to fatigue damage, it is necessary to experimentally determine the cyclic stress - strain curves of the RPV materials concerned and to recalculate the fatigue life assessment based on the information obtained.

### <span id="page-95-0"></span>**4.3. Reactor pressure vessel internals**

### *4.3.1. Description of RPVIs*

### **PWR**

The RPVIs consist of two structural assembly groupings: the "upper" consisting of all the internals' components above the core and "lower" internals (the remaining internals) assemblies. The fuel assemblies rest on the lower support structure of the lower internals assembly which transmits the resulting loads to the core barrel and to the core barrel flange, which rests on the RPV flange. The upper internals assembly is attached under the RPV head flange.

The vendor's designation of RVIs subcomponents is not necessarily the same for all PWR nuclear steam supply systems. The upper internals assembly is removed during each refuelling operation. The lower internals assembly is only removed during the RPV ISI period (in most cases each ten years). The core barrel provides a boundary for the reactor coolant. The primary coolant enters the reactor vessel via the inlet nozzles; impinges on the side of the core barrel and is directed downward through the annulus formed by the gap between the outside diameter of the core barrel and the inside diameter of the RPV. The primary coolant flow then enters the lower plenum between the bottom of the lower support plate and the RPV bottom head and is redirected upward through the core. After passing through the core, the coolant enters the upper core support region and then proceeds radially outward through the RPV outlet nozzles.

### **Typical PWR RPVIs – Westinghouse design**

Figure 4.8 shows the structural assembly grouping of a PWR RPVIs system which is the same for Westinghouse, Combustion Engineering, Babcock & Wilcox, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd. and Framatome. Siemens/KWU used a similar design at earlier plants, except that there was no instrumentation, mounted from the bottom of the RPV.

### **VVER RPVIs**

As mentioned in IAEA TECDOC-1 557, Section 2.2 [149]:

"Hot and cold leg RPV nozzles are located in VVER reactors at two different elevations; therefore, a horizontal distribution ring separates the cold and hot legs. After passing through the core, the hot coolant enters the hot leg nozzles through a perforated part in the top section of the core barrel.

The core barrel and its support structure (the core barrel bottom for VVER-440 and support tubes and distance grid for VVER-1 000) are important to safety because their primary functions are to confine, fix and support the shroud (basket) and provide a passageway for the reactor coolant flow. They direct the reactor coolant flow to the core, and after leaving the core, to the outlet nozzles. In addition, the VVER-1 000 core barrel support structure provides proper horizontal and vertical positioning of the fuel assembly and supports the core.

The core barrel keys are important to safety because they restrain large transverse motions of the core barrel while allowing unrestricted radial and axial thermal expansions."

The main components of the VVER RPVIs are the core barrel, the core baffle (core basket for VVER-440) at the level of the core and the block of guide tubes. These components are fixed together and to the reactor vessel in a way that allows their withdrawal, inspection, and partial repair as well as inspection of the RPV inner surface.

A detailed description of the design and the chemical composition of RPVIs base and bolting materials used in VVER-440 and VVER-1 000 RPVIs is presented in IAEA TECDOC-1 557: PWR Pressure Vessel Internals, Section 2.2 VVER type RPVIs [149].

### **BWR RPVIs**

BWR RPVIs were mainly designed and manufactured by ABB (now Westinghouse Atom AB), GE Nuclear Energy (now GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy.), Hitachi Ltd., Siemens/KWU (now Framatome) and Toshiba Co. Siemens/KWU BWRs and ABB BWR, with external recirculation pumps, are no longer in operation and are not described further.

The functions of the RPVIs may be divided into safety and non-safety functions. The safety functions are to support the core under all loading conditions, maintain a coolable geometry, ensure control rod insertion times, ensure reactivity control, direct and contain emergency cooling flows, ensure the availability of monitoring instruments and allow recovery to safe shutdown conditions. The added non-safety functions are to channel the incoming feedwater flow to the fuel, separate the water and steam, providing dry steam to the turbine and recirculating the saturated water after mixing it with the feedwater and providing support for operational instrumentation and surveillance sample holders.

GE Hitachi BWRs are the most common in operation and range from BWR/1 through BWR/6 series. RPVIs for no jet pump and jet pump plants and their general relationship to the RPV are illustrated in Figure 4.10 [53].

### *4.3.2. Physical ageing of RPVIs*

For PWR reactors, all the structures are made in SS (304 or 316 cold worked). The structures are potentially subject to high vibrations. Therefore, components must be screwed or welded and are subject to high temperatures (nearly 350°C – gamma heat) and high irradiations (some components are very close to the fuel assemblies).

Some of the BWR RPVIs, such as top guide, core shroud and core plate including the fuels supports, are located close to the active core and are therefore exposed to high neutron fluxes, which lead to high neutron fluences (E> 1 MeV) with increasing operating time, for example, > 1021 n/cm2 for 40 years of operation.

BWR internals, core shrouds, as well as other internals components fabricated from austenitic stainless steels have experienced significant levels of environmentally-induced cracking, while little cracking has been observed to date in PWR environments and mostly in bolting. Unlike the experience with BWR core shrouds and other components, environmentally-induced cracking has been very limited in PWR austenitic stainless steel components. This is due to the differences in reactor coolant chemistry between BWR and PWR designs (oxidising versus reducing conditions).

### *4.3.2.1 Inter-granular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC)*

SCC is the term given to crack initiation and subcritical crack growth of susceptible alloys under the influence of temperature, tensile stress and a "chemical" environment. There are two forms of SCC, which can proceed through a material in either of two modes: intergranular (along the grain boundaries) or trans-granular (through the grains).

IGSCC is a cracking phenomenon which develops along the grain boundaries. It occurs in austenitic stainless steel (such as 304 SS), under synergistic effects of three factors:

- 1. a susceptible material caused by e.g. sensitisation, cold work, irradiation;
- 2. tensile stress, for instance residual stress near welds;
- 3. environmental conditions, such as BWR NWC, that is high-purity water at ~280°C containing dissolved oxygen.

The statistics show that most SCC events occurred in very high numbers in SSs in BWR major components (not only in RPVIs), and were related to IGSCC, compared with major components of other reactor types (PWR, VVER, PHWR/CANDU).

The most critical locations for IGSCC for BWR reactor internals, based on the assessment of the extensive OPEX gathered within NEA SCAP database, are core shroud welds, and RPVI-pipe welds, as documented in the NEA Technical Basis for commendable practices on ageing management SCC and Cable Ageing Project (SCAP) final report, Table 2.2.5-1 [150]:

<span id="page-101-0"></span>

**Table 4.1. SCC events for BWR RPVIs** 

Source: SCAP database [150]

In addition to sensitisation, cold work operations such as bending, cutting, forming, rolling, and especially grinding, without subsequent solution anneal, can cause austenitic stainless steel to become susceptible to SCC in LWR environments. IGSCC susceptibility is also affected by other parameters such as corrosion potential (CP), water purity, stress, temperature, hydrogen, etc. (e.g. NUREG/CR-6 923 [151], NUREG/CR-7153, Vol. 2 [43], Ehrnstén paper: "Corrosion and Stress Corrosion Cracking of Austenitic Stainless Steels" [152] and R. J. M. Konings, T. R. Allen, R. E. Stoller, & S. Yamanaka article in *Comprehensive Nuclear Materials*, Vol. 5 [153]).

As shown in the reviews cited above, IGSCC has been observed in BWR components made of Type 304/304L austenitic stainless steel, nickel-based alloys 600 and X-750, as well as 182 weld metal. When SCC initiates in material with a cold-worked surface layer, subsequent crack propagation in the annealed material beyond the cold-worked region can be slower [154]. A solution of anneal heat treatment after fabrication significantly reduces SCC concerns for components with cold-worked regions, but such a step in the fabrication is not always practical or possible to introduce. Further details can be found in IAEA TECDOC-1 557 PWR Pressure Vessel Internals, Section 5.3.2.1 [149].

Detailed examples of recommended practices for IGSCC, IASCC, external chloride stress corrosion cracking (ECSCC) of SS or Ni-based alloys in Japan PWR and BWR plants are presented in NEA SCAP final report Appendix 1, Table A-1 to Table A-5 [150], all applicable for LTO beyond 60 years.

### **Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) of upper core barrel**

SCC of an upper core barrel girth weld was detected in a US PWR in 2022 [155]. This cracking was unexpected due to the low amount of irradiation exposure to this weld, since SCC of austenitic stainless steels is generally prevented by PWR water chemistry control. EPRI-MRP issued interim guidance in 2023 for inspections of this type of weld in PWRs (MRP-227 NEI 03-08 4 "Needed" Interim Guidance for WEC/CE Core Barrel Inspections, ADAMS Accession No. ML23 290A020, May 19, 2023) [156].

This recent OPEX event raises questions about SCC susceptibility of PWR internals, in regions without significant neutron fluence.

At present there are concerns in Swedish nuclear power plants regarding SS behaviour in the belt-line region: the prediction curves for irradiation degradation of material properties in both base and weld metals for LTO. This uncertainty might affect the outcome of a structural verification of the core barrel for extended LTO beyond 60 years.

### *4.3.2.2 Irradiation-assisted stress corrosion cracking (IASCC)*

The RPVIs of today's nuclear reactors are mainly made of austenitic stainless steels and nickel-based alloys exposed to oxygenated to hydrogenated water environments at ~270 to 340°C. The core of a nuclear reactor is an extreme environment consisting of high temperature water, imposed stresses and strains and an intense radiation field that affects the water chemistry, stress and microstructure of the core materials. IASCC has occurred in all water-cooled reactors.

Stress corrosion cracking, whether assisted by irradiation (SCC when the effect of irradiation is negligible and IASCC when it is significant), results from the simultaneous effect of mechanical loadings, temperature, and water chemistry, with or without the effect of irradiation.

RPVIs typically affected by SCC are baffle bolts and plates, the core shroud, its supports, the core spray lines and the jet pump riser pipes.

When components are exposed to high neutron fluence, they can become susceptible to IASCC, which is a type of SCC. IASCC, like IGSCC, is characterised by intergranular crack initiation and propagation. The IASCC mechanism concerns austenitic Cr-Ni steels and Ni-based alloys exposed to high neutron flux density during plant operation. As nuclear power plants are in operation for longer periods with more components or larger portions of components have accumulated an increased fluence, susceptibility of components to occurrence of IASCC can be expected. The summary of operational prerequisites for PWR and BWR water chemistry listed in Table 4.2 demonstrates that IASCC is not confined to a particular reactor design, material, component or water chemistry. On the other hand, IASCC cracking has so far been observed more frequently in BWRs than in PWRs, despite the higher dose rates and doses in PWR internals [127]. Historically, this is likely due to the high electrochemical potentials (ECPs) in BWRs under oxidising NWC conditions with fast unirradiated SCC rates and the high number of inspections performed to detect SCC in BWR internals.

PWR internals have high neutron exposure, reaching >75 dpa over an 80-year life in the regions with the highest exposure, such as baffle plates and baffle-former bolts. This creates a potential susceptibility to IASCC, which is currently managed by industry-developed programs such as MRP-227, Rev. 1-A [158]. Cracking of numerous baffle-former bolts (BFB) in Westinghouse-designed PWRs was discovered in 2016. Since that time, several US licensees have conducted extensive inspection and repair campaigns to mitigate BFB cracking. The US industry published guidance [159] [160] which has been assessed and accepted by the US NRC.

The US NRC staff's assessment [161] also provides an excellent summary of the issue:

- The EPRI-MRP has since incorporated the interim guidance in its PWR Internals Inspection and Evaluation Guidelines (MRP-227, Rev. 1-A) [162]. Analytical and predictive analyses have also been used to justify continued operation. The US NRC considers the BFB cracking issue to be generally well managed by inspection, replacements, and analysis conducted by the industry. Therefore, BFB cracking is a minor technical concern going forward.
- IASCC crack growth rates for SS PWR internals exposed to high neutron exposure show that, for neutron exposures greater than 20 dpa, they are somewhat limited. US NRC reviewed a proposed ASME Code Case on IASCC crack growth rates (CGR), which has since been published by ASME as Code Case N-889. The US NRC approved this code case conditionally in RG 1.147 [113] with the condition that the IASCC crack growth rates are not approved for neutron doses > 20 dpa. Industry and regulatory international community are working on addressing this gap by testing of harvested materials, including those from the Zorita plant (Spain) and in the SMILE project, which includes PWR internals materials from Ringhals, Unit 2 (Sweden). Results from the testing of Zorita RPVIs materials are summarised in US NRC Research Information Letter (RIL) 2022-05 "NRC Technical Assessment of Zorita Materials Testing Results" [163]. The Zorita CGR results for high fluence (>25 dpa) materials were higher than the Code Case N-889 CGR, supporting the US NRC condition.
- IGSCC and IASCC of BWR internals Although IGSCC of BWR internals appears to be well managed in the United States by inspection programmes and mitigation via water chemistry control, it is likely to continue to occur. Due to the lower neutron doses to BWR internals compared to PWR internals, IASCC is less likely, but may occur in a few areas. Hydrogen water chemistry, particularly coupled with online noble metal chemistry (OLNC), has been effective in mitigating IGSCC in US BWR internals. However, the long-term effectiveness of HWC/OLNC still needs to be verified.

As for VVER reactors, the material of the internals is Ti-stabilised 08CH18N10T steel, which is different from the structural steels of the PWR internals as mentioned in the previous text.

The neutron radiation dose received for the most heavily loaded VVER internals can reach 0.7 dpa per year for a VVER 440 reactor and approximately 1.5 dpa per year for VVER 1 000 and larger reactors. According to the recent works for Ukrainian nuclear power plants, the maximum values for VVER-1 000 can be even 1.8-2.2 dpa per year and for VVER-440 they can be 1-1.5 dpa per year.

The IASCC initiation threshold curves in VERLIFE procedures [148] and in the derived national standards of VVER reactor operators are derived for different steel types (A 304, A 316) and not for sufficiently high doses. Today's IASCC initiation threshold curves are supposed to be valid for 70 (100) dpa. To ensure the lifetime of the VVER internals for the required 80 years, further experimental data for the corresponding steel type for end-of-life neutron doses are required.

It is necessary to establish a reliable ISI method to determine any possible IASCC crack specifically in baffle-former bolts. These may have different designs for different VVERs and consequently different requirements for NDE inspection methods.

The input data for the development of the mechanical modelling and for the development of the assessment methodology should be based on neutron irradiation with similar parameters (neutron spectrum, temperature, environment) as in operating nuclear power plants and the level of neutron irradiation should be equivalent to the level of neutron irradiation of the internals components of operating RPVs at the end of life. It is therefore necessary to use material from harvesting activities during decommissioning of nuclear power plants.

This problem is of high importance for former bolts of VVER-440 units. Nevertheless, in VVER-1 000, swelling-induced changes in geometry, namely rings "bending", may also affect the LTO for the bolts for 80 years. Compared to VVER-440, bolts of VVER-1 000 could hardly be replaced or inspected.

### *4.3.2.3 Neutron embrittlement and loss of fracture toughness*

Irradiation embrittlement (also referred to as neutron embrittlement) changes the mechanical properties of metallic materials (low alloy steels, SS and nickel-base alloys) when exposed to high-energy neutrons (e.g. increasing yield strength, increasing ultimate strength, decreasing ductility, and a loss of FT). The irradiation embrittlement ageing mechanism is a function of composition, temperature, neutron flux and neutron fluence. While the mechanism's ageing effects are loss of ductility and toughness, the eventual ageing effect of concern is unstable crack extension, when the local applied stress intensity in an existing crack exceeds the reduced FT (EPRI MRP-227, Revision 1-A, para 3.2.6 [158]).

Loss of FT of CASS material due to thermal embrittlement is dependent on the material's casting method, composition e.g. molybdenum content, and ferrite content. Loss of FT of X-750 alloys, PH-martensitic SS, and martensitic SS, either from neutron or thermal embrittlement as applicable, cannot be identified by typical ISI activities, but through destructive examination. However, by performing visual (EVT-1, VT-1 examinations) or other volumetric inspections (e.g. UT), applicants can identify cracks that could lead to failure of a potentially embrittled component prior to component failure."

In PWR reactors, FT of wrought austenitic stainless steels (WASS) and austenitic stainless steel welds (ASSW) exposed to high neutron fluence is identified as a low knowledge, high susceptibility item in NUREG/CR-7153 Vol 2, "Expanded Materials Degradation Assessment (EMDA): Aging of Core Internals and Piping Systems" [43]. The industry and international regulatory community are pursuing additional data on FT of these materials through the Zorita work [163] and SMILE project. FT data for irradiated ASSW are lacking at high neutron fluences. US NRC had hoped to obtain high-fluence welds from a decommissioning US plant, but this harvesting effort was not able to be performed.

However, the following concerns, applicable to both PWRs and BWRs, are particularly under scrutiny by US NRC:

• FT of ASSW materials subject to neutron irradiation. US NRC approved topical report BWRVIP-100, Revision 1-A provided J-R toughness curves and recommended FT and flaw analysis methods for SS BWR internals, depending on neutron fluence levels [164]. After the approval of the report, the recommended FT method was found to be nonconservative for ASSW. The US NRC staff performed a technical assessment of the risk associated with the lower-than-expected FT [165]. The staff concluded that the increase in risk associated with the BWRVIP-100, Revision 1-A [165] non-conservatism is low. The database used to develop the lower bound J-R curves contained relatively few J-R curves for welds.

• FT of CASS reactor internals components subject to a combination of thermal ageing and neutron embrittlement for which there is little data on the FT of CASS subject to combined thermal ageing and neutron embrittlement.

#### Additional concern for VVERs is:

• FT of austenitic chromium – nickel Ti stabilised steels, the main construction material of VVER RPVIs, is evaluated according to the VERLIFE procedure [135] and derived national standards. The actual area of applicability is up to 100 dpa.

For the RPVIs close to the core, neutron embrittlement is an important ageing mechanism. Since these parts are not pressure retaining, it is not a very severe problem. But the embrittlement must be considered in structural integrity assessments, and it can facilitate other degradation mechanisms, like IASCC.

In VVER reactors, especially for the VVER-1 000, where thick parts of the core baffle are present, neutron embrittlement is a key degradation mechanism.
