FT drastically decreases (up to seven to ten times) for VVER 08CH18N10T steel when the dose is about five to ten dpa. According to the research irradiation-induced swelling leads to an abrupt degradation of material properties by stimulating the γ→α-phase transformation. A fully embrittle area may form if a void swelling exceeds seven to ten percent value, thus zones of high void swelling should be considered for crack postulations.

### *4.3.2.4 Void swelling and radiation creep*

EPRI MRP-227, Revision 1-A, para 3.2.7 [158] defines "Void swelling as a gradual increase in the volume of a component caused by formation of microscopic cavities in the material. Void swelling may produce dimensional changes that exceed the dimensional tolerances of a component. Severe swelling (>5% by volume) has been correlated with extremely low FT values. While the initial ageing effect is dimensional change and distortion, severe void swelling may result in cracking under stress."

The operation temperature of RPVIs is generally low enough to limit the effect of swelling. However, locally, if temperature increases, e.g. due to gamma heating in thick parts, swelling can occur and create local straining. The major possible swelling concern is related to the geometrical changes that could occur, which could have potential negative impact on control rod movement, or coolant flow.

The US NRC considers void swelling as a minor concern for US PWRs. Destructive examination of harvested components, including some from Zorita documented in [163] has shown insignificant amounts of void swelling in high dose components.

In the long term, the internal components most exposed to irradiation (baffle and former plates) are also likely to be susceptible to a swelling phenomenon. This mechanism is likely to appear in steel in high doses and high temperature. It has never been observed in France or in any Westinghouse design reactor from which the French reactors originated. On the other hand, it is suspected on thick parts equipping VVER reactors (but they operate under different conditions). It must be noted that results of the last 20 years of research on swelling (in particular the international GONDOLE project operated by French CEA) lead to consideration of a lower risk for this phenomenon (this is consistent with EPRI and IAEA visions).

The design of the VVER RPVIs is different (particularly of VVER 1 000 and other types with power output larger than 1 000 MW) than typical PWR designs. The components of RPVIs are subject to high neutron irradiation damage (the neutron dose may exceed 60 dpa for 40 years of operation and maximum irradiation temperature may reach 400°C) and therefore swelling and radiation creep are expected to develop. If operated for 80 years, the radiation dose can reach up to 120 dpa and information on the properties of such highly irradiated materials is very limited. The development of swelling may result in the formation of limit embrittlement area VERLIFE [148] and macroscopic changes in the geometry of the RPVIs components, which have already been demonstrated on some nuclear power plants of VVER type. Measurement of selected geometry changes due to radiation swelling and creep development and associated computational evaluation is part of the advanced RPVIs AMP VVER 1 000 and larger. Evaluation of radiation creep and swelling development is a requirement of the VERLIFE procedure and derived national standards.

RPVIs swelling evaluation is one of the most important issues in Ukraine and leads to limitation of LTO of VVER-1 000 nuclear power plant's units. This problem is less important for the VVER-440 units, due to the different core basket design, which is thinner and well cooled, so zones of internal heat generation (zones of high temperature), which significantly affect swelling, are limited. The core baffle material swelling model is described in the Ukrainian national standard (Assessment of the technical condition and extension service life of VVER-1 000 internals PM-T.0.03.333-15). It includes the determination of the void swelling of an elementary volume of the core baffle material depending on the neutron fluence in dpa and temperature (based on heat rate assessment). Also compared to other swelling models [166], the influence of the stress is accounted for.

Because of swelling and creep, a progressive shape change of the core baffle may lead to contact between the baffle and the barrel. It is believed that this possible contact is unacceptable from an LTO point of view, since it leads to additional stresses in the core barrel, change in the cooling conditions of baffle and a rise in the temperature in RPVIs elements. In other words, a possible contact is unacceptable from the operational point of view. On the other hand, there are no requirements in the reactor design documentation regarding the allowable value of the gap and the need for its presence. In more general sense, reliable failure/ limit state criteria for swelling components of RPVIs need to be established. Also, the swelling leads to the "bending" deformation of the rings, thus the bolts loading increases, together with forming a gap between the annulus (between baffle and barrel) and the core, which leads to leakage and additional core loading from the cross flow.

Residual stress and bolt/spring loads relax because of radiation creep and the stress may drop below the threshold stress for IASCC (~ 40% of irradiated yield strength) before initiation occurs. Under some specific conditions and locations in PWRs, reloading of components by differential swelling can potentially occur in a late stage of plant life, eventually causing IASCC ( [127], [157]).

### *4.3.2.5 Low cycle fatigue*

According to the VERLIFE procedures [148] and the national technical standards derived from it, the fatigue life of the internal parts of a VVER reactor must be assessed. This is even though the internal parts are not part of the pressure boundary. However, there are other critical safety functions that could be compromised by fatigue: support and maintenance of core geometry, support of control elements. Fatigue loading is caused by operating modes, including changes in temperature distribution, due to gamma heating, and stress evolution, due to volume swelling.

The Ukrainian national standard (assessment of the technical condition and extension service life of VVER-1 000 internals) [167] requires evaluation of fatigue for all RPVIs components, but it is critical for those with irradiation-induced material degradation. It is well-known that irradiation leads to a decrease in the plastic properties of the material; thus, the fatigue curves also change. Operational cycles and potential accidental conditions may lead to unacceptable results, especially in zones of concentration, which should be treated carefully.

### *4.3.2.6 Wear due to flow induced vibration*

Wear that affects several components: the lower guide parts (interfaces between radial holding keys and the M support slides), the upper guide tubes as well as the thermal sleeves and cluster guides. In this case, degradation results from the friction, possibly with impacts, of surfaces facing each other due to the relative movement of the internals concerned under the effect of the thermo-hydraulic loads to which they are subjected.

Heavy wear on these structural links can result in a change in the vibration state of the RPVIs and further damage development.

### *4.3.2.7 Core barrel degradation*

The hydrogen overpressure effectively scavenges all oxygen from the primary coolant system, which creates a low ECP environment in PWR primary water. This has not prevented SCC degradation of the core barrel as discussed in Section 4.3.2.4 and shown by K. J. Amberge, S. Davidsaver, J. McKinley in the paper: "An update on aging management of PWR reactor internals in U.S. plants" [168]. FT of austenitic stainless-steel welds in RPVIs (SS welds in core barrels and core shrouds) is not well characterised to date, as there are relatively few data on FT of irradiated welds, and some recent data showed industry models were non-conservative. This issue applies to analysis of found flaws for both BWRs and PWRs but does not affect existing ageing management programmes for detection of degradation.

Irradiation embrittlement and the effect of high neutron fluence on the FT of austenitic materials, in particular SS welds in e.g. core barrels and core shrouds, is a knowledge gap that needs to be addressed for LTO beyond 60 years.

### *4.3.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### *4.3.3.1 Current status of RPVIs non-destructive examination in the United States*

EPRI's team developed screening criteria with susceptibility levels for the eight postulated ageing mechanisms relevant to PWR internals and their effects and updated those screening criteria based on the latest research and the need to extend operation for the SLR from 60 to 80 years. Initial component screening, risk ranking, and categorisation were completed using susceptibility levels and failure modes, effects, and criticality analysis to identify the relative ranking of components. The team also completed engineering evaluations and safety assessments of degradation for components and assemblies of components. Ageing management strategy development, combining results of the engineering evaluations and safety assessments with component accessibility, OPEX, existing evaluations, and prior examination results, was completed to determine the appropriate ageing management methodology, baseline examination timing, and the need for and the timing of subsequent inspections (MRP-232, Revision 2 [169], issued in 2021). The information was compiled into the MRP-191 [170] and MRP-227 series of technical reports, as well as several supporting reports. The NDE inspection standard for PWR internals: MRP-228, Revision 5 issued in 2023 [171] is the companion document to these inspection and evaluation (I&E) guidelines, and it provides examination requirement standards for components listed in these guidelines.

The programme to develop and maintain these guidelines has been under way since the mid-2000s. It is organised around a framework and strategy for managing the effects of ageing in PWR internals (e.g. MRP-134 [172]) and is supported by a substantial database of material data and evaluation results. The latest version I&E of these guidelines is MRP-227, Revision 2, [166] issued in 2021, which supports LTO through 80 calendar years.

In the United States, RPVIs are inspected for ageing degradation under industry programmes that have been approved by the US NRC. The EPRI Boiling Water Reactor Vessel Integrity Program (BWRVIP) was started to address core shroud cracking in US BWRs during the 1990s and has since published inspection and evaluation guidelines for every major component group in BWRs, many of which have been approved by the US NRC. PWR internals are inspected under the guidelines in the MRP-227-A Rev. 1-A report [118]. MRP-227-A was approved by the US NRC in 2011 and most PWRs have completed initial baseline inspections for the first licence renewal period (40-60 years). Both the BWRVIP and the MRP-227 inspections are conducted in addition to the required ASME Code, Section XI examinations of RPVIs.

Inspections of both BWR and PWR internals in the United States rely largely on visual examination, including VT-3, VT-1, and Enhanced Visual Examination (EVT-1). UT is applied for some specific components (such as baffle-former bolts and BWR core shrouds) and welds and used for flaw characterisation of visually detected flaws. Physical measurements are also used for a few components, such as PWR hold-down springs.

EPRI's report MRP-227, Revision 1-A, 3 "Materials Reliability Programme: Pressurised Water Reactor Internals Inspection and Evaluation Guidelines." [158] contains a methodology that has been found acceptable for use for ageing management of PWR internals via a US NRC Safety Evaluation Report dated 25 April 2019 [162] which is incorporated in the report. MRP-227, Revision 1-A covers operation out to 60 years, but operation can be extended to 80 years with the addition of a gap analysis as described in the US NRC Generic Ageing Lessons Learned Report for Subsequent License Renewal (GALL-SLR), NUREG-2191 [173].

A revision to the MRP-227 report is currently under review by the US NRC, MRP-227, Rev. 2 [166], which extends the guidance of MRP-227, Rev. 1-A to an 80 calendar-year life.

EPRI published guidance for qualification of NDE methods in a companion report, "Materials Reliability Programme: Inspection Standard for Pressurised Water Reactor Internals – 2023 Update (MRP-228, Rev.5) [171].

The accessibility of some RPVI components for NDE is also restricted. For example, PWR core barrel welds are mostly inaccessible from the inner diameter due to the baffle plates and may only be accessible on the outer diameter through a narrow annulus created by the thermal shield. Other components that are difficult to access are the lower core support columns in Westinghouse-design RPVIs; to inspect these, remote visual examination equipment must be inserted through a small hole in the lower core plate.

A UT technique is used to detect cracking in baffle-former bolts. The technique is not used to size indications; so, if an indication is detected, the bolt is considered defective and either replaced or accepted via analysis that considers the bolt to be completely failed (non-load bearing).

Historically, methods such as acoustic monitoring have been used to monitor during operation for failures in reactor internals. These methods generally can identify if a loose part exists, but they cannot identify the part or exact failure location.

### *4.3.3.2 Status of RPVIs non-destructive examination in the EU countries*

In Czechia, a periodic NDE core-shroud measurement approach was chosen to quantify radiation-induced creep and swelling of a VVER-1 000 core shroud. The theoretical computational models used to evaluate the development of swelling and creep are verified and the results confirmed by experimental measurements. The first measurements were carried out in 2022 and 2023 at Temelin Nuclear Power Plant (Unit 2 and Unit 1). There are several different designs of measurement equipment using ultrasound, laser (Russian Federation), or a combination of inductive displacement sensors and optical fibres (Czechia). The key to successful detection of creep and swelling development is measurement accuracy.

The measuring of the actual geometry of core baffle during the nuclear power plant operation and its comparison with the calculated estimates are required for all Ukrainian VVER-1 000 units. First works were performed in the middle of the 2010s. For this aim a special tool was used, including four ultrasound gauges at the ends. The mutual movement of the tool in a vertical direction and rotation in a horizontal one allowed obtaining the shape of the whole internal geometry of the core barrel. Nowadays, a more advanced measurement tool is used; measurements are carried out between ten sides simultaneously using five measuring rods with ultrasound gauges. The rods are installed on the frame in such a way that the direction of measurements is perpendicular to the plane of the vertical surfaces of core baffle and measurements are made between the middles of the surfaces. According to regulatory requirements, periodic measurements of all core baffles of all units should be performed. The results of these measurements should not be only compared to each other (for a separate unit) but also be a basis for calculation verification and LTO assessment. It is assumed that periodic measurements will allow for the reduction of conservatism in the computation model by adjusting the coefficient in formulae, which has the most influence on the swelling process. Currently, a methodology of measurements analysis as well as a standardised design are being developed.

For the fleet of PWR reactors, SCC, assisted or not by irradiation, on the one hand, and internal wear (thermal sleeves, control rod guide tubes) on the other, are two well-identified degradation modes. As such, they are monitored over time. Their inspection methods are mainly based on VT. Depending on the phenomena, other techniques, such as UT can be used (guide tube support pins, or baffle bolts for instance). Specific applications can benefit from advanced technics as phased array (e.g. wear of the flange of the thermal sleeves under the vessel head). Neutronic noise monitoring is used for vibratory surveillance. Wear measurements are based on different metrology tools depending on the circumstances (VT, UT, laser).

The standard inspection methods for RPVIs in Swiss nuclear power plants are indirect VT by camera system, UT of baffle bolts and core shroud cracking. This technique could be applied, if necessary, on today's operating reactors, too.

In Sweden, the main concern is related to some welds in the core barrel which are behind thermal shields and are not inspectable. For a similar case, EPRI-MRP issued interim guidance in 2023 for inspections of this type of weld in PWRs (MRP-227 NEI 03-08 "Needed" Interim Guidance for WEC/CE Core Barrel Inspections, ADAMS Accession No. ML23290A020, 19 May 2023 [22] (as mentioned in section 4.3.2.1).

### *4.3.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

Since the 1970s, the RPVIs have shown several ageing degradations, such as irradiated assisted SCC on baffle-former bolts, PWSCC on support pins and flexure pins of guide tubes, wear on locking devices of support pins, and wear on thimble tubes.

In some cases, components have been replaced because of cracking, but in other cases unaffected components were replaced based on a life cycle cost/lifetime management consideration, considering the cost of future inspections and the potential risk of unplanned shutdowns in case flaws were to be detected.

### *4.3.4.1 Advances in welding for highly irradiated materials (PWR IMT-205)*

Weld repair techniques for highly irradiated RPVI components are not qualified. Helium accumulation in irradiated SS makes welding of such components challenging. US NRC regulations (e.g. 10 CFR 50.55a [174]) contain a condition on underwater welding of austenitic materials:

"(B) Underwater welding: Second provision. Licensees must obtain US NRC approval in accordance with paragraph (z) of this section regarding the welding technique to be used prior to performing welding on austenitic material other than P–No. 8 material exposed to thermal neutron fluence greater than 1 × 1017 n/cm2 (E < 0.5 eV). Licensees must obtain US NRC approval in accordance with paragraph (z) regarding the welding technique to be used prior to performing welding on P– No. 8 austenitic material exposed to thermal neutron fluence greater than 1 × 1017 n/cm2 (E < 0.5 eV) and measured or calculated helium concentration of the material greater than 0.1 atomic parts per million."

The time frame for needing weld repair techniques for RPVIs is uncertain. To date, repairs have been possible to achieve using mechanical repair methods, such as core shroud tie rods in BWRs.

### *4.3.4.2 Replacement of the reactor pressure vessel internals*

Unlike the RPV fuel management programmes (low leakage core) and reactor vessel annealing, irradiation embrittlement of the RPVIs can only be minimised by reducing the reactor power. Maintenance actions for managing IASCC, irradiation assisted cracking, or IGSCC can be modification of the coolant chemistry or replacement of RPVIs components with materials that are less susceptible to IGSCC.

RPVI components that have been determined by inspection to exhibit cracking, such as baffle plates, baffle bolts, guide tube support pins, can be replaced (IAEA TECDOC-1557, Section 8.1.5 [149]).

The first replacements of whole RPVIs have been completed in Japan since:

- 1998 at BWR nuclear power plants (see IAEA NP-T-3.2, Section 9 [147]);
- 2005 at PWR nuclear power plants (see IAEA NP-T-3.2, Table 1 [147]);

The entire replacement of the RPV internals in the context related to the re-evaluation of seismic assumptions.

The procedures for RPVIs replacement require measuring the gaps at the outlet nozzles and clevis inserts underwater, using remotely operated measurement systems, because of the difficulty to access the reactor vessel, due to high radiation exposure. Further details on the major steps for dismantling and installation of the new RPVIs, including the schematic outline for removing the original RPVIs, can be found in IAEA NP-T-3.2, Section 6 for PWRs and in Section 9 for BWRs [147].

The internals of ABB BWRs are designed to be dismantlable. Consequently, it is relatively easy to replace components. Components that have been replaced include core shroud support, core shroud, core shroud head with core spray system, and top guide (see L. Unneberg's report "Swedish Utility Experience With ASEA-ATOM-Design Top Guides" - EPRI NP-5947 [175], T. Graae's article "Repair and replacement of reactor internals for plant life extension" [176] and S. Haukeland's article "Internals replacements rejuvenates Forsmark" [177]).

In France, replacement of parts of RPVIs has also been completed (original hold down spring, baffle bolts, fuel pins, thermal sleeves, guide tubes, thermocouple guides, Guide Tube Support Pins, etc.). Based on specific needs, some tools are also developed within the framework of an insurance strategy.

Some mitigation techniques can also be implemented to prevent thermal sleeves wear for instance. Therefore, this is not considered as an issue. On the other hand, repair or replacement of all RPVIs are not considered today in France.

In Beznau Nuclear Power Plant (PWR) numerous baffle bolts were replaced by ones of less SCC susceptible material and optimised shape.

For BWRs, an important mitigative action is the usage of hydrogen water chemistry and its further development of the injection of noble metals like platinum (On-Line NobleChem® HWC/OLNC) to decrease the electrochemical CP.

Zinc, which is injected primarily for radiological reasons, seems to have an additional beneficial effect to the prevention of SCC. This is part of an ongoing research project.

In the 2024 outage at Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant (BWR), the SCC indications found on a riser pipe of the jet pumps were mitigated by a mechanical clamp.

### *4.3.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

Current knowledge regarding RPVI degradation mechanisms was continually boosted by the associated international research projects, such as the following activities:

- conducting additional independent testing of Zorita weld materials;
- continuous participation in NEA SMILE and FIDES projects;
- harvesting of high-fluence core shroud welds.

The SMILE research project, launched in 2021, aims to extract and test real plant-aged materials and components to improve and validate the knowledge of materials ageing phenomena and their kinetics, to improve the current knowledge level regarding RPVI degradation mechanisms described above (IGSCC, IASCC, neutron embrittlement, loss of FT, or void swelling). Details about the SMILE LWR materials library, the experimental testing and examination of the highly irradiated materials, harvested from the Oskarshamn 1 & 2 (BWR) and Ringhals 2 (PWR) nuclear power plants, can be found in the NEA WGIAGE presentation at the 46th Meeting [178].

EPRI identified in 2020 several high priority research gaps in relation to reactor internals ageing degradation assessment, repair and fabrication, as mentioned in PWR IMT-205, rev.4, Section 5.2 [47]. They comprise the need for:

- research to assess the significance of flow induced vibrations on the fatigue and wear of baffle assembly components (MRFA 1) and to determine the factors that lead to accelerated wear in control rod guide cards and other sections of the internals;
- improved techniques for highly irradiated SS, such as glow heat input welding based on laser or solid state joining, which offers the potential to overcome difficulties encountered when welding irradiated materials using conventional arc welding techniques.

However, as of the drafting of this status report, EPRI has not identified any significant gaps or challenges that would preclude a US or international PWR from operating to 60 or 80 years of total based on EPRI assessments performed consistent with US licence renewal methodologies and standards.

The US NRC provided guidance for reviewing gap analyses of PWR RPVIs AMPs based on MRP-227, Rev. 1-A in Final SLR-ISG-2021-01-PWRVI Updated Ageing Management Criteria for Reactor Vessel Internal Components for Pressurised-Water Reactors [179]. The US NRC has not identified any gaps related to RPVI ageing management that would preclude issuing renewed licences for 60-80 years.

As regards European countries, the approach proposed by Électricité de France (EDF) to justify the long-term behaviour of the French fleet's RPVIs is essentially based on the continuation of the ageing inspections. These actions are already in force at every ten-year inspection:

- the ageing management process;
- continued reactor checks and replacements when necessary to ensure that the RPVIs fulfilled their functions for the expected duration.

The acquisition of material data at high doses to anticipate the occurrence of damage beyond 60 years of operation is an essential element. This includes:

- SCC and IASCC susceptibility analyses;
- wear susceptibility analyses considering experimental conditions representative of in service conditions.

In Swiss nuclear power plants, the existing inspection and test programmes, especially preventative maintenance, are reviewed to determine whether ageing-induced degradation can be avoided or detected at an early stage. No gaps have been identified for LTO. In general, most RPVIs could be replaced with acceptable effort.

However, confirmatory research is desirable on the following topics:

- 1. IASCC behaviour in LWR environments for the full range of dose relevant for operation beyond 60 years (data and models).
  - o IASCC growth rates for highly irradiated (>20 dpa) austenitic stainless steels (wrought and welds), in PWRs, since BWR internals do not experience these fluence levels. The presence of numerous He bubbles in highly irradiated SSs noted above, as well as void swelling, affects analysis of found flaws but does not affect existing ageing management programs for detection of degradation.

- o IASCC behaviour in LWR environments for the full range of dose relevant for operation beyond 60 years, as well as long-term aspects related to SCC susceptibility. The presence of numerous tiny He bubbles in highly irradiated SSs noted above, as well as void swelling, could affect FT and IASCC susceptibility and therefore need better understanding.
- o VVER IASCC cracks in baffle-former bolts. A general understanding of IASCC development is not sufficient for LTO to 80 years. A comprehensive prediction methodology needs to be developed. The evaluation of the degradation of VVER RPVIs by IASCC is based on experimental data obtained for steels other than Ti-stabilised austenitic stainless steel 08CH18N10T, the main structural material of VVER internals.
- 2. Irradiation embrittlement of RPVIs SS and SS welds.
  - o FT of austenitic stainless-steel welds in RPVIs (SS welds in core barrels and core shrouds). There are relatively few data on FT of irradiated welds, and some recent data showed industry models were non-conservative. This issue applies to both BWRs and PWRs. This issue applies to analysis of found flaws but does not affect existing ageing management programmes for detection of degradation.
  - o Irradiation embrittlement and the effect of high neutron fluence on the FT of austenitic materials, in particular SS welds in e.g. core barrels and core shrouds, is a knowledge gap that needs to be addressed for LTO beyond 60 years.
- 3. R&D actions to better understand and model the RPVIs SCC, wear and swelling phenomena. This concerns the proven phenomena of SCC, (with or without the effect of irradiation) and wear phenomena affecting RPVIs need a better modelling, to optimise the mitigation methods and define robust maintenance strategies. For these two phenomena, more physical-based models will be developed by EDF. This concerns also the potential phenomenon of swelling. Nevertheless, it has to be noted that results of the last 20 years of research on swelling (in particular the international GONDOLE project operated by CEA) lead to consideration of a lower risk for this phenomenon (this is consistent with EPRI and IAEA visions).
- 4. Weld repair techniques for highly irradiated SS RPVIs components. Having such techniques available in the future would be useful but probably not essential due to the feasibility of mechanical repair methods.
- 5. Environmental effect on fatigue resistance of neutron irradiated materials and the lack of welding processes for repair of irradiated material.
- 6. LCF in VVERs. To ensure LTO beyond 60 years for VVER 440 reactor internals, it is necessary to revalidate the fatigue analysis based on the experimental cyclic stress – strain curves of the structural material of the most loaded subcomponents. Similarly, an evaluation of welded joints with incomplete penetration is required.
- 7. Void swelling and radiation creep in VVERs. The empirical phenomenological model of the RPVIs' material swelling/creep law is used in calculations and its conservatism can lead to unacceptable results. The main issue with the swelling of RPVIs is in the empirical mathematical model of irradiation-induced swelling/creep of 08Kh18N10T steel and the lack of the failure criteria for the irradiated components, for example core baffle and its fasteners (like the list of characteristics and their acceptable values in respect to safe state of RPVIs) (see results of GONDOLE Project).

Swell geometry measurements in VVERs. There is a lack of verified data and tools of actual RPVI geometry measurement (to measure core baffle internal geometry with the required accuracy), as well as the robust methodology for results postprocessing. A separate problem is the lack of initial geometry measurement, i.e. non-operated baffle for each unit.

8. Enhanced research for IASCC mitigation due to irradiation damage.

More IASCC incidents of reactor internals (SS, Ni-alloys) might be anticipated in LTO with increasing (high) fast neutron fluence and irradiation damage (e.g. due to channelling or He), although relaxation of weld residual stresses or bolt torques partially mitigates this concern and RIS and RIH tend to saturate at high fluence. Below are the topics for enhanced research for IASCC mitigation due to irradiation damage:

- radiation induced precipitation and transmutation at very high fast neutron fluence;
- role of He (and H) and swelling on IASCC in PWRs in LTO, e.g. at locations with high γ and thermal n flux and insufficient cooling. He by thermal (n,α) reactions from B-10 at low fluence and Ni-58 at high fluence, additional nuclear heating by α. B strongly segregates (thermal) to grain boundaries He within 10 µm around grain boundaries. Ni enrichment at grain boundaries by radiation induced segregation (RIS) with saturation above 10 dpa. Nuclear heating may raise temperature to swelling regime. Role of stress build-up by differential swelling in regions with gradients in T, influence and cold work;
- repair welding/methods for highly irradiated reactor internals (He-induced cracking);
- effect of ripple loading (thermal mixing from low leakage core, load follow, vibrations) on SCC in highly irradiated reactor internals;
- role of load follow on IASCC in PWRs;
- role of Si (and Si enrichment);
- IASCC & (environmental) fracture/HE of other internal materials such as X-750, A-286. Moderate irradiation hardening could drastically increase susceptibility;
- more radiation resistant reactor internal materials (cross-fertilisation from GEN-IV, Fusion & Spallation developments);
- 9. Needs for enhanced/new testing, monitoring, inspection and diagnostics methods.

### <span id="page-115-0"></span>**4.4. Steam generators**

### *4.4.1. Description of steam generators*

The most important safety function of the SGs is to ensure the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary and to constitute a separation between the primary and secondary side. It is the main heat sink during normal and upset operation.

The types of SGs used in water cooled nuclear power plants (IAEA TECDOC-1 668 [180], section 2) are:

- vertical tube sheet boiling SGs, commonly known as "recirculating vertical U tube steam generators" (RSG);
- vertical/tube sheet superheated SGs, commonly known as "once through steam generators" (OTSG);
- horizontal/collector boiling SGs, used in VVER reactors.

There are currently six types of SG tubes used in the world: mill annealed Alloy 600, thermally treated Alloy 600, thermally treated Alloy 690, Monel 400, Alloy 800 NG, and titanium-stabilised austenitic stainless steel 08Ch18N10T, used in VVER SGs (IGALL AMP 116 Steam Generators [181]). Most SGs designed by Westinghouse, AREVA NP, Babcock & Wilcox and Mitsubishi-Heavy Industries, Doosan Heavy Industries are being fabricated with thermally treated Alloy 690 (Alloy 690TT). AREVA NP and Babcock & Wilcox Canada are also supplying replacement SGs with Alloy-800 NG tubing or Alloy 690TT, as documented in TECDOC-1 668, Sect. 3.2.1 [180].

### **Typical Westinghouse Advanced PWR steam generator**

In RSGs, the most common SG construction type, the primary system coolant flows through U tubes with a tube sheet at the bottom of the generator and U bends at the top of the tube bundle (see Figure 4.12).

<span id="page-117-0"></span>**Figure 4.12. Schematic PWR recirculating SG cross section**

Source: TECDOC-1668 [180]

The primary coolant enters the SG usually at 315–330°C on the hot leg side and leaves at about 288°C on the cold leg side. The secondary system water (feedwater) is fed through a feedwater nozzle, to a feed-ring, into the downcomer, where it mixes with recirculating water draining from the moisture separators. This down-comer water flows to the bottom of the SG, across the top of the tube sheet, and then up-wards through the tube bundle, where steam is generated. About 25% of the secondary bulk water is converted to steam as it passes through the tube bundle up-wards, the remainder is recirculated.

The figure above is an update for US Westinghouse Advanced PWR type AP1 000 Unit, using two Delta 125 SGs with vertical shell U tube evaporator with integral moisture separating equipment. The tubes are fabricated from thermally treated nickel base Alloy 690 (Alloy 690 TT). Support of the tubes is provided by ferritic stainless steel support plates. The holes in the tube support plates (TSP) are broached with hole geometry (broached hole TSP) to promote high velocity flow along the tube. The thermal sleeve and feed-water nozzles are fabricated from Alloy 690 TT material, which is very resistant to erosion and corrosion. An improved design is to eliminate the conditions linked to the occurrence of SG water hammer (TECDOC-1 668, Section 2.1.2.1 [180]).

The US OTSG use straight heat exchanger tubes with tube sheets at both the top and bottom of the SG, as shown in Figure 4.13. Primary coolant is pumped through the tubes from top to bottom while the secondary coolant moves around the outside of the tubes from bottom to top in a counter-flow direction.

<span id="page-118-0"></span>The secondary system water enters a feed annulus above the ninth tube support plate level, where it mixes with steam aspirated from the tube bundle area and is preheated to saturation. The saturated water flows down the annulus, across the lower tube sheet, and up into the tube bundle, where it becomes steam. This superheated steam flows radially outward and then down the annulus to the steam outlet connection. Most of the secondary coolant is completely evaporated in a single pass through the SG.

![](_page_118_Picture_4.jpeg)

**Figure 4.13. PWR once through SG cross-section** 

Source: EPRI Report TR-103 824 [182]

The design features, materials and process parameters of both US OTSGs and RSGs are summarised in IAEA-TECDOC 1 668, Table 2.1 [180].

### **AREVA European pressurised water reactor steam generator**

The design features and the technical information of the new SGs designed by AREVA for the European pressurised water reactor plants are summarised below in Figure 4.14.

<span id="page-119-0"></span>![](_page_119_Figure_1.jpeg)

**Figure 4.14. AREVA European pressurised water reactor SG**

Source: TECDOC-1 668 [180]

Two out of three working nuclear power plants with three reactors in Switzerland are PWRs. These are Beznau Unit 1 and 2 (PWR, Westinghouse 2-loop, 1969, 1971) and Gösgen (PWR, KWU 3-loop, 1979). Detailed descriptions are given in the Technical Note TM-014-M 17 059, Topical Peer Review - Ageing Management of Nuclear Power Plants [183] for Beznau Nuclear Power Plant, respectively in Gösgen Nuclear Power Plant, Report BER-S-92 652, Contribution to the National Assessment Report, Topical Peer Review, 2017 [184].

The original SGs of Beznau Nuclear Power Plant were replaced in 1993 (Unit 1) and 1998 (Unit 2). The replacement SGs are of Westinghouse type 33, with additional installed antivibration bars, and in Gösgen Nuclear Power Plant they are Siemens Standard type MAN-GHH.

### **VVER steam generators**

The horizontal SG system for VVERs has significant differences compared to the U tube design of the PWR SGs, and nickel base alloys, like Alloy 600, are not employed in VVERs.

The primary coolant enters the SG through a vertical collector, travels through the horizontal U-shaped submerged SS tubing, and exits through a second vertical collector. The tube ends penetrate the collector wall (which performs the same function as the tube sheet in a PWR SG) and are expanded using either a hydraulic or explosive expansion process and then welded at the collector inside wall surface. The VVER-440 collectors (see Figure 2.8, page 15 in IAEA TECDOC-1668 [180]) are made of Ti-stabiliSed austenitic stainless steel.

The VVER-1 000 collectors are made of low alloy steel with higher tensile properties, clad with SS. The SG vessel is a carbon steel (VVER-440) or low alloy bainitic steel (all the newer VVER-1 000 SGs) horizontal cylinder, consisting of forged shells, stamped elliptical ends and stamped branch pipes and hatches welded together as shown in Figure 2.10, page 15 in IAEA TECDOC-1 668 [180].

The bent tubes are assembled into 2 U-bundles creating three vertical corridors to ensure organised hydrodynamics of boiler water circulation. The bent tubes are distanced from the tube bundle by special elements fixed in support structures located on the inner surface of the SG shell. The materials used for the pressure vessel, tubes and collectors pipeline production are:

- carbon steel No. 22K (unalloyed SS) VVER-440 SG vessel;
- alloyed steel 10GN2MFA (alloyed quality steel) VVER-1 000 SG vessel;
- austenitic stainless steel 08Ch18N10T- SG tubes for VVER-440/ WER-1 000.

Detailed information and construction details for both SG types are available in the IAEA report VVER-1 000 MW SGs integrity [185].

In VVER-1 000 MW the material of the collectors, austenitic stainless steel Ti-stabilised 08Chl8N10T, was replaced by low alloy steel 10GNMFA with higher mechanical (tensile) properties, due to the SGs problems, in particular cracking in the cold collectors (around 20 failures in the period 1986-1991), when a number of SGs had to be replaced due to the a combination of material aspects, design and operation loads in combination with water chemistry requirements violations, which were considered responsible for the damage [185].

#### **CANDU steam generators**

Although the size of CANDU reactor SGs (see Figure 2.6, page 13 in IAEA TECDOC-1 668 [180]) has escalated greatly with successive reactor designs, they are generally smaller than PWR RSGs, and operate at lower temperatures (290°C to 310°C primary inlet temperature). The lower temperatures generally delay the onset of thermally activated corrosion processes, such as PWSCC or IGSCC.

Because the primary coolant in a CANDU reactor is heavy water (D2O), relatively small tube sizes [12.7 mm (1/2") OD and, in more recent units, 15.9 mm (5/8") OD] have been used, to minimise the heavy water inventory. But this increases the difficulty in performing maintenance activities such as tube inspection, plugging and removal.

The most important area of diversity in the CANDU design is in the choice of tube material. The CANDU SGs currently operate with tubes made from high temperature, mill annealed Alloy 600 (Alloy 600 MA), Monel 400 and titanium stabilised Alloy 800 (TECDOC-1 668, Section 2.1.2.1 [180]).

### *4.4.2. Physical ageing of steam generators*

A synthetic, though comprehensive, description of the degradation mechanisms and their critical location, in every type of reactor and SG construction, are presented in a tabular form in connection with the indication of critical location on the SG schematic cross section in AMP 116 Steam Generators [181]. And a summary of the PWR SG tubes relevant ageing degradation processes is available in TECDOC-1 668, Table 4.1 [180].

As of 2013, it was already known that some environmentally assisted degradation modes of carbon and low alloy steel components were not considered at the design stage of LWR reactors (EDMA, Volume 2, [43], Section 5), including:

- corrosion of carbon steel tube support plates in the secondary side of PWR SGs due to complex concentrated environments occurring at heat transfer surfaces in the tube/support plate crevice;
- "high-cycle" (i.e. low strain amplitude/high frequency) fatigue due to flow-induced vibration or thermal stress cycles (e.g. in dead legs and in feedwater nozzles);
- flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) of carbon steel components (e.g. the PWR and PHWR SG tube support plates);
- enhanced SCC due to synergistic interactions with other degradation modes.

These concerns regarding the operational lives of 60 to 80 years of SGs are discussed below.

### *4.4.2.1 Stress corrosion cracking (SCC)*

Most PWR SGs are recirculating designs and most in-service PWSCC has occurred in the recirculating SGs. The locations where SCC most often occurs in Alloy 600 SG tubing are presented in Figure 4.15. The PWSCC of Alloy 600 SG tubing in the mill-annealed condition became a major degradation mechanism from the 1970s onwards for recirculating SGs (EMDA Vol. 2 [43], Sect. 3.6).

<span id="page-121-0"></span>**Figure 4.15. Locations where SCC most often occurs in Alloy 600 SG tubing**

Source: EMDA Vol. 2 [43]

"The first roll transitions experiencing PWSCC were located on the hot leg side, where the temperature is typically around 320°C and is 30 to 40°C hotter than the cold leg inlet at 280°C. Thus, it was clear that temperature had a significant influence on PWSCC, indicating a thermally activated mechanism. The apparent activation energy, calculated from fitting the temperature dependence to the Arrhenius equation, is rather high (~180 kJ/mole), so that a typical temperature difference of 30°C between hot and cold legs could easily account for a factor of four to five increase in the time to the onset of detectable cracking. Thus, a reduction of hot leg temperature by 4°C to even by 10°C was employed for mitigation."

As of 2020, the knowledge gap in PWSCC assessment of thermally treated Alloy 600 SG tubing (P-AS-20), denting, and SCC in SG Top of Tube-sheet (TTS) (P-AS-24), were still considered a high risk in EPRI PWR IMT (MRP-205) [47], Table 3-1. But with the replacement of the old SG tube bundles with Alloy 690TT, or Alloy 800 tubing, the degradation identified in the new SG tube bundles has been limited starting from 2008.

The problem remains for VVER SGs, where the most concerning degradation mechanism is stress corrosion induced by chlorides. Both VVER-440 and VVER-1 000 SGs use titanium stabilised SS tubes. This material is known to be susceptible to SCC initiated from secondary side (outer diameter) in acidic environment, but according to chromium oxide solubility curves the steel is susceptible to degradation in (highly) alkaline pH as well. Chloride stress corrosion is a type of intergranular corrosion and occurs in austenitic stainless steel under tensile stress in the presence of oxygen, chloride ions, and high temperature. SCC cracks on VVER SG tubes are located under tube support plates, but also on the outer tube diameter (secondary side), i.e. the outside diameter stress corrosion cracking or ODSCC (IAEA-TECDOC 1 577 [186]).

But VVER-440 and VVER-1 000 SGs with austenitic stainless-steel tubes have also experienced the SCC of dissimilar weld (shell to nozzle), which is a specific issue for both VVER reactor types. In several cases the repair of these welds is the "only solution" (as mentioned in IAEA AMP116 [181]).

Due to the horizontal positioning of the heat transfer tubing in VVERs there are more concerns for the effects of deposits on the secondary side of the tubing: Chemical treatments and water chemistry controls are needed to mitigate ODSCC of the stainlesssteel tubing. Some research is needed into how more optimised water chemistry controls can be implemented to minimise effects during plan restarts and, in particularly, after the plant extended layup, or after major component replacement. All current gaps, ranked as medium, refer to secondary water chemistry improvement (EPRI VVER IMT MRP-471, Table 3-5 ([55]).

Based on present knowledge and experience, the concerns and potential risks are:

- Corrosion of the threaded holes located on the flange joints of the primary and secondary headers of the SG. Based on the visual controls of the threaded holes, there is potential presence of corrosion. As per the present understanding, neither study nor calculation have been performed in case the threaded holes are repaired/cut in some way.
- Water chemistry regime and the concerns related such as corrosion of the inner space of the SG and corrosion of the heat-transfer tubes. The corrosion products arising inside the SG may create deposits on the internal part of the shell and on the heat-transfer tubes if the SG is insufficiently drained. Such deposits may lead to decreased heat-transfer, faster degradation of the inner space of the SG, or leakage.

The physical ageing of the SGs of the Swiss nuclear power plant is dominated by SCC of Incoloy 800 parts or other nickel base alloys or austenitic steels.

### *4.4.2.2 Fatigue crack initiation*

Fatigue refers to an ageing degradation mechanism where components undergo cyclic (low or high frequency) stresses, generated by thermal cycling, vibration, seismic events, or loading transients. Environmental factors may accelerate fatigue and may eventually result in a component failure. In LWRs, components such as the SG shells, and steam separators are among the ones mostly affected with increased operational time.

Each component was designed initially with expected loads and operating conditions specific for a lifetime of 40 years using established guidelines (typically those in Section III of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code). An 80-year reactor period of operation corresponds to over 600 000 hours of service (at a 90% service factor), while most longterm mechanical performance data used in design come from tests operating much less than 100 000 hours.

Although engineering judgments may offer justification for reactor operation up to 60 years based largely on the extrapolation of known phenomena after operating lives of 35– 40 years, there are concerns for the carbon and low alloy steels degradation, if operating beyond 60 years, related with time-limiting degradation modes (such as fatigue or thermal ageing) and synergisms between different degradation modes (e.g. fatigue and SCC).

Based on the systematic assessment of degradation mechanisms (i.e. using the Phenomena Identification and Ranking Table approach), for operation beyond 60 years, one key finding was corrosion fatigue of carbon and low alloy steels, due to changes in loading or chemical conditions over a long operating period of service, as of 2014 (EMDA vol. 2, Table 9.36) [43].

### **High cycle fatigue**

Over time, the physical ageing of the SGs of the Swiss nuclear power plants was dominated not only by SCC and other types of corrosion, but also by mechanical fatigue due to mechanical fluid-induced vibrations, thermomechanical fatigue induced by operational pressure or thermal transients.

Also, in CANDU SG tubes, a few failures were caused by HCF in CANDU SG tubes and the locations are typically related to where fluid-elastic instability is identified.

Fatigue failures due to HCF (vibrations) normally occur early in service life; however, tube fouling and tube support plate buildup may change the conditions and could contribute to tube vibrations. The flow field on the secondary side of a SG is complex and further understanding is desirable.

As of 2020, the assessment gap related to SG high- cycle fatigue was still ranked high risk for operation beyond 60 years, due to the current limitations of the SG tubes wear models (not always based on wear rates and improved materials or vibration conditions) which, together with improved CFD models, can improve the thermo-hydraulic analysis and enable a better understanding of how fouling, deposits and foreign materials contribute to SG tube vibrations (EPRI PWR IMT (MRP-205), Table 3-3, P-AS-22 [47]).

### **Low cycle fatigue**

The feedwater nozzle and connected piping are susceptible areas for fatigue. In 1979, the US NRC issued Bulletin 79-13 [187] to address the safety concerns and the need for extended inspections, raised by fatigue cracking in feedwater piping.

In the Westinghouse design two different layouts exist, one where the auxiliary feedwater connects to the main feedwater line before it enters the SG. The other layout is used for SGs with a preheater. In this case the auxiliary feedwater connects directly to the SG above the tube bundle.

In the feedwater and/or auxiliary feedwater nozzles LCF transients are present. First, many transients may be present when the plant is being maintained at hot standby or no-load conditions and the steam generation rate is made up by intermittent feeding of cold water into the SG. Due to the large temperature difference (and difference in density) of the fluid between the SG and the feedwater, a layer between hot and cold fluid (stratification) may arise.

The stratified layer introduces local through-wall stresses, whose magnitude depends on the top-to-bottom temperature difference and the level and thickness of the mixing layer. If the system is constrained, stratification may also introduce a global bending stress due to the difference in thermal expansion between the upper and lower part of the pipe. If the mixing level is wavy (striping) it could also introduce HCF at the inner surface of the nozzle (or in the piping). Stratification and striping may also affect the thermal sleeves, especially at the joints where alternating stresses could be very high and could cause an internal leakage. In cases where the thermal sleeve is damaged there is also a risk that the SG shell may be affected.

The feedwater piping is made of carbon steel while the nozzle and shell are made of low alloy ferritic steel. Therefore, these components may be susceptible to corrosion fatigue. Data indicates that steels with higher sulphur content together with highly oxygenated water may be more susceptible (NUREG/CR-6 909 rev. 1 [188]). However, in general, fatigue environmental effects associated with a normal secondary side chemistry with limited oxygen are anticipated to be limited (EPRI Materials Degradation Matrix, Revision 4, p5-8a "Problems related to off-chemistry conditions" [130]).

The transients in connection to the feedwater and/or auxiliary feedwater nozzles could be complex and may not be correctly described within original design transient specifications. The original operating conditions may also have changed over time, which can further complicate the situation. If there is an uncertainty about existing loading conditions, one recommendation is to implement temperature monitoring in the nozzle area. Based on results from such a system, better understanding of operation is achieved, and unfavourable operating modes could be avoided. Experience has shown that monitoring can serve as a basis for updating the design transient specification.

The CUFs at some SG nozzles due to operational pressure or thermal transients are among the highest recorded values.

### *4.4.2.3 Wear/fretting*

Tube wear in SGs can be caused by interaction of the tubes with tube support structures (e.g. tube support plates), foreign objects or other tubes. Tube fouling and tube support plate buildup can contribute to tube vibrations and loss of material/wear. The flow field on the secondary side of a SG is complex. State-of- the-art software is necessary to replace outdated codes and, combined with updated CFD models, could enable a better understanding of how fouling, deposits and foreign materials contribute to SG tube vibrations (see previous Sub-section 4.4.2.2).

Wear was considered a threat for Alloy 600 tubes and supports on the secondary coolant side of the SGs and was identified as a high knowledge, high susceptibility mode of degradation. This is a known fact for PWR reactors and is typically a result of design issues rather than specific material conditions (EMDA, vol.2, para 9.6.3 Summary of findings [43]). But with the replacement of many old SGs with new ones having tubes manufactured from Alloy 690TT (with increased Cr content), the susceptibility to wear/ loss of material decreased and no incidents have been reported in the past 20 years since they have been in service. In addition, the high-Cr weld metals have also been used extensively and without incident as a corrosion-resistant overlay for component repair (EMDA, vol.2, para 9.7 Scoring Summary for Alloy 690 and Alloy 152/52 weld metals [43]).

However, although the material susceptibility to wear decreased with the use of superior tube materials, there is still the risk of wear/cracking due to loose parts or foreign objects. In 2003, an adverse trend developed associated with SG tube damage caused by loose parts. This has become the main threat to SG tube integrity for replacement SGs.

The risk of "SG tube damage due to lose parts or foreign objects" is considered high, as there is a need for effective measures to minimise generation of loose parts and guidance for expansion of eddy current inspection scope and co-ordination with visual examinations on the secondary side. This knowledge gap ranked as "High" is currently addressed by a management plan to acknowledge the risk and recommending the development of a SG Foreign Object Handbook to be used by utilities together with extended Eddy current inspections and assessment criteria for management decision making and contingency plans, to ensure SG tube integrity (EPRI PWR IMT (MRP-205), Table 3-2, P-AS-26 Steam Generator Tube Damage due to Loose Parts or Foreign Objects [47]).

Other high risk gaps are related to the NDE inspection tools for the primary and secondary side of SGs and integrity evaluation capabilities related to the detection of foreign objects in the tube bundle, which represent a significant issue to the integrity of newer SGs with tubing fabricated from corrosion-resistant materials, but still prone to wear, as indicated in EPRI report PWR IMT (MRP-205) [47],Table 3-5:

- P-I&E-15 NDE of Steam Generator Tubing Eddy Current Technology Improvements;
- P-I&E-16 NDE Tools for Steam Generator Tubing Integrity Assessments;
- P-I&E-20 Steam Generator Foreign Object Detection and Evaluation Improvements.

### *4.4.2.4 Flow accelerated corrosion (FAC)*

The term "flow-accelerated corrosion" covers enhanced corrosion that can occur on copper-base alloys and carbon steels in LWRs in flowing water or steam under single- or two-phase conditions, with the major consequences of failure of the component due to wall thinning and loss of pressure by leakage.

The extent of FAC of carbon and low alloy steels in water-cooled reactors depends on the interactions between the following parameters: (a) temperature, (b) oxygen concentration (CP), (c) water chemistry and pH, (d) chemical composition of the metal, and (e) single- or two-phase flow and turbulence, as follows [189]:

- FAC of carbon steel reach its maximum around 130°C to 150°C, when the rates of metal loss result in wall thinning of up to 1 mm/year and piping failure in thinwalled pipes;
- the oxygen concentration in the secondary water is typically <5 ppb with hydrazine added as an oxygen scavenger (but too much hydrazine concentrations of 100 to 200 ppb have led to carbon steel support plates having disintegrated);
- for carbon steels, the pH at 25°C should be between nine and ten to minimise corrosion in water to the minimum oxide solubility of carbon steels;

- chromium levels >0.1 to 0.2 wt% are largely sufficient to avoid the problem of FAC in single-phase conditions in PWR SGs;
- FAC has been seen on the secondary side of PWR SGs, where significant loss was observed in upper support plates, steam separators, and blowdown piping.

Erosion corrosion occurs in pipe systems made of carbon steel with a fast-flowing medium, most often water, in which even small solid particles can be carried. The rate of natural corrosion is amplified by the flowing medium, which results in disruption of the passive layer. This creates various grooves, ripples, drop depressions, etc.

This degradation mechanism is manifested by a rapid weakening of the thickness of the pipe walls in places of turbulent flow, i.e. in places of high swirl with locally increased flow speed (diaphragms, nozzles, valves, cross-section reduction, elbows, etc.).

At present, flow-accelerated corrosion is a well-known form of degradation for low alloy and carbon steels, but changing water chemistry and flow conditions, as longer service life and exposure to FAC conditions may increase susceptibility and exacerbate FAC in elbows. Predictive models based on empirical observation or mechanistic understanding have been developed in the Europe, Japan and the United States. These complex interdependences between material, chemistry and hydrodynamics have been successfully modelled in the form of computer codes allowing estimations and predictions that lead to a safer and more economical operation, like COMSY (Germany) [190], CHECWORKS (EPRI) [191], or BRT-CICERO (EDF) [192], which have a very good prediction rate in identifying susceptible areas and orienting the UT inspection programme to those areas.

However, recent OPEX related to SGs (e.g. for VVER a heterogeneous weld joint affected by FAC and for CANDU the primary moisture separator degradation) show that longer operational time and changing operating conditions can lead to unwanted evolutions in some areas.

For instance, in a VVER-440, it is mainly a feed water nozzle and the subsequent part of the feed water distribution from carbon steel inside the SG to a heterogeneous weld joint that is affected by FAC.

Recently two-phase FAC have caused severe degradation of primary moisture separator vane cover of several CANDU SGs and resulted in costly replacement. The primary moisture separator was made from carbon steel with low Cr content. Foreign objects were generated, entered tube bundles and resulted in tube fretting damage.

### *4.4.2.5 Damage of the weld joint area between the SG shell and primary headers*

This is a specific degradation of the VVER-1000 SGs in Temelin Nuclear Power Plant, for which three main causes of the pocket area with a DN1 200 weld joint damage are known:

- High level of stress due to the prevention of free thermal expansion of the main circulation pipeline. VVER-1 000 MW SGs are not oriented perpendicularly to the main circulation pipeline axis, but at an angle of 27° between the main circulation pipeline axis and the SG axis. During unit start-up, the thermal expansion of the hot branch of the main circulation pipeline will induce supplementary loads.
- The corrosion environment in the closed pockets of the primary SG headers from trapped corrosion products (in pockets) and the susceptibility of 10GN2MFA steel to corrosion cracking.
- Frequent temperature changes in the lower part of the SG. Since the first start-up of the Temelin Nuclear Power Plant blocks, unusual temperature of the medium in

the lower part of the SG casing was observed during the start-up of the blocks and during power changes.

The cause of the damage in the DN1 200 weld area lies in the specific properties of the 10GN2MFA steel. The research of the chemical composition of 10GN2MFA steel and related properties was made [193]. It was found that cohesive strength of the steel and susceptibility to deformation embrittlement may be significantly reduced. Experimental work has shown that at five percent plastic deformation, the critical brittleness temperature shifts by up to 30°C. At a higher level of plastic deformation, the critical temperature shift is significantly higher, up to 60°C.

### *4.4.2.6 Transport of corrosion products and deposits build up*

Transport of corrosion products and other impurities that contributes to deposits and the formation of hard sludge on tubes, tube sheet and internal structures have been identified as the main technical issue for the SG secondary side.

Hard sludge on the Top of the Tube-sheet (TTS) can cause SG tubing corrosion or other degradation mechanisms. Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant has experienced TTS denting in areas with hard sludge in one SG. Deposit on tubes reduces the thermal efficiency and that deposit buildup on internal structures could result in tube wear and water level oscillations.

US NRC has no scientific safety concerns with the physical ageing of SGs related to operating beyond 60 years of service.

The Atomic Energy Association (ATENA) systematically reviewed the US practices on subsequent licence renewal and tried to find a gap from the Japanese Plant Life Management technical review based on the AESJ-SC-P005 standard[16](#page-127-0). The results published as ATENA 21-ME01 Rev.0[17](#page-127-1) are listed on pages 21 and 32:

- on page 21, Table 2.1.1-2 (5) PWR SG (Chanel Head and Tube Sheets);
- on page 32, Item 11-Thinning-Corrosion-Boric corrosion.

Regarding the SG, ATENA pointed out that Japanese practices may overlook the potential of BAC in channel head and tube sheets, made of ferric steels. Due to the immediate repairing (mechanical plug) of the damaged tube, potential of this degradation is low. Periodical monitoring by observation would be enough. This finding will be reflected in the AESJ-SC-P005.

### *4.4.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### *4.4.3.1 Eddy current testing (ECT)*

VVER SGs had not been designed for ECT, which is the usual testing method in SGs of western PWRs. Moreover, their supplier provided neither adequate methodology and criteria nor equipment for planning and implementing ISI. Consequently, VVER SG ISI infrastructure was established with a delay. Even today, there are still big differences in the eddy current inspection strategy and practice as well as in the approach to SG heat

<span id="page-127-0"></span><sup>16</sup> AESJ (2021), *Code on Implementation and Review of Nuclear Power Plant Ageing Management Programs: 2021*(*AESJ-SC-P005E:2021)*, [www.aesj.net/publish-2305.](http://www.aesj.net/publish-2305)

<span id="page-127-1"></span><sup>17</sup> ATENA (2022), ATENA 21-ME01 Rev.0, [www.atena](http://www.atena-j.jp/report/docs/e8737b82a1c5058a68b01bd3bf5e96c67e7fd4a1.pdf)[j.jp/report/docs/e8737b82a1c5058a68b01bd3bf5e96c67e7fd4a1.pdf.](http://www.atena-j.jp/report/docs/e8737b82a1c5058a68b01bd3bf5e96c67e7fd4a1.pdf)

exchanger tube structural integrity assessment (plugging criteria for defective tubes vary from 40 to 90% wall thickness degradation).

As a consequence, the IAEA co-ordinated a research project on Verification of VVER Steam Generator Tube Integrity, documented in TECDOC-1 577 Strategy for Assessment of VVER Steam Generator Tube Integrity [186], the results of a probabilistic safety assessment of the SG tube integrity using Monte-Carlo methodology, to predict the probability of tube bursts and to establish the tube plugging criteria.

However, maintaining structural integrity of VVER SG tubes is a dynamic process which must be performed at every outage considering the latest eddy current or any other new relevant information (for example from new pulled tube(s), forced shutdowns, operational events, etc.). Therefore, the prerequisite for efficient structural integrity monitoring is the use of advanced qualified eddy current inspection equipment, probes, and inspection personnel. Without these an effective structural integrity monitoring is not possible, as nonqualified equipment, probes and personnel lead to poor quality data and results which consequently may lead to misinterpretation of real situation and ultimately jeopardise the nuclear power plant operation.

### *4.4.3.2 Phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT)*

PAUT is a technique that offers many advantages compared to conventional UT methods. PAUT is a fully code-compliant UT method developed to test welds and materials accurately, efficiently and comprehensively in various industrial sectors in lieu of radiographic testing (RT) and other conventional UTs.

PAUT provides significant advantages over single-probe concepts and conventional radiography. These include:

- improved defect detection;
- rapid component coverage;
- compliance with inspection codes;
- the ability to have all data be digitally saved and stored for weld-record retention and analysis as well as future repeatable inspections for in-service applications.

A recent study about PAUT efficiency, as compared to the traditional round robin tests (RRT), was performed in Korea in 2022. It was an empirical study to evaluate the applicability of the PAUT technique to the inspection of boiler tube welds in thermal power plant facilities. The specimens of boiler tube welds were designed and fabricated with different materials (carbon steel, austenitic stainless steel, and dissimilar metals), and a reliability assessment was performed on data acquired through an RRT for various flaw types and materials.

The conclusion is: "The PAUT method significantly outperformed RT for planar flaws, but in the case of volumetric flaws it missed a flaw" (see [194]).

Array probes are being used more in the ISI programmes because the inspection speed is higher than that for the rotating probes that have been historically used in regions where bobbin probes have a lower probability of detection. More research is needed so that a correlation between the array probe inspection results and the rotating probes can be validated, allowing for the extensive inspection history with rotating probes to be used in the future. This topic is the subject of US NRC and EPRI sponsored research.

### *4.4.3.3 Time-of-flight diffraction (ToFD)*

ToFD was developed in the nuclear industry for monitoring cracks, being widely used in pressure vessels and thick-walled pipes as it demonstrated real time savings during construction and maintenance programmes and provides an excellent base line for future inspections. International acceptance criteria, codes and standards now include the facility to use TOFD. More details on the advantages and disadvantages of ToFD can be found in TUV's presentation Time of Flight Diffraction (ToFD) High Precision Weld Inspection [195].

However, the ToFD inspection technique has some limitations due to its operating principle and is related to the thickness of the material being inspected. "Consequently, the beam does not reach completely the work piece to be inspected, due to the limitation of the width of the ultrasonic beam. The internal region from which no diffraction pattern could be generated is known as the dead zone. Any discontinuity within this dead zone will not be detected, jeopardising the reliability of the inspection as a whole" (according to the paper: "A metrological approach to the time-of-flight diffraction method" [196]).

A possible solution to overcome the limitations described could be the use of more than one pair of transducers and the variation in probe centre separation (PCS) for the same cross section. However, the use of more than one pair of transducers leads to a higher cost in relation to the variation of PCS, due to the larger number of accessories and devices (transducers and cables, for example).

According to the paper, Section 3 Results and discussion [196]: "It is clear that the ToFD is a suitable technique for the identification of flaws and discontinuities in solid work pieces or equipment. Even scale the depth and height of discontinuities is possible under some circumstances. However, when it is necessary to measure the thickness of a testing object, the pulse-echo technique proves more to be reliable, making it a better test."

### *4.4.3.4. PAUT and ToFD working together*

While also a method of ultrasonic image generation, ToFD relies on a different principle than PAUT. While PAUT uses reflection, ToFD uses diffraction. The transducer produces pulsed ultrasonic waves, which are diffracted to various degrees by irregularities in the scanned material, then collected on the material's far side by a receiver. By analysing the differences in a beam's flight time from the transducer to the receiver, the instrument can detect and image the size and location of defects and flaws.

ToFD can find defects regardless of their orientation, which makes it an ideal complementary technology to PAUT. However, like PAUT, ToFD has certain imaging weaknesses. If only a single scan is made, technicians may encounter a lateral wave dead zone, off-axis errors, timing errors, and resolution errors. To gain a complete image of defects, it's necessary for technicians to use phased array techniques to vary beam width, angle, and point of entry. When ToFD imaging is used with phased array technology, technicians will be certain they have identified any weaknesses in the object being scanned.

To achieve rapid, accurate scans of welds, pipes, and other critical metallic components, NDE technicians should use a combination of PAUT and TOFD scanning technologies. Modern, cutting-edge ultrasonic test software, housed in portable equipment, is capable of compiling composite images from these dual technologies, to provide the most detailed picture of object interiors possible.

Adopting a combined scanning regimen significantly lowers the risk of missing defects and resulting equipment failures. To conclude, PAUT and ToFD are more effective working together than alone by compiling composite images from these dual technologies.

### *4.4.3.5. Guided wave ultrasonic testing (GWUT)*

As assessed and concluded in the paper "Review of Current Guided Wave Ultrasonic Testing (GWUT) Limitations and Future Directions" [197], there are two limitations that eliminate GWTU from the potential NDE advanced technologies for SG inspection:

- study on the effect of crack or breathing crack in a corroded area on GWUT parameters under varying temperature influences is yet to be studied;
- damage detection in the dynamic stressed thin plate under the influence of thermomechanical condition has not been explored using GWUT.

Most metallic structures are subjected to dynamic stress and environmental conditions while in service. These two conditions are detrimental to damage detection in structures using GWUT. Leveraging the potentialities of GWUT for structure health inspection, determining the effect of these combined conditions is significant in deciding damage severity, location, and orientation in a structure.

Understanding the dynamics of these challenges with respect to ultrasonic guided waves will open a new research discussion. The solution will increase the effectiveness of GWUT in achieving informed and reliable damage detection in metallic assets.

No new testing methods have been identified for the tubes on the secondary side of the SG, but the scope of the visual inspection of the tube bundle and deposit mapping with ECT needs to be expanded.

Use/install temperature monitoring to increase knowledge about conditions and how current operation affects structural integrity in different locations for e.g. feedwater, auxiliary feedwater.

As of this report's publication, there are no concerns regarding inspection methods and their efficiency in detecting ageing effects in the Swiss nuclear power plants. The scope of ageing management for KKB Unit 1 and 2 includes the SGs and the connecting pipes from the SGs to the reactor.

It is based on a review of the thermal-hydraulic ageing mechanisms. Fatigue monitoring (nozzles are instrumented with thermos-couples and integrated in the fatigue monitoring system) is standard. Other inspection methods include:

- ECT to determine the weakening of the SG tubes wall thickness;
- indirect VT by camera system;
- UT (phased array and TOFD);
- penetrant testing (PT) (Nozzles, Safe End);
- magnetic particle testing (MT) (nozzles outer surface, calotte round welds, manholes, support brackets).

Based on the operational experience at CEZ, the quality of controls performed and their results, the current approach to ensuring safe operation of the SGs in Czech nuclear power plants is considered adequate and striving for continuous improvement.

However, for the future needs, it would be useful to have some inspection method for more precise control of the threaded holes of the SG. Such a method could be the photogrammetry. Using this method, the robotic manipulator with camera would be put inside the threaded hole and would take many pictures of its surface. Then, these pictures would be digitally processed and evaluated. This method could offer higher precision of the record, higher repeatability, and the possibility to identify trends. Using this method, better information can be obtained about the potential pitting and surface corrosion inside the threaded holes, which cannot be easily repaired or replaced.

The other inspection method that could be enhanced is the indirect endoscopic control of the internal space of the SG. Nowadays, the internal space is controlled at the defined checkpoints, like spots. In the future, it would be more useful to inspect the vaster area of the internal space due to the free deposits. It can float inside the SG, or it could stay on the spot that is not controlled. Therefore, there is a lower chance to see/find the deposits when the control is performed only at the defined spots. For this enhancement, some robotic manipulator able to move inside the SG would be needed.

Beside the above-mentioned controls, the eddying current control with rotational probe could be useful in the future. This method could be used for control of the heat transfer tubes integrity; however, this is performed on the outer surface of the tube (from the secondary side of the SG).

### *4.4.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

In some cases, mitigation of fatigue can occur through improved operational procedures or equipment replacement to reduce transient occurrences or severity, for example mitigation of thermal shock in SG feeding, through replacement of feed water valves by better controlled ones. Mitigation of thermal stratification can be performed by hardware modifications (for instance the replacement of feed water valves for better feeding of the SGs) or by modification in operational regimes during startup and shutdown when thermal stratification may occur (IAEA AMP 101 Low cycle Fatigue [198]).

To be able to manage the ageing effects of the SGs secondary side connected to deposits, chemical cleanings need to be performed one or several times during the remaining time of operation. The condensate polishing, blowdown and other systems that reduce or remove corrosion products and other impurities have been identified also as important for LTO and projects to restore or improve the functions of these systems need to be implemented.

There are some design issues that have caused extensive numbers of tubes that have experienced tube-to-tube support wear; however, this mechanism is well understood and is being managed with inspection and plugging as necessary.

Some SGs have components in the upper steam drum (primary and secondary moisture separation equipment) that are susceptible to FAC. There are inspection techniques and repair options available to manage this degradation. The primary repair for flawed SG tubing is mechanical plugging. These plugs are also made with advanced material such as Alloy 690 and have a long history with no cracking or leakage. Sleeving, which is installing a tube inside a tube, is also an available repair method.

If SGs need to be replaced for the plant to operate beyond 60 years, there are design and manufacturing organisations that can accomplish this. The new SGs that will be in service world-wide beyond 60 years have advanced material such as Alloy 690, 800, or stainless tubing that has proven to be resistant to cracking.

When all the above repair solutions are exhausted, the last option to ensure safe operation beyond 60 years remains the SG replacement. As numerous SGs have been replaced to date, extensive guidance is available in NP-T-3.2 "Heavy Component Replacement in Nuclear Power Plants: Experience and Guidelines" [147]. For instance, in Japan five of the twelve operating PWR plants have experienced SG replacement. In April 2024, Takahama Unit 3 and Unit 4 (Kansai EPC) officially announced that they will replace all six SGs soon, but more as a strategic decision than due to degradation.

The entire range of SG replacement work presents a complex technical problem. Its complexity is due to the fact that during the processing of the layout solution of the reactor block with VVER-440 reactors, there was no presumption of the SG replacement. As a consequence, it is necessary to ensure high work efficiency during the replacement of the damaged SG, mainly due to the length of the shutdown and collective radiation doses for workers. SG replacement for nuclear power plants with VVER 1 000 reactors is carried out by pulling the SG out of its location to the reactor hall and further by lowering the dismantled SG into the transport corridor and transporting the new SG in an inclined position through the transport opening, which relates to the need to dismantle the closed hatch of the transport opening.

Replacing the SG also requires the dismantling of a significant amount of thermomechanical equipment, pipes, and steel structures of the block hermetic zone. The issues of disassembly and subsequent installation of SG must be solved in the technological documentation file.

To perform SG exchange with minimum block outage length and minimum radiation dose received by the maintenance personnel, the effectiveness of the main measures to reduce labour strength costs and doses received costs must be assessed.
