An appropriate technological equipment and decontamination procedure must be available.

The US NRC has no scientific safety concerns with the current repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions for managing the ageing effects in SGs related to operating beyond 60 years of service.

To be able to manage the ageing effects of the SGs secondary side connected to deposits, chemical cleanings need to be performed one or several times during the remaining time of operation. The condensate polishing, blow down and other systems that reduce or remove corrosion products and other impurities have been identified as important for LTO. Projects to restore or improve the functions of these systems need to be implemented soon (<5 years).

In Switzerland, during the yearly outage of Gösgen Nuclear Power Plant (PWR- three loops) in June 2022, the utility performed a scheduled eight-yearly in-service visual inspection of the SG cladding of the primary-side in and outlet. Three cracks were identified in the horizontal weldment (Filler Metal Alloy 82/182) between the tube sheet plate cladding (Alloy 182) and the divider plate (AISI 347) of the SG 2. The cracks did not extend through the wall, but their depth was unknown at this time. The cracking showed the characteristics of PWSCC. It is unclear how old the cracking is, since this area of the SG bottom dome was first visually inspected with a qualified remote controlled camera system during the outage in 2022.

Due to the findings in SG 2, the SG bottom domes of the other two SGs were consequently also visually inspected using the same remote controlled camera system. No indications for cracking were found. However, the cracking detected in the weldment of the SG 2 divider plate of Gösgen Nuclear Power Plant is the first of its kind for Siemens KWU units worldwide. Similar indications were found in some French nuclear power plants, but the design has significant differences (curved vs flat divider plate, stub runner).

The cracks were successfully removed during the 2023 outage by electrical discharge machining. The maximum depth was less than 18 mm. The remaining local wall thickness is sufficient, according ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC) Section III. A proven action is the plugging of defective or significantly weakened heat pipes. Some of the loose foreign objects on the secondary side could be removed. The cleaning of the tube sheets on secondary side is performed in a two-year interval.

The SGs have been replaced in numerous Westinghouse PWRs, including in Beznau Nuclear Power Plant in 1993 (Unit 1) and 1999 (Unit 2).

### *4.4.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

The latest version of the PWR IMT, Section 4.2.5 [47] includes an assessment of the knowledge of ageing plant material degradation that identifies and prioritises key knowledge gaps that should be addressed to better support proactive management of PWR SGs.

For SGs, the key remaining gaps include assessment gaps (e.g. SG tube and internals wear and HCF, denting and SCC in SG top of tube sheet region, SG tube damage due to loose parts or foreign objects, ODSCC of alloy 600 tubing, SG sludge deposits and scale buildup), mitigation gaps (e.g. ODSCC mitigation via water chemistry control, extended lay up of SGs), and inspection and examination gaps (e.g. ECT improvements, NDE tools for tube integrity assessments, foreign object detection and evaluation improvements). These gaps are the subject of ongoing research at EPRI.

For example, EPRI's Steam Generator Management Programme (SGMP) has guidance in place that will be sufficient for operating past 60 years. The guidelines are reviewed periodically to determine the need for revision based on current technology or OPEX. To sum up, these are the most relevant examples:

- ECT is the primary method for inspection of SG tubing. The EPRI PWR Steam Generator Examination Guidelines, currently Revision 8, 3 002 007 572, published in June 2016 provides guidance for performing SG tube inspections, including validation of NDE systems to detect and size flaws. It also contains requirements for qualification of techniques and personnel.
- The EPRI Steam Generator Integrity Assessment Guidelines, currently Revision 5, 3 002 020 909, published in December 2021, provides guidance for assessing the degradation identified during an inspection and covers the primary side as well as the secondary side components.
- EPRI's Primary-to-Secondary Leak Guidelines, currently Revision 5, published in December 2020, provides operators with guidance for monitoring for primary-tosecondary leakage, including actions to take in response to leakage.
- EPRI's PWR Primary Water Chemistry Guidelines, currently Revision 7, 3 002 000 505, published April 2014 and Secondary Water Chemistry Guidelines, currently Revision 8, 3 002 010 645, published September 2017, provide guidance to ensure state-of-the-art water chemistry programmes that ensure the integrity of the RCS materials.

Based on all the above information, it can be concluded that there are no high-priority gaps in research for SGs for LTO.

The AMP represents an essential, systematic expansion of the existing maintenance programmes in the Swiss nuclear power plants and is continually updated. In particular, the ageing mechanisms for safety relevant SSCs are identified by ageing management. Based on this, existing inspection and test programmes, especially preventative maintenance, are reviewed to determine whether ageing-induced degradation can be avoided or detected at an early stage. Any gaps revealed by the review can be closed in an accountable manner. As of this report's publication, no gaps were identified for LTO.

According to the current international ageing management practice and ageing effects identified to date, the following actions could be considered to address potential gaps for operation beyond 60 years:

- 1. Detailed procedures for the repair of the threaded holes of the hot and cold headers, and of the side manholes for the horizontal SG of the VVER-440 and VVER-1 000 MW nuclear power plants.
- 2. Detailed procedures for the replacement of VVER-1 000 MW SGs.
- 3. Detailed procedures focused on the secondary side cleaning using robotic manipulators. Based on the indirect endoscopic visual controls of the internal space of the secondary side of the SG, deposits used to be found on the surface of the heat transfer tubes inside the SG. The amount will be probably rising over time. Implementation of such cleaning robotic manipulators may enhance the heat transfer efficacy and extend the operational time span of the SG. Such cleaning procedures should be considered for both types of SG – VVER-440 and 1 000-MW, as well.
- 4. Optimisation of the crevice chemistry, or water chemistry of the secondary circuit. Secondary water chemistry has major influence on the amount of the deposits developed inside the SG, and on the conditions developed in the SG crevices. In the crevices, there is a high risk of corrosion development.
- 5. Conservation under nitrogen atmosphere during the outage to secure the internal space from the oxygen and developing atmospheric corrosion, preventing SG from the accelerated ageing. This should be considered for the SGs of the VVER-440 and VVER-1 000 MW nuclear power plants.
- 6. Research on transport of corrosion products and other impurities that contributes to deposits and the formation of hard sludge on the TTS and can cause SG tubing corrosion or other degradation mechanisms (TTS Denting). Deposits on tubes reduce the thermal efficiency and increase the risk that deposit buildup result in tube wear and water level oscillations.
- 7. Management of SGs' secondary side deposits through chemical cleaning performed one or several times during the remaining time of operation, enhanced condensate polishing, blow down and other systems that reduce or remove corrosion products and other impurities. Projects to restore or improve the functions of these systems need to be implemented soon (<5 years).
- 8. More research to validate a correlation between the array probe inspection results and the rotating probes, allowing for the extensive inspection history with rotating probes to be used in the future. This topic is the subject of US NRC and EPRI sponsored research.
- 9. More research on ODSCC in Alloy 800 NG tubing, as has been reported in some European SGs. It is anticipated that Alloy 800 tubing in CANDU SGs is also susceptible to ODSCC, especially at the expansion area near TTS. Activation energy for crack initiation and tensile stress due to tube expansion and potential denting due to hard sludge are key inputs for predicting the occurrence of cracks and providing risk-informed guidance for ISI.
- 10. More research to correlate flow velocities, foreign object shape and fretting rate. Foreign object-induced tube leakage has been observed in CANDU SGs. Integrity evaluation of tube damage due to foreign objects remains a challenge due to lack of test data specifically measured for CANDU SG design and operating conditions.

Per current practice and OPEX, the replacement of SGs has been feasible and well managed in many nuclear power plants aiming to operate beyond 40 years. However, life cycle management strategies could find significant cost savings, if attention is paid to:

- low-cost, low-exposure SG conservation methods;
- potential issues that are not currently visible (e.g. thermal ageing of weld metal over very long periods of time).

### <span id="page-135-0"></span>**4.5. Safety Class 1 piping**

### *4.5.1. Description of safety Class 1 piping*

Safety Class 1 systems contain fluid that directly transports the heat released by the fuel and whose failure leads to a LOCA of a magnitude that cannot be compensated for by systems relating to normal plant operation.

Safety Class 1 systems are designed to withstand high pressure, high velocities, high loads, and transient stresses, in accordance with ASME Section III, Section NB-3 000, which necessitates superior materials in terms of stress resistance for pressure boundary components. Safety Class 1 systems contain a multitude materials and manufacturing techniques, therefore several different ageing degradation mechanisms are applicable.

CASS are currently used in a variety of applications in both BWRs and PWRs including reactor coolant and auxiliary system piping, reactor coolant pump casings, reactor coolant valve bodies and fittings (EMDA, Volume 2 [43], Section 6).

### **Pressurised water reactors (PWRs)**

PWR Safety Class 1 pipelines cover:

- The primary loop:
  - ‒ MCL, connecting primary components with DMW, ensure the coolant flow from RPV to SG, then to reactor coolant pump and finally back to RPV. Each MCL is divided into a hot leg, a crossover leg and a cold leg which is composed of welded straight pipes and five elbows;
  - ‒ the surge line, which connects the pressuriser to the hot leg.
- The safety Class 1 auxiliary lines:
  - ‒ Safety Class 1 auxiliary lines ensure the coolant flow between primary components and connected safety systems. Their internal diameter is greater than or equal to two. Auxiliary pipes are safety Class 1 until the second isolation valve;
  - ‒ nozzles connecting the surge line and auxiliary lines to the MCL;
  - ‒ homogeneous welds connecting the above-mentioned components.
- Safety Class 1 pipes are manufactured with two types of SS:
  - ‒ wrought or stamped parts are made from austenitic stainless steels;
  - ‒ cast parts such as primary loop pipes, elbows and nozzles are made from Cast Austenitic-ferritic Stainless Steel (CASS).

Almost all safety class one pipelines are replaceable without major difficulty, except for cold leg primary loop elbows directly connected to RPV (called E-type elbows or Eelbows). The following subsections will therefore focus on CASS E-elbows because they constitute a major issue for LTO.

### **Boiling water reactors (BWRs)**

For BWR-type reactors the recirculation system, feedwater system and the main steam system mainly belong to the safety Class 1 piping.

In Sweden, the division is performed as per the provisions of the code ANS-52.1, edition 1983 for BWR plants and ANSI/ANS 51.1, edition 1983 for PWR plants.

According to the guideline ENSI-G01 all SSC of the pressure boundary up to and including the second isolation valve belong to the safety class one piping. Small diameter piping for measuring, drainage, and deaeration is considered as well.

### **Pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs)**

For PHWR designs, the main heat transport system includes the primary heat transport system (PHTS) and the auxiliary systems meet the definition of a safety Class 1 piping. In CANDU designs there are two loops in PHTS, each loop containing two pumps, two SGs, two reactor inlet headers, two reactor outlet headers, hundreds of fuel channels with their inlet and outlet feeders. Two lines connect reactor outlet header to a SG, connected further to a pump by a single suction line. Each pump delivers heavy water to one reactor inlet header through two lines.

Auxiliary systems act in conjunction with primary heat transport system to ensure that the design requirements of PHTS are satisfied. Auxiliary systems include a pressure and inventory control system, purification system and chemistry control system, shutdown cooling system, and emergency core cooling system. Large diameter CANDU primary heat transport system piping was fabricated from carbon steel SA-106 Grade B.

The feeders transporting heavy water (D2O) coolant to and from the fuel channels to cool the fuel bundles in the pressure tubes are integral part of the primary circuit in CANDU/PHWR reactors. CANDU feeders are carbon steel piping typically ranging from 4 to 10 cm (1.5 to 3.5 inches) nominal pipe size (NPS), configured in a combination of bends (external angles from 21° to 90°) and a straight pipe, with flow measuring elements made of Alloy 600 installed on certain outlet and inlet feeders by DMW.

The feeder pipes operate in an environment of high primary coolant pressure, temperature and high flow velocity, and are prone to FAC, PWSCC on DMWs connecting flow elements installed at some inlet and outlet feeders, and outside fretting between adjacent feeders (IGALL AMP 140 CANDU/PHWR Feeder piping [199]).

In CANDU reactors, the most susceptible areas for FAC are the elbows on the outlet feeders and Grayloc weld region and the AMP consists of periodic inspections and NDE surveillance activities for wall thinning and cracking, based on the CAN CSAN 285.4 standard requirements.

### *4.5.2. Physical ageing of safety Class 1 piping*

The NEA Component Operational Experience, Degradation & Ageing Programme (CODAP) project was launched in 2011 with the objective to collect information on passive metallic component degradation and failures of the primary system, RPV internals, main process and standby safety systems, and support systems (i.e. ASME Code Class 1, 2 and 3, or equivalent). The sources of information were 80% US databases (INPO, EPIX and CHECKWORKS) events reported between 1970-2012.

As shown by the CODAP report NEA/CSNI/R(2014)6 [200], although most of the piping failures encountered were caused by FAC, the largest population affected by FAC events represents non-code class piping (by ASME III Code Classes) and consists mostly of wall thinning, not leaking, nor cracking.

The PHTS event population consists of small bore (≤ DN100) reactor outlet feeder pipes of cold drawn carbon steel. This event population is unique to PHWR plants.
