### *4.5.2.1 Thermal fatigue*

Thermal fatigue occurrences were considered unanalysed since they are not normally captured in the original design fatigue evaluations (ASME Code, Section III or other). The US NRC issued US NRC Bulletin 88-0 [201] in 1988, which required licensees to evaluate their not isolable sections of piping connected to the RCS and implement a programme to ensure that these branch connections will not be subjected to high cycle thermal fatigue. A critical review of the available history, and inclusion of more recent thermal fatigue events, as of 2021, is documented in MRP-468 [202].

Two specific thermal fatigue mechanisms have been defined by significant research efforts over the past several decades:

- 1. Cyclic stratification induced by swirl penetration of hot RCS fluid into normally stagnant branch piping filled with lower temperature water. Stratification occurs in a horizontal or near horizontal pipe in which there is a sharp temperature difference between the fluid in the upper (hot) and lower (cold) regions of the pipe. Because of this temperature difference, large thermal stresses can be developed in the pipe wall. If the boundary level between the hot and cold fluids changes with time, the pipe will experience thermal stress cycles, which may lead to thermal fatigue cracks in the pipe wall. For the US PWR fleet, the cyclic stratification is managed by guidance provided in MRP-146 [203].
- 2. Thermal mixing of hot/cold fluids merging in piping tees. The resulting rapid temperature fluctuations on the inside surface of mixing tees or attached piping results in thermal cycling that may lead to cracking. For the US PWR fleet, thermal mixing is managed by guidance provided in MRP-192 [204].

Thermal fatigue is generally managed through plant fatigue monitoring systems or through valve in-leakage testing in the United States.

In some European nuclear power plants, thermal loads are determined using a specific fatigue monitoring system (e.g. FAMOS in Borssele Nuclear Power Plant and Gösgen Nuclear Power Plant, WESTEMS in Beznau Nuclear Power Plant, FATIGUE/PRO in Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant), measuring temperatures at fatigue relevant locations. By knowing the actual loads in the plant, excess conservatism in design transients can be reduced and anticipated modifications of operation to reduce fatigue loads can be tested numerically.

Thermal fatigue in dead-ended branch lines (HCF through flow in main pipe) led to numerous fatigue crack growth and leakage events; the last one was in September 2018 at DOEL 1 after 43 years of service, rated Level 2 on INES scale. To address this issue, Framatome and the Materials Testing Institute University of Stuttgart launched in 2024 the TEAR Project, aimed to improve code calculation (KWU-MIX for mixing flows and vortex formation) and to develop a local HCF Farley-Tihange fatigue monitoring approach (FAMOS-F, EMUS) based on artificial intelligence approaches (46th WGIAGE Meeting presentation of TEAR Project "Dead-end branch line" [166]).

However, HCF due to thermal cycling (turbulence penetration or thermal stratification) are design/location dependent phenomena and, generally well-characterised, and no additional research is needed. Although some modelling issues remain unresolved, these are anticipated to be addressed by analysis and not through additional testing.

### *4.5.2.2 Environmentally assisted fatigue (EAF)*

EAF is a degradation mechanism that can impact materials exposed to LWR environments in nuclear power plants. This degradation has been seen in materials when tested for fatigue life and exposed to LWR water chemistry conditions. The relationship between the life of a component and the magnitude and frequency of the cyclic loading is determined within structural codes through the fatigue-life curve, or S-N curve. Historically, the curves were determined by testing in air environments and adjustment factors were applied to account for a variety of effects not explicitly accounted for in the testing. One effect that was not originally explicitly accounted for in testing was exposure to LWR coolant during operation.

In the absence of explicit ASME Code rules to address the possible additional impact of water environments, the US NRC issued guidance based on additional research to address EAF; the guidance consisted of operating plant guidance for operation beyond 40 years in the [GALL Report \(NUREG-1801\)](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/staff/sr1801/index.html) [6], and later in the [Regulatory Guide \(RG\) 1.207](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML0703/ML070380586.pdf) Revision 0 [205], and its supporting technical basis report [NUREG/CR-6](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/contract/cr6909/initial/index.html) 909 for new reactors. The US NRC revised RG 1.207 (Rev. 1) [206] and NUREG/CR-6 909 (Rev. 1) [188] in 2018 to apply to both new and operating reactors, and GALL guidance for operation beyond 60 years, documented in NUREG-2 191 [8].

In 2005, based on a risk study reported in NUREG/CR-6 674, the US NRC concluded that reactor water environmental effects were not a safety issue for a 60 year operating life, but that some limited assessment of its effect would be required for a licence renewal extended operating period beyond 40 years (according to EPRI MRP-47, Revision 1 [207]). The EPRI document provides guidelines for performing environmental fatigue assessments using fatigue environmental factors from currently accepted Fen methodology, based on industry experience, consensus, and insight gained from the experience of licence renewal approval process. The guideline shows that NUREG/CR-6 260 [208] locations are considered an appropriate sample for Fen evaluation if none exceed the acceptance criteria with environmental effects considered. If this occurs, the sampling is to be extended to other locations for which similar evaluations to those conducted in NUREG/CR-6 260 [208] are required. In the extended operating period, fatigue monitoring is used for the sample of locations to show that ASME Code limits are not exceeded. If these limits are exceeded, corrective actions are identified for demonstrating acceptability for continued operation.

Later, to better understand the applicability of the available fatigue rules and EAF guidance, in 2018 EPRI re-assessed the documented 47 knowledge gaps from previous reports since 2011 for their progress status and documented this analysis in EPRI report 3 002 013 214 "Update and Revision of the EAF Knowledge Gaps" [209]. Using observations from these advanced experimental studies, partial explanation for the observed discrepancy between the predictions from Fen-based models and plant component field experience, improved predictive models have been developed that provide a better description of the observed behaviour in these recent laboratory tests. Based on a review of these data, a shorter list of 16 outstanding gaps is available in EPRI report 3 002 013 214 [209]. However, full validation for plant-representative component geometries and loading histories was not available yet.

In 2020, EPRI issued the technical bases and processes for three EAF screening methods for use in nuclear power plants in EPRI report 3 002 018 262 "Environmentally Assisted Fatigue Screening Methods", Revision 1 [210]. It provided three screening methods to identify appropriate limiting locations for systematic management of EAF effects on Class 1 reactor coolant pressure boundary components wetted with primary coolant. These methods will enable plant owners to demonstrate knowledge of the locations in their plants that can serve as locations requiring EAF management to satisfy long-term operation EAF guidance. The EAF screening methods also provide the rationale for selecting these locations, so that plant owners can minimise costs by avoiding the necessity of formal fatigue analyses, while still meeting the regulatory requirements to determine those EAF locations for explicit fatigue evaluation and/or management.

For BWRs, accurately accounting for the effects of environment on fatigue usage associated with primary system pressure boundary components remains a significant knowledge gap with increasing importance beyond 60 years.

Susceptibility is strongly affected by oxygen concentration, temperature, and Ph. Detailed information can be found in EPRI BWR and PWR guidelines: BWRVIP-351 "BWR Vessel and Internals Project\_ Type 304 Stainless Steel Base Material Intergranular Stress Corrosion Cracking Morphology Evaluation" [211], and MRP-386 for PWR: "Recommended Factors of Improvement for Evaluating Primary Water Stress Corrosion Cracking (PWSCC) Growth Rates of Thick-Wall Alloy 690 Materials and Alloy 52, 152 and Variants Welds" [121].

To sum up, the effect of LWR environments on fatigue behaviour in RCS structural materials has been an issue for decades among nuclear industries and safety regulators, particularly for the 60 years design life of advanced LWRs. In 2007, the US NRC issued RG 1.207 [205] for use in the design analyses of new reactors, incorporating the fatigue life reduction of pressure boundary components because of the LWR environment. As such, fatigue analysis is performed now considering the effects of LWR environments on carbon and low alloy steels, austenitic stainless steels and Ni–Cr–Fe alloys.

The draft for public comment of Rev. 1 of NUREG-2192 proposes to allow use of RG 1.207 Rev. 1 [206], or previous revisions of NUREG/CR-6 909. However, this is still somewhat of an evolving technical area. The US NRC-approved methodologies are very conservative. Additional research on environmental fatigue effects could contribute to reduced conservatism and allow some components to be demonstrated to be acceptable for longer periods of operation.

Currently R&D programmes continue to be developed around the world on EAF. For example, 16 organisations from nine European countries joined efforts in the European Commission Horizon 2020 funded project INCEFA+[18](#page-141-0) to obtain environmental fatigue experimental data points and derive an industrial methodology based on these results (details in IAEA NR-T-3.32, Section 5 [212])). The project ended in 2020, but it was followed by a new project, INCEFA Scale, launched in the same year for a five-year period and gathering 17 members. This new project aims at exploring scale effects in fatigue environmental phenomena, more specifically the challenges of transposition from the laboratory sample to the component scale.

### *4.5.2.3 Thermal embrittlement of cast austenitic stainless steel and welds (ASSW)*

Not all austenitic stainless steel material has the same susceptibility to experiencing a "significant" loss of FT due to thermal ageing embrittlement. The susceptibility of CASS to experiencing a significant loss of FT is related to the chemical composition (chromium and ferrite content), initial mechanical properties, operating time at temperature and casting method of the material. Details on the degradation mechanisms of LWR safety piping's most utilised materials and their vulnerabilities for extended operation beyond 60 years can be found in EMDA, volume 2, Sections 2 – 6 [43].

For instance, in the United States, methods for predicting the FT of thermally aged CASS materials with delta ferrite content up to 25% are provided in NUREG/CR–4 513, Revision 1 [213], since 1994.

Thermal ageing guidance for managing loss of FT of CASS due to thermal ageing embrittlement is provided in the GALL-SLR, XI.M12, which provides a screening methodology to determine the significance of the loss of FT due to thermal embrittlement. The current guidance is based on NUREG/CR-4 513, Rev. 2 [214], which provides lowerbound FT curves as a function of chemistry and ferrite content. The FT curves in NUREG/CR-4 513, Rev. 1[19](#page-141-1) are mostly based on materials aged in the laboratory at 400 degrees C for 10 000 hours. These results may not be bounding for very long operating times.

The US NRC would also like to obtain in-plant aged CASS materials to confirm the laboratory results. ASSWs are subject to a similar loss of FT due to thermal embrittlement as CASS. US NRC-sponsored research on thermal embrittlement of ASSW is contained in NUREG/CR-6 428, Rev. 1 [215]. Lower bound J-R curves for thermally aged material have been developed for welds made by different processes. The lower-bound curves in NUREG/CR-6 428 [215] are not endorsed in any US NRC guidance.

A model correlating aged FT with chemistry and ferrite content has not been developed for ASSW. Also, there is a greater degree of variability in the unaged (as-welded) properties for these welds. The US NRC would like to obtain more FT data to confirm the NUREG/CR-6 428, Rev. 1 [215] lower bound curves. In addition, the ASME Code, Section XI flaw evaluation procedures do not currently account for thermal ageing of ASSW.

In France, formulae were developed to predict the loss of FT due to the thermal ageing of all CASS components, which was made possible due to the large experimental database built at EDF/R&D since the 1980s. This database covers a large set of representative

<span id="page-141-0"></span><sup>18</sup> European Commission (n.d.), INcreasing Safety in NPPs by Covering gaps in Environmental Fatigue Assessment, [https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/662320.](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/662320)

<span id="page-141-1"></span><sup>19</sup> GALL-SLR, Rev. 1 [8] references NUREG/CR-4513 Rev. 2[7], which is mostly based on the same data.

materials and various ageing conditions up to 200 000 hours, between 285°C and 350°C. To validate these formulae, elbows were removed at the same time as the replacement of SGs and these aged components were studied in hot cells, with their actual properties compared to predictions (IGALL AMP112 [216]). Finite element analysis is performed using the most severe loading conditions and postulated flaws.

CASS pipelines are affected by thermal ageing. Because of its high chromium content, and other elements such as molybdenum and silicon, the ferrite phase present in these materials is subject to a spinodal decomposition which causes hardening. The consequence is a decrease of ductile toughness and tearing resistance with ageing. This mechanism is amplified by molybdenum (Mo) content. Therefore, CASS composition specifications have been improved with time: the initial choice of CF8-M material containing Mo has been abandoned and CF8, which is Mo-free, has been used instead. This modification benefits the whole 1 450 MWe series and most of the 1 300 MWe nuclear power plants.

Aged material properties are predicted by empirical formulae based on a large experimental database. They consider operating time and temperature, material chemical composition, estimated ferrite content and reception mechanical test results. They are applicable for at least 80 years of operation.

In addition to the above-mentioned thermal ageing of CASS, SS weldments with comparatively high ferrite contents are sensitive by the same mechanisms as above. Further, high strength materials, e.g. in bolts and valve stems, are thermally embrittled. Valve stems of 17-4PH that largely have been removed in PWRs are still in use in some BWRs, where operating temperatures are lower. The nickel base Alloy 690 and its weldments are also potentially sensitive to thermal ageing degradation (e.g. EPRI MRP-205 [47] P-DM-13).

A project dedicated to investigations of harvested components from LWRs is the SMILE research project launched in 2021, with the aim of improving and validating the knowledge of materials ageing phenomena and their kinetics, to improve the knowledge of long-term component behaviour. More details about the PWR and BWR materials library, the experimental testing and examination of the aged materials harvested from Oskarshamn 1 &2 (BWR) and Ringhals 2 (PWR) Nuclear Power Plants can be found in the NEA WGIAGE presentation at the 46th Meeting [178].

The Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers (JSME) has also introduced a thermal ageing degradation model for CASS as one of the important ageing management issues to be assessed for Fitness for Service condition, per the JSME Code.

### *4.5.2.4 Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) of SS piping*

As described in EMDA, volume 2 [43]: "Corrosion is a complex form of degradation that is strongly dependent on temperature, material condition, material composition, water purity, water pH, water impurities, and gas concentrations. The operating corrosion mechanism will vary from location to location within the reactor vessel and piping system and several different mechanisms may be operative simultaneously. These may include general corrosion mechanisms such as uniform corrosion, BAC, FAC, and/or erosion corrosion." Material degradation due to these corrosion mechanisms occurs over a reasonably large area in a homogenous manner. By contrast, localised corrosion modes occur over much smaller areas, but at much higher rates than general corrosion and includes crevice corrosion, pitting, and galvanic corrosion.

Finally, EAC includes other forms of degradation, which are assisted by localised or general corrosion with the additional contribution of stress. In an LWR, a number of different environmentally assisted cracking mechanisms are observed: IGSCC, transgranular stress corrosion cracking (TGSCC), PWSCC, IASCC and low-temperature crack propagation.

Stress corrosion crack initiation remains one of the most significant unknowns for potential failure time range prediction in LWR structural alloys, including highly resistant Alloy 690 materials. As discussed in the previous section, surface corrosion/oxidation in PWR primary water is another key aspect but many other materials variables must be considered. It is pertinent to evaluate the influence of microstructure damage due to cold work or surface grinding on SCC nucleation (EMDA, volume 2, Section 4.3.4 Stress Corrosion Crack Growth in Alloy 690 [43]). While the cracked areas could be removed or repaired, their proximity to the RPV material heightened the need for periodic inspection of Alloy 182 welds in the reactor. Improved inspection approaches were developed by the EPRI's BWR Vessel and Internals Project between 1995 and 1998 (EMDA, volume 2, Section 3.4 SCC OPEX of Ni alloys in BWRs [43]).

Service experience has demonstrated that most failures are due to either environmental effects or fatigue due to unanticipated loading conditions, not always encompassed by the plant's ISI programme. Consequently, nuclear plant operators are dedicating significant resources to inspection programmes that have proven to provide minimal benefit. EPRI developed an alternative approach based upon service experience and failure consequence. This risk-informed inspection approach allows for a more focused ISI programme that provides for a significant reduction in the examination scope (and associated costs and man-REM exposure) while continuing to maintain maximum integrity. This approach has been endorsed by the ASME Section XI Code Case N-560 (EPRI TR -110 701 Use of Risk Informed Inspection Methodology for BWR Class 1 Piping [217]).

Starting in October 2021, SCC was discovered in several French PWRs in austenitic stainless steel emergency core cooling system piping connected to the RCS. EDF embarked upon a massive inspection, repair and evaluation campaign in its plants. The US NRC is monitoring this issue and evaluating whether SCC of similar piping could occur in US plants ( [218]).

#### **4.5.2.4.1 Primary water stress corrosion cracking (PWSCC)**

PWSCC has caused cracking of nickel-based alloy full penetration welds and base and weld metal of partial-penetration welded components such as instrument nozzles. The main alloys affected are Alloy 600, 82 and 182. Many components and welds have been replaced with Alloy 690 base metal and Alloy 52 and 152 weld metal.

Numerous repair and mitigation methods have been developed and applied in the United States including weld overlays and inlays, through the mechanical stress improvement process (MSIP). Weld repair techniques and mechanical repair techniques have been developed and applied for instrument nozzles, pressuriser heater sleeves, and reactor vessel head penetrations and vessel nozzles. Inspection and mitigation have been addressed by several ASME code cases, some of which have been approved with conditions by the US NRC, such as Code Case N-770-5 [219] for butt welds made with Alloy 82 or 182, which is required to be implemented with conditions in 10 CFR 50.55a [174].

The most significant remaining technical issue is the cracking susceptibility and crack growth rates for Alloy 690/52/152. The CGR are known to be much slower in Alloy 690/52/152 compared to Alloy 600/82/182; however, the factors of improvement on CGR to be used for flaw analyses used to determine inspection intervals have not been agreed upon between US NRC and industry (represented by EPRI and the Code committees).

Another technical issue is long-term thermal ageing of Alloy 690/52/152 causing long range ordering or other hardening mechanisms could contribute to faster PWSCC CGR in Alloy 690/52/152. US NRC is conducting research in this area.

### **4.5.2.4.2 Intergranular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC)**

IGSCC is a cracking phenomenon which develops along the grain boundaries (a detailed description is provided in Section 4.3.2 of this report). It occurs in austenitic stainless steel (such as 304 SS), under synergistic effects of three factors:

- a susceptible material caused by e.g. sensitisation, cold work, irradiation;
- tensile stress, for instance residual stress near welds;
- an aggressive environment such as BWR NWC, that is high-purity water at ~280°C containing dissolved oxygen.

The initiation of SCC typically requires a long-term incubation period and increased operating time beyond 60 years will increase the likelihood of initiating cracks. Therefore, all influencing drivers of SCC that can be managed by optimal operating conditions, such as water chemistry and cycling of stress/strain by e.g. thermal or mechanical origin should be minimised.

Improvement of any of these factors will be beneficial for the resistance to SCC and use of the latest water chemistry recommendations as stated in e.g. EPRI Water Chemistry Guidelines [EPRI 3 002 000 505 [220], EPRI 3 002 002 623 [221] with revisions], in all regions of the piping (including dead legs), as well as minimising any off chemistry during start-up or shut-down periods.

The prediction of component cracking is advancing with the development of the extremely low probability of rupture (xLPR) code [222] , a state-of-the-art PFM code for piping applications to address PWSCC, but where also prediction of IGSCC will be added to the new version. For the case of SCC initiation, it is a statistical tool and difficult to describe the initiation probability of a specific component.

Recent failures in PWR piping have shown significant cracking of Type 316L stainless steel and such cases occur in the base metal region in the near vicinity of welds where high residual strains and high hardness are encountered (U. Ehrnsten's article in *Journal of Nuclear Materials* in 2020 [223]).

When SCC initiates in material with a cold-worked surface layer, subsequent crack propagation in the annealed material beyond the cold-worked region is slow and can even stop. In general, material work hardening accelerates SCC growth rate. Consequently, when a SCC crack leaves the highly work-hardened surface layer, it slows down. If the material is only susceptible to SCC in the work-hardened state (e.g. SS, hot-rolled Inconel 600 HT, Inconel 690), the SCC crack may stop when leaving the work-hardened layer. This is typically what makes the cracks detected on Inconel 600 HT not very dangerous (see EDF papers presented at Fontevraud [224], [225]).

### However:

- If crack-tip loading is high enough to generate local work-hardening, the crack can continue to propagate in the non-work-hardened zone (in the uncracked state).
- If surface hardening is severe enough to destroy the microstructure, crack initiation may be delayed.
- If compression is combined with surface work-hardening (as in the case of shotpeening material), crack initiation is not possible.

A solution is annealing after fabrication significantly reducing SCC concerns for components with cold-worked regions, but such a step in the fabrication is not always possible to introduce (details in IAEA TECDOC-1 557 PWR Pressure Vessel Internals, Section 5.3.2.1 [149]).

Some open issues relevant to operations beyond 60 years are B-AS-10 and B-DM-09 (see VVER IMT (MRP-471), Table 3-2 [49]) to envelop for initiation of austenitic materials the conditions where initiation occurs and for low alloy steels envelop both initiation and propagation conditions for SCC. For SCC growth rate of SS, issues are for example, high purity NWC data, discrepancies between field and laboratory data, effect of material grades for example, 304L, 316L, Ti-stabilised. Surface and grain boundary properties are likely not significantly aged since the alloys used are generally stable at BWR and PWR operating temperatures. Still, some questions remain since diffusion data below 600°C and especially for cold work or grain boundaries diffusion are limited and for example, cavity formation at grain boundaries indicates some microstructural evolution occurring (EMDA vol.2 [43]).

### *4.5.2.5 Leak before break two-step methodology for pipe integrity assessment*

LBB is a part of the break preclusion concept at Borssele Nuclear Power Plant [226], based on the assumption that a double ended guillotine break of piping is highly unlikely. In particular, the LBB argumentation contains time dependent assumptions regarding the growth of defects. The goal of the review for LTO was to demonstrate that the break preclusion concept, as implemented in 1997, remains valid until 2034.

The LBB demonstration includes two steps of time dependency:

- 1. The time for growth of a surface defect to develop into a through-wall defect the nuclear power plant must be able to operate for 60 years.
- 2. The time for a growth in a through-wall defect to become a critical through-wall defect (only when through-wall defect occurs).

Since no through-wall defect has been detected, this second time dependency always occurs after the first step mentioned above and is therefore not relevant for lifetime extension to 2034. Therefore, the relevance of time dependency in break preclusion of Borssele Nuclear Power Plant for operation until 2034 is concentrated on the first step. The assessment concluded that the time-dependent assumptions in TLAA on LBB are not restricting operation for 60 years (see the paper on NRG's experience in support of nuclear power plant ageing management and LTO [227]).

NRG has made significant progress in the development of LBB models and codes. Under the framework of the R6 development programme, NRG has been working on a probabilistic LBB model. The objective of this work was to obtain a better understanding of the factors that influence the criterion applicability, establish a probabilistic methodology and compare probabilistic results with current deterministic safety factors. The software DeMoT (Deterministic Modular Tool) [228] was created for this purpose. In 2021 DeMoT was discontinued and the new implementation in Python 3 was renamed LETO (LEak before break TOol). NRG also took part in a deterministic CSNI Leak Before Break benchmark organised by the US NRC to test the developed LBB code. In 2023, the deterministic modules of LETO [229] will be compared to the solutions of the other participants and further improved. The NRG development research on weld residual stress effects on LBB evaluations, as well as code modifications for the benchmark, are ongoing (NRG Annual Report 2023, Section 1.2 [87]).

Many US PWRs have LBB analyses that exempt a full break of the RCS main loop piping from having to be considered in design-basis analyses. PWSCC of Alloy 600/82/182 welds was not considered in original LBB analyses, since it was not a degradation mechanism that had occurred when these analyses were developed.

Regarding the pipe integrity assessment, the US NRC developed the xLPR PFM computer code jointly with EPRI. xLPR has been used to evaluate Safety Class 1 piping integrity, including the effects of PWSCC on LBB analyses [230]. Recently, xLPR has been used to evaluate the effect on piping failure risk of cracking similar to the French SCC and thermal ageing of CASS piping.

Deterministic LBB Code AP3 [231] and PFM code PRAISE-CANDU [232] have been developed by AtkinsRéalis for CANDU industry to reclassify large loss of coolant accident break sizes and to exclude some feeder welds from periodic inspection. PFM assessment was supplemental to deterministic LBB assessment to quantify the impact of periodic inspection and systematic treatment of input uncertainties.

In all Swiss PWR nuclear power plants LBB is applied to the main cooling lines to eliminate the double guillotined break as design load case. LLB was not applied for Swiss BWR.

### *4.5.2.6 Flow accelerated corrosion*

FAC is a complex phenomenon exhibiting attributes of corrosion, and often erosion in combination causing wall thinning in carbon and low alloy steels. The factors that influence whether FAC is an issue are velocity, dissolved oxygen, pH, moisture content (in the case of steam), and material composition e.g. chromium and Mo contents. BWR reactors of e.g. Swedish ASEA-Atom design include low alloy steel piping without cladding on both the steam and condensate/feed water sides. Plants with susceptible systems have FAC management programmes in place.

Swiss nuclear power plants, BWRs as well as PWRs, have periodic UT wall thickness measurement programmes for selected parts of the ferritic feedwater and steam piping (secondary piping within the containment is Class 1 in Switzerland) but also other piping that is assumed to be most susceptible to FAC and/or erosion. The outer radii of pipe elbows are the most relevant areas, as this is where the most erosive flow conditions and, due to the manufacturing process, the thinnest wall thicknesses can be found. These programmes were initiated after an incident in Surry-2 Nuclear Power Plant in 1986. The measurement positions are marked on the outer surface (180° circumference, full elbow length) of the pipes with a coloured dot grid to ensure that the locations can be unambiguously reproduced. By comparing measurements from different periods, it is possible to identify potential problems at an early stage, initiate countermeasures in a timely manner and establish a trend to predict the future development of the wall thickness.

There have been no signs of increased erosion to date. Some underruns of the nominal wall thicknesses discovered in the past at one plant were due to the manufacturing process, not to ageing. BWRs are using hydrogen water chemistry combined with noble metal injection. This ensures a low electrochemical CP, primary to prevent SCC, but a beneficial effect on FAC is expectable too (low oxygen level).

For PWR and BWR designs, recent recommendations for an Effective Flow-Accelerated Corrosion Programme are available in the EPRI Report NSAC-202L-R4 [233]. The report gives relevant information for FAC tasks for identifying susceptible systems, performing FAC analysis, selecting and scheduling components for inspection, assessing inspection data, and determining the remaining service life for worn components. The report also gives advice on a long-term strategy in relation to primary water chemistry (such as the effect of pH, hydrazine and amines on FAC for PWR plants, or of oxygen content on BWR plants).

A large diameter CANDU primary heat transport system piping was fabricated from carbon steel SA-106 Grade B. This material is susceptible to FAC. However, field inspections have not observed any noticeable wall loss in piping greater than NPS 8.

As for the PHWR feeder pipes, they are particularly prone to FAC due to their operating environment of high primary coolant pressure, temperature and high flow velocity, as well as to their twisted geometry (multiple elbows and changes in flowpath direction). In CANDU reactors the most susceptible areas for FAC are the elbows on the outlet feeders and Grayloc weld region.

A comprehensive programme for chemistry control, inspection, monitoring, and condition assessment is implemented to ensure primary circuit pressure envelope and the fitness for service of the feeder pipes (IGALL AMP 140 Feeder piping [199]).

This AMP includes monitoring and control of the primary coolant pH and O2 values in an optimal range to reduce the wall thinning rate and susceptibility to SCC. It also includes cleaning of the internal surfaces of the SGs tubes and improving the steam quality, leading to a decrease in temperature of the primary coolant at the inlet feeders, which helps in reducing the wall thinning rate and the susceptibility to SCC.

The selection of appropriate feeder pipe material with higher chromium content and tensile strength, and in some cases the use of increased nominal wall thickness, is also applied for replacement feeders or new builds. Stricter controls and improvements in feeder fabrication methods, such as heat treatment of welds and the use of updated bend fabrication methods, reduce the levels of residual stresses, improve the hydrodynamic conditions and reduce ageing degradation in feeder pipes.

### *4.5.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### *4.5.3.1 Ultrasonic examination for cast austenitic stainless steels (CASS)*

UT techniques are well developed for most nuclear power plant applications including carbon steel, wrought stainless steel, austenitic stainless steel and dissimilar metal piping welds. However, UT for CASS has proven to be very challenging due to the coarse grain structure of the material. Extensive research and development have been conducted to develop UT methods for the examination of CASS weldments.

To date, no UT examination techniques for CASS have been able to meet what would likely be the qualification criteria for detection and sizing in the ASME Code, Section XI, Appendix VIII, Supplement 9 [234] (which has been in the course of development since the initiation of Appendix VIII), if the acceptance criteria was modelled after other Appendix VIII acceptance criteria. Industry is completing the development of PFM tools for the evaluation of CASS which will be used to support the development of alternatives to Section XI, IWB-2 500 inspection requirements for CASS piping components, as well as potential changes to IWB-3 514 and IWB-3 640 flaw acceptance and flaw evaluation procedures.

Recently there has been interest and research in use of AI and ML to improve the efficiency of evaluating UT data by providing only the data that include potential flaws signals for evaluation by the qualified analyst.

A scarcity of qualified NDE examiners also exists in the United States. Qualification of examiners is time-consuming and expensive. Tools such as virtual and synthetic flaw technology which will enhance training of personnel and make testing scenarios less costly are being developed by industry and evaluated by the US NRC.

The material microstructure of CASS materials challenges the reliability of ultrasonic examination techniques. As such, the qualification requirements for ultrasonic procedures, personnel, and equipment used for examination of CASS piping in accordance with the ASME BPVC, Section XI, Mandatory Appendix VIII have not been developed.

Based on current research, it has been determined that some of the most difficult challenges for examination of CASS piping components are detection of axial cracks and depth sizing of circumferential cracks.

In addition to the limitations of UT examination, CASS material is subject to thermal ageing, which causes degradation of FT over time. The extent of toughness degradation depends on the delta ferrite (δ-Fe) content of the component. The failure mode of concern for CASS material is growth of a flaw (e.g. a pre-existing fabrication flaw) to a size that could challenge the integrity of the component, given the reduced critical crack size at the lower FT.

Currently, a PFM model for fully aged CASS piping was used to develop tolerable flaw sizes based on various levels of probability of failure. This model has been utilised to generate a series of flaw acceptance limits for the various service level conditions in the ASME Code. ASME Section XI Code Case N-838 has been developed based on PFM methodology for evaluating the effects of ageing and uncertainties in the CF8M CASS piping material properties [235]. This report presents the technical justification for the flaw tolerance evaluation of CASS piping to support ASME Section XI Code Case N-838, "Flaw Tolerance Evaluation of Cast Austenitic Stainless Steel Piping Components," approved by the ASME in 2015.

The credible crack growth mechanism in CASS material exposed to PWR coolant is fatigue cracking, as plant experience and testing show that austenitic stainless-steel material is generally resistant to SCC in PWR environments. The analysis of CASS components for extended operation often focuses on flaw tolerance evaluations, but EPRI has recently published ["Probabilistic Fracture Mechanics Evaluation of PWR Cast Austenitic Stainless](https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002025221)  Steel Piping Components – [Axial Cracking Methods and Results"](https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002025221) [236].

NDE are performed on CASS elbows at the end of manufacturing process to detect potential casting defects. Acceptance criteria of NDE indications are based on ASTM standards. Cracks are not tolerated.

A maintenance strategy has been defined on operating CASS elbows. Material sampling and NDE are performed on the base metal of selected elbows, depending on:

- the material sensitivity to ageing;
- the dimension of NDE indications (if any) on final manufacturing radiographs.

Material sampling makes it possible to check the accurateness of ageing prediction formulae and NDE so that indications do not grow in service.

In addition, the assessment of components' mechanical integrity is based on ductile fast fracture analysis. The steps of this analysis are detailed as follows:

- prediction of the ductile tearing resistance of the aged material (for a given operating life);
- identification of penalising loadings (mechanical and thermal);
- ductile fast fracture analysis considering a severe hypothetical flaw (hypothetical semi-elliptical crack called "reference defect");

• verification of code criteria (risks of initiation and instability): the ductile tearing resistance must be greater than the cracking force, including safety coefficients.

This assessment is applied to various sections of the elbows, including far away from welds. It is very conservative due to several penalising assumptions (the hypothetical flaw) and the demanding criteria (no initiation is required in second and third categories of situations, for all types of loadings including thermal).

### *4.5.3.2 Ultrasonic examinations of dissimilar metal welds (DMWs)*

Although the A600 family of materials is well managed across the fleet with a variety of established inspection strategies, an expanding set of mitigation and repair options, and a proven set of PWSCC-resistant replacement materials (A690, A52, and A152), EPRI continues to address both short and long-term nickel-based alloy degradation management issues.

The primary driver for continued research into the legacy A600 materials is to ensure that inspection regimes, mitigation strategy options, and flaw disposition curves remain current relative to operational experience and laboratory data as long as the materials are in service within the fleet. One of the most recent EPRI guides on performing UT inspections is "Guideline for Conducting Ultrasonic Examinations of Dissimilar Metal Welds", Revision 3 [237]. This report provides enhanced guidance and NEI 03-08 "needed" requirements and "good practice" recommendations for nuclear power plant owners in planning and executing efficient, complete examinations of DMWs. DMW examinations must be implemented in a manner that minimises the probability of significant human errors, improves flaw detection, reduces false calls, and improves the overall quality of the examinations.

However, future research should include understanding the role of fabrication processes on material properties; developing, improving and/or expanding applicability of inspection, repair, and mitigation methodologies; and improving capabilities to analyse phenomena that may impact the integrity of components composed of nickel-based alloys.

Recent events in French nuclear power plants reveal the need for comprehensive inspection methods. The UT inspection of austenitic stainless steel piping welds and dissimilar welds on Swiss PWRs and BWRs is considering both SCC and fatigue as potential failure modes. The used and qualified UT inspection systems vary by application case and nuclear power plant, but their performance in SCC detection is based on enhanced UT signal evaluation.

In general, UT inspection is carried out manually or mechanically. Mechanised inspection is always used for DMW. Conventional UT with a single element probe and PAUT with 2 MHz to 4 MHz transversal UT waves are used in case of dual side accessibility. Longitudinal waves are used in case of single side accessibility. In addition to probes with specific angles (45°, 60° and 70°, 35°-70° for PAUT), probes which are dedicated to high focus on inner surface are also applied. The TOFD is not in use.

The applied "state-of-the art" UT inspection systems are able to detect SCC defects with a depth extension of > 10% of the wall thickness. The smallest detectable depth extension is 2 mm. The linear expansion corresponds mostly to a depth-to-width ratio of 1/6.

The detection of SCC is mainly based on a dedicated UT signal evaluation. Compared to the common UT signal evaluation by amplitude, the characteristics of the UT signal are rated and evaluated on a micro level. Evaluation on micro level means that even UT signals slightly above noise are considered. In combination with the swaying of UT probes, evidence of SCC can be given and is part of the UT signal characterisation.

### *4.5.3.3 Thermal fatigue*

Currently many plants use online temperature monitoring systems for the assessment of thermal fatigue. Fatigue monitoring system used are Fatigue Pro (EPRI/Structural Integrity), FAMOSi (Framatome) and WESTEMS (Westinghouse). Environmental assisted effects have to be considered also. The cumulative fatigue usage factor needs to be extrapolated to the end of the next ten-year period and the expected end of operation (which is 60 years now).

For many reactors there are no indications that thermal fatigue will be a limiting factor for the intended operating time, as of 2024.

### *4.5.3.4 Advanced NDE inspection tools for PHWR feeders*

For CANDU feeder piping, the Canadian nuclear industry has developed in recent years many advanced non-destructive inspection techniques to be applied safely in hazardous environments. Automated systems, manual tooling and specialised software modules have been designed since the early 2000s to provide complete and efficient fitness for service inspections of primary heat transport system carbon steel feeder pipes. These techniques deal with complex geometries, difficult access and radioactive environments. Complementary NDE techniques, namely UT, ECT, PAUT and automated scanners, are used.

Over time, several inspection tools have been developed (see the paper "Overview of Improvements in Work Practices and Instrumentation for CANDU Primary Heat Transport Feeders In-Service Inspections" [238]), such as:

- Bend Cracking Crawler, to detect feeder bend cracking;
- MÉTAR bracelet, a feeder thinning tool;
- the Grayloc Area Inspection Tool (GAIT), a manually fed driving mechanism that revolves on the feeder pipe axis a wall thickness measurement head.

All these advanced inspection tools specific to CANDU/PHWR pressure tubes and feeders are important for crack initiation, thinning rate, to predict the progression based on computer models, to maintain the critical safety functions and avoid unplanned shutdown and economic penalties, and not necessarily from the perspective of a limitation to operate beyond 60 years, since in CANDU design, the feeders, as well as the pressure tubes, are replaced at mid-life (after approximately 30 years) in a refurbishment outage (more details on feeders' inspection tools and prediction models are available in Romania's NAR-TPR on Ageing [239]).

### *4.5.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

### *4.5.4.1 Repair*

A wide variety of repair, mitigation and replacement solutions have been applied or developed to Safety Class 1 piping in US PWRs and BWRs. These include weld overlays and inlays for mitigation of SCC and PWSCC, MSIP for mitigation of PWSCC susceptibility, and replacement of whole piping sections. Some of the methodologies are provided as alternatives in ASME Code Cases, which may not be currently approved by US NRC. The US NRC is working with the US industry to resolve issues with these code cases. US licensees are free to propose unapproved repair methodologies to the US NRC as alternatives under 10 CFR 50.55a [174].

Major repair or refurbishment activities are relatively rare in Safety Class 1 piping systems, especially for the MCLs. Therefore, it is very important to have both a comprehensive maintenance programme and an effective AMP in place. For the latter, a strict monitoring of the operating conditions (e.g. water chemistry and transients) but also a tight inspection scheme (e.g. NDE and fatigue monitoring) are a must. MSIP and the full structural weld overlay are options which were or will be also used in Switzerland in case of existing indications or cracks in welds but also as a preventive measure.

### *4.5.4.2 Mitigation through operating conditions/re-design*

There is a need to investigate thermal fatigue mitigation and repair techniques that can be cost effectively backfit to existing plants. For fatigue modes that result in more frequent component failures, it is appropriate to focus on redesign and mitigation to prevent online outages and degraded system reliability(Issue P-MT-14 - Develop Recommendations and Guidance for Mitigating Fatigue Failures in Piping new and ranked high, PWR Issue Management Tables (MRP-205) [ [47]).

Since the root cause of fatigue-related failures are system/plant operation or design configuration, mitigation of fatigue damage is accomplished by reducing the magnitude of the applied loads or thermal conditions, or by reducing the number of loading cycles. For thermal transients, a reduction in the rate of temperature change for extreme temperature cycles can be effective. In case of pipe replacement, new design solutions are adopted to improve the process configuration, the geometry and loading, to minimise the flow-induced vibrations. Special care is taken to avoid thermal stratification caused by valve in–leakage in up-horizontal running safety injection line configurations and swirl-penetration thermal cycling in down–horizontal drain lines.

Special attention should be given to the surge line isometry and the operation regime for the pressuriser. Unfavourable design and/or operation regime can lead to high cumulative fatigue usage factors.

### *4.5.4.3 Replacement*

In 1998, a leak on the reactor heat removal circuit at Civaux 1 (a four loops PWR of 1 450 MW(e) in France) was found and the root cause of the event was characterised as thermal fatigue resulting in leakage from a mixing zone area due to high differential temperature (high ΔT). The utility initiated engineering studies and investigations to identify other areas on the RCL circuit that could be under the same conditions.

An area on the cold leg at the chemical volume control system (CVCS) line connection (Figure 4.18) was identified as a potential zone for thermal fatigue. In 2002, at Fessenheim 1 in France, an RCL cold leg part of a pipe was replaced to remove the real potential for thermal fatigue of this zone (NP-T-3.2, Section 2.1.5. Reactor coolant piping/recirculation piping [147]).

<span id="page-152-0"></span>

**Figure 4.18. Reactor coolant piping replacement in France**

Source: NP-T-3.2 [147]

Components which are projected to be unacceptably degraded due to thermal ageing embrittlement may be replaced in a proactive manner. For instance, susceptible primary circuit elbows may be replaced at the same time with the SGs or the pressuriser. Extensive guidance that resulted from the valuable experience gathered from the RCL replacements carried out in France, Switzerland and the United States is available in NP-T-3.2, Section 8. RCL replacement in PWRs ( [147]).

<span id="page-153-0"></span>**Figure 4.19. Location of replaced RCL parts in a typical Westinghouse reactor**

Source: NP-T-3.2 [147]

Due to their location on the primary circuit, E-elbows are deemed difficult to replace (they connect the cold leg to the RPV).

Except for E-elbows, all safety class one lines are considered replaceable. The replacement strategy is specific to each location on the primary circuit. For example, several primary loop CASS elbows (but not E-type) have already been replaced. Also, several portions of the auxiliary lines (safety injection system (SIS) and reactor heat removal system (RHRS)) have been replaced due to SCC in strain-hardened areas adjacent to welds.

When replacing the SGs in Beznau Nuclear Power Plant, parts of the main cooling lines were also replaced. In another Swiss PWR, the surge lines were redesigned and replaced because of a high fatigue usage factor.

Continuous improvement in CANDU designs based on OPEX, R&D findings, inspection results and maintenance needs has resulted in a robust fuel channel design that is easier to construct with predictable, safe and reliable performance, and which is easy to maintain over the life of the plant.

Fuel channel and feeders' removal and replacements are part of a life management strategy for CANDU reactors to extend their operating life. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL) has specialised tooling and procedures for the safe and effective removal of irradiated fuel channel and feeders and reinstallation of new fuel channel assemblies. Details about the tooling for removal and replacement of fuel channels are available in NP-T-3.2, Section 10.2.3 [147].

### *4.5.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

Although significant progress has been made to date to understand, monitor, assess and mitigate the operational conditions, there are still uncertainties regarding Safety Class 1 piping failure main causes: if induced by SCC, thermal fatigue, changing operating conditions, or a combination of them. For example, the US NRC has not identified any gaps related to ageing management of Safety Class 1 piping that would preclude licensing plants for 60-80 years of operation.

In the Swiss nuclear power plants, the AMP represents an essential, systematic expansion of the existing maintenance programmes and is continually updated. In particular, the ageing mechanisms for safety-relevant SSCs are identified by ageing management. Based on this, existing inspection and test programmes, especially preventative maintenance, are reviewed to determine whether ageing-induced degradation can be avoided or detected at an early stage. Any gaps revealed by the review can be closed in an accountable manner. Currently, no gaps were identified for LTO.

However, there are some areas where additional research could be beneficial.

- 1. Factors of improvement for PWSCC growth rates in Alloy 690/52/152 welds. If factors of improvement could be approved by the US NRC, required inspection intervals for these welds could be increased. Thermal ageing could potentially affect Alloy 690/52/152 CGRs so this is also an area where more knowledge is desirable. Additionally, confirmatory research may be needed if new nickel-based alloy weld metals are introduced by industry. Understanding of the ageing characteristics of high strength martensitic or precipitation hardened SSs requires additional research [e.g. P-DM-15 in EPRI MRP-205].
- 2. Research to better understand the French SCC experience and determine if similar piping in US plants is also susceptible. If susceptible, the likelihood of such cracking in US plants would increase as plants age.
- 3. Thermal ageing of CASS. While the US NRC has regulatory guidance for ageing management of CASS piping that is adequate, it would be beneficial to have more FT data from actual plant materials that have been aged for long times. Such data could be acquired from harvested piping components.
- 4. Thermal ageing of ASSW. The US NRC regulatory guidance for Safety Class 1 piping ageing management does not address loss of FT due to thermal ageing of ASSW. US NRC would like to develop a better understanding of the factors affecting FT of thermally aged ASSW, and either confirm or refine existing lower bound toughness curves for ASSW, which could inform changes to ageing management (if necessary). This information could also be used to inform changes in the ASME Code, Section XI flaw evaluation procedures which currently do not account for the effects of thermal ageing on toughness of ASSW.
- 5. Environmental fatigue. Additional research could potentially reduce unnecessary conservatism in US NRC-approved evaluation methods for environmental fatigue. Industry may need to improve understanding of environmental fatigue effects, in regard to chemistry factors (PWR IMT (MRP-205) [47], VVER IMT (MRP-471) [49]):
  - a) P-AS-02 Environmental Effects on Fatigue Resistance of Pressure Boundary Components (High risk);
  - b) V-AS-18 Environmental Effects on Fatigue Resistance: Pressure Boundary;
  - c) Components (High risk);
  - d) V-AS-28 Methods for Determination of Locations of Class 1 Piping Susceptible to Thermal Fatigue (High risk).

- 6. Improvement of knowledge and predictive tools for long-term SCC and thermal ageing. Safety Class 1 piping materials in VVER reactors are susceptible to SCC for base material, weld as well as cladding, due to the Ti stabilised SS used on primary system piping. DMW of VVER-440 SG collectors are also affected by SCC. More knowledge is needed on the cracking mechanism, on material properties, residual stresses, crack growth rates, NDE, LBB issues and on the consequences of a failure (see VVER IMT (MRP-471), Table 3-2 [49]):
  - a) V-DM-03 Long Term SCC Susceptibility (Medium risk);
  - b) V-AS-03 SCC of Stainless Steels Exposed to Primary Water (Medium risk);
  - c) V-AS-04 Thermal Embrittlement Combined Effects on SS Welds (Medium risk);
  - d) BWR reactors are also affected by of long-term SCC and thermal ageing of Class 1 piping materials and DMW (see EPRI IMT BWRVIP-167 [48]);
  - e) B-AS-10 Stainless Steel SCC Crack Growth (High risk);
  - f) B-AS-27 Alloy 82/ 182 SCC Crack Growth (High risk).
- 7. Solution to address the excessive conservatism from current LBB methodologies:
  - a) For operation beyond 60 years of BWR Class 1 piping, the knowledge gaps refer mainly to the SCC Crack Growth assessment methodologies, as mentioned in EPRI BWR IMT (BWRVIP-167)/rev.4, Section 3 [48]: B-AS-10 Stainless Steel SCC Crack Growth (High risk).
  - b) To support the 60-year operation of some small diameter CANDU piping, robust LBB methodologies such as modelling entire piping system with postulated through-wall cracks is needed.
- 8. Improvement of guidance for system/plant operation or design configuration. More information is needed to "Develop Recommendations and Guidance for Mitigating Fatigue Failures in Piping" - P-MT-14 (PWR IMT (MRP-205), rev.1, Table 3-2 [47]).
- 9. Validation of PFM codes and development of best practice document. Various PFM codes such as PRAISE-CANDU [232] and xLPR [222] have been applied to support the LTO. Continuous development and validation of these PFM codes are needed to provide ongoing assurance. The forthcoming NEA report (NEA/CSNI/R(2024)1) also recommends the development of a best practice document to guide PFM code developers and users in areas such as selecting appropriate fracture models, determining input distributions, and selecting sampling algorithms.
- 10. Improvement of vibration monitoring methods and constructive solutions to mitigate vibrations. HCF caused by vibrations in small piping results relatively frequently in incidents. The root causes of such vibrations are manifold and complex. If they exceed the fatigue threshold level, a crack can initiate and propagate relatively fast. Therefore, improved vibration monitoring methods and constructive solutions to mitigate vibrations would be favourable. The usage of sockets weld should be avoided because of their disadvantageous notch effect factors.
- 11. Thermal ageing of CASS E-elbows. This is the only strong LTO issue for safety class one lines. Many ageing management actions are already ongoing and will

continue, in the scopes of R&D, engineering and plant operation. Additional new actions have been undertaken to address the CASS E-elbows gap for LTO beyond 60 years, as follows:

- a. improvement of the mechanical analysis methods and associated hypotheses to reduce conservatism and better account for physics to determine in a more representative way the margins available on CASS elbows;
- b. performance of in situ examinations: the development of a NDE of inservice E-elbows has been launched, to confirm the absence of indications larger than the size of the justified flaw. This new NDE aims at controlling the entire inner wall of the E-elbows over several millimetres of depth;
- c. preparations of E-elbow repair solutions by elimination of NDE indications, in case of need;
- d. studies of the feasibility of replacing E-elbows to support LTO beyond 60 years if all other methods have failed.
- e. Regarding the improvement of mechanical analysis methods, following the lessons learnt from academic overview, EDF has identified new methods to reduce conservatisms of the current analytical approach:
  - For the assessment of flaw initiation: a specific criterion considering the lower harmfulness of casting defects, whose morphology is different from a postulate plane crack;
  - For the assessment of instability: use of Gfr parameter [240], which is more accurate than J parameter (Rice integral) thanks to a distinction between plastic and fracture energies;
  - In the long term, investigations of PFM and local approach models of ductile fracture.

### <span id="page-156-0"></span>**4.6. Buried and underground piping**

### *4.6.1. Description of buried and underground piping*

In this section, buried and underground piping is defined as piping that is generally inaccessible for inspection using conventional techniques. This means that the piping is either buried in the ground, embedded in concrete or located within inaccessible shafts with restricted access. Gaining access to it may may require the removal of a permanent construction. Accordingly, building penetrations are not further considered here because these sections are very short and the external surface on both sides can be monitored.

Buried and underground piping are used in both safety and non-safety related applications in a nuclear power plant and may contain liquids or gases. The act of placing a pipe underground can provide protection from certain design basis hazards such as tornado missile strikes. Applications may include, but are not limited to:

- fuel and oil handling systems (for diesels/standby generators, lubrication systems);
- gas systems (service water, condensate, demineralised water, circulating water systems, emergency core cooling, chilled water systems, fire protection systems, heavy water transfer (PHWRs), drinking water, service water, feed water, demineralised water, domestic water, fire protection systems);

- water systems (service water, feed water, demineralised water, domestic water, fire protection systems);
- sewage, drains, collection and sampling systems;
- chemical handling systems (chlorination, de-chlorination, boron recycling system);
- electrical systems (those utilising buried conduit);
- miscellaneous systems (radioactive waste systems, cooling tower blowdown system, frazil ice protection, off gas system, etc.).

Fuel oil transfer systems provide onsite storage and delivery of diesel or fuel oil to emergency diesel or standby generators.

Water handling systems in nuclear power plants include service water, condensate, demineralised water, circulating water systems, emergency core cooling, chilled water systems, fire protection systems, heavy water transfer (PHWRs), drinking water and others. Buried or underground piping is typically used as part of the connection of the nuclear power plant to its main heat sinks (lake, sea, river, or cooling towers). Buried piping is also used for the fire protection systems (buried piping and fire hydrants in a ring configuration to make water available for firefighting activities).

Sewage and floor drainage systems are designed to collect drainage from potentially radioactive equipment and floor drains can be processed in liquid waste treatment systems. Monitoring capability is provided to ensure that inadvertent releases of radioactivity are prevented. The importance of floor, storm and yard drainage systems has been highlighted in relation to their role in external flood protection. Degradation of such drainage systems can negatively impact the ability of stations to respond to heavy rainfall and other similar events. Detailed information about every buried pipe application can be found in IAEA NP-T-3.20, Section 3 [241].

Most buried metal piping is constructed from welded carbon steel (bare, coated or lined) or cast iron (including ductile iron) joined via mechanical joints. Corrosion-resistant alloys, including austenitic stainless steels such as Types 304 and 316 (including low carbon "L" grades), more highly corrosion resistant SS (typically the 6% molybdenum stainless steels) and non-ferrous materials (most commonly copper-based alloys including brasses, bronzes and copper-nickel alloys), may also be used for some buried lines. Some plants have installed titanium piping in critical locations.

Super austenitic stainless steels with > 6% Mo and increased nickel and nitrogen levels are also under consideration, as replacement piping at nuclear power plants. This material is resistant to corrosion by soil. While the use of super austenitic stainless steels is quite effective in the prevention of external corrosion. They are even more valuable in preventing internal corrosion due to their resistance to microbiologically induced corrosion (MIC) and chloride-induced corrosion.

A detailed description of the mechanical properties, advantages and the recommended application resulting from these characteristics for all the materials used in buried piping construction: metallic, non-metallic and concrete, as well as different connection types, coatings, liners are provided in IAEA report NP-T-3.20, Sections 4.1- 4.2 [241].

In case of buried piping of the water supply systems, the inner and the outer surfaces must be differentiated. As these systems are mainly carrying river water, the main degradation mechanism is uniform corrosion of low alloyed steels or shallow pit formation. The latter is more critical as it leads to a localised attack and accelerates the formation of leakages. Usually, the critical surface of such piping is the inner surface of the pipes with contact to the water. Here, stagnant conditions or partly filled pipes are an important contributing factor for inner corrosion. For buried pipes, the corrosion attack can start from the outer surface as well. Different measures of corrosion protection such as zinc plating, several types of coating (e.g. bitumen, epoxy) or even cathodic protection are used. SS pipes are usually not susceptible to inner or outer corrosion.

In Switzerland, only one nuclear power plant has safety relevant piping in several water supply systems that are either buried in ground or laid in inaccessible channels (Safety Class 3). A long-term maintenance and inspection concept is in place. Further information is provided in Chapter 4 of the Swiss "National Assessment Report for the Topical Peer Review: Ageing Management in Nuclear Power Plants" [242].

### *4.6.2. Physical ageing of buried and underground piping*

Degradation of buried piping may occur in any kind of pipe materials (metals, concrete, polymers, etc.) from the inside and/or from the outside. Its origin may be linked to poor design, construction, maintenance or the internal or external environment of the buried pipe. Depending on its components, a buried pipe may be sensitive to such degradation mechanisms as: corrosion; fatigue; tuberculation or occlusion; freeze-thaw cycling; settlement and soil displacements; wear (erosion), or selective leaching (Gray cast iron and copper alloys material).

In Ukraine, mechanical damage of buried piping is also considered a potential degradation mechanism. Mechanical damage can lead to local defects (dent as a rule) or local stability lost. The mechanical damage is the result of loads from traffic on the surface over the piping.
