In the case of RCC, the presence of reinforcements in a material can modify the homogeneous spatial swelling of the paste. The stress field created by the reaction of the reinforcements to the swelling is likely to "orient" the directions of crystallisation of ettringite. Anisotropic expansions can therefore be expected. Unfortunately, insufficient research work to date seems to be available in the open literature.

The main recommendations for future work, which resulted from an investigation conducted by the University of Florida and documented in EPRI report 3002007577 [283], are to:

- improve the finite element modelling prediction of temperature differentials, temperature gradients and thermal stresses;
- further investigate the ability of alternative supplementary cementitious materials to reduce heat of hydration as well as reduce the corrected sulphate to alumina ratio to reduce the potential for DEF;
- improve construction specifications and ensure sound structural facilities until the end of their design life.

For more details on DEF, refer to IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262], ACES Project Report [265] and EPRI Report 3002007577 [283] and ACES [265].

#### **Black corrosion**

RCC structures in water saturated or submerged conditions such as intake structures with high availability of chlorides may be susceptible to black corrosion in absence of oxygen. If the iron solution can leak out to the concrete surface, then nodule-like precipitates or stains can be observed. However, if the iron solution is prevented from reaching the concrete surface, it could lack any signs of rust. The black corrosion product is less expansive and hence exerts less internal stress within the surrounding material. As a result, no visible cracks, spalling or scaling will appear in the concrete cover and the corrosion process stays unnoticed. Therefore, black rust is difficult to detect by visual methods. When the material is exposed to an aeriated environment the colour change from dark/black to red. The red rust colour may be dominating the concrete surface, even though it can have a black core/interior (Refer to [284] for more information on black rust).

There is a lack of knowledge about detecting ageing effects associated with this degradation mechanism due to the absence of visual signs on the concrete surface.

### **Thaumasite sulphate attack**

Thaumasite is a calcium-silicate-sulphate-carbonate mineral. A rare form of sulphate attack involves thaumasite formation due to reactions between calcium silicates in the cement, calcium carbonate from limestone aggregates or fillers and sulphates, usually from external sources. Thaumasite sulphate attack in susceptible concrete typically requires sulphate sources, mobile groundwater, calcium silicate hydrate sources, the presence of carbonate and low temperatures (<10°C). Vulnerable structures in nuclear power plant are intake structures. The attack forms slowly and can destroy a significant part of the calcium silicate hydrate, resulting in a soft, white, pulpy mass that causes total disintegration of the concrete and exposed rebar, as shown in IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262].

### **Specific gaps related to well understood ageing processes**

Specific gaps exist even in the processes which are well understood. Consequences of degradation effects on safety-related SSCs in nuclear power plant are not well documented (or are not identified) in literature – as such it is not recognised under which conditions the consequences can cause severe deterioration of concrete structures. Some ageing processes that require further research are:

- Microbiological processes linked to concrete/steel.
- Deterioration of concrete under high temperature in the steam exhaust rooms with very high humidity (very specific conditions in a nuclear power plant). As a result, these concrete structures will be damaged more easily, under the influence of elevated temperatures, compared to structures located in a dry environment.
- Acid-induced dissolution of calcium-bearing cement phases with other processes.
- Coupled effects AAR and creep/shrinkage especially in the case of bi-axially loaded structures (such as the nuclear power plant containment building).
- Coupled effects of DEF and creep/shrinkage especially in the case of bi-axially loaded structures (such as the nuclear power plant containment building).
- Coupled effects of freeze-thaw AARs and leaching.
- Drying, creep, and shrinkage behaviours at high temperatures.
- Synergistic effect of carbonation and chloride ingress, which is not well studied and little is known how both processes effect corrosion at the same time.
- Crack corrosion and the behaviour of cracks exposed to freezing and thawing and chemical attacks (ACES [265]).

### *4.7.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### **Inspection and diagnostic technologies**

### **Visual inspections**

Visual inspections are performed in accordance with applicable codes, standards, specifications and procedures (e.g. ASME Section XI Subsection IWL [234] , ACI PRC-349.3 [285], CSA N287.7 [286]). Age-related visible effects on the structure's surface such as cracks, pop-outs, spall, blistering, delamination, discoloration, staining, efflorescence, abrasion and corrosion can be detected by visual inspection. Tools such as measuring tapes, callipers, crack comparators, levels, chipping hammers and sounding lines are traditionally used to perform visual inspections.

Optical aids, such as fiberscopes and borescopes, allow inspection of inaccessible regions. Video cameras can be used to record current conditions for future reference. A video microscope with image acquisition, image display and image analysis capabilities has been developed to monitor cracks in structures [287].

Scuba divers are used to inspect underwater concrete structures. Where scuba divers can be used, many types of test devices in use above water have been adapted for use below water, for example rebound hammers and ultrasonic pulse velocity systems. These tools provide good readings on the general condition of underwater concrete [288]. Remotely operated underwater vehicles, also sometimes known as an underwater drones or underwater robots, can be a useful tool for visual inspection of underwater structures.

However, some underwater structures, notably SFPs, are associated with radiation hazards that can make the use of scuba divers problematic. To minimise personnel hazards, underwater vehicles (tethered or remotely operated vehicles) that use video or still cameras and other sensors, can be used. Visual inspections can be done in clear water; however, many types of structures are in water that is not clear enough to perform a visual examination.

The use of unmanned aerial systems or drones for inspection of structures has grown rapidly over the recent years. The technology can be used to perform inspections of structures and components that require extensive scaffolding and could pose risks of injury to personnel if done by traditional methods. EPRI field-tested the use of drones equipped with various payloads to inspect a containment building at a nuclear plant in the United States [289]. Inspectors used the drones to collect photos, thermal images and videos, then analysed them to locate areas of degradation and compared the results with those from traditional visual inspections (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262].

### **Non-destructive evaluations (NDEs)**

NDEs utilise non-invasive techniques to determine the integrity of a material, component or structure, or to quantitatively measure some object characteristic. NDE methods can be used to indicate concrete strength, density and quality, locate and characterise voids or cracks, locate rebar and embedment, indicate concrete cover depth and indicate corrosion of reinforcing materials. A summary of common NDE methods and techniques is provided below:

- Stress-wave methods for structures: Ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV), ultrasonicecho, impact-echo, spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) and impulse response.
- Low-strain stress wave methods for deep foundations: Sonic-echo, impulseresponse (mobility), impedance logging, crosshole sonic logging and parallelseismic method.

- Nuclear methods: Direct transmission radiometry, backscatter radiometry, radiography, gamma-gamma logging for deep foundations, radiography, neutron based methods.
- Magnetic and electrical methods: Covermeter, half-cell potential, concrete resistivity, linear polarisation resistance, magnetic flux leakage.
- Methods for measuring transport properties: Initial surface-absorption test, figg water-absorption test, covercrete-absorption test, surface sorptivity test, steinert method, figg air-permeability test, schönlin test, surface airflow test, surface airpermeability test, ion diffusion test.
- Electrochemical methods: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, tafelextrapolation.
- Audio methods.
- Rebound hammer.
- Infrared thermography.
- Radar.

These methods are described in detail in ACI 228.2R [290], IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]. Some of the advanced techniques are described here.

#### **Pulsed phase thermography**

Pulsed phase thermography provides a means to image the internal structure of a component. It combines the features of impulse thermography and lock-in thermography and records the cooling down process with an infrared camera so that at each surface position, a transient curve of temperature, is recorded as a function of time. Fast Fourier transformation analysis is used to separate information according to different frequencies of thermal waves and delivers amplitude and phase images. The analysis of transient curves permits a qualitative location mapping of defects (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

### **Acoustic emission technique**

Acoustic emission (AE) is the term used to define transient stress waves emitted from the sudden release of energy due to a deformation in the monitored material, such as crack formation or growth. As a passive piezoelectric sensing technique, AE is suitable for realtime long-term monitoring of structures. AE sensors are very sensitive, which enables them to detect active cracks long before they are visible (microcracks). Many degradation mechanisms of concrete, such as corrosion and AAR, take years to progress and are associated with the formation of microcracks. The sensitivity of AE can be used to monitor the progression of these degradation mechanisms (ACES Report [265]).

#### **Automatic image-based crack detection**

Manual inspection has been the acclaimed method for crack inspection where the sketch of the crack is prepared manually, and the conditions of the irregularities are noted. Since the manual approach completely depends on the specialist's knowledge and experience, it lacks objectivity in the quantitative analysis. So, automatic image-based crack detection is proposed as a replacement which can be done using some of the NDE techniques such as infrared and thermal testing, UT, laser testing, and radiographic testing. All of them are based on image processing but the crack detection criteria can be based on different parameters: surface (most often), length, width, depth, direction of propagation. More details on these techniques can be found in Mohan and Poobal [291].

### **Galvanostatic pulse technique**

The galvanostatic pulse technique is a transient polarisation method and can be used for detecting corrosion in wet and anaerobic environments. Rebar is polarised in the anodic direction relative to its free CP. The extent of polarisation depends on the corrosion state. Rebar is easy to polarise in the passive state, as noted by the large difference between free corrosion and polarised potential. The difference is much smaller when corrosion is occurring. The method is superior to the half-cell potential method, when testing wet concrete where there is a risk of misinterpretation of results. Galvanostatic pulse technique measurements take considerably longer to execute than half-cell potential measurements and require an experienced person to perform the technique (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

### **Tafel extrapolation**

Tafel extrapolation is an electrochemical method for calculating corrosion rate through use of current intensity and Tafel slopes. The technique is based on application of either steady fixed levels of current followed by monitoring of potential (galvanostatic), or application of specific potential followed by monitoring of current (potentio-static). Tafel slope values for anodic and cathodic curves in the Tafel graph are used to obtain corrosion current, which is then used to calculate corrosion rate. With this technique, very low corrosion rates can be measured, monitoring can be continuous and corrosion rate can be measured directly (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

### **Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy**

AC electrochemical impedance spectroscopy has been investigated as a tool for quantifying corrosion of steel rebar embedded in concrete and chloride diffusivity in concrete. The technique enables information to be obtained about mechanisms occurring within the system by applying a perturbation to reinforcing steel and measuring current flow and phase shift in the resulting current. AC electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can estimate a steady state corrosion rate from the impedance spectrum and can be used to study effects of corrosion inhibitors, coatings and pitting corrosion. It can, however, be labour intensive and time consuming, requiring lengthy data acquisition times, a physical connection to the steel embedded in concrete, and is presently more suitable for laboratory studies (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

#### **Machine learning, data fusion and post-processing visualisation**

ML is a technique of data analysis and a branch of AI. ML is being implemented in NDE inspections to aid in detecting and understanding signals and outputs from the performed inspections and help the evaluation process. Artificial neural networks are commonly used to aid in the detection of defects.

Data fusion is the process of combining different data sources, that vary in information, size, and behaviour, into a single model to create more coherent and useful information than that provided by the individual data sets. In NDE, data fusion uses data from complimentary techniques, like radiography and UT, to not only create diverse and redundant data sets but to avoid uncertainty, lack of precision, and conflicts of information. Data fusion can also work as way of gathering different information from ML models.

After the applied energy interacts with the material properties and condition, the resulting output signal is processed and evaluated. Some of this processing includes sparse reconstruction, the Fourier transform method, and the modified Feldkamp–Davis–Kress reconstruction method. Further details on these methods can be found in [292].

#### **Destructive testing**

Some common semi-destructive and destructive testing methods are:

- core testing;
- break-off;
- probe penetration;
- pull-out;
- pull-off;
- chemical analysis (e.g. chloride ion content, carbonation depth, AAR and sulphate attack);
- laser induced breakdown spectroscopy;
- petrographic examinations.

These methods are described in detail in IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262].

### **Monitoring**

Instrumentation helps in detecting and monitoring overall and local strain, stress, deformation and temperature changes in concrete structures. Results may be helpful in assessing concrete volumetric changes (i.e. creep and shrinkage), loss of force in prestressing systems and monitoring the moisture content of RCC in the constructions of the internal spaces of the containment. These are the changes that cannot be detected through common visual inspection techniques. Instruments used in nuclear power plants include:

- vibrating wire strain gauges (VWSGs);
- thermocouples;
- pendulums;
- extensometers (e.g. invar wire);

- linear variable differential transformer (LVDT)
- load cells (also called dynamometers);
- liquid level gauges;
- humidity gauges;
- embedded corrosion monitoring sensors;
- precision level surveying;
- fiber optic sensors;
- acoustic emission monitoring.

The details of these instrumentations can be found in IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262].

The possible failure of some of the embedded sensors during construction and over the lifetime of the structure needs to be considered when determining the quantity of the instruments. It is preferred to use different types of instruments for measurements of the same parameters to ensure redundancy and proper functionality of the sensors. The limitations of using this instrumentation for monitoring include the following, according to IAEA NP-T-3.5 [1]:

- instruments typically provide structure data only at discrete points;
- the redundancy of instruments is required to protect against individual instrument failure or damage;
- reference conditions apply when instruments are placed in service and read (which may not reflect full structure history);
- post-construction installation may cause local damage.

#### **Inspection of inaccessible areas and elements**

Examples of inaccessible areas are below-grade surfaces exposed to foundation soil/material, backfill, or groundwater, portions of concrete surfaces that are covered by metallic liners, fully embedded or inaccessible containment shell or liner portions, liner anchors, portions of surfaces where visual access is obstructed by adjacent permanent plant structures, and portions of steel components that are embedded or encased in concrete or encapsulated or otherwise made inaccessible during construction or as a result of repair/replacement activities.

Subsections IWL and IWE of ASME Code Section XI [234] exempt inaccessible areas from examination; however, specific requirements for examination of suspect conditions by the responsible engineer and evaluations to be performed on inaccessible areas are mentioned.

An exhaustive list of inaccessible areas should be developed associated with the reasons of their inaccessibility to be able to demonstrate for each area, with adapted methods, their ability to fulfil their behaviour requirements for LTO beyond 60 years. Assessments of inaccessible concrete components can be done by removing material to expose the component of interest and directly applying the standard testing methods, indirectly through environmental evaluations (i.e. quantification of aggressiveness of the ambient environment), or via assessment of adjacent accessible structures exposed to similar environments. This is often supported by a more detailed assessment of design, construction, and operational history to demonstrate that significant degradation is unlikely. If the ambient environment is determined to be aggressive, additional testing and

evaluation is required that may involve removal of material to expose components for direct inspection and testing. Non-destructive testing methods suitable for inspection of inaccessible portions of the metal pressure boundary where it is embedded in concrete have not been identified.

Methods employed for indirect inspection of below grade concrete are based on a chemical evaluation to assess the presence and concentration of potentially aggressive ions (e.g. sulphates or chlorides). Foundation piles can be evaluated using sonic echo and impulse response testing even under inaccessible head conditions. Parallel seismic method can be used for inaccessible head conditions. AAR and DEF in inaccessible areas of concrete structures such as base slabs of buildings, water intake and discharge structures, service water pump house, and below grade walls of the spent fuel pool covered with a liner plate, can be monitored with embedded strain sensors (IGALL AMP 324, IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262].

### **Inspection of specific structures**

Various inspection methods used for detection of ageing effect in concrete structures and inspection examples of some specific structures are discussed in this section.

### **Containment concrete**

Visual inspection can be carried out for the accessible surfaces of the containment. An example of visual inspection for containments of EDF in France is given below:

- Single-wall containments: Visual inspection is done for the external facing (dome and parts of the skirt visible from the outside). The aim is to look for traces of corrosion of the rebars, concrete facing defects and to verify the integrity of the tightness coating.
- Double-wall containments: Visual inspection is done for the second wall containment (the parts visible from outside of the second containment building and for the inner part, those visible from the annulus and opposite the former). Either partial inspection (search for traces of rebar corrosion) or complete inspection (search for traces of corrosion and survey of cracks) is carried out.

Containment integrity test is used to measure the leak-tightness of the containment structure. The frequency of these leak rate tests is usually ten years. But, since the concrete contributes to the leak-tightness, a defect that penetrates the liner in an embedded area might not lead to that the integrity test will not meet the acceptance criteria.

Instrumentation can also be used to measure tendon prestressing force (in case of nongrouted tendons). For existing prestressed concrete structures with grouted post-tensioning systems, retrofitted sensors need to be considered to enable monitoring of structure's response to apply loading and prestressing force. When sensors are installed on the outside surface of the containment structure, sufficient protection needs to be provided from the environment, as temperature fluctuations and ultraviolet exposure significantly affect sensor readings, making interpretation of results difficult (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262], IGALL AMP 311).

In some countries, nuclear power plant containment buildings are continuously monitored. For example, in France, as of the construction stage, the containment is equipped with instrumentation, distributed around the basement, the gusset, the cylindrical part and the dome, except for the outer containment of double-wall containments, which is not instrumented. The instrumentation system comprises:

• VWSGs, embedded in the cylindrical wall and dome to measure concrete strain;

- thermocouples to assess the volumetric strain due to temperature;
- pendulums for horizontal displacement monitoring;
- Invar wire extensometers for containment height variation monitoring;
- LVDT to measure the radial and circumferential deformation of openings;
- dynamometers on four pure grease-injected vertical tendons on the first reactor of each site. The main requirement is the measurement after the prestressing phase, to check the cables relaxation coefficients and the friction coefficients.
- direct levelling references (placed in the prestressing galleries).

Additional special inspections can be carried out because of new internal or external findings. For example, the condition of the prestressing in the ring girder between the dome and the outer cylinder of the reactor building shell was assessed as a special inspection in the KKB (Beznau Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland). In connection with the replacement of the SGs in 1993 and 1999 and the replacement of the RPV head in 2015, the outer reactor building shell and the steel liner in the KKB required large openings. As part of such interventions, information required for ageing monitoring was also collected, such as the condition of the concrete, the reinforcement, the steel liner and its anchoring.

### **Metallic liners**

General visual examination of accessible liner surfaces can uncover evidence of possible degradation that could affect containment integrity or cause unacceptable leakage. Corrosion of uncoated areas of metallic liner, due to excessive moisture or aggressive adjacent containment environments, may also be revealed. Examination of DMW will identify material defects in the weld and base metal (adjacent to weld edges). Supplemental testing (e.g. ultrasonic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant or electromagnetic) can be also performed. Phased array ultrasound testing may be used for measuring the thickness of liners.

Containment leak-tightness is verified periodically through leakage rate testing. To be able to detect local leakage through the structure an inspection can be performed while the containment is pressurised. By using acoustic methods, either by listening with a microphone or using an acoustic camera, it is possible to detect leakage through the structure at embedded parts of the liner. Applying soap water to the concrete structure could also give indication of leakage. The disadvantage of this method is that a degradation of the liner will only be indicated after the discontinuity in the liner has developed due to corrosion. A leakage through the concrete will indicate in what area a defect could be found. But it is still hard to tell the exact position of the degradation since the leakage through concrete is transported by the easiest means (through cracks, etc.), and not via the shortest way out.

For portions of metallic liner embedded in concrete, there are no available NDE methods that can detect degradation of the liner plate. For example, in the Swedish containments, the larger part of the liner is embedded in concrete and the only visible part is in the dome. To find different deviations in connection to embedded liner is not possible with the current techniques.

### **Non-metallic liners**

Visual examination of non-metallic liners and coatings is effective in identifying potential problem areas (e.g. blistering, peeling, delamination, and voids). The integrity of nonmetallic liners can be also evaluated by leak rate testing of the containment.

The integrity of corrosion inhibiting coatings applied to metallic liners can be evaluated visually, with supplemental testing of suspect areas to measure dry film coating thickness and adhesion, and to determine if uncoated areas exist. Liner coating thickness can be determined using magnetic pull-off gauges, magnetic flux gauges and tooke gauges. Evaluation of sealing and coating systems can be done through adhesion measurements by tape adhesion, direct tension (elcometer) or direct peel.

### **Pre-stressing tendons**

For non-grouted tendons, the tendon forces can be measured through a lift-off test. Also, for non-grouted tendons that are protected from corrosion by grease, it is important to ensure that the quality of the grease is sufficient to protect the tendons from corrosion for the operating life including life extensions. Material samples of grease and steel threads can be taken during lift-off tests for testing.

On the other hand, grouted tendons are well protected against corrosion. However, for grouted tendons it is not possible to perform lift-off tests. The tendon forces can be evaluated using the following techniques:

- monitoring of the tensile strains in the wires of tendons and evaluating the prestress level at a section in the containment structure from readings of appropriately located strain gauges or strain or stress meters at the section, and a pressure test at certain time intervals;
- evaluating elastic response of containment subjected to pressure testing at certain time intervals.

The prestress level thus evaluated is then compared with initial structural integrity test (ISIT), performed during the pre-operational test of the containment and predicted prestress force.

Refer to NEA/CSNI/R(2015)5 "Bonded or Unbonded Technologies for Nuclear Reactor Prestressed Concrete Containments"[28](#page-192-0) for details of monitoring integrity of grouted and ungrouted prestressing systems.

### **Conventional reinforcement**

To assess the risk of corrosion, visual inspection is performed to detect the signs of degradation. In addition, the reinforcement cover is measured and compared with the depth of carbonation determined on drilled cores and further laboratory tests are carried out, such as determining the concrete density, chloride content, the compressive and tensile strength and the quality of the concrete structure using thin sections. If active reinforcement corrosion is suspected, potential measurements and potential field measurements are carried out on the reinforcement.

#### **Spent fuel pools**

SFPs typically have limited access for visual inspection. Accessibility is limited due to radiation hazards and obstructions such as spent fuel, fuel racks and equipment. Surveillance is used to monitor pool water levels, temperature, chemistry and presence and amount of any leakage. Ultrasound method can be used for inspection of spent fuel pool welds. Inspections of pool liners can be done visually, for example using remotely operated vehicles. Visual inspection of accessible parts and parts above the water level is used to detect ageing effects. Where external surfaces of SFPs are in contact with soil, indirect

<span id="page-192-0"></span><sup>28</sup> NEA(2015), "Bonded or Unbonded Technologies for Nuclear Reactor Prestressed Concrete Containments", OECD Publishing, Paris[, www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl\\_19604.](http://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_19604)

methods of monitoring environmental parameters can be used as described in Section 4.7.3.1.5 to assess degradation potential (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262], IAEA IGALL 315).

If there is a leakage through the welds of the fuel pools this will go through the leakage detecting system. It has been noticed that the pipes collecting leakage in some cases are clogged by boric crystals or calcium carbonate from the concrete. Since the pipes are narrow and have more than one 90° angle there are now no suitable methods that make it possible to inspect or clean the pipes. A clogged pipe means that it will not be possible to identify the leakage and there is also a risk that the leakage will go through the concrete structure instead.

#### **Cooling towers**

Typical specific inspection methodologies for cooling towers include checking for structure tilt using topography equipment, detailed visual inspections of concrete surfaces to map the shape and size of cracks and other damage such as corrosion and 3-D laser scanning. Increasingly regular assessments are being augmented by embedded monitoring systems to enhance diagnostic capabilities.

In Belgium, monitoring of cooling towers is based on results obtained from topographic surveys, inventory of deterioration types and analysis of structural materials. Photographs covering the entire shell surface are taken from ground level. Computer aided interpretation of the photographs permits mapping of cracks and defects and their evolution and the development of crack distribution, length and orientation statistics. Cataloguing of photographs shows shell changes with time. Additional inspections include measurements to determine rebar corrosion and depth of concrete carbonation. Laboratory tests are performed on samples removed from the towers. Results of inspections (e.g. deformation of the shell and degradation in material properties) are used to perform analyses to demonstrate that required safety factors are being maintained (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262], IGALL AMP 307).

### **Water intake structures**

Routine monitoring of water intake structures involves visual inspections of above water level structures and video recording of underwater structures. The examination could be performed visually, by use of a NDE method, or by destructive testing to detect voids in concrete or excessively corroded rebars. Joints seals are examined to check if they can perform their design function. Water passage section functionality is checked (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262], IGALL AMP 307).

### *4.7.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

Actions such as repair, refurbishment or replacement may be taken to restore a failed SSC's ability to function within acceptance criteria. Final repair technique selection needs to consider durability, life cycle costs and labour skill and equipment requirements. Following any repair, follow up inspections need to be conducted periodically to confirm repair effectiveness. Materials used need to be qualified for nuclear applications. Specifically, materials used inside containment structures need to be qualified for accident conditions so that they do not interfere with safety related systems. Qualification tests are given in standards such as N287.2 [293]. Repair techniques related to major ageing issues and repairs related to specific structures of nuclear power plants along with international experience are described in subsequent sub-sections. Repair techniques are described in detail in literature such as IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262] and ACI-546 [294].

### **Repair for major ageing-related issues**

### **Cracks**

Surveys of general civil engineering construction and nuclear power plant structures indicate that cracking is by far the most frequently occurring problem. Concrete structures have two categories of cracks: microcracks and macrocracks. Microcracks necessitate no repair action, but they are important because under increased loading they become wider and propagate and can eventually reach a size (i.e. macrocracks) sufficient to deteriorate concrete further, accelerate embedded steel corrosion or produce leakage. Macrocracks are important to service life. After identifying that a crack is of sufficient size to require repair, it is important to determine if the crack is active or dormant and then the following repairs may be carried out:

- Dormant pattern or fine cracking: penetration sealers, coatings, high molecular weight methacrylate or epoxy treatment.
- Dormant isolated large cracking: Epoxy injection, rout and seal, flexible sealing, drilling and plugging, grout injection or dry packing, stitching, additional reinforcing, strengthening.
- Active cracks: Penetrating sealer, flexible sealing, rout and seal, install expansion joint, drilling and plugging, stitching, additional reinforcing.
- Seepage: Eliminate moisture source, chemical grouting, coatings, hydraulic cement dry packing.

#### **Spalls**

Shallow spalls (<20 mm) are generally repaired using Portland cement-based mortar materials however, polymer concretes containing epoxies or methyl methacrylate have also been successfully used. Deep spalls are treated in a similar manner to shallow spalls except that coarse aggregate is added to the repair material. For mass concrete requiring extensive material replacement, the repair patch may be built in two or more layers to prevent excessive heat buildup due to cement hydration. If the spall to be repaired is on a vertical or overhead surface, generally dry packing is used in which a very harsh mix (i.e. dry) is applied and compacted using a blunt instrument, to overcome issues due to gravity effects.

#### **Water seepage**

When moisture is present, chemical grouting using silicate, acrylamide, lignin or resin (i.e. epoxy, polyester and urethane) systems is the most effective non-structural repair technique. The reaction of chemical grout, which may be purely chemical or physiochemical, produces a decrease in fluidity and a tendency to solidify and form occlusions in channels or fill voids in the material. Chemical grout reaction can be in the form of soft, flexible, semi-rigid or rigid gels. When seepage is intermittent and the path through the concrete periodically dries, it can be injected with epoxy resins, or water can be incorporated into a urethane injection system to promote expansion and curing to form a flexible foam material.

To protect the structure, coatings and sealers can be applied and water stops, and joint sealants need to be maintained. Repair of waterproofing is typically performed by the individual treatment of discontinuities such as cracks and joints and/or by a concrete surface treatment (i.e. application of water proofing sealant, coating or a membrane). For additional waterproofing of some structures, sealants and coatings can be used in combination or a coating system may include FRP sheets [295].

### **Alkali–aggregate reactions**

Mitigation of AAR in existing concrete structures can be carried out by interfering with the reaction mechanisms (e.g. drying and sealants) or treating symptoms (i.e. restraint and crack filling). The application of surface film coatings (e.g. acrylic/ polyvinyl acetate) to prevent moisture penetration has not always been found to be effective over the long term; however, solvent-based silicone coatings have been shown to provide good protection against water penetration for over two years and reduce expansions caused by the ASR.

If AAR has stopped, the only repair generally required is filling surface cracks with cement grout or resin. Other methods that have been used, not to mitigate but to counteract the effects of AAR, include strengthening by adding external rebar and cutting joints into the structure to accommodate expansion. Mitigation of the ASR in nuclear power plant concrete structures could potentially be challenging owing to the concrete section thicknesses involved, and it may be difficult to reduce water sources.

#### **Corrosion**

When corrosion damage is localised on exposed surfaces, replacement or partial reconstruction may be the most feasible solution. Because anodic, cathodic and electrolytic processes are necessary for corrosion occurrence, repair activities are directed at halting one or more of these processes. Brief descriptions of the repair processes are provided below:

- Re-passivation: Three methods for rebar re-passivation are available which are using alkaline cement or mortar, electrochemical re-alkalisation and chloride extraction. Using alkaline cement or mortar relies on the migration of alkalis into the old concrete. Electrochemical re-alkalisation is used to restore high pH to concrete which has been shown to arrest corrosion, but its long-term effectiveness is questionable. Chloride extraction removes chloride ions from concrete to achieve a residual chloride ion concentration low enough to stop the corrosion process.
- Steel reinforcement (rebar) coating: This includes applying a physical barrier (e.g. epoxy) to protect the steel and provide electrical resistance. The procedure requires concrete removal to a depth below the rebar, a clean steel surface free of rust, and sometimes, if badly corroded, replacement of portions of the rebar. The bond strength of the epoxy coated bars is reduced because the coating prevents adhesion and lowers the coefficient of friction between the bar and the concrete (ACI 318 [296]). Also, if the remainder of the steel is uncoated, and the coating in the repaired area is damaged and becomes corrosively active, a high rate of corrosion can occur. In chloride environments, chlorides may penetrate the coating ends and cause crevice corrosion where steel has not been re-passivated. Use of low water to cement ratio cementitious coatings may be preferred in chloride contaminated concrete (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).
- Cathodic protection: This does not eliminate corrosion, it transfers it to a less expensive, consumable, non-dangerous, known location, specifically the anode. Corrosion can be effectively halted, or its rate decreased, by applying a small direct current to rebar, making it slightly cathodic relative to an externally applied anode at or near the concrete surface. Two types of cathodic protection systems are available: impressed current, and sacrificial anode. Cathodic protection has been successfully used for several decades and is best suited for applications where the concrete is extensively contaminated and high chloride levels exist at the level of the steel. Applications of cathodic protection systems to nuclear power plant

concrete structures are somewhat limited and have generally involved safety related concrete structures other than containments.

### **Repair examples of specific structures**

### **Containment shell**

In the case of the Swiss Mühleberg Nuclear Power Plant, cracks were found in the foot ring of the dome, which threatened the leak-tightness of the outer reactor building envelope. The load bearing capacity was not an issue, but measures were required to ensure the serviceability and leak-tightness. After the application of a vapour barrier as a seal, the dome was thermally insulated to reduce the variations in temperature and provided with an outer plastic sealing sheet. The measures carried out over 30 years ago have remained effective to this day. In another example, the coating on the outer torus was renewed in 1991. This permanently eliminated moist spots on the inside of the reactor building shell.

### **Prestressing tendons**

Tendons and anchor heads of ungrouted systems can be re-tensioned or replaced. Corrosion preventive medium (grease) can be replaced. This has been done at a few stations where larger than expected loss of prestressing force occurred (e.g. Crystal River 3 in the United States). Grouted tendons cannot be re-tensioned or replaced. If prestressing levels fall below minimum design requirements, supplemental prestressing may need to be considered.

#### **Metallic liners**

Corrosion initiating from the part of the liner that is in contact with concrete has been documented in multiple nuclear power plants around the world and is the most common occurrence of documented cases of liner corrosion. Corrosion initiating from the concrete side of the liner has been associated with objects embedded in the concrete that are in direct contact with the liner, lack of consolidation or large voids behind the liner that were created during initial construction, and construction joints that were left open and exposed during construction for extended periods in coastal plants. More examples of degradation of liner and operational experiences are found in [EPRI report 3 002 021 004 Deterioration and Evaluation of Steel Liners and Vessels: Operating Experience].

Another example of location where corrosion occurs in metallic liners is along the liner circumference adjacent to upper portions of the concrete basemat. The cause is attributed to waterstop breakdown allowing fluids to accumulate in this region. Remedial measures involve inspecting the region, cleaning, recoating and reapplication of the waterstop. In some cases, material loss is sufficient to require weld overlays or application of replacement material patches. Another liner repair method involved replacement of a liner steel plate section.

In one instance where corrosion had progressed to the state that 1 cm diameter holes had penetrated the liner, repairs involved removing concrete adjacent to the region, sandblasting the liner, inspecting, welding plates over areas where holes were present and painting. In addition, corrosion inhibitor was injected into the space between the liner and floor slab and a redesigned, more durable, waterstop was installed.

In the case of EDF's 900 MWe PWRs, the containment liner was successfully repaired with a steel patch in the 1990s because some corrosion holes appeared in the bottom of the containment, due to the seal material between the concrete and the liner in this area [297]. For the double-wall containments (1 300 MWe reactors and N4 reactors), the leakage evolution is mitigated with polymer coating put at the inner or the outer face of the containment wall.

#### **Non-metallic liners**

Areas of non-metallic liner can be visually inspected for degradation, and leak tightness can be re-established by applying an additional qualified coating such as polyurethane. Repairs are typically performed by installing new liners on top of old ones after the surface has been properly prepared and compatibility of materials and qualification of the resultant liner system evaluated and confirmed.

Alternatively, the old liner can be completely removed, the substrate properly prepared and new liner applied. In either case, the repaired liner system needs to be qualified for application by tests that include the substrate, surface preparation and combination of old and new material, including the thickness and all layers of each material.

### **Spent fuel pools**

For SFP with metallic liners provided with a leak chase system behind seam welds, it is important to ensure that drainage system channels are free from obstructions to allow for leakage collection and prevention from exposure of concrete and carbon steel components to water. Underwater welding techniques, described in ANSI/AWS D3.3M [298], are available for application if the leakage location can be detected. Accessibility may also be an issue due to obstructions present in SFPs.

For SFPs with non-metallic liners, underwater repairs can be considered by recoating. However, this approach requires accessibility, careful surface preparation, material selection and application to ensure a long-lasting solution. For rigid liners, concrete cracks or joint movements may cause cracks in the repair material. EPRI and EDF have documented a robotised process for polymer repairs of spent fuel pools in [299].

In the case of EDF SFPs, in some specific areas such as fuel transfer area, the pool liner can be repaired with SS patch or silicon patch.

#### **Cooling towers**

Repairing corrosion-induced deterioration in cooling towers typically involves removing deteriorated concrete, undercutting, cleaning, and protecting reinforcing steel and reestablishing the original concrete section. Corrosion reoccurrence can be reduced by installing a sacrificial cathodic protection system for the affected concrete components. In cases of severe degradation, repair involves replacing selected beams and columns (usually in mechanical towers). Epoxy coated rebar is generally used for this purpose despite its higher cost (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

In the case of French cooling towers (refer to [300] for details), some repairs were carried out which consisted of passivating the rebars in case of corrosion, applying coating on the top of the tower, and adding structural reinforcement, in case of cracking. Some columns, affected by ASR or DEF, have been covered with a coating based on ultra highperformance fiber reinforced concrete (UHPFRC). The swelling has been stopped and the strength capacity restored. In the case of Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant in Sweden, there have been issues regarding corrosion in cooling water structures due to difficulty in accessing the affected areas.

#### **Water intake structures**

Repair of intake structures typically involves sealing of cracks and spalls using specialty epoxies, grouts, and patch materials. Specialty grouts are used for concrete surfaces under water. For underwater repairs further guidance is available in ACI 546.2R [301]. Cathodic protection can be used to prevent corrosion damage; however, its use is not common in these types of structures. Concrete deterioration by biofouling (micro-organisms attached to surfaces) is to be regularly addressed to avoid further multiplication of organisms that can be detrimental to mechanical equipment. Additional measures, such chemical treatment systems are often necessary.

### **Foundations**

Repairs to nuclear power plant basemats are like those in general civil structures, though access can be a problem. Typical remedial measures can include additional piles, groundwater level control (e.g. pumping), crack or anchorage repairs, waterproofing, machine foundation modification or soil strengthening by cementitious grout injection. Soil strengthening by cementitious grout injection is used for water control and/or structural improvement. Its advantages over removal and replacement of poor soils are that it is an in-situ treatment that is less disruptive to surrounding areas. Polyurethane grouts can be used for some applications such as concrete levelling and void filling. Structural improvements include densification, compaction grouting, soil fracturing, settlement mitigation and restoration, slab jacking, soil fracturing, pre-construction grouting, ground strengthening, liquefaction mitigation measures and slope stabilisation.

Soil permeation/chemical grouting was carried out at the Pickering Unit 8 Nuclear Power Plant to reduce settlement of its main output transformer (IAEA NP-T-3.5 [262]).

### *4.7.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

The US NRC has not identified technical gaps in concrete containments and concrete structures other than containments that would preclude licensing plants to operate from 60- 80 years. The guidance in NUREG-2191 [8], as well as the guidance in and NUREG-2192 [18] are considered adequate to address ageing issues for 60-80 years of operation.

The US NRC continues to monitor OPEX, participate in international co-operative research, continue its own confirmatory research and participate in codes and standards organisations to enhance knowledge and, as appropriate, adjusts ageing management guidance to maximise its effectiveness.

In principle, the ageing mechanisms of concrete structures that are relevant to Swiss nuclear facilities have been sufficiently researched and are compiled fully in the nuclear power plant owners' ageing management documentation. The Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate (ENSI) sees no knowledge gap here and therefore no need for action. Therefore, regular monitoring of environmental conditions is sufficient to counteract ageing effects at an early stage.

ENSI sees technological development opportunities in the preparation and performance of inspections and in the diagnosis of ageing effects. The necessary, sometimes costly preparatory work and the indirect engineering assessment of areas that are difficult or impossible to access and the evaluation of findings and test results could be reduced or improved by new technologies such as the use of drones and artificial intelligence.

The increased use of non-destructive diagnostics in favour of the waiver of destructive testing would support the long-term preservation of the existing concrete structures.

The main potential identified gaps for LTO beyond 60 years for the French nuclear power plant fleet are:

- 1. Concrete containment mechanical behaviour Based on measurement and up to date modelling, the behaviour of the containment and the steel liner in case of severe accident at 80 years will be demonstrated. A continuous effort to improve the modelling is sustained.
- 2. Concrete pathologies Given the very slow evolution kinetics, concrete swelling pathologies do not present a safety challenge (ability to detect the phenomenon in

anticipation) but could be a factor limiting the operating time because no repair solution is currently known. The planned work programme consists of better understanding and modelling the reactions, predicting their effects on the structure, and maintaining the best international state of the art R&D actions are envisaged in this direction. For sites where a pathology is proven, measures are taken where possible to limit the inflow of water which contributes to the development of the swelling reaction.

- 3. Double-wall containments leak tightness (1 300 MWe and N4 reactors) The strategy concerning the leakage evolution will stay the same: based on prevention, the areas where the leaks are anticipated are coated with polymeric coating, inside and outside the containment, and the leakage rate is periodically checked to ensure that the criterion is met. Future efforts concern the robustness of the coatings, to improve their adhesion to the wall. They also concern methods for detecting and quantifying leakage, as well as the contributions of numerical models to predict the evolution of leakage rates.
- 4. Biological shield mechanical behaviour For the biological shield, the fluence is calculated up to 80 years, considering the fuel type. If the fluence is enough to influence the concrete, calculations will be done, based on concrete properties published. If necessary (it means if the calculations with published properties do not allow to conclude), the property of the in-place concrete, considering the fluence effect, will be determined.
- 5. NDE NDE is a way of gaining access to information on the behaviour of the structure where it is not instrumented, or when the instrumentation is not relevant to the phenomenon. The main actions underway in this area are:
  - a. detection of corroded thickness and corrosion activity for coated reinforcement and liner;
  - b. detection of honeycombs, delamination, cracking, concrete defects, with an application for swelling pathologies;
  - c. measurement of the concrete stress.

Potential areas for enhancement to ensure concrete containment and civil structures operation beyond 60 years:

- 6. Enhancing considerations for ageing management during design and construction (applicable only to new builds/repairs/modifications);
- 7. Assessing synergetic effects of coupled degradation mechanisms;
- 8. Enhancing means for detecting degradation (visual inspections, NDEs);
- 9. Facilitating periodic inspections (developing tools/database to enable trending and facilitating decision making);
- 10. Enhancing protection and repairs:
  - a. incorporating better understanding of ageing in addressing the root cause;
  - b. incorporating advancements in repair techniques and materials;
  - c. taking advantage of previously performed repairs with good field performance;
  - d. documenting repairs.

- 11. Increasing use of new non-destructive diagnostics technologies such as the use of drones instead of destructive testing to reach inaccessible areas.
- 12. Increasing use of artificial intelligence to support the evaluation of test results, the comparison and trending with existing inspection results and the final assessment
- 13. Increasing research on irradiation of concrete. The areas that are affected are hard and almost impossible to reach. This makes it hard to control/inspect the structure. It is not possible to give general conclusions regarding degradation since the effect on the concrete differs depending on the constituent elements. (NDE-methods, inspections etc.).
- 14. Developing NDE methods to be able to detect degradation in embedded steel liners.

Understanding the development of degradation and corresponding pathologies in massive structures (being complex due to e.g. hydric, thermal and chemical gradients and linked with processes such as drying, leaching, mechanical loading) relevant to a nuclear power plant is crucial for different processes, and relevant for AAR, DEF and crack corrosion.

For some processes, there is further need for experimental data or studies for specific phenomena:

- Irradiation: Rate effects/annealing, requires the characterisation of in-service LWRs' concrete at high dose, i.e. > 1019 n.cm-2 E > 0.1 MeV with substantial silica content in the aggregate.
- Irradiation: Irradiated steel-concrete bond strength; possible loss on bond due to the irradiation-induced damage of concrete around reinforcement bars and anchorages.
- Irradiation: Irradiated concrete creep; higher irradiated concrete creep would limit/prevent irradiation-induced cracking.
- Harvesting service irradiated concrete from decommissioned plant and comparing the data from accelerated test specimens: This will provide valuable insights and reduce uncertainty.
- Creep and relaxation: It is still not well understood what physical phenomena create the Pickett effect (desiccation creep, Section 4.12.2.1).
- AAR: All three stages of progression are poorly understood; (1) the exact features resulting in aggregate dissolution remain ambiguous, (2) the influence of both aggregate and cement paste chemistry on resulting AAR gel mechanical properties remains ambiguous, and (3) the mechanism and kinetics of resulting swelling and damage (dependent on moisture and mechanical properties) also remains ambiguous. These are all compounded by a lack of standardisation in assessing and cataloguing relevant data, both in standard practice and laboratory studies.
- Pitting corrosion: The impacts of features of the steel-concrete interface on pitting corrosion are largely unknown and need to be further studied. The effect of steel surface condition and steel microstructure on the pitting corrosion processes in concrete is understudied and requires more attention.
- Crack corrosion: Parallel cracks pose a more serious threat to reinforcement than transverse cracks, as they sustain higher corrosion rates. The behaviour of cracks submitted to dynamic loading induces a variation in the crack widths. Indeed, the variation in the crack width may inhibit the sealing effect of the corrosion products and inhibit the re-passivation. Comparisons can be made between real crack shapes

on structures with those obtained in laboratories (by flexion) to verify if they are in accordance: shape, profile, damage length along the rebar.

Even for processes that are well understood, there are specific gaps in knowledge in these areas:

- The consequences of degradation effects on safety relevant SSCs in nuclear power plants. As such, it is not recognised how, and under which conditions, the consequences can cause a severe deterioration of concrete structures. This is relevant for microbiological processes.
- Deterioration of concrete under high temperature in the steam exhaust rooms with very high humidity. As a result, these concrete structures will be damaged more easily under the influence of temperatures of up to 150°C compared with structures located in a dry environment.
- Acid-induced dissolution of calcium-bearing cement phases, with other processes.
- The coupling between AAR and creep/shrinkage especially in the case of bi-axially loaded structures (such as the nuclear power plant containment building).
- The coupling between DEF and creep/shrinkage especially in the case of bi-axially loaded structures (such as the nuclear power plant containment building).
- The effect of a coupled deterioration mechanism on freeze-thaw loading, for example linked to AAR or leaching.
- The drying, creep and shrinkage behaviours at high temperatures.
- The synergistic effect of carbonation and chloride ingress, including how both processes effect corrosion at the same time.
- The combination of several factors that influence degradation processes, which must be considered with comprehensive and satisfactory studies on this complexity e.g. for AAR, DEF and general corrosion.

### <span id="page-201-0"></span>**4.8. Electrical cable systems**

### *4.8.1. Description of electrical cable systems*

### *4.8.1.1 Function and typical features of cables*

In nuclear power plants, cables are vital components of all systems installed in large quantities (few thousand km). Based on their specific purposes and characteristics, here are the most common functional types of cables:

- Instrumentation and control cables: These cables are used to transmit low voltage and low current analogue or digital signals from instruments. They are often composed of twisted pairs, coaxial, triaxial and shielded to minimise interference. Examples include cables for resistance temperature detectors (RTDs), pressure transmitters, and thermocouple leads. Radiation detection and neutron monitoring circuits. Often used insulation materials are cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE), ethylene propylene-based materials (EPR/EPDM), ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA), chloro-sulfonated polyethylene (CSPE), polyethylene (PE), and PVC. Modern cables do not use some of the mentioned materials like PE or PVC.
- Low and medium voltage cables: These cables are responsible for supplying power to low voltage (less than 1 kV) and medium voltage (less than 35 kV) auxiliary

devices and systems within the power plant. They can be single conductor or multiconductor cables. Low voltage power cables are used for devices such as motors, motor control centres, heaters, and small transformers. Typically, the insulation materials are XLPE, EPR, PVC.

- High voltage cables: Voltage cables over 50 kV. High voltage cables have a simple design consisting of a few parts, the same as MV cables: the conductor with the insulation, screen (semi-conducting layer with a copper type screen covering each core), the inner sheath, armour (mechanical protection) or metallic outer screen and jacket. Other layers can include water blocking tapes, ripcords. Numerous types of cable insulation materials like - XLPE, Rubber or PVC have been employed since the historical development of cables. Some types of jackets are LDPE, HDPE, polypropylene, PVC, low smoke zero halogen (LSZH), etc.
- Special cables: Special cables serve specific purposes or are designed to withstand challenging conditions. Examples include articulating cables, which are flexible and used in applications where frequent movement or bending is required. Special cables can also be designed to withstand high levels of radiation found in certain areas of the nuclear power plant.
- General service cables: These cables encompass a range of cables used for general purposes such as grounding, telecommunication and other non-specific applications.

### *4.8.1.2 Design features of nuclear power plant cable systems*

The operational time span of nuclear power plants was originally established as 30 and/or 40 years through qualification testing. Extensions to 60 years to the original operational basis of nuclear power plants are allowed for many nuclear power plants; prolongations to 80 years have been approved for some nuclear power plants and are currently being evaluated by many nuclear utilities.

For the nuclear power plants constructed in 1970s and 1980s, LTO beyond 60 years could be a concern because:

- manufacturing quality was lower at the time (for example, it is possible to identify at the plant different batches of the same type of cables that have changes in material composition);
- not all cables from the 1970s and 1980s were tested, and in some cases the cables were delivered to the nuclear power plant without information about their lifetime;
- at that time, cables were not as topical as they are now, and cable qualification was not carried out according to current knowledge, but sometimes very quickly.

To ensure the reliability of cable systems in nuclear power plants over the LTO licence extensions, more focus has been given to improve accelerated ageing models to in-service electrical cable ageing. Understanding major factors for cable ageing behaviours enables the development of technology to monitor cable condition and assess cables' residual lifetime. If the qualified life is to be extended, a thorough evaluation (including detailed knowledge of degradation mechanisms) supported by an adequate basis for the lifetime extension should be provided. The technical basis for extending the qualified life means the determination of changes in documented material composition and parameters, or in assumed environmental conditions, load cycles and other parameters. Often there is still not enough information for this decision.

The evaluation of the situation with old cables requires a specific approach, because:

- cables are in all areas of the nuclear power plant;
- often a given cable passes through several rooms with different environmental parameters, different stressors, meaning its service life may vary in individual rooms;
- different batches of the same cable can be produced in different years;
- exceptionally, the same types of cables can be found from several manufacturers with different properties;
- the exact routing is not always available;
- old cables may have been later covered with additional fire-retardant layers.

While the focus of ageing management and lifetime extension for cables often centres on the insulation material due to its critical role in maintaining electrical integrity, it is essential to consider the entire cabling system, which consists of conductors, connectors, splices, penetrations and cable constructions. Each component plays a crucial role in ensuring the overall reliability and performance of the whole cable system.

### *4.8.1.3 Construction of a typical electric cable*

The construction of a typical electric cable consists of a polymer insulating material covering a metallic copper or aluminium electrical conductor. The metallic conductor may be a single strand of solid wire or a bundled group of smaller diameter wires. The insulating material of individual cable conductors are often covered by a layer of polymer jacket material to protect the integrity of the insulating material from physical damage; multiple conductor cables will typically include an overall polymer jacket to protect the individual insulated cables that make up the cable.

Cables are qualified by their manufacturers to provide a specified service life (e.g. 40 years for nuclear power plants) for a specified voltage class (based on the qualified dielectric strength of the polymer insulation) operating continuously at or below a specified maximum ambient temperature (e.g. 90o C). If the insulation and outer jacket material are undamaged, most cables can tolerate occasional wetting but are not qualified for extended operation in a submerged state.

Electric cables operating in nuclear power plant service can be exposed to a variety of environmental and operational stressors. Environmental stressors can include elevated temperature, high radiation, high humidity, submersion, and exposure to dust, dirt, and corrosive contaminants. Operational stressors can include high voltage, electrical transients, internal ohmic heating, vibration, installation damage, manufacturing defects, and damage inflicted by operating and maintenance activity. Over time, these stressors, and combinations of these stressors, can cause ageing and degradation mechanisms that will result in ageing effects such as gradual degradation of the cable insulation and jacket materials.

A nuclear power plant, depending on the design, may contain more than 50 000 electric cable circuits, of which about 60% are control circuits, 20% are instrumentation, 13% are AC power, 1% are DC power, and the remainder are miscellaneous communications circuits. Most of these electric cable circuits are in dry, mild operating environments that are well within their qualified operating limits, and therefore perform reliably throughout their qualified service life.

Many cable circuits, however, may normally be exposed to one or more of the stressors described above and must be qualified to operate under more harsh operating environments. Electric equipment important to safety, including electric cables, that are required to continue to successfully perform their safety function in the harsh environment throughout the duration of and following design basis events occurring at the end of their qualified life, must be environmentally qualified in accordance with the requirements of 10 CFR 50.49 [16].

Cable splices are exposed to the same environmental and operational stressors as the cables on which they are installed. Since cable splices are constructed of many of the same or similar materials as the electric cables on which they are installed, these stressors can also cause ageing degradation of the polymer insulating materials used in the cable splice. In addition, the other subcomponents that make up an electric cable splice (insulating tape, fillers, sleeves, insulating compounds, and compression connectors) are also susceptible to ageing degradation due to the various stressors to which they are exposed. Connectors are susceptible to stressors such as moisture, condensation, vibration, and thermal cycling that can lead to corrosion and loosening of the conductor compression joints or solder joints.

When cable splices that are not qualified for wetted or continuous submersion are exposed to moisture, or are submerged in water, they can be affected more rapidly and more severely than a cable with intact insulation in the same environment. A poorly installed or designed splice can result in multiple penetration pathways for moisture into the interior of the splice, not only around the splice materials where they interface with the surface of the cable insulation, but also through the damaged or cracked outer jacket or insulation (EMDA, Volume 5 "Aging of Cables and Cable Systems" [46]).

Stressors affecting cable termination connections at terminal blocks, fuse holders, circuit breaker and disconnect switch terminal connectors, electric motor leads, electrical equipment insulating bushings, electrical bus bars, or other electrical equipment termination points are generally the same as those affecting electric cables. The resulting ageing and degradation mechanisms acting on the terminations, however, can be very different than for cables and splices because of the variations in the types and designs for these cable system components.

Descriptions of cables commonly used in nuclear power plant applications, which can be used as guides or knowledge transfer tools for the future AMPs owners, can be found in the following EPRI reports:

- 3002013173 "Cable Polymer Material Handbook Instrument Cable" [302], a guide for recent knowledge of degradation of polymers, efficiency and limitations of the monitoring techniques;
- 3002010637 "Cable Polymer Material Handbook Low Voltage Power and Control Cable" [303], explaining how to properly classify and apply the proper ageing management and assessment/CM techniques for cables, or to prepare design and work order packages for cable installation or cable replacement;
- 3002005322 "Cable Polymer Handbook Medium Voltage Insulations" [304], providing useful information for cable repair, replacement and ageing management, or new installations.

Depending on EDF plant series, different polymeric materials have been used for cables insulation and sheath:

- Cables of the 900 Megawatts plants are first generation cables. For LOCA resistant cables, insulation is based on EPR and outer sheath is based on CSPE. Other cables (safety classified or not) have insulation and outer sheath based on PVC;
- Starting from 1300 Megawatts plants, high voltage cables with an insulation based on XLPE are used;
- Halogen Free materials are used starting from 1 450 Megawatts plants.

All these cables were procured during the construction of the EDF nuclear fleet applying generic technical specifications, including severe qualification test sequences. This allowed the installation of cables of very much higher quality than the cable manufacturers' "catalogue" products.

More detailed information is available in France National Ageing Management Report [146] of EDF.

### *4.8.2. Physical ageing of electrical cables*

Cable ageing has been identified as one of the most important issues in relation to plant life management and life extension. To assess cable lifetime, these appropriate stressors have to be considered during accelerated ageing and qualification process. A crucial topic for long-term cable operation beyond 60 years is the appropriate and reliable ageing stressors' simulation and detection. Some specific challenges have been identified over the time related to the cables' qualification process, in particular:

- identifying which stressors are to be simulated;
- understanding how selected stressors are simulated;
- understanding in which order accelerated ageing is performed, sequentially or simultaneously;
- using appropriate ageing model;
- setting limiting conditions;
- using margins;
- monitoring cable conditions.

Knowledge of the stressors causing cable degradation helps to manage them and better assess cable lifetime. The list of degradation mechanisms, their descriptions, effects on the functional of cable/entire system and their control option are described in detail in many documents, for example [305], [200], [306], [7]. The existing documents also summarise the degradation effects for individual components of the entire cable system (cables, connectors, penetrations, drives, sensors, etc.), the significance of individual degradation effects and kinetics, their control options and other information.

Basic degradation mechanisms in the context of ageing effects on cables are presented below:

- degradation due to ionising radiation;
- temperature effect;
- moisture, steam, water;

- catalytic reaction;
- action of chemicals;
- joule (ohmic) heating;
- mechanical stress.

Gamma radiation is the most significant stressor for cables exposed to radiation during normal operation of a nuclear power plant, especially in the presence of oxygen. During accidents, beta radiation may also play an important role if the cable is not protected by a conduit. The effect of radiation degradation consists mainly of oxidative degradation. In general, the cable properties degrade with increasing absorbed doses, but many polymers are also sensitive to the radiation dose rate. The rate of degradation can be a very complicated function of the absorbed dose and is usually non-linear.

In qualification testing, the assumption is usually made that thermal degradation and radiation degradation are additive, and that there are no synergistic effects. However, for many polymers, synergistic effects can be significant so that the degradation becomes a complex function of temperature, dose and dose rate.

### *4.8.2.1 Ageing models*

Ageing models are used for:

- Simulating stressor and accelerated ageing to simulate LTO at elevated temperatures (typically the Arrhenius model). If the Arrhenius approach for thermal lifetime is used, the activation energy value needs to be known.
- Using such models, the cable condition after a specific period, e.g. 60 years, can be simulated. Models assume that the short-term simulation of thermal ageing at a higher temperature or irradiation at higher dose rates causes the same degradation as the real-life (i.e. service) long-term ageing at a lower temperature and/or lower dose rates.
- Other models are used for assessing cable lifetime at normal operational temperature. How the cables will change their properties and the time when the end point is reached. This is mostly based on the knowledge of actual cable condition and real environmental parameters.

Different ageing models have been presented during the last few decades and still new models are being developed. When using any model, it must be kept in mind that cables of concern for LTO beyond 60 years were manufactured in the 1970s and 1980s. Recent modern models, which use knowledge on antioxidants or stabilisers, cannot be easily used for these old cables as such information is not available or is difficult to obtain. Ageing models are used for stressors' simulation as well as to calculate residual lifetime, the time left to reach the limiting condition in operational conditions.

### *4.8.2.2 Accelerated ageing model*

Initially, simulations of the effects of exposure to plant temperature conditions and the postaccident temperature conditions were based on the Arrhenius equation for accelerated ageing for a life of 30 or 40 years. The radiation ageing was based on the operational dose plus the accident dose, administered as a total integrated dose. The testing was conducted in sequence with either thermal ageing followed by radiation ageing or vice versa. Based on the successful test results, the equipment was considered qualified for 40 years, and no CM was required. These test results were then used to extrapolate the known margins for extending the life for an additional ten years or more.

As a better understanding of the ageing behaviour of polymeric materials has been developed, concerns have been raised over the original approach to qualification. The main sources of the uncertainties in environmental qualification and accelerated cable ageing are diffusion limited oxidation, dose rate effects, using very high temperatures for thermal ageing, limitations of activation energy values, synergistic effects and the complex problem of the design basis accident (DBA) and post-DBA simulations. These areas of uncertainty are discussed in more detail in IAEA NP-T-3.6, Annex A–1 [305], which gives a brief summary of the ageing mechanisms in polymeric cable materials and the effects of accelerated ageing versus operational ageing that are relevant to the qualification process.

In the case of EPR/EPDM and XLPO/XLPE materials, aged under combined radiation/thermal environments, the possible presence of the "inverse temperature" effect requires further investigation. Data suggesting that the inverse temperature effect exists should be considered in any predictive models. For radiation studies, where the inverse temperature effect is absent, the dose-equivalent damage (DED) approach is the best methodology for the development of predictive models.

However, recent research conducted by the US Department of Energy (DOE), in PNNL-30041 Rev.1 Sequential Versus Simultaneous Aging of XLPE and EPDM Nuclear Cable Insulation Subjected to Elevated Temperature and Gamma Radiation [307], suggest that the sequential ageing commonly used in cable qualification may be conservative relative to in-service ageing and that conclusions regarding that conservatism likely require addition consideration of the specific materials and conditions in question. This report also demonstrates that mass change may be a useful technique for estimating the degradation of cables insulated with EPDM, particularly with the simultaneous (T/R) and sequential irradiation followed by thermal (R+T) ageing scenarios, because a sharp decrease in mass was observed to correlate to a reduction in elongation at break (EAB). In addition, total colour difference was observed to be possibly advantageous for non-destructive characterisation based on principal component analysis correlation between EAB and total colour difference and based on the sensitivity of the technique.

### *4.8.2.3 Limiting condition (end point criterion) model*

Limiting condition means a cable condition that achieves the acceptance criterion, i.e. value of the selected property, including safety margin, beyond which the rate of degradation is so significant that it can jeopardise the capability of the cable to perform its functions in normal and mainly accident operations. Setting the appropriate limiting condition(s) is one of the basic steps for cable lifetime assessment.

The conditions should be conservative enough to cover potential material nonhomogeneities, uncertainties in the assessment methods applied, etc., but not so conservative that they give needless results. Some recommended limiting condition criteria are referred to in the IAEA, EPRI and other international references (i.e. NP-T-3.6 [305], NEA/CNSI SCAP final report [150], IAEA-TECDOC-1825 [306], the final report "Assessment of cable ageing for nuclear power plants" [308], EPRI 1020804 "Aging Management Program Development Guidance for AC and DC Low-Voltage Power Cable Systems for nuclear power plants, [309], EPRI, Report No. 1008211 "Initial Acceptance Criteria Concepts and Data for Assessing Longevity of Low-Voltage Cable Insulations and Jackets" [310]).

Degradation of cable insulations is manifested most by embrittlement. Maintenance of the elastic properties of insulations is directly linked to their capability to retain mechanical integrity and geometric dimensions, even in case of movements during maintenance, minor modifications in the cable distribution systems or transfer of stress during installation (bends, clips, etc.).
