Material embrittlement may be most easily assessed by mechanical tests, measurement of EAB. EAB of jacket and conductor insulation is often the essential limiting criterion for cables. Its value must not fall below 50% for cables important to safety.

Other methods for the determination of lifetime are developed and tested in the world, which are based on measurement of electrical properties over the total length of cables. Methods for combining measurements of several electrical parameters offer the relevant potential to determine cable condition with the possibility of indicating changes (degradation). It is necessary, however, to carry out long-term measurements and set the parameters individually for specific cables. The advantage is that these measurements can be applied to inaccessible cables.

For high-voltage cables, testing partial discharges and dissipation factor tg δ is the appropriate method to determine cable condition.

As of the drafting of this report, there is no known chemical, physical or electrical method that would make it possible to clearly define an absolute acceptance criterion for a wide range of cables.

Although the current guidance on cable ageing management for long-term operation is adequate, there are two main areas where the US NRC may benefit from additional research. These areas are: 1) ageing of cables in wet and submerged environments, 2) ageing of cables in temperature and radiation environments.

#### **Ageing of cables in inaccessible and underground environments**

Cables in inaccessible and submerged environments may experience accelerated insulation degradation due to water-related ageing mechanisms. Direct contact with water or moisture intrusion in the cable insulation system has been identified as a significant ageing stressor that can affect performance and life of electric cables. Progressive reduction of the dielectric strength is commonly a result of water treeing which involves the development of permanent hydrophilic structures in the insulation coinciding with the absorption of water into the cable.

Water treeing is a phenomenon in which dendritic micro-voids are formed in electric cable insulation due to electrochemical reactions, electromechanical forces, and diffusion of contaminants over time. These reactions are caused by the combined effects of water presence and high electrical stresses in the material. Water tree growth follows a tree-like branching pattern, increasing in volume and length over time. Although these cables can be "dried out," water tree degradation, specifically the growth of hydrophilic regions, is believed to be permanent and typically worsens over time.

Based on established research, water treeing or water-induced damage can occur in a variety of electric cables including XLPE, TR-XLPE and other insulating materials, such as EPR and butyl rubber. Once water trees or water induced damage form, the dielectric strength of an insulation material will decrease gradually with time as the water trees grow in length, which could turn into an electrical tree resulting in the failure of the insulating material.

Under wet conditions or in inaccessible or submerged environments, several environmental and operational parameters can influence water tree initiation and affect water tree growth. These parameters include voltage cycling, field frequency, temperature, ion concentration and chemistry, type of insulation material, and the characteristics of its defects. Cables in inaccessible and underground environments are generally routed through underground conduits, concrete duct banks, cable trenches, cable troughs, and underground vaults, or they may be directly buried.

The concern for cables in inaccessible and underground environments is that cables that are subject to wet and submerged environments could develop water trees that could possibly transitions into electrical trees causing the cable to degrade and fail prematurely compared to the cable's expected life. This concern was substantiated by the results of Generic Letter (GL-2007-01), where the licensees were asked to provide a history of inaccessible and/or underground power cable failures that are within the scope of 10 CFR 50.65

The review of licensees' responses identified 269 cable failures for 104 reactor units. The data obtained from the generic letter responses showed an increasing trend of cable failures. These cables were failing within the plants' 40-year licensing periods. However, over the last 15 years, EPRI has issued several ageing management guidelines that included performing CM that have demonstrated the ability to manage the ageing of cables in wet and submerged environments.

#### **Ageing of cables due to temperature and radiation**

The qualification approach used for cables in US plants was specified in two Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) documents (formerly used IEEE 323-1974 and 383-1974) issued in 1974. Since these standards were published, additional knowledge has been acquired to improve qualification methodology. For example, per the IEEE documents, lifetime predictions could be developed by measuring physical properties (EAB) at elevated temperatures and subsequently extrapolating physical property behaviour to lower temperatures relevant to power plant conditions, assuming Arrhenius behaviour (i.e. no change in activation energy).

Regarding radiation induced ageing, the equal damage/equal dose assumption was employed such that the total dose of interest was typically simulated at high dose rates, such as 10 kGy/h (1 Mrad/h). Additionally, accelerated ageing simulation was usually done sequentially, with the thermal environment preceding the radiation environment. Over the past 35 years, substantial efforts have been devoted to determining whether the ageing assumptions employed by the original IEEE standards could be improved. The studies have led to a better understanding of accelerated ageing methods and more confident lifetime predictions.

During qualification of cable materials (as required by IEEE 323-1974 and 383-1974), prior to performing the LOCA test, the cables were pre-aged to degradation levels equivalent to the expected lifetime of the nuclear power plant (end-of-life condition). In semicrystalline polymers, such as XLPE and some EPR materials (where the crystalline melting points lie below the temperatures employed to pre-age the samples), there is a concern that the ageing that came as a result is not representative of the ageing the cables undergo in the nuclear plants under normal operating conditions.

Therefore, performing the temperature ageing at temperatures above the melting point of the semicrystalline polymers and the radiation ageing at high radiation dose rates (10 kGy/h 1 Mrad/h) may have given rise to several uncertainties associated with how the accelerated pre-ageing for the qualification was carried out. Mainly, these are that performing the ageing sequentially and at high temperatures and high radiation dose rates may not properly age the cables (ageing the cables to their end-of-life condition) prior to the LOCA test compared to performing the ageing concurrently and at lower temperatures and lower radiation dose rates as the cables experience in the containment of nuclear power plants.

The uncertainties associated with how the accelerated ageing for the qualification process was performed (sequentially and at high temperature and high radiation dose rates) are as follows:

- activation energy;
- diffusion limited oxidation;
- dose rate effects;
- synergistic effects between thermal and radiation ageing;
- sequential versus concurrent ageing;
- inverse temperature effects;
- pre-ageing of semi-crystalline materials.

Important sources of information are:

- NRC, NUREG-6384, "Literature Review of Environmental Qualification of Safety-Related Electric Cables", Washington, DC, April 1996. (Agency Document and Access Management System (ADAMS) Number ML031600732) [311];
- NRC, GL-2007-01, "Inaccessible or Underground Power Cable Failures that Disable Accident Mitigation Systems or Cause Plant Transient: Summary Report," Washington, DC. (Agency Document and Access Management System (ADAMS) Number ML0827603850) [312];
- SANDIA, REPORT, SAND2005-7331, "Nuclear Energy Plant Optimization (NEPO) Final Report on Ageing and Condition Monitoring of Low-Voltage Cable Materials," Albuquerque, NM, November 2005 [313];
- PNNL. Technical Letter Report, PNNL-28542, "Assessment of EPRI's Tan Delta Approach to Manage Cables in Submerged Environments: Statistical Review of EPRI Data," Richland, WA, March 2020 [314].

Medium-voltage cables degrade primarily due to dielectric effects (water treeing, partial discharge) not thermal ageing (there are known, but rare instances). The following cable ageing management guides provide more insights into common ageing modes:

- 1021070 "Medium-Voltage Cable Aging Management Guide", Revision 1 [315]. Although issued in 2010 the report provides practical information to help in choosing the correct assessment tests to apply and to help understand critical issues about selection and installation of cables and terminations that affect cable longevity;
- 1013187 "Plant Support Engineering: Life Cycle Management Planning Sourcebooks: Medium-Voltage (MV) Cables and Accessories (Terminations and Splices)" [316], providing system engineers with generic information, data, and guidance they can use to generate a long-term equipment reliability plan for the plant-specific SSC (ageing and obsolescence management plan optimised in terms of plant performance and financial risk).

As for Low-Voltage Cables, EPRI report 3002000924, "Low-Voltage Cable Aging Management Guidance" [317] provides sufficient information to enable personnel to readily understand cable system ageing management and the activities that must be performed to control the ageing of cables during remaining plant life. All the common adverse localised environments (ALE) shown have been seen in plants, but thermal oxidative ageing from external heating (not ohmic heating) is most common cause identified for cable degradation. The below EPRI guides cover identification and evaluation of cables and associated ALEs:

- 3002010641 "Low-Voltage and Instrumentation and Control Cable Aging Management Guide, Revision 1" [318]. The report describes a common approach for developing and implementing a low-voltage power, control, and instrument cable system ageing management programme that focuses on worst-case adverse environmental conditions. Verifying that cables in such conditions are not ageing significantly indicates that the cables in less severe environments are in satisfactory condition. If not, the scope of assessment broadens, and further action is needed.
- TR-109619 "Guideline for the Management of Adverse Localised Equipment Environments" [319]. The guideline presents a systematic approach for identifying and managing ALE at reasonable cost and effort and is very useful for development of an equipment qualification surveillance tasks.

Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant has concluded that they need to consider different ageing mechanisms (oxidation, embrittlement, etc.) and different ageing stressors (temperature, radiation, humidity, etc.) that might accelerate ageing and ageing effects. Ringhals states that the effect (loss of flexibility, hardening, decreased insulation resistance, etc.) of ageing mechanisms and detection of different ageing stressors are easier to detect than the detection of ageing mechanisms. Therefore, Ringhals Cables AMP is mainly focusing on detecting these different ageing effects and stressors to handle the different ageing mechanisms.

Of the three important ageing stressors mentioned above, temperature is the most significant stressor since it causes the material to harden (loses its elasticity) and eventually loses its tensile properties. Obviously, cables exposed to radiation are also important to consider but a major part of cables at Ringhals units are routed in rather radiation mild environment. The existence of ALE "hot spots" for rooms including cables might challenge cable performance.

Ringhals has notice that there can be batch-related ageing problems. If the supplier does not use the same mixture of the polymer every time in the manufacturing process or if the cable has two types of polymer on the wire insulation it can be a problem because of different ageing mechanism stressor or behaviours.

The main ageing mechanisms affecting electrical cables are related to the ageing of the organic materials (polymers) making up the insulating jackets and outer sheaths under the effect of temperature, irradiation, or even humidity. This ageing results in an evolution of the electrical and physico-chemical characteristics of these polymers. OPEX and studies carried out show that the main ageing mechanisms that can affect cables are:

- Oxidation This is the predominant mode of degradation of polyethylene-based polymers (XLPE, EPR). To inhibit, or at least slow down, oxidation-related degradation, antioxidants are used in polymer formulations. The first stage in the ageing process of polymers used in the insulation and sheathing of electrical cables is to consume these antioxidants. The oxidation reaction, associated with the production of polymer oxidation products, will only begin once all the antioxidants have been consumed.
- Additives migration Some additives present in polymers, such as the plasticisers used in PVC formulations, are liable to migrate over time, by exudation or evaporation. A typical case is the exudation of phthalate or phosphate plasticisers present in PVC. The loss of additives leads to the loss of the properties they confer.

In the case of PVC, migration of plasticisers leads to changes in mechanical properties and, in some cases, a reduction in insulation.

- Water trees linked to the presence of moisture For high voltage cables with polyethylene-based insulation (XLPE, EPR), the combination of humidity and electric field causes electrochemical reactions leading to the appearance of microcracks, and then progressively to the formation of water trees in the insulation. This can eventually lead to breakdown.
- Dehydrochlorination in the case of PVC It is initiated by temperature under aerobic or anaerobic conditions (absence of oxygen), and therefore also affects confined materials such as cable insulation. It consists of the formation of carboncarbon double bonds and hydrochloric acid (HCl) following the departure of chlorine and hydrogen atoms present in PVC. This phenomenon can cause some drop of insulation on some PVC cables.
- Ageing mechanisms occurring on a macromolecular scale Modifications affecting polymers on a macromolecular scale are chain cutting and chain welding (cross-linking). These have a major impact on the mechanical behaviour of polymers.

There may also be modifications to the side groups (grafting of oxygenated groups), which have little influence on mechanical behaviour but can, for example, modify the dielectric properties of the material.

These three mechanisms coexist (cutting, cross-linking, grafting) and will be preponderant depending on environmental conditions (temperature, irradiation, type of radiation, etc.) and the nature of the polymer.

### *4.8.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### *4.8.3.1 Cable condition*

Models and pre-ageing tests predict cable service lifetime. However, real ageing may be different: environmental parameters may differ and models may not be exact. Therefore, it is important to determine actual cable condition and compare with predicted values.

The best way for cable condition determination is measurement of cables harvested from the plant. If the main limiting condition criterion is EAB, exact cable condition can be known. Cables can be harvested from the cable deposits, if available, or during maintenance, cable replacement, or modernisation. The history and operational conditions shall always be known. Measured parameters are used not only for cable actual condition, but also to improve model precision.

If it is not possible to measure cables removed from the plant, other CM strategies for old cables in nuclear power plants can be implemented, as per IAEA No. NP-T-3.6 [305] and IAEA TECDOC-1825 [306]. Some of the proposed methods have already been standardised (see IEC/IEEE 62582 Electrical equipment condition monitoring methods - Part 3: Elongation at break [320], IEC/IEEE 62582 - Electrical equipment condition monitoring methods - Part 4: Oxidation induction techniques [321] and IEC/IEEE 62582 - Electrical equipment condition monitoring methods - Part 5: Optical time domain reflectometry [322]). When it comes to determining the actual condition of cables, there are several methods available. However, it's important to note that each method may have its own limitations and confidence levels.

Unanticipated operating conditions are caused by defective installation, operation, or manipulation with the cable, which can lead to enhanced degradation. These conditions are usually only identified through thorough visual inspection walkdown observations. This involves physically examining the cables and associated components, such as for example junction boxes, for signs of damage, degradation, or wear. It helps to find cracks and surface cracking, hardened insulations, mechanical stress (for example compression by clamp), incorrectly attached cables to the equipment, cable bended around sharp edge, too small bending radius of the cable, chemical contamination (paint, oil, boric acid), source of heat (melting of the jacket), hot spots, etc. All findings need to be documented, and managed; important findings need to be solved immediately. As stated in RG 1.218 [323], research and experience have shown that no single, nonintrusive, condition-monitoring method currently available, if used alone, is effective to predict the performance of electric cables under accident conditions. A combination of condition-monitoring techniques provides significant insights into the condition of cables.

### *4.8.3.2 Methods to determine cable system conditions*

To determine the condition of cables and to verify whether important cables for safety functions are still reliable or need to be replaced for LTO, the following areas are important:

- qualification processes, including pre-installation laboratory qualification testing as well as post-installation measures to verify adequate cable performance while the plant is operating and in case of DBA;
- condition-based qualification (CBQ), a method that compares the current cable condition with results provided through the qualification process;
- cable ageing management programme (CAMP), providing support to the current and future licence renewal activities calling nuclear power plants to operate for up to 80 years or more;
- cable condition monitoring as a part of CAMP involving methods that can be used to determine the performance of cable insulation material.

The qualification process may be accomplished in several ways: type testing, OPEX, and analysis. These may be used individually or in any combination depending upon the situation. The preferred method of qualification is type testing which is described in various standards, national requirements or recommendations (IEEE, IAEA). It begins with a detailed qualification specification, described in standards, continues with pre-ageing, DBA simulation and functional properties measurement to verify that sample is functional during the whole time, and test results are described in a final qualification report.

The equipment qualification (EQ) of cables has evolved in the decades to provide methods suitable for providing an increasing level of confidence in cable performance. The early cable qualification tests involved operational ageing and DBA tests with cable functionality proven. The service life of the component is projected based on the operational ageing and adjustments to that period based on the actual service environment. However, the actual environment could be severe, model for accelerated ageing activation energy could change or the cable materials qualified vs. delivered could change. These combined effects and impact on cable ageing may influence the total cable lifetime.

CBQ is an improved method of EQ that provides improved confidence in equipment performance in that it requires CM activities to measure and record the level of cable degradation and keep track of the degradation rate in any of the cable characteristics. In this procedure, the cable samples are aged to various equivalents of normal operating time (i.e. without DBA), up to 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, or 80 years.

For aged samples, a suitable condition indicator is measured that varies with the rate of degradation caused by ageing. For cables, this is most often the EAB measurement., but other indicators, including electrical ones, are being explored. In this way, the trend of change of the given property with time is obtained. The trend is then compared to an aged cable sampled in service. Thus, the degree of degradation of the operated cable is determined. Extensive guidance about the qualification process and all the assessment phases are described in IAEA NP-T-3.6, Section 3 Qualification methodology and Section 4 Qualification monitoring [305] and IAEA SSG-69 on Equipment Qualification for Nuclear Installations [12].

To provide reasonable assurance that the intended functions of electrical cables and connections are maintained consistent with the current licensing basis through the expected operation period, as well as through the period of extended operation, a CAMP must be implemented. The basic goal of CAMP and qualification is assessment and determination of the residual lifetime of cables. it is necessary to know the influence of degradation mechanisms on the ageing process; to find out what degradation mechanisms affect the individual cables at different locations of the nuclear power plant and to establish a suitable criterion to estimate the residual lifetime. The cable lifetime model is shown in Figure 4.24.

<span id="page-215-0"></span>

**Figure 4.24. Time representation of the residual lifetime**

Source: Vit Placek, UJV Rez

Focusing on cables exposed to harsh conditions, particularly due to high temperature and radiation dose, there is sufficient information to determine the limiting service conditions of various insulation materials for LTO from 40 to 60-year period, e.g. in Table 10-1 of EPRI 1013475 [324]. The "60 Year Service Limiting Environment" defined in the aforementioned table is understood as an environment, in terms of temperature and radiation dose, to which insulation materials indicated in the Table could be exposed to for 60 years and still perform its design function. It is possible then, considering the information gathered in this Table, to determine specific limiting conditions for cables based on the insulation materials within the scope of CAMP.

Considering the specific conditions of a nuclear power plant, it is possible to determine nuclear power plants ALE locations for different type of insulation materials. When operating from 40 to 60 years these locations are defined as areas where temperature and radiation dose conditions exceed the "60 Year Service Limiting Conditions" for a certain type of insulation material included in Table 10-1 of EPRI 1013475 [324]. To identify ALEs for different types of insulation materials, trays/conduits routing diagrams related to potential areas with harsh environments are evaluated. Once cables exposed to ALEs are identified, its monitoring/inspection should be considered, and potential ageing effect and degradation mechanisms should be managed, at least if these cables are not subject to Environmental Qualification requirements.

In addition, according to Regulatory Guide 1.211 [325], qualification by analysis alone does not ensure that safety-related cables and field splices can be demonstrated to perform their safety functions under postulated DBEs, and that no failure mechanism exists that could lead to common cause failures under postulated service conditions. Therefore, in accordance with RG 1.211 [325], programmes for monitoring of environmental conditions (such as temperature, radiation levels) and CM should be also implemented for safety related power, instrumentation, and control cables subject to Environmental Qualification requirements. CAMP may include, for a representative sample of this type of cables, any appropriate inspection techniques, supplemented with walkdowns to look for visible signs of anomalies attributable to ageing, with particular emphasis on the identification of ALE or "hot spots."

A reliable assessment model of cable lifetime evaluation is crucial for long-term cable operation beyond 60 years. The basic factors influencing cable lifetime calculation are:

- selecting an appropriate ageing model;
- setting the appropriate limiting conditions;
- continuously maintaining model precision.

Close collaboration with nuclear power plant operators and staff is a very important part of the CAMP and significantly improves the CAMP outputs.

### *4.8.3.3 Testing methods relevant for cables condition beyond 60 years*

In practice, to fully utilise the concept of qualified condition for cables in a nuclear power plant, it is necessary to carry out qualification monitoring to confirm that the qualification is still valid and the cables are in the expected limits. Qualification monitoring covers both environmental monitoring of actual conditions in the plant and CM of the cables.

A lot of documents propose, describe and discuss different CM techniques, like IAEA No. NP-T-3.6 [305], SCAP final report NEA/CSNI/R(2010)15 [150], IAEA Safety Reports Series No. 82 [7], EPRI report 1020804, Aging Management Program Development Guidance for AC and DC Low-Voltage Power Cable Systems for nuclear power plants, [309], IEC/IEEE [62582-3: 2012 \[320\]62582-4: 2012](https://standards.ieee.org/findstds/standard/62582-4-2011.html) [321]62582-5: 2012 [322].

A detailed international benchmark test on different CM methods was carried out within IAEA activities. The goal of the benchmark analysis was to provide guidelines on how to monitor the performance of insulation and jacket materials of aged low voltage cables and to establish a programme for monitoring cable degradation in nuclear power plants. The results have been published in the IAEA TECDOC-1825 [306] and show what the ideal CM methodology for cable systems assessment should provide:

- cables' structural integrity and electrical functionality;
- ability to differentiate between global and localised degradation and localise the degraded points;
- unambiguous trend in the degradation level;
- a limiting condition, or one that is correlated with a property providing end point criterion;
- assurance that the method and values uncertainty are within reasonable limits.

### 4.8.3.3.1 Electrical testing techniques

Some examples of electrical functionality tests are insulation resistance, polarisation index, voltage withstand and dielectric breakdown. Most of these tests are certainly effective as pass/fail indicators of functionality, but studies over many years in the nuclear industry suggest that there are no reliable data yet available that allow an appropriate correlation between these measurements and cable ageing. Some of these tests require high voltages (dielectric breakdown is a destructive test) and thus may be considered inappropriate for use on I&C cables in situ for fear of insulation damage.

Electrical measurements are mostly applicable to cabling systems, including conductors, connectors, splices, and penetrations although they can also reveal problems in cable insulation material. Some techniques are sensitive to insulation degradation (polarisation and depolarisation current (PDC), Tan Delta, dielectric spectroscopy, time domain reflectometry (TDR)/frequency domain reflectometry FDR, etc), others are sensitive to conductor integrity (e.g. loose connections, corrosion of connectors). The advantage of electrical techniques is in their in-situ and remote testing capability. Many of the electrical measurements can be performed on installed cables in an operating plant and can often reveal problems along the whole length of a cable.

Currently known CM methods based on electrical measurements are mostly useful in identifying and locating problems in nuclear power plant cable systems and confirming functional performance. Some have shown potential for measuring ageing degradation, but more research is needed to validate their use. One of the practical limitations is often in determining a suitable ground plane for electrical measurements. For unshielded cables, this is a major disadvantage. Where cable is shielded, the shield can often be used as a more reliable ground plane for measurements.

IAEA NP-T-3.6 "Assessing and Managing Cable Ageing in Nuclear Power Plants", in Section 4.7 [305] and IAEA TECDOC-1825 in Table 33 [306] give a comprehensive view of every technique available, with advantages, disadvantages and applicability of different non-destructive CM methods:

- partial discharges;
- FDR;
- TDR;
- reverse time domain reflectometry (RTDR);
- dielectric loss measurement;
- inductance, capacitance and resistance (LCR) measurements;
- insulation resistance measurements;
- embedded microsensors.

Methods requiring samples:

- EAB;
- indenter modulus;
- density;
- oxidative induction time.

According to EDMA, vol. 5, Section 3.1 Ageing [46], specifically, ultrasonic inspection, infrared thermography, and chemical sensing of by-products are demonstrated as diagnostic tools to characterise cable insulation. A nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) relaxation technique for detecting ageing in XLPO insulations and CSPE cable jackets has been demonstrated. Broadband impedance is discussed and shown to be sensitive to changes in the physical and chemical state of aircraft wiring. In addition, wire impedance was measured for wires exposed to humidity, and it was shown that the resistance increases. To determine the remaining life of insulation through detection of micro-void characteristics, the energy stored within the electric field between the wires is affected by micro-void growth and thus, capacitance can be correlated to micro-void content, as presented in "Proceedings of the International Conference on Wire System Ageing" NUREG/CP-0179 [326], held in April 2002.

A promising new method is dielectric spectroscopy. The method was developed at University of Bologna within the European Research Projects ADVANCE and TEAM Cables and was further developed by EPRI in the report EPRI 3002020818 "Test Protocol for Condition Monitoring of Low/Voltage Cable using Dielectrically Based Methods" [327]. At present, this method is being applied in nuclear power plants.

In medium voltage cables, Tan Delta and withstand testing are typically used for condition assessment. The below references describe application of Tan Delta to ageing of cable systems:

- EPRI 3002000557 "Aging Management Program Guidance for Medium-Voltage Cable Systems for Nuclear Power Plants", Revision 1 [328]. This report describes the scope of the cable circuits to be evaluated, those conditions that are ALE, and the actions to be taken to assess the conditions of the cable circuits subject to adverse conditions. For key test methodology, assessment criteria are described, along with possible corrective actions that could be implemented.
- EPRI 1021070 "Medium-Voltage Cable Aging Management Guide", Revision 1 [329] . The report is unique in that it focuses on the cable types used in the nuclear power industry and the conditions that challenge them, allowing staff to understand the specifics of their cable systems without being confused by the much broader range of cable information associated with power distribution systems that do not apply to nuclear power plants.

For low voltage power and instrumentation cables, a combination array of tests including Dielectric Spectroscopy, Pol/Depol, TDR, and FDR can be used. This is described in the reference below:

- EPRI 3002020818 "Test Protocol for Condition Monitoring of Low Voltage Cable Using Dielectrically Based Methods", [327]. The report is linked with another EPRI report 3002010403 "Initial Findings on Use of Dielectric Spectroscopy for Condition Monitoring of Low Voltage Nuclear Power Plant Cables ( [330]), where commonly used cross-linked polyethylene and ethylene propylene rubber insulations were subjected to accelerated thermal ageing of whole cable assemblies (multiconductor cables) and single-conductor test specimens and were periodically assessed using various mechanical (EAB, indenter), physiochemical (for example, oxidation induced temperature (OIT), density), and electrical testing (insulation resistance, low frequency dielectric spectroscopy (LFDS), PDC) methods. The report documents the results of both the laboratory and field testing and shows promising results, but more modelling and confirmatory physical testing are needed to support remaining life estimations.
- EPRI 1022969 "Plant Engineering: Electrical Cable Test Applicability Matrix for Nuclear Power Plants" [331]. The report indicates whether the test is a standard test or under development, whether acceptance criteria are available, and whether an expert is necessary to interpret the results. The fault-locating techniques are also described in the main body of the report. The report ensures that the correct test is chosen for a given situation, reducing greatly that the wrong test will be chosen, and confusing results or erroneous information be obtained.

Electric cable condition-monitoring tests may be grouped by whether the inspection or test is performed in situ on electric cables in the plant or if a laboratory-type test performed on representative material specimens in a controlled laboratory setting. These conditionmonitoring test techniques may be performed to measure and assess the following:

- electrical properties (such as insulation resistance test, voltage withstand, dielectric loss/dissipation factor, time domain reflectometry, and partial discharge);
- mechanical properties (such as hardness, EAB, and compressive modulus/polymer indenter test);
- chemical and physical properties (such as density, oxidation induction time, oxidation induction temperature, and infrared spectroscopy);
- physical condition and appearance (visual inspection).

As said in RG 1.218 [323], research and experience have shown that no single CM method currently available, if used alone, is effective to predict the performance of electric cables under accident conditions. A combination of CM techniques provides significant insights into the condition and level of degradation of cables.

Based on the operating parameters, cable insulation and jacket materials, cable construction (e.g. solid/extruded versus laminated, shielded versus unshielded), and environmental and operating stressors for each cable system application, the user should select CM inspection and testing techniques to detect, quantify, and monitor the status of the ageing mechanisms that may cause the degradation of the cable system. By selecting the CM techniques that are best suited to the detection and monitoring of the anticipated stressors and associated ageing and degradation mechanisms, the user can more accurately monitor the condition of critical plant cables, assess their operating condition, and implement corrective actions to manage ageing and degradation in those cables that are found to be experiencing stressors and ageing and degradation rates beyond specified design conditions.

The realistic and timely assessment of cable condition is the best means for managing cable degradation and avoiding unexpected early cable failures. Sections 3 and 4.5 of NUREG/CR-7 000 "Essential Elements of an Electric Cable Condition Monitoring Program" [332] provides guidance on the selection of condition monitoring techniques for electric cables. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Std. 1205-2000/Cor 1-2006, "Guide for Assessing, Monitoring, and Mitigating Aging Effects on Class 1E Equipment Used in Nuclear Power Generating Stations" [333] provides guidelines for assessing, monitoring, and mitigating ageing degradation effects on Class 1E equipment used in nuclear power generating stations.

Provided that the cable successfully passes the LOCA test after pre-ageing, the CM values can then be used to determine the qualified level of degradation (QLD) that can be applied to the installed cable as acceptance criteria.

The recently completed NUREG/CR 7 300 [334], concluded that "except for the wellestablished Elongation-At-Break (EAB) condition monitoring method, no single condition monitoring method was found to be suitable for condition-based qualification for cables." Instead, the user would have to employ a combination of CM techniques to manage the ageing of cables based on the environmental conditions to which the cables are subject.

Additionally, there is a need to develop and validate suitable acceptance criteria to employ in the use of non-destructive examination techniques capable of assessing the ageing of the cables in-situ. (US NRC, RG 1.218, "Condition-Monitoring Techniques for Electric Cables used in Nuclear Power Plants [323]).

The non-destructive methods used by Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant Units-3&4 are visual inspection, indenter, line resonance analysis (LIRA), very low frequency Tan-Delta testing, partial discharge testing, insulation resistance testing, and outer sheath insulation resistance and TDR. The destructive methods used by Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant are EAB and high voltage withstand test (if cable deficiencies exist).

Identification of "hot spots" is mainly done by usage of thermography camera, but usage of temperature- and radiation loggers was introduced in for inaccessible rooms, when inspections are performed, i.e. during "plant walk down". The result of a "plant walk down" and temporary installation of temperature- and radiation loggers is documented and, if necessary, used to update the preventive maintenance plan. Or to initiate a corrective action (e.g. to insert shielding such as double insulation of hot pipes or establish a new cable routing to avoid identified "hot spots").

Testing of harvested cables installed from the beginning in the containment area of Ringhals Unit 3 and 4 was performed with the EAB method. The result of these measurements was summarised in the research report "In situ NMR condition monitoring of cable insulations in Nuclear Power Plants" [335] [\(2021-01 In situ NMR CM of cable](https://www.stralsakerhetsmyndigheten.se/contentassets/dc0b8a1af99c45c3b47a3e2a192d1bb9/202101-in-situ-nmr-condition-monitoring-of-cable-insulations-in-nuclear-power-plants.pdf)  [insulations in Nuclear Power Plants\).](https://www.stralsakerhetsmyndigheten.se/contentassets/dc0b8a1af99c45c3b47a3e2a192d1bb9/202101-in-situ-nmr-condition-monitoring-of-cable-insulations-in-nuclear-power-plants.pdf)

There are several methods with different levels of maturity to characterise the ageing of an electric cable at a given moment in time. These complementary methods are suitable to identify and understand cable ageing mechanisms and estimate cable service life:

- Visual inspection is a very simple means of diagnosis that allows detection of the first signs of cable ageing and severe environmental conditions that could speed up the cable ageing process. Visual inspection also enables the state of the cable raceways to be checked (for corrosion, mechanical damage, etc.).
- Insulation resistance measurements consist in measuring the current passing through the insulated when a continuous voltage is applied. A linear resistance value of 30 Megohm.km is the internationally accepted threshold below which investigations must be carried out to identify the cause of the drop in insulation resistance. The insulation resistance measurement alone cannot constitute a cable operability criterion. The detection of a drop in insulation resistance on a cable must therefore be supplemented by measurements to refine the diagnosis.
- Tan-Delta measurements can also be used. The dissipation factor value is reserved for high-voltage or medium-voltage cables, and it is the ratio between the resistive current Ir and the capacitive current Ic crossing the insulation. If the insulant is degraded, the Ir/Ic ratio is higher and increases with the voltage applied. The dissipation factor value and how it changes with voltage are used to establish a diagnosis of the overall condition (dielectric losses) of high-voltage or mediumvoltage cable insulation. It does not however enable a fault to be located, or to distinguish global ageing from a serious isolated fault. To do this, the Tan-Delta measurement must be combined with Partial Discharge measurements, as detailed below.
- Partial discharge measurements are also reserved for high-voltage or mediumvoltage cables. They supplement the Tan-Delta measurement to locate one or more isolated defects along the length of a cable. Partial discharges are microbreakdowns occurring in the insulation under the effect of the electric field around certain defects such as micro-voids or treeing (associated with the presence of moisture). The principle that permits the locating of partial discharges is comparable to that used in reflectometry.

- The TDR principle is to generate an electrical pulse at the end of a cable and to observe the signal reflected from that pulse: The electrical pulse is propagated along the entire length of the cable and reflected when it reaches the other end, but also if it encounters a defect in the insulation or a variation in the impedance of the cable. Knowing the speed of propagation of the pulse, it is possible to determine the location of the defects along the length of the cable.
- This technique, which can be used on low-voltage cables, is like the principle of partial discharge measurement used on high-voltage or medium-voltage cables. It does not enable the state of degradation of a cable to be assessed directly but is used as a complement to other diagnostic methods.

For high-voltage or medium-voltage cables, the Tan-Delta and partial discharge measurements have been used on the French nuclear power plants since 2012 in line with international recommendations. Their effectiveness was confirmed by EPRI in 2015 and by the US NRC in 2022. Partial discharge measurements complement Tan-Delta measurements as a means of resolving doubts.

Studies on low-voltage cables continue, but to date no relevant technique has been identified that can be used in the field.

The European ADVANCE project (Ageing diagnostics and prognostics of low voltage I&C cables) ended in 2013. It did not identify any NDE techniques (mechanical, chemical, or electrical) that could be used directly in the field, but some techniques (such as dielectric spectroscopy) look promising. The use of reflectometry, most likely reserved for the detection of point defects, remains under investigation.

Following the ADVANCE project, a co-ordinated research project with the IAEA was launched in 2013. As part of this project, a brochure entitled "Benchmark Analysis for Condition Monitoring Test Techniques of Aged Low Voltage Cables in Nuclear Power Plants" was published in 2017.

In addition to these diagnostic methods, a programme of on-site cable sampling has been put in place on the nuclear French fleet for several years. This multi-year programme covers all high-voltage, medium-voltage and low-voltage cable ranges installed (manufacturer, polymer). The results of characterisation of cables that have aged naturally on site have improved the understanding of cable ageing mechanisms, confirmed the interest of the predictive approach and validated cable operability up to at least 60 years of operation. Some of the cables sampled have been in service for over 35 years, giving a solid understanding of the ageing phenomena of the various polymers.

The criterion for serviceability of cables is a mechanical one (EAB) whose value must remain above 50% in absolute value (internationally shared acceptance criterion for cables).

### *4.8.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

EPRI has created high-level guidance on use cases for wireless as a substitute for degraded wire:

• 3002018281 "Wireless Technologies as a Replacement for Degraded Cable Systems" [336]. The report shows that replacing degraded cables with new cables can be cost-prohibitive when many cables are involved. Wireless and other modern digital communication technologies provide a cost-effective alternative to allow plants to remain competitive. Wireless technologies are already in use throughout industrial areas within plants to support mobile workforce initiatives and conditionbased monitoring applications. Through plant modernisation efforts, wireless will gradually become ubiquitous throughout the plant. Also, wireless sensors and adaptors can be deployed at low cost and integrated with an existing network infrastructure quickly. By initially targeting systems that are not safety-related, the regulatory burden and concerns over cybersecurity and reliability are reduced, making the wireless option more appealing. As another option for upgrades and replacements, fibreoptic cables could also serve as an effective alternative that might provide similar cost and installation benefits.

• 3002000551 "Plant Engineering: Results of Cable Rejuvenation of Severely Degraded Black Ethylene Propylene Rubber Medium-Voltage Cables" [337]. This report describes results for proof-of-concept research for using commercially available cable rejuvenation processes on severely degraded, service-aged, medium-voltage, black EPR cables that were submerged or wet for much of their service life. The cable rejuvenation provides an alternative to immediate cable replacement. As a proof of concept, this research did not evaluate the long-term effect of rejuvenation to determine how long lasting the rejuvenated cable's insulation breakdown strength will be. In lieu of additional research, this process should be considered an interim action. Further evaluation would be needed to understand how the process affects change over time.

Ringhals Unit 3 and 4 have replaced all Hypalon/Lipalon insulated safety-related cable installed in with function criteria in an accident scenario inside the containment.

At Ringhals Unit 3 and 4 there were oil-insulated high voltage cables between 130 kV switchgears and the startup transformers T93 and T94. The cables were more than 40 years old and demonstrated signs of ageing degradation. At T93 there was indication of an oil leakage at the phase terminals which was not considered to be repairable because there are no spare parts available. The conclusion and assessment were to exchange these cables to oil-free XLPE insulated cables.

When cables above 1 kV are spliced, the ambition is to do partial discharge measurement to verify that the splice and end termination are correctly installed. The measurement gives a fingerprint from the installation date and can be compared to future measurements, to look for deviations over time. This is for detecting irregularities in the installation process that can result in high thermal loads at these points and the discharges will eventually break down the insulation.

As already mentioned, repair and replacement are not a technical issue for cables. It is only the massive replacement of cables, especially if a sudden cliff effect occurs, that could be an issue.

- Research that supports cable thermal ageing and thermal ageing model improvement.
- The use of so-called sensor cables that monitor the temperature load. These are hybrid cables that monitor the temperature along their entire length. It can also be used for cables in hermetic cable penetrations.

### *4.8.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

### **Research open issues**

It may be correct to assume that all cables between 40 and 60 years old should be considered as being near their end of life, unless there is demonstrable evidence to the contrary. This might include detailed CM and environmental monitoring, combined with life curves generated during EQ pre-ageing which was carried out under conditions that minimised uncertainties. Where practical, PVC cables should not be considered for life extension because of their fire hazard, even if their degradation levels are low. Cable penetrations containing PVC should also be considered for replacement.

Ageing model precision: the used model is compared with the actual cable condition at the plant. Using these results, that model shall be regularly improved. One important parameter is the appropriate value of activation energy, which needs to be validated for each cable type, for jacket as well as insulation material. There are several other areas where specific experimental and analytical research could provide better methods for ageing effects simulations beyond 60 years using accelerated ambient nuclear-power ageing environmental conditions, as mentioned in EDMA, Volume 5, Section 5.9 [46]:

- Activation energies Most of the ageing models use the Arrhenius approach and need activation energy values. Values used in the past were not always appropriately justified. To specify the ageing model, more reliable activation energy determination would be beneficial. Experiments to derive Arrhenius activation energies with reduced uncertainty at low temperatures for the specific cable materials is of interest.
- Diffusion limited oxidation (DLO) and dose rate effects With respect to choosing combined radiation plus temperature-accelerated ageing conditions, and for refining DLO calculations on cables under those conditions, the following experimental methods are suggested for consideration in the future.
  - $\circ$  The dependency of ageing on oxygen partial pressure can be studied under radiation conditions to provide information on oxygen consumption and to provide data for estimating values of  $\beta$  for DLO modelling.
  - Oxygen permeability measurements on actual cable jackets and insulations up to at least 100°C.
  - Development of two-dimensional finite element models for typical cable crosssections to improve the accuracy of DLO modelling.
- Inverse Temperature Effects Research to better understand inverse-temperature effects, identify which cable materials are most susceptible to these effects, and develop suitable methods to accelerate the ageing of these materials are of significance for understanding the expected behaviour for operation beyond 60 years.
- Moisture Effects The effect of long-term wetting of both low- and medium-voltage cables is still not well understood. Research in this area would provide information on the extent of the significance of potential degradation in cable performance during long-term submergence. Wet-energised ageing is yet to be better-understood technical issue for medium-voltage cable. Results are available from a large volume of wet-ageing research on medium-voltage XLPE cable, which is the most common distribution industry cable insulation. Less information on wet ageing is available for medium-voltage EPR cables used in nuclear power plants.
- CM techniques A wide range of methods are now available for the cable materials used at nuclear power plants. These methods are an essential part of condition-based qualification and is a useful technique to support life extension planning. The test results can provide information on the remaining lifetime of the cable and how the degradation continues to support or refute life extension. Most valuable are cables with known history harvested from the plant. Continuous research should be

focused on further development of methods for reliable cable CM. Methods, that will track cable degradation within the whole cable length as well only localised failure. Development of the methods up to the real application at nuclear power plant.

- Joule heating Heating through the passage of electric current, so-called Joule heating or Ohmic heating, is a significant factor in the degradation of power cables. The mechanism of degradation due to this heating is like the effects of heat from the surrounding environment. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can accelerate the ageing of the cable insulation material. This can result in the loss of mechanical strength, flexibility, and electrical properties over time. This ageing effect is described in many documents, e.g. IAEA SRS No 82 [7]. Not all the cables are affected by the effect of joule heating. Only a limited group of power cables continually energising motors could be affected by joule heating. However, only limited amount of equipment important to safety is in steadily operation. Moreover, cables are mostly oversized. A detailed analysis of the real effect of joule heating on nuclear power plant cables should be carried out.
- Ageing models improvement Ageing models for both accelerated ageing as well as for tracking of continuous cable ageing at operational parameters need to be improved.
- Continuous and future activities at the plant Preservation of cable technical data is needed. It is important that the documentation (specification) of the cables, which is normally obtained during their procurement, is maintained. During the life of the plant (now typically 40 more years), design modifications and maintenance activities are likely to change the original plant cabling or wiring. Cable ageing assessment is critical to life extension operations and requires detailed information on cable types, materials, and locations. Without traceability of this information, evaluation of cable life extension is very difficult. However, often the original cable manufacturers do not exist or information is not available from other sources, with documentation from the 1980s being incomplete or missing.
- Review of existing EQ documentation This should be the first stage of any cable ageing management programme to extend life. The value of the activation energy should be known, at least if it has been measured or taken from the literature. In many cases, literature activation energy values were used for thermal pre-ageing, but rarely they were used for identical cable materials. The value of the activation energy used is critical to the calculation of the qualified life, as a 10% error in the value can change the qualified life by a significant factor. The activation energy value should be obtained by laboratory testing rather than from the literature to include the uncertainties associated with accelerated thermal ageing. Where little information is available on the types of cable materials installed, it is recommended that the existing cable be replaced with a qualified cable.
- Hot spot identification The main problem with hot spots, or adverse localised environments, is that the cable in these places will probably fail much earlier than expected from the general condition of the cable. Hot spots need to be properly identified and the cause corrected, or the cable replaced/repaired. Electrical CM methods show some potential for identifying the presence of hot spots along a cable by detecting localised cable degradation. Regular in-situ testing of cables can determine their location before degradation becomes fatal.
- Environmental monitoring Systematic measurement of environmental parameters is essential. Obtaining detailed knowledge of temperature and dose rate is an

essential part of CAMP. Real measured values are usually lower than design parameters and it allows LTO.

- CM A wide range of methods are now available for the cable materials used at nuclear power plants. These methods are an essential part of condition-based qualification and is a useful technique to support life extension planning. The test results can provide information on the remaining lifetime of the cable and how the degradation continues to support or refute life extension. Most valuable are cables with known history harvested from the plant.
- Cable deposit The placement of cable samples for measurements of mechanical and electrical properties, in a temperature and/or dose rate region typical of the most severe operational conditions at a nuclear power plant, is a very useful element of CAMP. If enough space in the plant, the cables should age at different conditions, temperatures, and dose rates. It enables to assess the degradation of real operated cables. They can be placed there "as received" or pre-aged before installation. It serves as the best source of cables, where their history and environment are well known.
- Cable replacement This can be an effective way to deal with equipment life extension for cables that are exposed to harsh environments and have been in service for 30-35 years. The planned replacement with new modern cable materials can provide nuclear power plants with additional benefits in terms of better fire protection, halogen-free materials, and degradation characteristics. The new cable with measured condition indicators can also be used in condition-based qualification.

Though current regulatory guidance on cable ageing for LTO is suitable, there are a few areas in the realm of cable ageing where the US NRC may benefit from additional research. Specifically, Chapter 5 of NUREG-7153 [46] lists the areas where additional research could be performed to enhance the US NRC's understanding of the uncertainties associated with the qualification and moisture related knowledge gaps, as follows:

- activation energy values used for thermal ageing;
- diffusion limited oxidation;
- dose rate effects;
- synergism between thermal and radiation ageing;
- sequential vs concurrent ageing;
- pre-ageing of semi-crystalline materials;
- moisture effects;
- ohmic heating.

In addition to the uncertainties associated with the knowledge gaps listed above, there is a need to perform additional research on non-destructive examination techniques that could be used to manage the ageing of cables in-situ.

Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant cables installed in harsh environments with or without function under accident condition and non-safety related cable are tested and qualified for the planned lifetime of 60 years. With an extension of the Unit 3 and 4 planned lifetime, installed cable types may have to be verified and tested to prolong qualified lifetime.

The main possible gaps for LTO beyond 60 years and the corresponding action plan are as follows:

1. Prediction of the evolution of cable characteristics over time

The predictive approach is one of the key elements for LTO beyond 60 years. The predictive approach needs an in-depth understanding of degradation phenomena affecting polymers and their kinetics.

Studies carried out to date have enabled to identify and understand the main modes of polymer degradation. Particularly, EDF has been contributing to the development of a new analytical model, the "multi-scale" model, which is based on an in-depth understanding of the various polymer degradation mechanisms. The aim is to simulate the changes in the material on the most appropriate scale for predicting the consequences of the changes on the targeted macroscopic property.

Developing a multi-scale model is a complex task. Complete modelling of the degradation kinetics of an industrial formulation, sometimes containing several polymer bases, fillers, and numerous additives, requires several steps.

The development of this approach has not yet been fully finalised, even if the work carried out has enabled significant progress in understanding the ageing phenomena affecting cable polymers. Further studies are planned to better predict degradation kinetics.

### 2. On-site cable sampling for expertise

The methodology of on-site cable sampling, put in place for the French nuclear fleet for several years, was recognised as a good practice at the end of the first Topical Peer Review on the topic of cable ageing management organised by ENSREG/Western European Nuclear Regulators Association (WENRA) in 2017.

On site cables sampling for expertise and the development of related polymers' characterisation techniques will continue to ensure that cables behave properly for LTO beyond 60 years, and to contribute to validate the results of the predictive approach.

#### 3. NDE techniques

As already mentioned, for low-voltage cables, there are currently no relevant NDE techniques that can be used on site (today monitoring is essentially based on visual checks for that type of cables).

Work will continue developing new NDE, particularly for low-voltage cables, to improve the monitoring of cables in operation.

4. Pursuit of ageing management process and enhancement to consider new knowledge when available, as described above.

The research gaps for LTO beyond 60 years are:

- research that supports cable thermal ageing and thermal ageing model improvement;
- the use of so-called sensor cables that monitor the temperature load. These are hybrid cables that monitor the temperature along their entire length. They can also be used for cables in hermetic cable penetrations.

Areas for potential for improvement include:

• cable ageing knowledge in cable penetration;

- diagnostic methods of electrical measurements so that they can evaluate the state of cables ageing;
- the development of functional CBQ into practice in the conditions of a nuclear power plant operated for several decades, so that the qualification programme and the AMP are aligned.

### <span id="page-227-0"></span>**4.9. I&C safety systems**

### *4.9.1. Description of I&C safety systems*

The I&C system is a plant's brain, a system of systems and the most complex system in the nuclear power plant. It ensures automatic control of plant functions and provides means for manual control. Instrumentation and control are an engineering discipline for which designers, licensees, and regulators need specialised knowledge and skill.

The I&C systems important to safety of nuclear power plants generally consists of:

- control systems important to safety;
- reactor protection system;
- actuation systems for engineered safety features;
- systems required for safe shutdown (including passive systems);
- information systems important to safety (accident monitoring);
- interlock systems important to safety;
- diverse actuation system;
- data communication systems;
- instrumentation and control in the main and supplementary control rooms;
- digital I&C systems.

Typical representatives of components in I&C systems include:

- sensors (e.g. RTDs, thermocouples, pressure transmitter including level and flow, pressure switch, neutron detectors, sensing lines);
- actuators (motors and solenoid drives);
- cables and connection interfaces (splices, terminations, connection interfaces, etc.);
- junction boxes;
- containment penetrations (electrical and sealing function);
- limit switches/position indicators;
- relay, microswitch;
- power sources;
- capacitators resistors, diodes, transistors integrated circuits;
- digital electronics cards;
- potentiometers;
- different types of batteries and power supplies for electronic cabinets;

• various types of displays at the control rooms (main control room, supplementary control room) and local control stations (e.g. I&C and electrical cabinets).

The overall I&C architecture of a nuclear power plant includes multiple I&C systems, each playing a specific role. Although the architecture of an I&C system is plant-specific, various constituent elements (e.g. equipment, modules, subsystems, redundancies, systems) can be used in different reactor designs, e.g. PWR, BWR, CANDU, as well as SMRs.

A number of nuclear power plants are in the process of upgrading ageing and obsolete analogue I&C systems to digital systems. Substitution of the relay-based technology with digital has become almost unavoidable, even in sensitive areas such as I&C systems important to safety, mostly due to expired service lifetime and difficulties with maintenance of the obsolete analogue devices.

The I&C modernisations include small as well as large-scale digital upgrades of I&C systems at nuclear power plants. The replacement of the original (analogue) I&C system based on digital hardware which is either hardware programmed devices (HPD) or computer-based system with software. While small digital upgrades focus on modification/replacement of individual I&C components (e.g. local controllers, feedwater control system, turbine control system), the large-scale modification involved a complete replacement of reactor protection and control systems. Large scale digital upgrades also involved changes to human system interface (HSI), which had an impact on layout of main control room (MCR) controls, alarms and displays.

The nuclear industry is increasingly using devices designed for non-nuclear applications (industrial digital devices), which often contain non-analogue or digital components (socalled smart devices), in systems important to safety in nuclear power plants. Examples of I&C equipment which includes embedded industrial digital devices include:

- time delay relay, relay, timer;
- process switch, controller, or transducer (temperature, pressure);
- circuit breaker;
- isolator, delay module;
- variable frequency drive, motor starters, motors and damper motor;
- controller or valve positioner;
- meter or indicator;
- inverter/uninterrupted power supply (UPS), power supply;
- components with battery backup;
- signal conditioner and electrical filters;
- components with the following attributes/features: selector switches;
- potentiometers, LCD/digital display, external connection (i.e. USB or Ethernet), JTAG port and BDM port.

Although advanced digital I&C systems have been used extensively in many other industries, their use in the nuclear industry is still very limited. This is mainly because very few new nuclear power plants have been built since the mid 1980s and the licensing process of digital I&C systems is challenging and complex. Digital upgrades are an effective means to enhance plant safety and system functionality, manage obsolescence, and mitigate the increasing failure liability of ageing analogue systems, see [338].

### *4.9.2. Physical ageing of I&C safety systems*

The nuclear industry has been slow to incorporate digital sensor technology into nuclear plant designs due to concerns with digital qualification issues. However, the benefits of digital sensor technology for nuclear plant instrumentation are substantial in terms of accuracy and reliability. This paper [339], which refers to a final report issued in 2013, demonstrates these benefits in direct comparisons of digital and analogue sensor applications. Improved accuracy results from the superior operating characteristics of digital sensors.

These include improvements in sensor accuracy and drift and other related parameters which reduce total loop uncertainty and thereby increase safety and operating margins.

In the following, the most important ageing degradation mechanisms are discussed in terms of complete or incomplete knowledge and possible R&D gaps.

### *4.9.2.1. Ageing and obsolescence management*

Ageing or obsolescence may cause the service life of some I&C systems to be significantly shorter than the lifetime of the plant. The ageing degradation may be latent and sometimes difficult to detect on time. Nuclear power plants typically have a set of specific programmes that help managing the ageing degradations of passive and active system and component (SC). The main objective of these programmes is to timely detect any ageing degradation and provide set of preventive measures to avoid premature SSC failures.

The ageing mechanisms could significantly affect I&C components. The means for detecting the effects of these mechanisms are identified during design. Identification of the potential impacts of ageing first involves an understanding of the relevant ageing phenomena for the various I&C components. Ageing of I&C components most commonly results from exposure to heat or radiation. Nevertheless, the possibility that other phenomena (e.g. electromigration in microcircuits, formation of "tin whiskers," mechanical vibration or chemical degradation) might be relevant to a specific component need to be considered.

Although the physical ageing is an important factor for I&C components, the non-physical ageing due to obsolescence is equally important to consider for digital I&C systems. The obsolescence is becoming an important factor to considered in the I&C system life. For example, there might not be sufficient spare parts or even suppliers over the long span of the plant lifetime.

Maintenance programmes for I&C systems typically include activities for the identification of trends that might cause degradation (ageing), including the detection of precursors that could cause reduction of functional reliability or even equipment to become incapable of performing its safety function. The risk of obsolescence is critical with new digital I&C systems because of the shorter lifetime of new digital technology. As the I&C systems provide the vital support for the safe and reliable operation of nuclear power plants, the I&C system functions must be maintained throughout plant life. This is ensured by implementation of an appropriate AMP and obsolescence management. The basic ageing management process includes the following:

• understanding the ageing and obsolescence phenomena and identifying the (potential) effects on I&C systems and components;

- addressing the specific impact of these effects on the plant in all plant states and operating profiles;
- analysing the associated risks for the plant operation;
- carrying out necessary mitigating actions to counteract the effects of ageing and obsolescence.

The ageing management and obsolescence programme is an iterative process throughout the plant life. For digital I&C systems, the software is not subject to physical ageing, which is relevant for hardware. However, due to rapid advancement of digital technology, both the software and hardware are subject to obsolescence. Despite the software does not age, it is often necessary to change software together with hardware during digital upgrades.

### *4.9.2.2. Ageing effects and related degradation mechanisms for I&C systems and component (physical ageing)*

The I&C equipment can be affected by a wide range of degradation mechanisms, the impact of which will vary due to several factors, such as:

- how the equipment has been designed, fabricated, and installed,
- the materials used to manufacture the equipment,
- the equipment's tolerance to drift and failure,
- the equipment's operating environment (i.e. its exposure to degradation mechanisms),
- how the equipment is maintained,
- the potential for the degradation mechanisms to interact with each other.
- The duty cycle of the equipment (i.e. continuous or intermittent use).

Equipment designed for intermittent use is likely to degrade at a greater rate if used for continuous operations. Identification of degradation mechanisms and the assessment of their impact may not be a straightforward activity and is likely to require inputs from a wide range of competent personnel with specialist skills and knowledge.

### *4.9.2.3. Examples of ageing-related degradation mechanisms*

Ageing-related degradation mechanisms may cause I&C equipment to degrade and if left without proper maintenance and ageing management, may eventually affect the equipment's ability to deliver its required function(s) considering specified service conditions associated with plant states (i.e. operational states and accident conditions).

The following list includes typical examples of environments or stressors to which I&C equipment can be exposed during plant life, in operational states and accident conditions, and which may lead to degradation mechanism/ageing effect:

- temperature;
- moisture/humidity;
- thermal and humidity cycling;
- erosion;
- thermomechanical and/or thermodynamic constraints during the manufacturing process;

- vibration;
- repetitive rapid acceleration/deceleration (e.g. a seismic event);
- repetitive mechanical shock;
- handling (that may lead to electrostatic discharge (ESD) for instance);
- radiation exposure;
- chemical exposure;
- electromagnetic interference (EMI)/radiofrequency interference (RFI) exposure;
- ultraviolet light exposure (this mainly has an impact on polymers);
- surface contamination (e.g. dust, dirt, sand, fluff, mould);
- wear;
- electrical stress (e.g. power surges);
- salt fog (this degradation mechanism is pertinent to nuclear power plants on coastal sites);
- fatigue.

Examples of ageing effects that have an impact on I&C equipment that have been identified by nuclear power plant operators around the world include:

- calibration drift and deviation of set points;
- accuracy and reproducibility degradation;
- changes in equipment response time(s);
- changes in equipment signals (amplitude and frequency);
- output data corruption;
- introduction of signal noise;
- loss of output signals/data;
- changes in switching voltages;
- changes in resistance (e.g. insulation, coil, loop and contact);
- corrosion of equipment supports, housing and components;
- loss of conductor mechanical strength;
- cracking of equipment supports, housings, seals, coatings and solder joints.

In addition to the above, the following are some specific examples of ageing effects relevant to specific I&C components:

- Electrolytic capacitators Elevated ambient temperatures can increase the rate at which electrolytic capacitors lose their liquid electrolyte because of degraded end cap seals (e.g. through evaporation), which in turn can result in the capacitors drying out and failing to open or causing a short circuit.
- I&C cables Exposing cables to high temperatures can cause their insulation polymers to degrade, which can lead to the cables failing and causing a short circuit.

Chemicals, such as grease, oil, acids and cleaning fluids, can degrade the integrity of cable insulation polymers, which can lead to cable failure and short circuits.

- Fiber optic cables Ionising radiation can cause fibre optic cables to darken, which can affect the propagation of optical signals through the cables.
- Circuit boards and components Thermal cycling can cause circuit boards and components to expand or contract at different rates, which can place solder joints under mechanical stress. This can lead to fatigue in the solder joints and failure.
- Whiskers' formation on circuit boards Inadvertent electrically conductive connections can be formed through growing whiskers which can lead to malfunctions or short circuits on the affected components. The growing of whiskers is a stochastic process which could lead to an increasing failure rate of electrical or I&C components if no measures are taken.
- Semiconductors High levels of ionising radiation can cause semiconductor "bulk damage", which can cause electronic equipment to fail.

Other factors that may cause premature ageing of I&C equipment include:

- Mechanical damage to connectors (e.g. wear, fatigue) due to periodic removal of I&C equipment for inspection, test or outages. This can lead to a loss of continuity or arcing between contacts.
- High levels of vibration when the I&C equipment is located on or next to rotating equipment, which can lead to fatigue in component connections and failure.
- Chemical degradation of neoprene rubber insulation sleeves that can result in hygroscopic salts forming within the rubber, which can absorb moisture from the air and lead to highly conductive droplets forming on the outsides of the insulation sleeves. The insulation sleeves may become conductive and short circuits occurring between the touching of sleeves to earth through metal structures.

Implementation of plant programmes, such as preventive maintenance, CM and surveillance programmes, ageing management and EQ programmes, ensure an early detection of any premature ageing degradation of I&C components. Also, regular equipment parameter monitoring, recording and trending is implemented to determine if these limits are being approached and thus allow appropriate and timely mitigating measures to be taken. The identification of such parameters is more of a challenge for digital devices than for analogue devices.

### *4.9.2.4. Ageing-related operating experience*

OPEX from nuclear power plants worldwide provides information on ageing-related faults of I&C systems and components (see Ref. [340] for further information). Although digital systems performing protective functions are equipped with internal diagnostic failures to detect faults early, OPEX shows that failures of electronic cards and electrolytic capacitators belong to the most represented causes in the I&C commodity group. Whisker's formation can result in malfunctions or short circuits of electronic cards. For this reason, the surveillance programmes should contain appropriate preventive inspection measures to identify whisker formation. In addition to the surveillance programme improvement, the upgrades in the design of sensitive components which eliminate whisker development and consequent progressive replacement could be also considered as an effective solution.

Monitoring of reliability trends could be helpful to identify in time the ageing problem without "waiting" for a safety significant event occurrence. Degradation of electrolytic capacitators is not always easy to identify. Therefore, electrolytic capacitators should be replaced at a specified time interval, given by the manufacturer. Other degradation mechanisms observed in the evaluation of ageing-related events were electrical failure, loss of insulation resistance, setpoint drift, and wear. In most cases, the ageing degradation was detected by components failure. Replacement of the failed component is the preferred corrective action.

The EPRI Annual I&C OE Report contains a collection of industry lessons learnt and best practices, primarily focused on digital I&C equipment. The report is issued annually to continue to accumulate, analyse and synthesise I&C OPEX. The 2022 baseline report represents the analysis and synthesis of I&C equipment failure events dating from the 1970s through 31 December 2022 (Reference 3002023750 "Annual Instrumentation and Control Operating Experience Review: 2022 Baseline Report", 2023).

### *4.9.2.5. International support for effective ageing management*

The IAEA IGALL Ref. [7] provides a technical basis and practical guidance based on proven practices on managing the ageing of mechanical, electrical and I&C components and civil structures of nuclear power plants important to safety. Regarding SSCs important to safety, this publication contains the following:

- a generic sample of AMR tables;
- a collection of proven AMPs;
- a collection of typical TLAAs.

This information is based on approaches developed and implemented in various types of water moderated reactor in participating IAEA Member States and will be periodically updated.
