This publication serves as a roadmap to available information on ageing management and provides a common, internationally recognised basis on what constitutes an effective AMP and TLAA for operation of existing plants, as well as a knowledge base on ageing management for the design of new plants, design reviews and safety reviews (i.e. PSRs).

### *4.9.2.6. Summary of physical ageing challenges*

Physical ageing of I&C systems and components (except of cables) is managed through various plant programmes (e.g. maintenance, EQ and AMPs). Considering operation beyond 60 years, the most challenging factor appears to be the determination and prognosis of ageing degradation of I&C cables, in particular for harsh environment (cable system ageing is covered in Section 4.8. of this report). With this regard, there is a good international knowledge and understanding of the ageing effects/degradation on I&C systems important to safety.

The lack of competence in using old equipment is another challenge. Highly skilled personnel have retired and "old" knowledge has not been sufficiently transferred to younger staff.

The main issue is obsolescence, meaning problems in purchasing spare parts. Old workstations to handle programming and tuning parameters run under old operating systems that are not supported any more. This creates problems in obtaining the correct drivers for hardware and software packages.

Another aspect is the technical ageing. Equipment ages but remains functionally correct. The problem is more, as mentioned earlier, that the knowledge of how to use/calibrate/maintain the equipment can be lost.

### *4.9.3. Inspection and diagnostics methods*

### *4.9.3.1. General inspection and diagnostic methods for I&C systems*

Description of the latest testing and diagnostic methods applied to I&C equipment in IAEA Member States, is provided in recently published IAEA Technical Report NR-T-3.34 [341]. The following paragraphs shortly introduce each diagnostic method.

Visual inspections are one of the most practical ways of identifying ageing effects in I&C equipment (especially for analogue devices and cabling). The visual inspection is typically included in all system health/performance monitoring programmes. For accessible components, the visual inspection (internal/external) has the potential to reveal damage to the equipment and/or surrounding equipment. Where it is not practicable or desirable to remove equipment for inspection, the use of specific tools needs to be considered (e.g. magnifying glasses, endoscopes, inspection mirrors and torches). Some equipment may not be accessible during operation and is therefore scheduled during outages. Visual inspections are undertaken by competent personnel (i.e. by trained personnel who have a good working knowledge of typical I&C equipment degradation mechanisms and ageing effects). Although visual inspections could easily identify visible degradations or deterioration, they will not be able to detect all ageing effects (especially for digital equipment, where ageing effects are usually associated with the die of electronic components) and that other methods/techniques may be more effective in identifying certain types of ageing effects.

Real-time monitoring includes monitoring and trend plant operating parameters such as temperature, pressure, flow, and neutron flux level. Variations in these parameters over time may indicate the onset of ageing-related equipment degradation (for example, a gradual reduction in thermocouple loop resistance would result in a gradual increase in output temperature). Digital systems and devices are often able to self‑monitor their performance and to automatically report the early onset of issues to operators and vendors before they threaten the delivery of the equipment's required function(s). This in turn has the benefit of enabling timely mitigating measures to be introduced to prevent equipment failures.

The infrared thermography involves detecting heat radiation and converting it into images that represent the amount of radiated heat. Thermography is a useful technique for identifying equipment "hot spots" that are the result of ageing-related degradation (e.g. due to degradation of equipment insulation and increased contact resistance), or heat sources that could cause surrounding equipment to degrade. Consideration should be given to the fact that hot spots may only develop during certain system/equipment operating modes, and it is therefore important that infrared thermography is undertaken across the equipment's full operating spectrum.

### *4.9.3.2. Inspection and diagnostic methods for digital I&C systems*

The safety implications of an increased use of digital I&C in new reactor designs and upgrades on operating plants resulted in the need to develop a common understanding from the perspectives of regulatory authorities on inspection practices related to digital I&C systems. The NEA Committee on Nuclear Regulatory Activities (CNRA) Working Group on Digital Instrumentation and Controls (WGDIC) developed "Consensus Position on Regulatory Inspections of Digital Instrumentation and Control Systems and Components Important to Safety used at Nuclear Power Plants" (CP-15), Ref. [342]. This consensus position provides guidance for facilitating the process of preparing and conducting regulatory inspections of digital I&C hardware and software for systems and components during design and manufacturing at the manufacturer's facility as well as during installation, commissioning, operation, and maintenance in nuclear power plants. This applies to the following I&C system lifecycle activities:

- quality management system for I&C system lifecycle processes;
- system requirements;
- system design;
- implementation and integration;
- hardware qualification;
- installation and commissioning;
- operation and maintenance;
- verification and validation;
- I&C system lifecycle activities with computer security programmes.

Additional information on digital I&C inspections can be found in the "Proceedings of the Special International Nuclear Regulatory Inspection Workshop on Digital Instrumentation & Control (DI&C)" developed by the NEA WGDIC and the NEA CNRA Working Group on Inspection Practices (WGIP), Ref. [343]. This document describes a series of regulatory inspection practices that apply to digital I&C systems in operating reactors and new reactors, which can help verify that they are designed, manufactured, installed, commissioned, operated and maintained in accordance with the regulatory requirements, the manufacturer's design, operating recommendations and the facility's licensing basis.

### *4.9.3.3. Preventive maintenance strategies for digital I&C components*

With nuclear power plants implementing digital I&C systems there is a need for industryaccepted preventive maintenance guidance. Often, plants attempt to adapt their existing preventive maintenance procedures for the original equipment to the new systems, which may be insufficient or overly conservative, and can consequently be leading to equipment failures and inadequate maintenance activities. Considering this, EPRI report 3002000502 "Preventive Maintenance Practices for Digital Instrumentation and Control Systems" [344] collected and assessed the current preventive maintenance tasks, identified weaknesses, and recommend preventive maintenance strategies for digital I&C systems.

Besides this, EPRI report 1023281 "Collected Field Data on Electronic Part Failures and Guidelines for the Monitoring and Aging of Instrumentation and Control (I&C) Electronic Components" [345] provides generic guidelines to monitor the ageing of electronic components and boards, describing also several tools that were designed and tested to measure ageing indicators.

### *4.9.3.4 Summary gaps/challenges*

Inspection methods and diagnostics methods for I&C systems and components are generally applied in the same manner during operation, as well as in LTO. These methods and tools are continuously improving (e.g. better inspection tools and detection techniques) and thus help improving timely detection of various ageing degradation in LTO.

Currently, there seem to be no gaps and challenges for I&C systems and components for LTO beyond 60 years.

The I&C safety systems are closely monitored and a significant amount of preventive maintenance/testing is performed. No need for additional testing/monitoring is identified.

Surveillance demands for the equipment means that it is worked with on a frequent base, leading to problems usually being found before they become troublesome.

### *4.9.4. Repair, refurbishment and replacement solutions*

### *4.9.4.1. Digital upgrades of the existing nuclear power plants*

Digital upgrade projects at nuclear power plants provide a solution to replace the aged and obsolete analogue I&C systems. Substitution of the relay-based technology with digital has become a common option, even in sensitive areas such as safety I&C systems. Digital upgrades may consist of a small, or large-scale modernisations of I&C systems at nuclear power plants. While small digital upgrades focused on modification/replacement of individual I&C components in I&C systems (e.g. local controllers, feedwater control system, turbine control system), the large-scale modification involved a complete replacement of reactor protection and control systems. Large scale digital upgrades also involved changes to HSI, which had an impact on layout of MCR controls, alarms and displays. Consequently, this resulted in modification of full scope simulators, operating procedures, and operator training.

The large scale I&C modifications (i.e. replacement of the original reactor protection system) are always performed in phases, typically during several extended outages, to make the balance between time necessary to implemented modification steps, considering risks of limiting plant availability, increased operation and maintenance costs and the risk of not meeting future regulatory requirements. As an example, the scope of large-scale digital upgrades may include the following replacement phases:

- Phase 1, consisting of safety and safety-related systems such as the reactor trip system, engineered safety features actuation system, emergency load sequencer, reactor power control and limitation system and post-accident monitoring;
- Phase 2, consisting of process computer systems, including in-core measurements processing;
- Phase 3, consisting of control systems of the primary circuit components;
- Phase 4, consisting of turbine and generator control and protection systems;
- Phase 5, consisting of control systems of the secondary circuit components.

The replacement process at multi-unit sites always includes several phases starting at the pilot unit and continued as replication of modifications at remaining units that have already been done at the pilot unit.

The large-scale digital I&C upgrades at existing nuclear power plants need to consider several challenges that were not present in original analogue I&C systems:

- modification of the HSI at the MCR because of the new digital technology (e.g. visual displays, soft controls);
- integration with the existing installation and interface that has not been modernised;
- activities relating to the development of computer software, including design, verification and validation;
- implementation of diagnostic functions to reduce repair times;

- evaluation of the required time between periodic tests;
- the launch of this type of project with sufficient time to prepare.

Although the large-scale digital upgrades try to limit changes to HSI, the replacement of the original analogue technology by digital technology often requires changes to the layout of controls and displays at the MCR, as well as in local control panels. Modification to the original HSI design, however, requires conducting verification and validation activities relating to human factors engineering.

Use of digital assets in I&C systems performing safety functions requires consideration of other engineering discipline, such as the cybersecurity. As a result, the overall I&C architecture and individual I&C systems for the plant needs to implement specific security measures to protect important digital assets from potential cyberattack.

An example of successful replacements of analogue with digital I&C systems is Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant. A review of the technical results of Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant I&C modernisation project, including the lessons learnt and the recommended practices helpful to other nuclear power plants contemplating large nuclear power plant I&C modernisation projects, is documented in EPRI report 3002002986 "Instrumentation and Control Modernization at Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant – Lessons Learned" [346], issued in 2015.

This OPEX example can be supported by other recent EPRI guidelines:

- EPRI's Digital Engineering Guide (DEG), which uses a systems engineering framework and a graded approach to conduct plant modifications that add or modify digital technologies, such as major analogue to digital facility change or a minor update to a software module in an installed digital system. (Reference 3002011816 "Digital Engineering Guide: Decision Making Using Systems Engineering (DEG)" [347], 2021);
- The EPRI Digital Systems Engineering Users Group (DSEUG) was formed to promote the utilisation and evolution of the Digital Systems Engineering Framework also to collect digital project OPEX. The 2023 report is a compilation of the current state of nuclear power plant digitisation, strategies, as well as plans for future digital projects. It includes approaches to digital equipment selection and documentation, division of responsibilities of the digital plant change process, and digital project lessons learned. (Reference 3002026368 "DSEUG Nuclear Plant Digital Project Experience" [348], 2023).

### *4.9.4.2. Use of smart devices in I&C systems important to safety*

Industrial or commercial grade digital (smart) devices are increasingly used in digital upgrades at nuclear power plants. These devices are developed according to non-nuclearindustry standards and are certified by non-nuclear organisations using those non-nuclear standards in industrial applications (e.g. the oil, gas, rail and aircraft industries). However, the safe use of these devices in I&C systems performing safety functions requires further assessment (qualification) to demonstrate their suitability for a given safety application at a nuclear power plant.

The qualification of an industrial or commercial smart device for applications in nuclear power plant systems important to safety may often be more difficult than it would be for a device specifically developed for nuclear applications because its commercial development processes may be less transparent and controlled than those described in the IAEA Safety Standards. Often, the qualification is challenging if there is no co-operation from the manufacturer. The difficulty associated with the use of these devices may relate to the unavailability of information to demonstrate quality and reliability.

### *4.9.4.3. Licensing issues related to smart devices acceptance in nuclear safety applications*

Most industrial digital devices (smart devices) are certified to International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 61508 [349] on the basis of the development process, but some devices are certified on the basis of prior use or proven-in-use arguments (this approach is very rarely used for safety integrity level (SIL) 3). Depending on the certifying body, this type of certification may be quite rigorous in terms of the quantity and type of OPEX needed (e.g. more than 30 million hours of applicable operation for SIL 3), which may include operating conditions that are at least as challenging as those of the target application, and the expected stability of the particular version of the product. For nuclear qualification, it is important to clarify that this certification path is used only where there are weaknesses in the documentation of the development process.

Smart devices for intended nuclear application may be assessed by reviewing manufacturer documentation and performing a clause-by-clause compliance analysis to a suitable national or international nuclear standard. However, this will depend on the standard applied during the original development and requires access to development documentation that can sometimes be difficult to obtain. Evidence of a manufacturer's compliance with a widely accepted industrial standard such as IEC 61508 [349] is usually accepted towards the demonstration of development quality. IEC 62671 [350] provides a framework for assessing predeveloped smart devices of limited functionality, which may or may not have been developed to nuclear or industrial standards. Some specific criteria to examine industrial digital device include the following:

- use of a design life cycle that involves stages of development such as functional requirements, architecture design of hardware and software, high level software design and low-level software design;
- independence of detailed verification at each stage of the life cycle;
- effective use of configuration management tools to control all design products (e.g. specifications, test procedures, board design, code, software tools);
- design change control, including impact analysis;
- use of design constraints such as coding standards and verification tools;
- use of design analysis techniques to confirm the correct structure of the code (e.g. static analysis) and to measure the code complexity;
- use of design tools (e.g. compilers) justified by certification or testing or otherwise demonstrated to be acceptable;
- use of verification techniques and tools to confirm the degree of completeness of testing (e.g. tools that verify that every path in the code has been tested).

Another possibility is the approach adopted in the United States, which uses the EPRI Technical Reports 3002002982 [351] and TR-106439 [352], which have been reviewed and endorsed by US NRC for justification or dedication of commercial grade items and services used for nuclear power plants. EPRI report 3002002982 [351], with exceptions and clarifications, is the updated commercial grade item dedication guidance to supersede Revision 1 to EPRI NP-5652 and TR-102260, which is specifically endorsed in Regulatory Guide 1.164 [353]. EPRI TR-107330 [169] can also be used as a reference, although it was created for the qualification of commercially available programmed logic controllers.

The approach used in France is provided in the RCC-E:2016 standard [354], which provides two qualification paths for smart devices: either using IEC 62671 [350], or using smart devices that are already certified to IEC 61508 [349] and for which appropriate evidence is available. A graded audit by the level of SIL requirement is also determined by the safety class.

The approach in the United Kingdom is derived from safety assessment principle ESS.27 [355], which requires the assessment of the production excellence of a smart device. This includes the quality of the development process and of its verification and validation and additional independent confidence building measures to confirm the suitability of a digital device for a nuclear application. Further information on qualification of smart devices for their safe use in in systems important to safety can be found in IAEA SRS No. 111 (Ref. [356]).

### *4.9.4.4. Considerations for coping with common cause failures of smart devices*

Although CCF is not unique to smart devices, the presence of software or firmware in smart components means that they present additional challenges compared with their analogue counterparts, because of the introduction of additional sources of systematic failure. Unlike random failures, systematic failures are "failures related in a deterministic way to a certain cause, which can only be eliminated by a modification of the design or of the manufacturing process, operational procedures, documentation or other relevant factors" (see IEC 61508 (Vol. 4) [349]). Such failures are potentially dangerous from a CCF perspective, as multiple devices can be affected. Examples of causes of systematic failures in smart devices include the following:

- erroneous or incomplete specification of requirements;
- undetected errors introduced during software or firmware development;
- errors in configuration control, leading to incorrect equipment settings;
- vulnerability to cyberthreats;
- vulnerability to other external factors, such as stressing environmental conditions (e.g. the effects of EMI, RFI or radiation on digital components);
- inclusion of common low level software components that may not all be revealed in the documentation available to the user (or even the manufacturer, where reliance is placed on lower levels of the supply chain).

Systematic failures can arise from the software or firmware of a smart device (e.g. the same product is used in two or more places within a plant architecture design) or from common software or firmware elements used in various smart devices of different types (e.g. operating systems, tools or embedded modules that are not disclosed).

### *4.9.4.5. Smart device cybersecurity considerations*

Smart devices, because of their digital nature, can be susceptible to cyberthreats. Smart devices offer a level of resilience against cyberthreats compared with other complex digital systems. There are, however, various scenarios in which cyber vulnerabilities of smart devices can be exploited.

Some of the cyberthreats identified above arise from the supply chain. For example, malware inserted into a software library or module could affect several devices. Similarly, malware inserted into a software tool such as a compiler could affect all devices that are produced using that software tool. Overall architectural solutions are generally an effective means of reducing the impact of any cyberattack, as is the use of technology types whose vulnerability to cyberattack may be easier to identify and manage (e.g. use of HPDs, such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA)s, instead of microprocessors).

### *4.9.4.6. Summary gaps/challenges*

The physical ageing of I&C systems and components can be acceptably managed by various plant programmes (e.g. maintenance, EQ and ageing management) to support safe and reliable operation beyond 60 years. The equipment obsolescence and availability of "nuclear grade" equipment as replacement parts, however, has been identified as the main challenge for LTO. Due to the fast evolution of digital technology, digital I&C equipment in nuclear power plants become obsolete much faster than mechanical and structural equipment.

Unlike analogue technology, there are several areas (e.g. reliability determination for digital safety systems, assessment of CCF in safety systems and diverse actuation) where the academic bases or engineering practice supporting the design criteria for I&C safety are not widely accepted by all member states. It may be expected that the practices of member states will evolve over time.

Application of digital (smart) devices developed according to industrial standards (i.e. not specifically designed and manufactured according to nuclear standards) requires additional assessment to ensure their safe use. Gaining access to information concerning the design and manufacturing of such devices to enable their evaluation and the implementation of the necessary compensatory measures for their acceptance can be difficult.

Currently, there is limited regulatory consensus on the safe use of smart devices in nuclear safety systems. Safe use entails selecting and evaluating smart devices for use in nuclear power plants, making use of third-party certification within the framework of the assessment process and adequately implementing safety design criteria based on a graded approach.

Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant benefits from a highly skilled electronics workshop with good possibility for repairs and refurbishments campaigns. This work process is well established and functions well. To be able to fulfil this in the future it is necessary for spare components and documentation to be available and for competent personnel to be maintained.

One department at Ringhals is directed to work and handle the obsolescence issues. They receive obsolescence findings and needs mostly from the maintenance departments. They work and share information within the POMS database (Proactive Obsolescence Management System) [357].

### *4.9.5. Potential gaps for LTO beyond 60 years*

### *4.9.5.1. Considerations for managing the physical ageing*

The ageing effects of I&C systems and components are managed by several plant programmes, such as maintenance programme, AMP EQ programme, which provide good basis for early detection of ageing degradation of I&C systems and components. Because nuclear power plants remain in operation well beyond the originally established time frame, these plant programmes are essential to ensure the safe and reliable operation of nuclear power plant in LTO. To credit these programs for LTO, they need to be evaluated and modified to ensure that ageing effects will continue to be identified and managed for the planned period of LTO.

The ageing effects of passive I&C components (e.g. cables, connections, containment electrical penetrations) are managed either by AMPs, or for qualified equipment, by EQ programme. Not all the passive I&C components are easily replaceable. The longer the period of LTO is (e.g. beyond 60 years), the more important the review of AMPs and TLAAs is to demonstrate that these components will have sufficient safety margins to perform their intended safety functions in the period beyond 60 years. Demonstration that the passive I&C components still have sufficient margins for much longer service time than originally envisaged is, however, challenging. This is valid for I&C cables (see Section 4.8. of this report).

For environmentally qualified I&C equipment, a comprehensive re-qualification programme is essential to be capable of functioning within acceptance criteria during specific operating conditions while retaining the ability to perform its safety functions in accident conditions for a design basis accident or a design basis earthquake. This can be ensured by equipment refurbishment, or replacement on time specified intervals (e.g. sensors, transmitters, connectors), or re-qualification [358]. The equipment qualified status can be evaluated by appropriate re-qualification methods to determine whether any changes in documented material composition and parameters, or in assumed environmental conditions, load cycles and other parameters, are needed to support this evaluation. The evaluation method, such as re-evaluation of the conservativism of assumptions made in the original EQ, type testing of naturally aged equipment with additional ageing to support the extension of the qualified life.

IGALL Ref. [7] provides a technical basis and practical guidance based on proven practices on managing ageing of mechanical, electrical and I&C components and civil structures of nuclear power plants important to safety, which is regularly updated and can be considered as useful technical basis for management of ageing for LTO beyond 60 years.

### *4.9.5.2. Considerations for managing the obsolescence*

Digital I&C system and components are susceptible to obsolescence more than to physical ageing. Although the digital system could retain its intended functional and performance characteristics for a long period of time, advances in digital technology, a lack of genuine spare parts, or an end to product support result in difficulty to keep the I&C systems in operation. Implementation of the obsolescence programme is necessary to predict nonphysical ageing of I&C equipment and prepare procurement plans to ensure sufficient stock of spare parts, or plan for replacement, either partial or of the entire system, to ensure further safe and reliable operation in an extended LTO.

For major digital upgrades, long-term vendor support is also necessary. Ideally it should commence no later than the handover of the system to the nuclear power plant operator and, ideally, before that. The nuclear power plant operator also needs to have access to the necessary spare parts for the planned LTO time span. Operational spares are generally calculated based on the number installed combined with the expected failure rates and the design life of the equipment. During operation, failure rates need to be monitored and spares holding adjusted if failure rates are different than predicted.

A key decision affecting the spares holdings is also whether to repair failed components (in which case guaranteed repair time is significant) or discard and replace. Further information on management of obsolescence can be found in Refs [4], IAEA NR-T-3.34 [341] and EPRI 3002002852 [359].

EPRI Guide 3002023438 "Digital Systems Engineering: Digital I&C Lifecycle Strategy Guide" [360] highlights key aspects of digital I&C life cycle management planning, including both the potential benefits associated with reducing operations and maintenance (O&M) costs and the reality that digital I&C and information technology products have shorter life cycles than their analogue predecessors, as of 2022. This guide describes the factors that impact digital life cycle plans and recommends formats for life cycle documents. (Interfaces with the DEG, 3002011816 [347])

### *4.9.5.3Potential challenges for I&C systems going digital*

- 1. One of the biggest challenges as I&C systems become obsolete is that the replacements are increasingly digital. These digital replacements perform the same functions but may require additional programs to be in place (i.e. cybersecurity). They also require additional safety evaluations and common cause failure analyses that would not be required for a like for like replacement. Additionally, as digital upgrades to I&C systems are implemented, there needs to be consideration for the digital lifespan being shorter than for the analogue systems. Plans must be in place for the digital lifecycle, including software changes and more frequent hardware upgrades as necessary.
- 2. Original I&C systems do not always have thorough documentation that describes how the design functions are implemented. There is a potential challenge to upgrading or replacing the original I&C system equipment, if personnel knowledgeable on the system are no longer available.
- 3. I&C system managers need to be aware of the obsolete parts in their systems and ensure there is a plan in place to address the concerns. This plan would lead to a resolution to the obsolesce, normally system/component replacement. It should also include a risk assessment based on the obsolete components' functions and a bridging strategy to ensure system functionality until a permanent solution can be put in place. It is imperative for the system manager to advocate the system obsolescence plan and ensure plant leadership is aware of the risk (i.e. worst-case scenario if obsolete components fail and cannot be replaced/repaired in a timely manner).
- 4. Competence is the main issue; beyond that, no specific gap has been identified for I&C safety systems to reach beyond 60 years. Equipment issues are handled by the obsolescence group or by replacement throughout projects.

### **5. Safety requirements important for LTO beyond 60 years**

### <span id="page-243-1"></span><span id="page-243-0"></span>**5.1. Availability of original design basis documentation**

The nuclear power plants that are currently being considered for LTO beyond 60 years were designed in the 1960s or 1970s and were commissioned in the 1970s. At that time, operators usually did not require, as a part of nuclear power plant delivery, the design basis documentation (DBD). In many cases the DBD remained in the designers' and manufactures' possession. Many original designers and manufacturers have already disappeared from the market; others are focused on new designs and new builds rather than providing services for older nuclear power plants.

The importance of the availability of original DBD for the existing nuclear power plants increases with the age of nuclear power plants. DBD must be available or accessible for establishing the appropriate configuration and modification management at the plant, particularly for evaluation of the impact of safety SSC modifications on maintaining their design functions. While SSCs important for the production of electricity are being replaced throughout the lifetime of the plant based on economic decisions, major safety SSCs are usually replaced, refurbished or upgraded only in connection with the plant LTO (including LTO beyond 60 years). Thus, the availability of DBD is particularly important prior to entering the LTO period.

The second reason why nuclear power plants need access to DBD, particularly prior to entering an LTO period, is the necessity to revalidate TLAAs. Designers and manufacturers used TLAAs to demonstrate fulfilment of SCs' intended functions for the design period.

TLAAs involve two types of parameters. The first parameter, a time dependent parameter, is used to evaluate an analysis parameter, which is then compared to a regulatory limit or criterion to determine acceptability of the component for service. Examples of time dependent parameters include component operating time, neutron fluence or number of thermal cycles on a component. The analysis parameters associated with these timedependent parameters could include FT of thermally aged CASS, neutron embrittlement of RPV materials and fatigue CUFs, respectively.

Nuclear power plants usually possess information on time dependent parameters and their values (e.g. number of years for which the SC was designed). But nuclear power plants frequently do not have access to the supporting analysis, which contains the calculation of the analysis parameter's values based on the given time limited assumptions.

Numerous nuclear power plant operating organisations have difficulties with TLAA's identification as there are components with safety impact (for example pumps, valves and heat exchangers) that do not have documented safety analysis in the form of TLAAs but may contain lifetime limitations in their technical specifications (e.g. number of cycles or several years of operation). Proven practice to manage this situation is provided in the IAEA IGALL Safety Report [7], programme ORP404 "Components with operational restrictions that have no documented safety analysis (version 2021)".

Unavailability of an original TLAA excludes the possibility of its revalidation for the intended period of LTO. Nuclear power plants must perform much more complicated corrective actions, e.g. perform completely new analyses which become TLAAs (which can be sometimes difficult due to a lack of input design values), supersede the TLAA by implementing an AMP or replace the SC.

Besides identification and revalidation of TLAAs, another important challenge might be availability of the updated DBD over the time to support appropriate modification/ configuration management. Decisions for LTO as well as LTO beyond 60 years are frequently connected with commitments for safety modifications, refurbishment or replacement of safety systems where availability of updated DBD is an important precondition.

Some nuclear power plants lost the access to the original design calculations or safety analysis from various reasons or did not maintain DBD up-to-date or accessible. Therefore, they need to retrieve or even reconstitute the DBD to support LTO, both for appropriate modification/configuration management and identification and revalidation of TLAAs. It is a complex, expensive and long-term task. An important starting point is a definition of the scope of the SSCs and the level of detail (equipment, component) for which DBD will be collected. It is suitable to continue with collection and structuring of all relevant information which is available at the plant or in the operating company. Useful information can be found in the SAR, other safety analyses, technical specifications, operation manuals, etc. Then it is important to decide for a suitable method of design basis reconstitution. Several plants successfully used reverse failure mode and effect analysis, others rely more on engineering judgement of the plant and contractors` engineers.

In the United States, plants would generally have their original design basis information necessary for beyond 60 years as they would have had to gather it to receive licence extensions to 60 years. In the cases where design basis documentation could not be retrieved, evaluations would have been performed to determine alternate means to maintain safety long term (i.e. increased inspection/monitoring, testing). An example of this is when reactor vessel surveillance capsules do not contain representative material for their plant, but the industry was able to develop integrated industry surveillance capsule programs that allow sites to use data/materials from host plants to understand their reactor vessel material ageing. Supplemental surveillance programmes have been developed at EPRI to gather high fluence data for extended operating periods (see [70]). This would all be documented in the licence renewal application and responses to US NRC requests for additional information on the application.

TLAAs for previous licence extensions should be documented and tracked so that they are updated prior to the end of their evaluation period. That would need to be done to meet the US regulations and periodic inspections by US NRC inspectors validate the plants are maintaining their TLAAs. As for means to support identification of new TLAAs after licence extensions are granted, site corrective action programs would document any identified deficiencies that required acceptance by evaluation. Also, the US renewal regulations require that plants with a renewed licence continue to identify any newly added SSCs and update their SAR to include any new AMPs and TLAAs (10 CFR 54.37) [13]. A site should have a procedure or process to identify new TLAAs in the licence renewal period to incorporate part of the licence renewal application.

Sites maintain their design basis documentation and ensure configuration management when modifications and replacements are performed through procedures describing all the requirements for completing design changes. Common design change package content for US plants was also developed as part of the NEI Delivering the Nuclear Promise effort several years ago to try and standardise the way sites did design changes across the US fleet (reference NEI Efficiency Bulletin 17-06, Revision 3, Implement Standard Design Change Process [361]). The US NRC also does periodic inspections to confirm plants are maintaining their design basis documentation and configuration management. Any identified deficiencies from those inspections would be captured in the site corrective action program and addressed. Some plants have had challenges in the past with maintaining their design basis such that it is a vulnerability to sites to lose focus on maintaining that documentation. However, restoring configuration management to ensure the safe operation of SSCs long term is considered reasonably achievable if a site finds itself in this situation, albeit not without significant time and cost associated with this effort.

The United Kingdom is embarking on a new era of nuclear reactor design, build and operation. At the same time, it has several older generation reactor technologies at various phases in the operational lifecycle including PWRs, advanced gas-cooled reactors (AGRs) and magnesium oxide reactors (Magnox). The United Kingdom also has many historical nuclear legacy facilities, some of which date from the very earliest days of the post-war 1940s nuclear industry which are entering decommissioning or long-term care and maintenance before eventual demolition.

Nuclear facilities contain SSCs important to safety which are required to operate and perform reliably and predictably throughout their life in service. That is often beyond their design life.

SSCs are typically designed to a design life which takes account of the operational demands and expectations throughout that period to achieve the performance characteristics. With intervention throughout the design life of SSCs through examination, inspection, maintenance and testing, a level of confidence can be established on which performance expectations are based.

When designing SSCs against codes and standards, service life assumptions determine the basis on which materials and components are selected. Often design conservatisms are built into the codes and standards for SSCs which provide operational margins and beyond design life tolerance. However, SSCs rarely have an unlimited life expectancy and are unlikely to contain materials or components without wear out characteristics which requires consideration when entering beyond design life operations.

The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) has recently undertaken research projects (ONR-RRR-061 Phase 1 [362] and ONR-RRR-061 Phase 2 [363]) to identify relevant good practice operation beyond the initial design life for nuclear facilities. This includes the need to consider enhanced examination, inspection, maintenance and testing. This is summarised within of the "Technical Assessment Guides on Ageing and Degradation Management NS-TAST-GD-109" [364] (Appendix 1) and makes up part of the "Mitigation Actions" detailed in Section 3 of TAG 17 (Annex 5).

As such, without an in depth understanding of the design basis of SSCs, there is a risk that when the design life is reached or exceeded, materials or components may deteriorate in reliability and performance to the point where either enhanced examination, inspection, maintenance and testing becomes necessary to monitor performance characteristics more closely, re-validation of the SSC design basis may be necessary, or replacement becomes necessary.

In the years 2016-2021/2023 for Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant/Temelin Nuclear Power Plant the DBD was made in co-operation with the original general designer of both Czech nuclear power plants. It was processed in the reconstitution form. DBD has a hierarchical structure in three levels:

- DBD1-1 document, design basis/design report and other information processed comprehensively for the entire nuclear power plant;
- DBD2-app. 160 documents processed in a graded approach only for systems executed safety functions, or safety supported functions (nuclear safety); and

• DBD3-app. 350 documents processed in a graded approach only for significant equipment groups forming relevant DBD2 (above).

Reconstituted DBD is regularly up to date in a specific software application and once a year is saved as shared documents in the nuclear power plant archive, where is digitally available for all relevant nuclear power plant employees. DBD is used as a key and fundamental concept documentation containing design basis/design report (located in the upper peak of CM=Configuration management equilibrium) especially during change configurations and modifications of nuclear power plant. Important information from the DBD is also reflected in the licence and safety documentation (SAR, PSR, etc.).

### <span id="page-246-0"></span>**5.2. Development of codes, standards and regulations**

Because of technology development, development of new diagnostic, inspection and monitoring methods and primarily with increasing experience from operation, ageing safety related events OPEX, the number and level of safety requirements and recommendations for design, operation and maintenance of existing nuclear power plants fleet are gradually increasing.

As described in Section 2.4, the IAEA has developed a comprehensive set of safety standards which are regularly updated to reflect the latest scientific and technical development and state-of-the-art knowledge and OPEX. The IAEA safety standards reflect an international consensus on what constitutes a high level of safety for protecting people and the environment from harmful effects of ionising radiation. Safety standards are complemented with several layers of lower-level publications which provide best practices and experience on how to implement safety standards.

The latest IAEA safety standards introduced many new requirements and recommendations which are also being applied for existing fleet of nuclear power plants through the process of PSR [5]. New safety requirements and recommendations can be very challenging for the existing fleet, and it is not always possible to fully comply with them, so alternative solutions must be sometimes undertaken. New requirements of IAEA SSR-2/1 (Rev.1) [365] and SSR-2/2 (Rev.1) [3] are further developed into guidance such as recommendations of:

- SSG-34 on "Design of Electrical Power Systems for Nuclear Power Plants" [366], Section 5 for physical separation of redundant safety systems (redundant divisions), physical separation of cables (safety and non-safety, different safety divisions, different voltage classes);
- SSG-69 on "Equipment Qualification for Nuclear Installations" [12], Section 3 and 4 for qualified equipment to perform safety functions throughout design extension conditions in severe accidents;
- SSG-53 on "Design of the Reactor Containment and Associated Systems for Nuclear Power Plants" [367], Section 3 for considering design extension conditions for the reactor containment function;
- SSG-67 on "Seismic Design for Nuclear Installations" [368], Section 3 for minimum earthquake level to withstand.

As of this report's publication there are no new IAEA safety standards requiring/recommending the use of passive safety functions (instead of active), redundancy of safety systems in connection with probabilistic safety analysis (PSA) (e.g. not in SSG-34, SSG-76, SSG-74 and SSG-70).

In the aftermath of the Fukushima Daiichi accident, WENRA Safety Reference Levels for Existing Reactors [369] introduced challenging requirements in:

- Section 6, Issue F on Design Extension of Existing Reactors. Requirements to consider design extension conditions;
- Section 19, Issue TU: External Hazards
- Section 18, Issue SV: Internal Hazards which introduces "a protection concept".

Para SV5.5 states that "SSCs identified as part of the protection concept with respect to design basis events shall be considered as important to safety." This leads to a significant increase of the number of SSCs important to safety and consequently increased requirements on these SSCs including significant increase of SSCs within ageing management.

Regulating safety is a national responsibility, and many countries have decided to adopt the IAEA safety standards for use in their national regulations. The IAEA safety standards are applied by regulatory bodies and operators around the world to enhance safety in nuclear power generation. The IAEA safety standards and informational publications also create sound basis for development and update of national and international codes, standards and regulations.

Most countries operating nuclear power plants (with exception of the United States where alternative arrangements exist) perform a PSR every 10 years [5] based on a comparison of the plant status against the latest national and international requirements, codes and standards. PSR is recognised as a mature and comprehensive approach to ensure that the latest codes, standards and regulations are properly addressed by nuclear power plants. The conclusions of this review typically lead to improvement of processes, procedures and organisational arrangements, but also to major modernisations and safety improvements of the original plant design.

Other sources of safety improvements including major modernisation are direct requirements of national regulators as corrective actions after major accidents (e.g. Three Mile Island, Chernobyl or Fukushima Daiichi accidents) or based on OPEX or enhanced safety analyses.

These requirements for modernisation and safety improvements of original plant design assume significant financial resources and extended outages, which may lead to operators' decisions to permanently phase out nuclear power plant units. This was in connection with economic aspects, which were for example the reason for the shutting down of four nuclear power plant units in Sweden in 2015-2020 (PWR and BWR 1 and 2 units at Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant and BWR Units 1 and 2 at the Oskarshamn Nuclear Power Plant).

Safety standards are only effective if they are properly applied in practice. The IAEA's safety services encompass design, siting and engineering safety, operational safety, radiation safety, safe transport of radioactive material and safe management of radioactive waste, as well as governmental organisation, regulatory matters and safety culture in organisations. These safety services assist IAEA Member States in the application of the IAEA safety standards and enable valuable experience and insights to be shared. Technical Safety Review service on PSR [370] is designed to support nuclear power plants in proper preparation and conduct of a PSR. The SALTO peer review service also reviews the plants` PSR approach and results with a focus on its use for justification of safe LTO. As mentioned earlier, the SALTO peer review service [371] was designed to review the preparedness of nuclear power plants for LTO (including LTO beyond 60 years) and is broadly used for this purpose.

The IAEA peer review services on PSR reviews shall "… address, in an appropriate manner: the consequences of the cumulative effects of plant ageing and plant modification; equipment requalification; OPEX, including national and international OPEX; current national and international standards; technical developments; organisational and management issues; and site related aspects." as stated in Requirement 12 of SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1) [3]. They also verify if "a recent PSR can provide reassurance that there continues to be a valid licensing basis taking account of, for example, plant ageing and current safety standards and operating practices" as stated in para 2.3 of SSG-25 [5] and "the extent to which the plant conforms to current national and/or international safety standards and operating practices" as stated in para 2.3 of SSG-25 [5].

### *5.2.1. Codes, standards and regulations harmonisation and enhancement needs*

In the United States, the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 requires that regulatory agencies participate in the development, and use, of technical standards that are created by voluntary consensus standard bodies (both domestic and international) to the extent practical. The US Office of Management and Budget Circular No. A-119 (1998) provides additional clarification on the purpose of this Act (e.g. reduce government costs, provide incentives for private industry to establish standards that serve national needs) and how agencies are to implement this direction.

As a result, the US NRC references consensus standards in its LTO beyond 60 years (subsequent licence renewal) guidance documents where practical. For example, for the main pressure equipment, NUREG-2191, "Generic Ageing Lessons Learned for Subsequent Licence Renewal (GALL-SLR) Report" [8] references American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, "Rules of Inservice Inspection and Testing of Components of Light-Water-Cooled Plants."

In addition, when a consensus standard is not available, the US NRC (as appropriate) endorses or references other industry standards/guidance related to ageing management. Examples relevant to the main pressure equipment include the EPRI guidelines for water chemistry, flow-accelerated corrosion (NSAC-202L-R4 [233]), and "Materials Reliability Program: Pressurized Water Reactor Internals Inspection and Evaluations Guidelines" (MRP-227, Rev. 2 [166]).

Finally, when consensus and industry standards do not fully address the scope of ageing issues, the US NRC addresses those gaps in its own guidance in NUREG-2191 [8] and NUREG-2192, "Standard Review Plan for Review of Subsequent Licence Renewal Applications for Nuclear Power Plants." The US NRC considers its current guidance in NUREG-2191 [8] and NUREG-2192 [18] (including the standards they reference) to sufficiently address ageing issues for 60-80 years of operation. However, the US NRC continues to participate in standards development committees to strengthen the availability of robust, effective standards that address ageing.

In the United Kingdom, ON[R Safety Assessment Principles](https://gbr01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.onr.org.uk%2Fsaps%2Fsaps2014.pdf&data=05%7C01%7CToby.Forster%40onr.gov.uk%7C44916c71f86240f9878108dbdb962800%7C742775df807748d681d01e82a1f52cb8%7C0%7C0%7C638345210183853151%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7VcHcGsFz2zbytRwExEhi3b0V5Mu%2BvkOvvIkQlmsVu8%3D&reserved=0) (SAPs) [372] recognise that as a facility ages the potential exists for SSCs to operate beyond the original design life, safety margins may be eroded and a duty holder may argue that making improvements is not worthwhile. The short remaining lifetime of the facility may be invoked as part of a safety case argument. However, this factor should not be accepted to justify the facility operating outside legal requirements, or at levels of risk that are unacceptably high.

A safety case which argues for not making an improvement based predominantly on limited future lifetime should only be accepted where the maximum extent of the future operational life is irrevocably fixed and provides a suitable margin of safety. In cases where the planned lifetime is not irrevocably fixed, a minimum period of ten years (or the unavoidable necessary life of the facility, if longer) should be considered for the purposes of judging whether the risk have been reduced as low as reasonably practicable.

In addition, the introductory paragraphs to the SAPs also identify that the principle of continuous improvement is central to achieving sustained high standards of nuclear safety. The SAPs record that the legal requirements for risk reduction "so far as is reasonably practicable". Application of this principle ensures that, no matter how high the standards of nuclear design and subsequent operations are, improvements should always be sought.

Seeking and applying lessons learnt from events, new knowledge and experience, both nationally and internationally, must be a fundamental feature of the safety culture of the nuclear industry. With respect to SSCs and beyond design life operation, continuous improvement should contribute to improving confidence in the actual condition of SSCs or to gain greater knowledge of what contributes to the Safety Margins, and how extended operation will impact on these margins.

The SAPs are also intended to be applied in the assessment of PSRs. This includes a comprehensive assessment of the facility's condition, OPEX, safety case, safety management arrangements, and culture, looking forward at least the next ten years and normally to the end of life. The review is carried out at appropriate intervals through the different lifecycle phases of the facility usually every ten years starting at the commencement of active commissioning.

In Japan, the industrial codes contribute to evaluation of components for LTO. As typical codes, the situation of the JSME codes is introduced below.

JSME nuclear design and construction codes cover the main safety classified SSCs for PWRs and BWRs: design and construction for LWR (JSME S NC1 [373]), concrete containment vessels (JSME S NE1 [374]), welding (JSME S NB1 [375]), materials (JSME S NJ1 [376]) and fitness-for-service (JSME S NA1 [377]). They include requirements and rules supporting the activities needed for the safety demonstration. For LTO, the Japanese government approved over the 60-year operation of nuclear power plants, and the revision of the law was promulgated in June 2023. Evaluation of SSCs for ageing is required for 30 years of operation and every ten years thereafter. Also, a special examination for SSCs is required at 40 years of operation. Operation beyond 60 years will be permitted if the evaluation is approved on the basis of scientific evidence.

The key evaluations of main pressure equipment for LTO are the seismic evaluation and the environmental fatigue evaluation for nuclear power plants. The JSME Design and Construction Code (JSME S NC1 [373]) refers the JEA (Japan Electric Association) seismic code (JEAC4601 [378]), and the JSME developed a code case for elastic-plastic analysis method of piping for seismic condition (JSME S NC-CC-008 [379]). The JSME Environmental Fatigue Evaluation Method (JSME S NF1 [380]) is used in the evaluation for the safety review. Some components are replaced because of SCC, and the JSME Code Case on Protection against SCC (JSME S NC-CC-002 [381]) is applied to the design of the replaced component. The JSME Rules on Pipe Wall Thinning Management for Nuclear Power Plants (JSME S NH1 [382], JSME S NG1 [383]) are also effective for LTO.

The requirement for seismic evaluation by the Japanese regulatory side is higher than in other countries. Also, environmental fatigue is important for PSR. So, advanced and accurate evaluation methods are needed for the seismic evaluation and environmental fatigue evaluation methods. The JSME is developing methods such as elastic-plastic analysis methods and accurate design fatigue curves. Regarding elastic-plastic analysis, the elastic-plastic analysis method of piping for seismic condition (JSME S NC-CC-008 [379]), which can perform fatigue evaluation using strain calculated by elastic-plastic analysis for a seismic wave, was published. Regarding design fatigue curves, the new design fatigue curves, which consist of the best-fit curve using tensile strength as a variable, factors on stress and number of cycles developed by statistical analysis, mean stress correction by the Smith-Watson-Topper approach, considering variable loading amplitude, and surface finish effect, were developed and incorporated into the JSME Environmental Fatigue Evaluation Method.

In France, AFCEN nuclear design and construction codes cover the main safety classified structures, systems and components, mainly for pressurised water reactors: civil work structures (RCC-CW code [384]), mechanical pressure equipment (RCC-M code [385]), electrical and I&C systems and equipment (RCC-E code [386]) and in-service surveillance and maintenance rules for mechanical equipment (RSE-M code [387]). They include requirements and rules supporting the activities needed for the safety demonstration. For LTO, the design of SSC must be reassessed to meet new assumptions related to an extended operating lifetime and upgraded safety requirements. Also, LTO might lead to additional ISI, to the reinforcement or replacement of existing SSC, and to the procurement and erection of new SSC. In that regard, LTO beyond 40 or 60 years does not differ from the periodic safety assessments: it mainly needs to reconsider the effects of ageing on SSCs on a larger timescale.

AFCEN nuclear codes being periodically updated, they align with the latest regulatory and safety requirements when enforced and applicable (including the consideration of IAEA standards and their updates), and benefit from the OPEX and R&D results related to degradation mechanisms and ageing effects. The latest recognised editions of AFCEN nuclear codes should then be specified for the reassessment of SSC and the procurement of new SSC.

AFCEN nuclear codes include requirements and rules to prevent and address degradation mechanisms and ageing effects on safety classified structures, equipment and components, at the design and construction stages (selection of materials, design and analysis, fabrication and examination), with regular updates to account for OPEX. In that regard, the RCC-M [385] covers mechanical pressure equipment, the RCC-CW code [384] covers civil work structures, and the RCC-E code [386] covers electrical and I&C equipment.

AFCEN nuclear codes also provide requirements and rules to preserve the justification and qualification of SSC during operation (surveillance/monitoring, examination and periodic testing, classification and justification of defects or deviations, maintenance rules for repairs and replacements), based on the assumptions and outcome of the safety analysis. For mechanical equipment, these requirements and rules are provided in the RSE-M code. The RCC-CW code [384] includes dedicated chapters on ageing management (AM), providing guidance for in-service rules. The RCC-E code [386] also addresses activities for electrical, automation and control equipment during operation (permanent monitoring, periodic testing, preventive and corrective maintenance), supporting the preservation or reassessment of EQ.

In all regulatory contexts, it would be advantageous to enhance methodologies for assessing the impact of constraint effects on FT, for applications in PTS analysis and in other contexts. An additional area of interest involves further investigations regarding material properties of irradiated SS and continue to develop methodologies for evaluation of internals, such as the Core barrel. With respect to fatigue there is also a need for additional data/methods for evaluating the effect of environmental assisted fatigue in the high temperature regime (325°C -345°C).

In some cases, it might make sense to adopt and adapt approaches from non-nuclear industries. A good example are the rules according to fatigue design and assessment. It seems the fatigue rules in ASME BPVC VIII are more advanced than this in ASME III/XI. They incorporate for instance approaches for mean stress correction and surface roughness. More generally, there is very extensive experience with fatigue over all branches of industry, e.g. fossil fuels, aerospace, automotive, rail, offshore and others.

### *5.2.2. Challenges of codes, standards and regulations increasing requirements*

In the United States, the Congressional Review Act (CRA) requires that the US NRC submit many of its final rulemakings (new or revised regulations) and guidance documents to the US Congress for notification purposes before the rulemaking or guidance document can take effect. The CRA establishes a process whereby the US Congress is made aware of certain types of agency actions and can enact laws to void them. This is a means by which Congress can reject a new US NRC regulation or guidance document if Congress considers the action to be too burdensome to the industry.

For those regulations and guidance documents covered by the CRA, the US NRC must provide a summary of their economic impacts. A regulatory basis document is an analysis that describes the technical, legal, and policy information that supports changes to the US NRC's regulations. It describes why the current regulation needs to be updated, explains how a change in the regulations will resolve the problem, and discusses other regulatory options to potentially address the problem. It provides a high-level discussion of the costs and benefits of each option and identifies any backfitting and forward fitting considerations.

The agency will sometimes issue preliminary proposed rule language to provide the public an opportunity to comment on the US NRC staff's proposal and to prepare for detailed discussions during a public meeting.

In Japan, methods for AMR are specified by the Atomic Energy Society of Japan (AESJ) as AESJ-SC-P005. This code covers ageing degradation to be considered for the regulatory requirement at 30, 40, and 50 years of operation. Considerable ageing phenomena were summarised based on SSC, functional requirement, environment, and materials, and the summary sheets are periodically updated based after the regulatory review of all Japanese Nuclear power plants. A systematic comparison of AESJ-SC-P005 and US SLRs was recently conducted, and the gap between the two was limited, confirming that the code is almost valid even for operation beyond 60 years.

Some specific evaluation methods for important SSCs have been standardised by Japan Electric Association (JEA). For example, the surveillance programme for irradiation embrittlement of RPV is specified in JEAC-4201, and the FT verification method is specified in JEAC-4206, respectively. The former has been revised periodically based on the expansion of surveillance data and research on irradiation embrittlement mechanisms. The latter incorporates the master curve method. Both are still in dialogue with the regulations for endorsement.

For LTO beyond 60 years in France, AFCEN nuclear codes could need updates on how degradation mechanisms and ageing effects are assessed and justified, considering further experimental data at laboratory scale and experience gained on actual equipment in nuclear power plants. The knowledge acquired could provide enhanced data and assessment methods to support the justification of safety classified equipment with regards to suspected degradation mechanisms beyond 60 years.

Ageing of materials generally leads to a decrease of their mechanical ductile properties. More specifically, fracture resistance of several mechanical components is altered by ageing (thermal or irradiation ageing), the latter leading for example to RPV embrittlement. Hence, justification of the integrity of components prone to ageing is increasingly difficult with the existing codified methods which, because of their conservatism, may provide a pessimistic margin estimation.

The use of initial design criteria established when the plants were built may not be adequate for the need of LTO (SSCs are aged, ageing phenomena are not linear, knowledge has increased…). This is a concern for utilities and stakeholders which, with the LTO perspective, chiefly need to refine their margin assessment thanks to advanced methods. AFCEN nuclear codes for mechanical pressure equipment, namely RCC-M [385] and RSE-M [387], already provide advanced methods:

- The WPS model is proposed by EDF for the RPV irradiated zone analysis. The WPS effect is the favourable effect of a prestress applied at "high temperature" (i.e. service temperature) on the effective toughness of ferritic steel submitted to a pressurised thermal shock.
- The GFr criterion [240] is proposed by EDF for Elbow E of the cold leg of MCL, close to the RPV, made in cast SS and prone to thermal ageing. This criterion is an alternative to classical evaluation of instability based on tearing resistance curve (J,da). GFr parameter [240] has the advantage of measuring energy dissipated specifically by fracture, whereas J parameter mixes both fracture and plastic deformation energies.
- The development of other advanced fracture mechanics methods is underway in R&D programmes, with the purpose of providing more precise and physical (but still conservative) margin estimates: Beremin, master curve, J-Q. Beremin and J-Q methods take into account local plastic effects at crack tip (constraint effects), which enables to model geometry effects between specimens and equipment. Master curve is a way to better make use of RPV irradiation surveillance programme.

The objective is to pave the way for these three methods in a new AFCEN technical publication bringing together all currently acceptable mechanical models for flaw evaluation, to be published and referenced by the next edition of RCC-M [385] code at the end of 2024.

However, even if the French Nuclear Regulator (ASNR) does not officially endorse these codes, the assessment by the ASNR of these methods (WPS, master curve, Beremin, Gfr), for use in future plant safety review is still pending.

The target of LTO beyond 60 years will probably imply other evolutions of codes but, at this stage, it is too early to draw an exhaustive list.

To adopt the requirements of the recently published new WENRA Safety Reference Levels [369], the IAEA SSG-48 [4] and the recommendations from ENSREG Topical Peer Review 2018, the Swiss Regulatory Guideline ENSI-B01 (Ageing Management) [388] is currently under revision.

The Regulatory Guideline ENSI-A03 (Periodic Safety Review of Nuclear Power Plant) [389] was updated in 2018 and now defines requirements for an LTO assessment if a nuclear power plant exceeds 40 years of operation. This LTO assessment must be renewed at least every ten years.

Equipment qualification is addressed by the Regulatory Guidelines ENSI-A04 (Documents for approval of modifications) [390] and ENSI-G11 (Safety-classified vessels and pipelines: planning, fabrication and installation) [391]. The ENSI-G11 will be revised soon.

In addition to the regulatory guidelines and the nuclear legislation, Switzerland, as a small country, does not have national nuclear codes. So, international codes are used, and the possibilities for influencing code development are limited. One possibility is to participate in appropriate working groups.

### <span id="page-253-0"></span>**5.3. Technological obsolescence**

### *5.3.1. Overview*

Obsolescence of components can eventually lead to difficulty acquiring spare parts or difficulty getting technical support from the original manufacturer, longer procurement lead-times and higher prices. It is important to identify and prioritise obsolescence, so that measures can be taken to identify and approve alternative replacement parts or components to maintain the reliability of plant equipment.

Guidance in EPRI 1019161 "Plant Support Engineering: Proactive Obsolescence Management" [392] involves the following key elements to proactively manage obsolescence:

- identification of obsolete items by maintaining a list of equipment and associated items in the plant, periodic communication with vendors and monitoring precursors to obsolescence such as increases in price and lead-time, to identify the plant equipment and items that are already obsolete or likely to become obsolete in the near future;
- prioritisation of obsolescence issues based on a cross-functional evaluation of factors including equipment criticality, system health, and upcoming demand;
- proactive development and implementation of solutions, which may range from minor design changes and equivalency evaluations to reverse engineering and major modifications.

It is important to mention also other type of obsolescence - obsolescence of knowledge, knowledge retention and transfer of knowledge from experienced members to unexperienced staff. Lack of relevant knowledge of research staff, manufactures, suppliers and operators can also lead to lack of capability to address technological obsolescence and physical ageing issues and consequently to permanent shut down of nuclear power plants. This section does not focus on obsolescence of knowledge and will further discuss solely technological obsolescence, which refers to the condition where the plant's equipment and systems become outdated or inferior compared to newer technologies, increasing the difficulty of obtaining spare and replacement items, original manufacturer support, and potentially impairing operational efficiency, safety, or regulatory compliance.

Technological obsolescence has become an issue for many nuclear power plants. This topic has been addressed since 2005 using several commercially developed solutions. A modern approach to proactive technological obsolescence management was implemented in Canada and the United States . This issue is being solved also in other parts of the world mostly using similar approaches (e.g. in Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, France, Hungary, Sweden). International co-operation is of a key importance to identify and quantify current and future needs of individual operators and jointly motivate manufacturers and suppliers to produce, supply and provide maintenance services for existing equipment.

Technological obsolescence is important particularly for I&C and electrical equipment, both safety and non-safety related. I&C systems are a typical example, but their obsolescence is frequently combined with physical ageing. I&C refurbishments are regularly performed and are both from technical and safety side well managed. But regulations in some countries (e.g. US) still does not allow routine shift from analogue to completely digital safety I&C systems. This can eventually lead to the situation when the

units could be phased out due to lack of maintainability of I&C systems. Another important aspect is the high financial cost of I&C refurbishment (investment costs, extended outages, tests).

### *5.3.2. Guidelines, standards and regulation*

EPRI developed several reports on managing obsolescence, "Plant Support Engineering: Proactive Obsolescence Management, Program Implementation and Lessons Learned"[29](#page-254-0), presents an obsolescence management process that can be implemented as a separate programme of integrated in existing plant maintenance, procurement, inventory management, and engineering processes. EPRI 3002013813, "Obsolescence Program Manager Computer Based Training (CBT) v1.0" provides basic training for individuals involved in managing obsolescence in an on-demand, computer-based format available to EPRI members and the public.

The IAEA has described technological obsolescence and its importance for nuclear safety in Specific Safety Guide SSG-48 on "Ageing Management and Development of a Programme for Long Term Operation of Nuclear Power Plants" in 2018 [4]. Section 6 of this safety guide provides basic recommendation for development and implementation of a proactive technological obsolescence programme. Further details on proactive technological obsolescence programme are provided in Safety Report Series No. 82 (Rev.2) "Ageing Management for Nuclear Power Plants: International Generic Lessons Learned (IGALL)" [7]. TOP 401 Technological Obsolescence Programme, in its 2023 version is available on the IGALL public website[30.](#page-254-1) It is a document that provides practical guidance on establishment and implementation of a proactive technological obsolescence programme, new metrics for monitoring and trending and new possible solutions to address it.

An obsolescence programme can be developed as a stand-alone programme or incorporated into existing plant processes, as shown by IAEA SSG-48 [4] (e.g. maintenance programme, equipment reliability programme) and used in a way that regularly and proactively identifies obsolete equipment, prioritises obsolescence issues, and enables proactive development and implementation of replacement solutions.

EPRI documents 3002002852 [359], EPRI 1015391 [393], EPRI 1016692 [394], EPRI 1019161 [392], INPO document NX-1037, Revision 3 [395], INUOG document INUOG-2019/001, Rev.0 [396], and industry successful experiences can be used as references for the development of a proactive obsolescence programme at the plant.

EPRI 1019161 "Plant Support Engineering: Proactive Obsolescence Management" [392] [\(www.epri.com/research/products/1019161\)](https://www.epri.com/research/products/1019161) provides guidance for developing and implementing an obsolescence management programme with three basic elements: identification of obsolescence issues, prioritisation of the issues, and solution implementation. The methodologies presented can be used to minimise the impact that obsolescence has on plant production and cost. In this paper, engineering solutions are suggested as common solutions to address obsolescence issues.

Equivalency evaluation or design changes can be used to approve alternative replacements as discussed in EPRI 1008254 [397] (["Guidelines for Optimizing the Engineering Change](https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001008254) 

<span id="page-254-0"></span><sup>29</sup> EPRI (2009), "Plant Support Engineering: Proactive Obsolescence Management, Program Implementation and Lessons Learned", [https://www.epri.com/research/products/1019161.](https://www.epri.com/research/products/1019161)

<span id="page-254-1"></span><sup>30</sup> IAEA (2025), IGALL[, https://gnssn.iaea.org/NSNI/PoS/IGALL/SitePages/Home.aspx.](https://gnssn.iaea.org/NSNI/PoS/IGALL/SitePages/Home.aspx)

[Process for Nuclear Power Plants, Revision 2"](https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001008254)). The current EPRI guidance related to digital equivalency evaluation comprises:

- 3002018279 "Digital Equivalency Evaluation: Screening Checklist and Considerations, Revision 1 – An Updated Approach That Considers Item Configurability and Consequences of Error" (2020) [398]
- 3002020837 "Determining Configurability and Consequences of Error of Digital Devices" (2021) [399].

These two evaluations are both available to EPRI members at no cost.

When items are no longer available from a supplier with a nuclear quality management programme, potential solutions may involve replacement items that are only able to be procured as commercial grade. In these cases, the commercial-grade dedication process may be used to accept the commercial-grade item for use in a safety related application.

Additional guidance on the commercial-grade dedication process can be found in EPRI 3002002982, "Plant Engineering: Guideline for the Acceptance of Commercial-Grade Items in Nuclear Safety-Related Applications: Revision 1 to EPRI NP-5652 and TR-102260" [\(www.epri.com/research/products/3002002982\)](https://www.epri.com/research/products/3002002982) [351]. The process involves a technical evaluation that includes identification of critical characteristics of the item and development of acceptance criteria, acceptance methods and an acceptance plan, as well as verification of each critical characteristic to demonstrate acceptability.

Acceptance methods may include inspections, tests, or analyses by the nuclear operator or third-party dedicating entity, survey of the commercial supplier, and surveillance of activities at the supplier's facility. Critical characteristics are the important design, material, and performance characteristics of a commercial-grade items that once verified will provide reasonable assurance that the item will perform its intended safety function (more details in EPRI 3002002982 [351]).

It can become a good practice, for the dedicator, to share defect reporting (for instance [400] and [401]).

Other international standards may also be used when applicable, such as IEC [350] or IAEA NR-T-3.31 [402]. IAEA NR-T-3.31 [402] identifies the key challenges associated with the use of digital COTS (Commercial Off the Shelf) devices in nuclear safety applications and provides guidance on the requirements for what would constitute an adequate justification process.
