IAEA NR-T-3.34 [403] "Management of Ageing and Obsolescence of Instrumentation and Control Systems and Equipment in Nuclear Power Plant and Related Facilities Through Modernization" provides pertinent IAEA recommendations and guidance on I&C system/equipment ageing and obsolescence management and relevant good practice, describes key ageing and obsolescence related issues that need to be taken into consideration when modernising I&C systems/equipment and provides strategies that could be employed to address such issues.

### *5.3.3. Industry joint groups*

Most of the equipment found in any nuclear power plant can typically be found in one or more other operating organisations. Therefore, opportunity exists to collaborate with other nuclear power plants when developing proactive replacement solutions that involve external suppliers and engineering services. Collaboration enables participants to share the cost of solution development that is suitable for multiple applications. Therefore, industry databases can be effective in solving obsolescence issues.

A good example of this collaboration is the Nuclear Utility Obsolescence Group (NUOG) [395] and the International Nuclear Utility Obsolescence Group (INUOG) [396]. Both were formed to share information and solutions for dealing with equipment obsolescence at nuclear power plants. For example, INUOG developed "Guideline for Establishing Obsolescence Indicators" [404] in 2018. Sharing best practices may also come from other areas in the industry such as benchmarking trips to other utilities or World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO) and SALTO Peer reviews. EPRI's Procurement Engineering and Related Topics Symposium (PEARTS) is the working group that led development of the EPRI products that address obsolescence management. EPRI performs obsolescence assessments and has invited INUOG participation for international assessments.

There are also commercial products such as POMS supported by Westinghouse [357] for identification, prioritisation, and determining solutions of obsolescence issues.

Other provider of obsolescence solutions is Paragon (PeAKS database) [405], Curtiss-Wright Nuclear Division (RAPID database) [406], EPRI's Utility/ Supplier Obsolescence Notification and Exchange (UsOne) and Pending Obsolescence Protocol (POP) databases [407]. Such databases help nuclear power plants to get information in a quicker way than approaching to it separately.

The IAEA and NEA Nuclear Harmonisation and Standardisation Initiative (NHSI) was launched in 2022 to bring together policymakers, [regulators,](https://www.reutersevents.com/nuclear/nrc-cnsc-see-eventual-path-multi-lateral-licensing) designers, vendors, and operators to develop common regulatory and industrial approaches that view nuclear as a global fleet.

### *5.3.4. Possible challenges for LTO beyond 60 years*

Although there are some guidelines and successful experiences managing the obsolescence problems in some nuclear power plant, there are some key challenges on obsolescence management that all the industry faces when talking about LTO beyond 60 years. Many SSCs which might not need a replacement before the end of 60 years of operation or whose lifetime was expanded when working until 60 years, will have the need to be replaced or could be obsolete when going for operation beyond 60 years.

When looking to obsolete equipment, the main concerns that utilities have, their impact and possible solutions, are summarised below:

- 1. Spare parts procurement To mitigate the effect of longer lead times for spare parts procurement and more frequent obsolete components, the obsolescence management and planning must be done in a much timely manner. This means that organisational changes and procedures have to be developed or improved to deal better with spare parts issues. This also means that the maintenance activities have to be planned well in advance, to give the supply chain approximately two years to procure and solve upcoming obsolescence issues. This will ensure no material shortage in the upcoming overhaul period. Long-term supply contracts and bridging strategies must be in place where needed and used considering upcoming needs regarding some components.
- 2. Common cause failures safety impact If the obsolescence programme proactively identifies and finds solutions to replace the obsolete equipment, there should be a time slot big enough to introduce the replacement component gradually in the facility. This gradual introduction of new equipment will be beneficial before a complete exchange of product series is performed taking into consideration OPEXs in different utilities.

- 3. Increased O&M costs The concern with the increased O&M costs is mostly not related to the cost itself if the need for resources is identified in time, in order to support the economic budgetary process within the plant. This means that the obsolescence problems as well as the proposed method of solution must be identified timely and implement gradually in time, avoiding sudden O&M increase in costs. Close exchange of information within the industry and OEM is the key to understand the upcoming obsolescence challenges and be able to plan them on time.
- 4. Qualifying commercial items, industrial digital instrumentation Procedures to use COTS (commercial off-the-self) or commercial components have to be updated and in compliance with any directive. If the all the nuclear power plants do it according to the same directive, such as EPRI best practice, makes it possible to use already performed qualification of other entities and to support the methodology of perform commercial grade dedication (CGD) in a standardised way. This include electrical and I&C components, as well as mechanical.
- 5. Decreased reliability performance Obsolescence of knowledge by the plant technical resources, as well as the OEM experts, has a significant impact on the reliability as well as when trying to understand the root cause of the failures. In case they are not correctly identified, would the failure not be well mitigated. In the other hand, most equipment replaced by the obsolescence programme is expected to have an increased level of reliability due to modern design features and OPEX.

The main difficulties that the industry faces in terms of obsolescence beyond 60 years are:

- 1. The nuclear industry is constantly managing obsolescence, and still finds it challenging to proactively identify, prioritise, and solve obsolescence issues to minimising impact (see items "1" to "5" above). The discovery that an obsolete item is needed typically occurs when the item is ordered, leaving little time to find a replacement and perform the engineering evaluations necessary to accept it for use. Nowadays this is still a main challenge of nuclear power plants, even for operation up to 60 years.
- *2.* Sharing information on an obsolescence issue remains a challenge. In many cases, applicable intellectual property laws prohibit sharing proprietary information about a proposed replacement device without permission of the manufacturer. However, there are different companies which place in the market commercial databases that include some information on how the industry solved this issue, or which manufacturer could deliver that potential replacement piece or part, which can be accessed in return of a fee. Use of EPRI's Utility/Supplier Obsolescence Notification Exchange (UsOne) database is available at no charge. EPRI members can upload lists of obsolete items for which replacements are needed and suppliers can upload lists of items for which they already have replacements. When a utility uploads a list, they can see and download a list of existing replacement solutions that match their needs. When a supplier uploads a list, they can see and download a list of utilities that need their existing solutions. This reduces the time spent searching for a solution when one already exists, as well as duplication of reverse engineering. It can also reduce engineering time spent on equivalency evaluations.
- 3. The modernisation of I&C systems/equipment is another important challenge for nuclear power plants to identify suitable replacement equipment technology, maintain the required operating capabilities and adequate safety margins, and integrate new replacement systems with older systems based on different technologies, among others.

- 4. Once an obsolescence issue has led to the replacement of an SSC system/equipment, the new process of qualification of the component and the manufacturing process of it can be laborious, especially when the SSC is safety related.
- 5. Despite there being some industry guidelines available, digital equivalency evaluations often present a challenge due to the complex nature of digital devices and the training required to understand the potential risks a replacement digital device can present to the nuclear power plant.
- 6. There is a lack of simple performance measurement tools to track performance of the obsolescence management programme.
- 7. Maintaining a supply chain running and up to date with manufacturers for complex and pieces/parts remains a challenge.

To meet the above-mentioned challenges, the nuclear sector (policymakers, regulators, designers, vendors and operators) must work along similar, if not identical, international guidelines that allow for a standardisation of common regulatory and industrial approaches to obsolescence issues.

### **6. Conclusions for LTO beyond 60 years**

<span id="page-259-0"></span>The descriptive parts of the report, particularly Sections 2, 3, 4 and 5, contain subsections listing preliminary conclusions or gaps. These conclusions and gaps represent the opinion of individual contributors to given sections and were used as a source of information for the development of Section 6.2, "Identified areas for enhancement" (AFE). Section 6.2 represents a consensus of the project task team members on the AFEs that need attention to support safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years in an agreed structure. The "proposals for dispositioning", which are a part of each AFE, should provide descriptions of suitable solutions for the dispositioning of the identified AFEs to support nuclear power plant operation beyond 60 years. They can include:

- further R&D projects to fully characterise and manage ageing effects;
- new/enhanced testing, monitoring, inspection, diagnostics or repair methods;
- training on ageing management and LTO preparation;
- development of codes, standards, procedures, methodologies;
- other solutions (e.g. extended collaborative network for obsolescence/supply chain issues).

Section 6.1 "Areas properly addressed" (APA) was also developed by the project task team members based on information collected in Sections 2, 3, 4 and 5. Section 6.1 represents a consensus of the project task team members on APAs and provides the technical audience with information and advice on what is available, documented and can be used as a knowledge basis for assessment, justification and preparation for safe LTO beyond 60 years. APAs have the same structure but do not contain "proposals for dispositioning".

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* A2.3-01

*Conclusion title:* IAEA guidance for LTO beyond 60 years

*Description of conclusion:* As discussed in Sections 2.3 and 2.4, the IAEA has developed a set of safety standards and other publications to support its member states in preparation for safe LTO. Safety standards and guides are based on the member states' experiences. Safety standards are not legally binding but represent an international consensus on the area. Safety standards are written on a higher-level providing requirements and recommended ways how to address requirements (in safety guides). Safety standards are applicable to the whole period of nuclear power plant operation and thus do not distinguish between LTO beyond 30 or 40 years of operation and LTO beyond 60 years of operation. The IAEA safety standards are regularly updated to include the latest experience of the member states and reflect the recommended approach to ageing management and preparation for safe LTO, including LTO beyond 60 years. IAEA publications below the level of safety standards (e.g. safety reports) provide good practices and examples of how safety standards can be implemented. They may distinguish between LTO up to 60 years and beyond 60 years. IAEA informational documents other than the safety standards and guides (like the TECDOCs and technical report for main components) provide other relevant and detailed data for the development of comprehensive and systematic ageing management programmatic documentation.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* The IAEA safety standards represent the fundamental guidance for most of the IAEA member states for demonstration of preparedness for LTO. They are also used as a reference for IAEA peer review services focused on LTO such as SALTO and OSART.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* A2.3-02

*Conclusion title:* Sharing operating experience feedback and proven practices in ageing management

*Description of conclusion:* The IAEA IGALL programme has an essential role in collecting, monitoring and sharing the latest proven practices in ageing management (AMPs, TLAAs etc.) The IGALL programme maintains a continuously updated database of known ageing effects and degradation mechanisms and proven AMPs and TLAAs to manage them. US NRC GALL [6] as well as GALL SLR [8] (supporting LTO from 60 to 80 years for US plants) have been also incorporated into IGALL documents and database.

Based on the increasing number of nuclear power plants going through comprehensive safety assessments to demonstrate safe operation during LTO beyond the original design lifetime (30 or 40 years), the current experience is continuously collected, analysed and shared in the IGALL Safety Report [7], supported by the publicly available, consolidated IGALL programme database[31.](#page-260-0)

This ensures incorporating latest OPEX and knowledge, keeping the IGALL as a living programme and an efficient tool to maintain the ageing management in nuclear power plants effective and on the state-of-the-art level.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* As the age of operating nuclear power plants increases, the probability of adverse ageing effects on SSCs will also increase. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that the latest OPEX feedback and proven practices in ageing management are shared among all operating nuclear power plants.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.4. US NRC regulatory framework for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* A2.4-01

*Conclusion title:* US NRC regulatory framework

*Description of conclusion:* Regarding national regulatory frameworks, the US NRC regulatory framework is the most mature in terms of specific regulations and practical experience with conducting the safety evaluation and licensing renewal to allow safe operation of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years. The general approach and methodology for licensing renewal from 60 to 80 years is the same as for the licensing renewal from 40 to 60 years, with only minor updates. The GALL Report [6] provides an acceptable approach to assess and manage ageing effects, and it is periodically updated based on industry OPEX and research. NRC inspectors evaluate each plant's implementation of their

ageing management programmes at the beginning of, and during, the period of extended operation.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* The US NRC regulatory framework for licensing renewal from 60 to 80 years is fully developed and practically used, so it can serve as an example for other countries operating PWR or BWR nuclear power plants approaching this step.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.5. Typical national regulatory frameworks to support LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* A2.5-01

*Conclusion title:* Approaches to LTO justification

*Description of conclusion:* Although each country and each reactor technology may have its needs and LTO justification methods, most countries rely mainly on IAEA safety standards and many of them also use the US NRC approach, or the regulatory approach from the country of the design origin. The various national approaches can be grouped into two main categories:

- the PSR-based approach, typically used in countries with unlimited or continuing licences (with a PSR for LTO typically more rigorous, with greater focus on ageing aspects and covers the whole intended period of LTO);
- the licence renewal-based approach, typically used in countries with a limited licence, typically for 30 or 40 years and usually allowing an additional 20 years of license extension.

Both approaches can be successfully used also for LTO beyond 60 years.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* There are proven approaches to justify safe LTO based on IAEA safety standards which apply also to operation beyond 60 years.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 3.5 Human resources, knowledge and competence management

*Conclusion number:* A3.5-01

*Conclusion title:* Education and training of personnel for LTO

*Description of conclusion:* A lot of work has been done in recent decades in training based on systematic approach to training methodology and significantly in relationships between the nuclear sector, educational institutions and training systems. Closer co-operation between nuclear organisations, universities and governmental organisations has been recognised by many countries as an important factor in developing adequate nuclear education and in creating the new HR pipelines for LTO.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Competent and qualified personnel represent one of the most important prerequisites for implementation of safe LTO programmes beyond 60 years. Well-planned training processes, the development of talent pipelines and close co-operation between academia and nuclear industry make it possible to bridge the generational gap and ensure that knowledge and expertise are transferred effectively. It is also necessary to ensure that the latest lessons learnt and good practices in training and qualification management are shared among all operating nuclear power plants.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 3.5 Human resources, knowledge and competence management

*Conclusion number:* A3.5-02

*Conclusion title:* Talent and succession programmes in LTO

*Description of conclusion:* Many nuclear organisations have developed comprehensive talent and succession programmes supporting the critical knowledge transfer from experienced professionals to newer employees, maintaining operational continuity and safety standards. These programmes also identify and prepare future leaders, ensuring that the organisation has capable individuals ready to step into key roles as needed.

The IAEA supports member states by providing guidance, conducting SALTO missions, and organising assist visits to help meet the safety standards. The most relevant requirement related to the importance of talent and succession programmes in LTO is outlined in SSR-2/2 (Rev. 1) - Requirement 4: Staffing of the operating organization [3]. The IAEA offers comprehensive guidance in managing human resources in the field of nuclear energy which can be utilised to benchmark excellence.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Succession planning helps to mitigate the risks associated with unexpected departures or retirements, ensuring that there are always qualified personnel ready to take over. By fostering the culture of continuous learning and development, these programmes also help the organisation to stay innovative and adaptable to new challenges and technologies in implementation of its LTO plans.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* A4.2-01

*Conclusion title:* Extension of existing RPV surveillance programmes for LTO beyond 60 years

*Description of the conclusion:* The need to monitor changes in the mechanical and fracture properties of the RPV structural material throughout its lifetime is well known. The surveillance programmes are updated for LTO beyond 60 years operation plans in accordance with the requirements of the national regulation and standards. Material resources to cover the full planned service life may sometimes be limited. The technology of reconstituted surveillance specimens, material harvested from decommissioned RPV, as well as specifically designed replacement material are used.

EPRI has multiple ongoing or future projects to generate high fluence surveillance capsule data, and update ETCs as necessary. MRP-326, Revision 1 [69] details the co-ordinated reactor vessel surveillance programme (CRVSP) which moved out US plant surveillance capsules to generate high fluence results. The PWR Supplemental Surveillance Programme (MRP-412) also has a goal to gather high fluence test results. These two capsules will be withdrawn in 2027 and 2028, with 24 new transition temperature shift measurements, and three new USE results at high fluence levels (between 4.5 x 1019 – 1.2 x 1020 n/cm2 ). EPRI has a future pending programme to investigate and potentially propose enhancements to the main, international consensus ETC from ASTM, E900.

A critical issue is often the lack of remaining surveillance specimens, but it is managed properly by usage of reconstituted specimen and reintroducing into RPV for continued irradiation at the positions with the highest allowed lead factors. Alternatively, miniaturised specimens could be used. If the combination of lead factor and remaining operating time is sufficient, new specimens from archive material, with the required chemical composition, should be used. Another possibility is to use material from decommissioned, nonoperational RPVs.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* The mechanical and fracture properties of the RPV material deteriorate during operation due to the synergistic effect of irradiation and operating temperature. To demonstrate the structural integrity of the RPV under normal, abnormal, and emergency conditions, it is necessary to know the mechanical and fracture properties of RPV steels as input data for the necessary analysis.

The main ageing mechanism of the RPV from a lifetime point of view is the embrittlement of the ferritic steel core zone (core shells and their joining welds) due to irradiation. Embrittlement affects the strength of the material with respect to the fast fracture risk, which is the design-basis damage mode in the core zone. Collecting data to extend the ETC coverage to the targeted life extension is mandatory.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel/4.4 Steam Generators/4.5 Safety Class 1 piping/4.6 Buried and underground piping

*Conclusion number:* A4.2-02

*Conclusion title:* Fatigue monitoring programmes

*Description of the conclusion:* Fatigue has been identified as one of the degradation mechanisms which require ongoing monitoring for LTO justification, including for:

- some parts of the RPV, especially nozzles and head bolts;
- some parts of the SG, especially nozzles;
- the surge line and the pressuriser;
- buried service water systems and underground pipelines.

The most susceptible components are in the primary circuit, where the parameters' cycling could reach the highest amplitude. In some Swiss PWR SGs there were found positions with the highest CUFs. But also, for service water system pipelines that do not have strict requirements for the number of cycles, as they operate at almost constant pressure and temperature, different seasonal levels of underground water may lead to additional settlements. Surface live loads from transport, draining of buried pipelines for short periods of time could add significant influence of cycling loading.

Currently, state-of-the art online fatigue monitoring systems are available to be used for real time counting of transients and sometimes even of CUF. Also, temporary monitoring of the temperature on selected part of the piping is a good practice to improve the knowledge of the thermal loading. Selection of location should be based on the existing knowledge of dead legs' behaviour influence on mechanical damage risk. Environmental effects should be also considered. With these tools the fatigue issue caused by thermal and pressure transients, as well as thermal stratification, is generally considered sufficiently addressed. But these online fatigue monitoring tools are less appropriate to detect highcyclic fatigue phenomena, like thermal mixing and mechanical vibrations. This requires complementary actions (see AFE E4.5-07 and E4.5-08).

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Fatigue is a continuously progressive ageing mechanism. Extending the service life leads to higher CUFs. Increasing demands on flexible operation of nuclear power plants can also have a negative impact on fatigue. Power up rates have often a significant effect on vibration levels.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.4. Steam generators

*Conclusion number:* A4.4-01

*Conclusion title:* Steam generator guidance for inspection, repair, cleaning, and

replacement technology

*Description of conclusion:* EPRI's Steam Generator Management Program developed guidance for inspection, repair, cleaning, and replacement technology of SGs that will be sufficient for operating beyond 60 years. The guidelines are reviewed periodically to determine the need for revision based on current technology or OPEX.

In Japan and in France, there is also a great deal of experience with SGs inspection, repair, cleaning, and replacement, which is sufficient to enable operation for more than 60 years.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* With the ageing of SGs worldwide, the ageing effects of SGs will increasingly require inspections, cleaning, repairs and even replacements of SGs. It will be important to have in place appropriate guidance and technology to perform these tasks.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.5 Safety Class 1 piping

*Conclusion number:* A4.5-01

*Conclusion title:* Thermal fatigue in non-isolable branch lines connected to the reactor

coolant loop

*Description of conclusion:* Although thermal fatigue occurrences were considered not analysed in the original design fatigue evaluations, industry guidance has since been put into place to monitor and detect instances of thermal fatigue. In the US cyclic stratification and thermal mixing are handled by MRP-146 [203] and MRP-192 [194], respectively. Thermal fatigue is generally well-characterised and susceptible locations are identified and managed.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Thermal fatigue has led to numerous failures in nonisolable branch lines connected to the RCL and could pose and important safety and economic threat if not properly anticipated and addressed. Methods are available to carry out investigations and assessments, but they still can be improved, as well as the knowledge of dead legs thermal hydraulic loadings (see AFE E4.5-08 entitled "Thermal cycling due to vortex penetration and other complex thermo-hydraulic phenomena").

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.5 Safety Class 1 piping

*Conclusion number:* A4.5-02

*Conclusion title:* Database of thermal ageing of CASS

*Description of conclusion:* Thermal ageing of CASS has been studied extensively since the mid-1980s through laboratory testing on a wide range of materials (CF8M, CF8…), including samples harvested from site. The database is now sufficient to cover the equivalent of 80 years of operation for both cold and hot leg primary piping of PWRs. These data feed empirical prediction formulae that enable prediction of ductile FT properties for the need of LTO beyond 60 years.

Laboratory work continues to enrich the database and to consider feedback (OPEX, international state of the art)*.*

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* This topic is important from two main reasons:

- impact on maintenance programmes if some CASS components have to be replaced;
- impact on reactor lifetime for CASS components that could not be replaced (namely CASS elbows next to RPV on cold leg).

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.5 Safety Class 1 piping

*Conclusion number:* A4.5-03

*Conclusion title:* Current methods enable EAF management

*Description of conclusion:* Methods have been developed for appropriately addressing the effects of the LWR environment on the fatigue calculations of nuclear power plants. These methods will enable plant owners to demonstrate knowledge of the locations in their plants that can serve as locations requiring EAF management, to satisfy long-term operation EAF guidance.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* In the absence of explicit ASME code rules to address the possible additional impact of water environments, the US NRC issued guidance based on additional research to address EAF; the guidance consisted of operating plant guidance for operation beyond 40 years in the [GALL Report \(NUREG-1801\)](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/staff/sr1801/index.html) [6], and later in the [RG 1.207](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML0703/ML070380586.pdf) Revision 0 [205], and its supporting technical basis report [NUREG/CR-](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/contract/cr6909/initial/index.html)[6909](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/nuregs/contract/cr6909/initial/index.html) [188] for new reactors. The US NRC revised RG 1.207 (Rev. 1) [206] and NUREG/CR-6909 (Rev. 1) [188] in 2018, to apply to both new and operating reactors, and GALL guidance for operation beyond 60 years, documented in NUREG-2191 [8]. Regulatory requirements are well developed for addressing EAF during licence renewal activities.

RCC-M code [385] provides explicit rules to address EAF (Rule in Probationary Phase #3). They are based on NUREG/CR 6909 report [188] and are optimised to better account for the effect of influent parameters, following extensive experimental programmes.

Although the relationship between the life of a component and the magnitude and frequency of the cyclic loading in LWR environments is well understood, additional testing is recommended to further reduce uncertainties, especially for cases where data are in a more limited number (see AFEs E4.3-05 and E4.5-01).

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.6. Buried and underground piping

*Conclusion number:* A4.6-01

*Conclusion title:* Guidance for buried and underground piping

*Description of conclusion:* The degradation mechanisms for buried and underground piping are generally well understood, and regulatory and industry guidance describes appropriate material selection, preventive measures (e.g. coatings, cathodic protection) and inspection approaches to manage ageing. In addition, industry guidelines describe current repair, refurbishment, and replacement solutions, including polymeric liners and complete pipe replacements.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Long-term degradation of buried and underground piping may impact nuclear plant safety functions. Effective ageing management by proper material selection, preventive measures, inspections, and repair/replacement activities is necessary to prevent failures, ensure safety, and maintain regulatory compliance.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.8 Electrical cable systems

*Conclusion number:* A4.8-01

*Conclusion title:* Comprehensive cable ageing management programme

*Description of conclusion:* Many nuclear power plants worldwide have developed and implemented a comprehensive CAMP. It consists of the following steps:

- Monitoring environmental parameters extensive temperature and dose rate monitoring within the whole plant. Moisture monitoring is important for some plants.
- Identifying stressors and expected ageing mechanisms.
- Installing cable deposits even plants in operation can introduce cable deposits. Cables harvested from the plant can be installed in cable deposits. Cable degradation of such cables is more accurate than cables artificially aged before placing into the deposit.
- Condition monitoring of cables , including visual inspections and cable harvesting at the plant.
- Collecting all the possible information on cables in scope.
- Developing a database for monitored cables.
- Carrying out in-laboratory ageing experiments of cable types in scope determining properties change with time of ageing and degree of deterioration.
- Selecting condition-monitoring techniques suitable to monitored cables.
- Establishing the baseline condition of monitored cables.
- Identifying cable characteristics and ageing effects being monitored by each selected CM technique.
- Performing test and inspection activities for periodic CM of cables.
- Periodically reviewing and incorporating plant and industry experience.
- Periodically reviewing, assessing and trending the condition of monitored cables.
- Identifying degraded conditions and taking prompt corrective actions.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Comprehensive CAMP is a key precondition to allow extension of cable lifetime beyond 60 years.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.2. Development of codes, standards and regulations

*Conclusion number:* A5.2-01

*Conclusion title:* Contribution of industrial codes for LTO

*Description of conclusion:* Several codes and standards support the evaluation of components for LTO, including JSME (Japan), AFCEN (France), and ASME (United States). These codes provide acceptable approaches to address such issues as seismic evaluations, irradiation embrittlement of the RPV, thermal ageing of cast stainless steels, fatigue, and several additional important LTO topics.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Codes and standards are an essential aspect of safe and reliable nuclear operations. Based on state-of-the-art knowledge, they provide important criteria for quality controls, inspections, repairs, and other activities to support LTO.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.3. Technical obsolescence

*Description of conclusion:* A5.3-01

*Conclusion title:* Support for addressing obsolescence

*Description of conclusion:* Industry and IAEA guidance and industry joint groups provide support for establishing an obsolescence management programme. These provide strategies to address important LTO challenges, such as the identification of obsolete items, acquiring replacement parts, and maintaining adequate technical support.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Obsolescence of components can lead to difficulty in acquiring spare parts or difficulty in getting technical support from the original manufacturer, longer procurement lead-times and higher prices. It is important to identify and prioritise obsolescence so that measures can be taken to maintain the reliability of plant equipment.

### <span id="page-267-0"></span>**6.2. Identified areas for enhancement**

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* E2.3-01

*Conclusion title:* Identification of SSCs

*Description of conclusion:* The IAEA requires in *Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Commissioning and Operation (Specific Safety Requirements SSR 2/2 (Rev.1)* [33] setting the scope of SSCs for justification of safe LTO. Potential ageing effects and degradation mechanisms of these SSCs shall be assessed and managed for the intended period of LTO. Ageing effects and degradation mechanisms can be properly assessed only on the level of components and in some cases on the level of the components` parts.

To properly set the scope of SSCs for LTO assessment and properly perform AMR, there must be a good identification system of the SSCs of a nuclear power plant. Identification of SSCs must go to a sufficient level of detail and a plant SSC identification system must provide a unique ID for each SC at the plant. Nuclear power plants must ensure completeness and consistency between databases and lists of SSCs used as a source of information for scope setting.

As can be seen from the results of the IAEA SALTO peer review service, which are analysed in SALTO Highlights 2005-2015 [408], SALTO Highlights 2015-2018 [409] and SALTO Highlights 2018-2022 [39], issues in scope setting of SSCs for ageing management and LTO belong to the most frequent issues and have an impact on all further steps in ageing management.

In some nuclear power plants, unique IDs are not assigned for all SSCs important for the LTO assessment. Cables, pipelines, penetrations and I&C components are among the SSC that are typically poorly identified. It is notable also that particularly cables and pipelines are a very important part of LTO assessment. For cables, cable routing is sometimes not developed or not properly recorded.

A poor identification system of SSCs in many nuclear power plants results in an incomplete or unclear scope of SSCs for LTO assessment. It is difficult to demonstrate completeness of the scope of SSCs, create commodity groups, collect all relevant data, and determine boundaries among professions (e.g. mechanical and electrical parts of pumps and valves, mechanical and civil parts of supports, penetrations, I&C and mechanical part of field measurement). AMR, which is supposed to be a periodic activity, is also a difficult task without comprehensive identification of SSCs.

Development of a database of all SSCs, or a comprehensive system of identification of nuclear power plants SSCs, cable routing and their maintenance is a difficult and long-term task which requires a firm, high-level management decision and significant human resources. But it is an essential step towards justification of safe LTO and demonstration of preparedness for LTO.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Systematic and complete identification of SSCs for LTO assessment is a key step in effective ageing management and is essential to ensure safe operation in the long term.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* In order to ensure that all relevant SSCs are identified, the plant should implement a clear and robust process for scope setting as per SSG-48 [4], considering also SRS-106 [9], Section 3, which can ensure an adequate selection of SSCs to be included in the AMPs, considering safety functions, boundaries, commodity groups. Besides selection on technical grounds, administrative measure (e.g. labelling SCs, customised software platforms for managing, controlled SSC databases) could be used. It is advisable to co-ordinate efforts among countries operating nuclear power plants in order to share practices and experiences in scope setting and management of databases. Training and benchmarking on the identification of SSCs and scope setting for LTO may be carried out.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* E2.3-02

*Conclusion title:* Data management for ageing management and LTO assessment

*Description of conclusion:* The scope of SSCs and consequently AMR typically encompasses tens of thousands of SCs and their parts. To handle this number of SSCs, SCs are usually grouped into commodity groups of similar SCs, with similar internal and external conditions, and similar operational requirements (e.g. valves of the same manufacturer, type, system and working conditions).

For AMR, relevant data from design, manufacturing, commissioning, operation and maintenance history, tests, inspections, and monitoring must be collected for each SC or commodity group in the scope for LTO assessment. AMR for each SC or commodity group results in a demonstration of effective management of ageing effects of the SC or commodity group or in the development of corrective actions to improve the management of ageing effects of the given SC or commodity group. AMPs and other plant programmes to manage ageing are typically developed or enhanced as corrective actions.

AMPs typically request other plant programmes to perform activities i.e. monitoring, testing, inspection and return results to ageing management. Then the status of each SC or commodity group is evaluated using the new results. AMR and ageing management itself are a periodic activity, so this data is collected, evaluated and archived with a high frequency, depending on the significance of the finding. This closed circle of data flow requires good comprehensive data management as this concerns about tens of thousands of SSCs and many inputs for each SC or commodity group.

A good quality list of SSCs for LTO assessment, interconnected with a nuclear power plant master list, is an important starting point. It is essential that all programmes at the plant use the same basic information about SSCs (e.g. ID, manufacturer, type, system, intended functions, safety classification, working conditions, year of installation) which is shared from the plant SSCs' master list. From the long-term perspective and quality assurance point of view, nuclear power plants are encouraged to keep one master list of SSCs.

It is also important to establish clear data flow among the ageing management database (which is interconnected with or part of plant's SSCs master list) and other plant programmes performing field activities important for ageing management.

The structure of the data in the ageing management database is also of key importance. It should allow assessment of the status of each commodity group but also of each SC. It should further allow recording of the history of previous assessments, creating trending of monitored parameters, establishing and checking acceptance criteria, etc.

The existence of multiple databases at a nuclear power plant which are not interconnected with the plant master list (i.e. basic SSCs attributes are not shared throughout the whole nuclear power plant but rather exist separately and redundantly in more than one database) is an issue in many nuclear power plants. Due to constant modification and replacement processes in nuclear power plants, it is extremely difficult to maintain consistency among data in several different databases. Consequently, different plant databases after a few years of separate existence may have inconsistencies with different SSC IDs, manufacturer's types, installation dates or operational and maintenance information. It is then almost impossible to collect all inputs for each SC or commodity group for AMR and later establish routine data workflow for a periodic collection and assessment of inspections, testing and monitoring results in AMPs.

Ageing management requires co-ordination with many other plant programmes which are performing activities like preventive maintenance, inspections, monitoring and testing for ageing management purposes and then return results to the AMPs for periodic assessment. This process involves tens of thousands of SCs and many activities for each of them. It requires clearly established data flow among these programmes. This process is currently an issue in many nuclear power plants. It is sometimes done manually by downloading and uploading required data from one database to another. Data compatibility and quality assurance is then a significant issue.

Another frequent issue in this area is the existence of operational and maintenance history and results of inspections, monitoring and testing only in a paper form (or not completely recorded). It generates significant workload to properly collect and analyse complete information about each SC and commodity group in a scope for LTO.

As can be seen from the results of the IAEA SALTO peer review service, which are analysed in SALTO Highlights 2005-2015 [408], SALTO Highlights 2015-2018 [409] and SALTO Highlights 2018-2022 [39], issues in data management are frequent as separate issues but are also often contributing factor to issues in other areas. This topic is also described in [410].

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Proper data management is essential to ensure for effective ageing management and LTO assessment.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Implement robust process to control data relevant for ageing management, as well as the flow of information between different databases and other IT systems, as per SSG-48 [4], considering also SRS-106 [9], Section 2. Implement coordinated efforts among countries operating nuclear power plants to share practices and experiences in scope setting and management of databases. Conduct trainings and benchmarking on data management relevant for ageing management and LTO.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3. IAEA safety standards for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* E2.3-03

*Conclusion title:* Enhancement of equipment qualification programme

*Description of conclusion:* A comprehensive EQ programme is an essential precondition for successful demonstration of preparedness for safe LTO. Particularly the environmental part of a qualification programme, which contains time limited assumptions, is of key importance for LTO activities. The IAEA established requirements for a comprehensive EQ programme in *Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Design (Specific Safety Requirements SSR 2/1, Vienna, 2016)* [365] and *Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Commissioning and Operation (Specific Safety Requirements SSR 2/2, Vienna, 2016)* [3].

Environmental qualification should establish the qualified life of equipment within which ageing effects would not prevent satisfactory performance of the equipment if a postulated accident were to occur within the established operating period (possibly including LTO). Environmental qualification should demonstrate that, at the end of its qualified life, the equipment will still be capable of performing its intended function(s) under the full range of specified service conditions.

The qualification status of equipment should be properly documented and maintained throughout the plant lifetime. The documentation relating to EQ, which is typically part of the EQ programme, should include:

- a master list of qualified equipment;
- results of temperature monitoring and radiation monitoring in the plant;
- the evaluation report for EQ;
- test reports related to EQ.
- Reports of TLAAs related to EQ (for evaluation for LTO), or reports of another suitable equivalent analysis.

Monitoring of actual environmental conditions should be implemented to get additional information necessary for the assessment of ageing effects on the equipment in its actual operating environment.

The qualified life of equipment should be reassessed during its lifetime, considering the progress in the knowledge and understanding of degradation mechanisms and the actual operating environment of the equipment. If the qualified life is to be increased, a thorough safety demonstration should be provided by the operating organisation.

The current situation in many nuclear power plants is very different from this status. Most of the plants were designed and manufactured as seismically and environmentally qualified but many of them do not have access to the qualification documentation (qualification files for qualified equipment containing normal and accident conditions, pre-ageing parameters, test procedures, test parameters and results).

A master list of qualified equipment is not always available at the plant. The identification system of qualified equipment is sometimes incomplete. Equipment like I&C components, cables and penetrations frequently do not have their own unique IDs. Cable routing of qualified cables is sometimes not developed which does not allow determining the worst operating and accident conditions for each qualified cable. Also qualified life is not always determined for qualified equipment.

During nuclear power plant operation, it is important to maintain the qualified status of qualified equipment. Monitoring of environmental conditions of qualified equipment (like replacement of seals, rubber parts, and lubricants) are not always systematically performed with the requested periodicity by the maintenance programme and confirmation is not recorded within the EQ programme. Operational temperatures, doses, and other parameters relevant to ageing are not always monitored for qualified SCs. "Hotspot" areas, where real operational conditions can exceed tests conditions, are not always identified for qualified SCs.

Qualified life should be revalidated prior to its exceedance. It is a complex and expensive task which can be properly performed only if a comprehensive EQ programme is fully implemented. Having a comprehensive qualification programme in place, the margins between qualification pre-ageing and test parameters and real operating parameters can be used for justification of extended qualified life of qualified equipment. Also margins between qualification test accident conditions and calculated design accident conditions can be used for the same purpose.

Without a comprehensive qualification programme, the only solution to demonstrate fulfilment of the intended function of qualified equipment during the period of LTO is replacement or refurbishment of this equipment. This solution is extremely expensive and requires extended outages connected with a loss of production for a significant period and may have a significant cost in terms of collective dose.

As can be seen from the results of the IAEA SALTO peer review service, which are analysed in SALTO Highlights 2005-2015 [408], SALTO Highlights 2015-2018 [409] and SALTO Highlights 2018-2022 [39], issues in EQ and particularly environmental qualification belong to the most frequent issues. This topic is also described in [410].

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* SSCs were designed and for 30 or 40 years. Then the qualified life was for most of the SSCs successfully extended up to 60 years of operation. Further extension of qualified life up to 80 years will be very challenging for many SSCs. To avoid massive replacement of qualified SSCs, it will be necessary to have comprehensive qualification programme implemented to provide for this step.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* To ensure the capability of the SSCs to fulfil their intended function during the postulated accident, the operators should implement a comprehensive EQ programme covering the full intended period of operation.

A comprehensive qualification programme consists of many steps. They are basically described in SSG-69 [12]. The main activities necessary for re-assessment of the qualified life for LTO beyond 60 years to preserve qualification and effectiveness of the EQ programme are:

- Environmental monitoring: Compare real measured values with the values for which the equipment was qualified.
- Equipment CM: Check the actual equipment condition and evaluate it against the prediction made by initial qualification.
- Periodic surveillance and maintenance: Equipment shall be installed and operated in accordance with prescribed rules. Equipment needs to be checked against real installation, operation and performed maintenance.
- Supply chain: Not all the equipment will be able to operate beyond 60 years without spare parts. Sealing and gaskets are typical representatives of parts with limited operation time.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.3 IAEA safety standards LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* E2.3-04

*Conclusion title:* Development of a methodology to assess the effectiveness of AMPs in a nuclear power plant

*Description of conclusion:* Keeping AMPs alive, based on the feedback from implementation, is one of the most important key factors for an effective programme during extended LTO periods.

Furthermore, as shown in international guides and standards developed by the IAEA (SSG-48 [4], SRS-82 (Rev.2) [7], and SRS-106 [9]), the implementation of AMPs is necessary to be evaluated, but currently, there is no methodology established defining which information is relevant and describing how to properly collect all these aspects to address this need.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* By using this methodology, nuclear power plants could be able to obtain qualitative and quantitative information to assess the effectiveness of any AMP and develop a way to keep the programme alive based on the conclusions of the implementation report.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* It is necessary to develop a reliable methodology for collecting the most important information related to the implementation of an AMP such as: possible changes in the programme scope, results of activities collected by the nuclear power plants' maintenance and other existing programmes (including events and degradations), frequency with which these activities have been carried out and their alignment with international recommendations, the need for any corrective action, and the assessment of the OPEX. All this information should be gathered and analysed periodically within a single document for each AMP to serve as a tool to evaluate performance indicators (both qualitative and quantitative) that determine the effectiveness of AMPs over the implementation period. This analysis will make it possible to derive conclusions about how AMPs are working and will allow the definition of action plans to improve them, if necessary, based on effectiveness measurement of the results obtained.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 2.5. Typical national regulatory frameworks to support for LTO beyond 60 years

*Conclusion number:* E2.5-01

*Conclusion title:* Clarity of regulatory authority expectations

*Description of conclusion:* Many countries operating nuclear power plants facing LTO or even with nuclear power plants already in LTO, particularly those with a smaller fleet of nuclear power plants and smaller regulatory authority, have not yet developed a comprehensive set of national regulations for preparation for safe LTO. They typically rely on IAEA safety standards and sometimes also on the US NRC regulatory framework or the regulatory framework from the designer's country as a practical reference. Poor communication between operator and regulator regarding expectations for safe LTO is also frequently observed. Lack in clarity of expectations for safe LTO has been observed in ten out of 27 SALTO peer review missions in last analysed period of 2015 to 2022 [409], [39]. Lack in clarity of expectations for safe LTO can lead to wrong assumptions of operators regarding preparation for and demonstration of safe LTO and consequently to gaps in preparation for safe LTO.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Unclear regulatory authority expectations led in many countries to difficulties and delays in licensing renewal.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Co-ordinated effort among regulatory authorities of countries operating nuclear power plants is necessary to develop clear regulatory expectations and share experience on regulatory oversight practices. Recent guidance for regulatory oversight specific for ageing management and LTO was issued (SRS-109 [10] and WENRA Safety Reference Levels [369]) and could be a useful tool for regulatory authorities to set a clear set of national regulations for preparation for safe LTO. Training activities could be developed for the regulatory authorities of member states who are facing LTO projects for the first time. Activities such as international workshops, experience sharing groups, regional forums or technology-oriented groups can be used for harmonising regulatory practices. As an example, the IAEA IGALL project includes a specific working group (WG4) for sharing experience on regulatory practices. Workshops and trainings can be used for disseminating information and ensuring early involvement of regulators in the LTO process.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 3.4 Supply chain issues

*Conclusion number:* E3.4-01

*Conclusion title:* Supply chain strategic management and long-term planning

*Description of conclusion:* Major equipment replacement and the refurbishment of integral components to LTO of 60+ years, rely on a limited supply chain that involves specialised resources such as high-capacity cranes, advanced robotics and a skilled workforce. However, the availability of such resources is constrained due to the niche nature of the nuclear sector, and the necessary investments in equipment, training and workforce development are considerable.

Therefore, the supply chain for these resources requires strategic management and longterm planning to ensure their availability when required. This involves fostering partnerships with suppliers, investing in training and development to build a skilled workforce, and promoting research and development into advanced robotics and other technologies relevant to equipment replacement and refurbishment.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* As nuclear power plants operate beyond 60 years, the need for very specialised (niche) resources becomes increasingly critical to ensure safe and economical operations. Therefore, a sustainable and resilient supply chain needs to be maintained to support the extended LTO of nuclear power plants.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Each nuclear power plant needs to assess the availability of its original equipment suppliers and their manufacturing and provide new solutions, when necessary, as relevant to LTO. This involves several generic key recommendations for the sector, to be used individually, such as:

- 1. collaborative industry wide forecasting and foresight of LTO refurbishment needs and identification of futures issues in manufacturing or suppliers (corporate decision-making factors such as ESG, circular economy, and sustainable manufacturing need to consider the evolving societal and environmental standards);
- 2. investing in modern technologies and upgrade programmes (adopting new enhanced equipment inspection, monitoring and assessment tools: "digital twin" technology, additive manufacturing and artificial intelligence) to have alternative products when needed;
- 3. leveraging the resurgence of the nuclear industry/nuclear supply chain (using the modern supply chain created for new nuclear builds to address older nuclear power plants' needs);

4. adopting proven, high-quality industrial products (e.g. extending the commercial grade dedication approach, successfully applied in some countries, in safety-critical applications).

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 3.5 Human resources, knowledge and competence management

*Conclusion number:* E3.5-01

*Conclusion title:* Human resources strategy and workforce planning for LTO

*Description of conclusion:* As mentioned in Section 3.5, independent IAEA peer reviews over the past decades have identified that the lack of long-term HR strategy and inadequate workforce planning for the whole period of LTO remain common problems in many operating organisations. Having a long-term HR strategy is critical because it determines how HR processes (workforce planning, training and development, succession, and talent management, etc.) are aligned with the LTO goals. It is crucial to collaborate with policymakers to ensure that universities and other educational organisations and institutions have sufficient facilities and student slots. This will help develop a pool of individuals with the necessary skills and competence to support the nuclear power plants' talent pipeline for a skilled workforce required for LTO.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* A long-term HR strategy ensures that all HR processes, such as workforce planning, training and development, and succession management, are aligned with the goals of LTO. This alignment is essential for maintaining operational efficiency and safety over extended periods. Effective workforce planning and development are critical for ensuring that there are enough skilled personnel. This is particularly important in the nuclear industry, where specialised knowledge and skill are required for the whole period of operation.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* To ensure the implementation of a safe and efficient LTO programme, the operators should develop a long-term HR strategy including a detailed workforce plan covering the full intended period of operation. The IAEA has multiple ongoing and future programmes, tools and guidance to further enhance the area of human resources and workforce planning. More emphasis should be focused on the LTO aspect.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 3.5 Human resources, knowledge and competence management

*Conclusion number:* E3.5-02

*Conclusion title:* Knowledge and competence management and its important role in LTO

*Description of conclusion:* As discussed in Section 3.5 and based on the observations from SALTO reviews performed by the IAEA, maintaining the knowledge and competence in the organisations of the nuclear industry and nuclear regulatory bodies will soon become one of the sector's most serious problems. The loss of workers possessing critical operational knowledge could become a significant internal threat to safe and reliable operation, especially when considering long-term operation beyond 60 years. Most operating organisations around the world can demonstrate the implementation of various knowledge management tools. The problem is that the concept of knowledge management rarely includes the whole cycle of people, processes and technology and is rarely fully integrated and embedded in the management system. As a result, this leads to errors in long-term resource planning and an increased risk of loss of critical knowledge.

Another important factor of the successful implementation of LTO programmes is the need for systematic assessment and mapping of personnel competencies. This process helps identify gaps in knowledge and skills, allowing for more efficient training planning. Well established competence management also helps to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements, improves the plant operation efficiency, and ensures that staff are prepared to handle potential emergency risks. During the SALTO missions conducted by the IAEA it was observed that the regular and systematic assessment of competencies is not performed adequately.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Fully implemented and integrated knowledge and competence management represents one of the most significant prerequisites for successful LTO. The transfer of critical nuclear knowledge between old and new generations, well established sharing platforms, systematic assessment of competence, succession programmes and communities of practice, coaching and mentoring are among a number of efficient tools supporting LTO. However, a crucial factor is the establishment of a robust organisation and management strategy and policy that effectively incorporates knowledge management as an important management component.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* To ensure the implementation of a safe and efficient LTO programme, it is recommended that the operators integrate the guidance on knowledge and competence management into their own organisational standards. The IAEA support (such as guidance, knowledge management assist visits, knowledge management schools, trainings etc.) needs to be focused on long-term aspects, beyond 60 years. Additionally, the establishment of extended collaborative networks and communities of practice in this area is also suggested.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-01

*Conclusion title:* Enhance research to maintain RPV fluence within the embrittlement trend curves limits

*Description of conclusion:* During LTO the RPV will receive neutron fluence greater than or equal to 6 x 1019 n/cm2 during the 60-80 calendar year period, and improved embrittlement trend curves are needed. This issue can be researched by gathering higher fluence data from plant surveillance capsule programmes, or by mitigating the fluence level using flux decreasing techniques.

Embrittlement projections will have to cover fluence up to 8 x 1019 n/cm² to meet the objective of LTO beyond 60 years (up to 80 years). The embrittlement trend curve needs to be consolidated at such fluence through the analysis of the most irradiated samples from the irradiation surveillance programme. An adaptation of the sample retrieving calendar can be necessary to gather higher fluence data from plant capsules surveillance programmes to cover the fluence projection at 80 years.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Many plants around the world will exceed this fluence threshold at the end of life, beyond 60 years of operation. Thus, it is of utmost importance to have accurately calculated RPV embrittlement, with minimal calculational uncertainties, or a different approach, an enhancement in research to limit the fluence level by using the latest generation of shielding to minimise the core leakage.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Generation of low-flux high fluence data relevant for European nuclear power plants - Integrated surveillance programmes should be established in Europe like EPRI CRVSP (MRP-326/rev.1) [69], PSSP Capsule Fabrication Report (MRP-412) [70] in the United States, to generate the required low-flux high fluence data relevant for European nuclear power plants.

A way to limit the fluence level is to use flux reduction techniques. Today's standard is low leakage core loading, but there are also more potent techniques available. These are the application of shielding rod assemblies, applied in numerous units already. It offers in its latest generation shielding factors up to seven. Also, the usage of shielding pads or plates outside the core was already successfully applied (examples: Kori Unit 1, Joseph M. Farley Unit 1 and 2) and could be combined with shielding rods. For example, France implements hafnium rods inside the core [411]. The effectiveness of flux reduction measures is a question of starting the implementation as early as possible. Licensees should be encouraged to implement such measures proactively.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-02

*Conclusion title:* Use of master curve direct fracture toughness technology

*Description of conclusion:* The use of master curve technology is one avenue to reduce conservatism in evaluating RPV toughness, which is currently mainly calculated using CVN based approaches.

The results of surveillance capsule testing are used for reactor vessel embrittlement projections to determine the increase in the reference transition temperature (RTNDT) which is used to index the reference FT curves as specified in the applicable national regulation. Alternatively, the master curve approach is used to monitor FT in RPVs as a complement to the existing regulatory surveillance programme, to demonstrate the conservatism of the regulatory approach. Efforts are needed to incorporate such methodologies in the corpus of accepted methods to describe more precisely the embrittlement of RPV low-alloy steels.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* At higher fluence levels, and when extending operating time, there is a possibility that plants will not be able to meet RPV FT regulations using traditional means (Charpy-based technology). The master curve approach may provide a more accurate evaluation of RPV beltline toughness than the Charpy-based approach.

The main ageing mechanism of RPV from a lifetime point of view is the embrittlement of the ferritic steel core zone (core shells and their joining welds) due to irradiation. Embrittlement affects the strength of the material with respect to the fast fracture risk, which is the design-basis damage mode in the core zone. Assessing precisely the strength of the aged material without conservatism is of the utmost importance in the context of LTO beyond 60 years.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* EPRI and other institutes in Europe and Japan have multiple ongoing or future projects to further enhance and justify the use of master curve technology including:

- development of CC N-830-2 (MRP-418, Revision 2) for direct use of master curve technologies in support of evaluations using ASME Section XI Appendices A, G and E (N-830-1 is approved for Appendices A and G, work is ongoing to revise the code case for Appendix E);
- development of CC N-914 (MRP-462, Revision 1) for methods to account for embrittlement in ASME Section XI calculations, including those involving master curve;

- development of a ΔT<sup>0</sup> ETC to support CC N-914 with a direct ETC for irradiated master curve T0 determination (ongoing programme);
- codification of the master curve approach in RCC-M [385] or RSE-M code [387];
- development ofstrategies regarding the potential lack of specimens (see AFE E4.2- 01). Usage of mini-CT-specimen is one possibility. Measures are needed to increase acceptance. An important up-to-date project is the EU funded FRACTESUS.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-03

*Conclusion title:* Advanced mechanical assessment methods – local versus global approach to brittle fracture assessment

*Description of conclusion:* The main degradation mechanism of the RPV from a lifetime point of view is the embrittlement of the ferritic steel core zone (core shells and their joining welds) due to irradiation. Embrittlement affects the strength of the material with respect to the brittle fracture risk. The mechanical assessment of the brittle fracture risk is usually based on conservative methodologies such as the global approach of fracture. Compared to the global approach currently in use, the local approach provides a more precise description of loading variables which govern the fracture behaviour of RPV, such as local plasticity effects at crack tips (constraint effects, such as in case of small defects) and scale effects. In France, the local approach of brittle fracture assessment uses the Beremin model [412]*,* [413]*.*

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* In addition to the mitigation strategy on nuclear power plant management such as neutron flux control for the RPV, several methodological levers are needed to reduce the conservatism of brittle fracture analyses and to secure the demonstration of LTO beyond 60 years. The local approach provides a more precise description of the brittle fracture risk and therefore its implementation would be beneficial to secure LTO beyond 60 years.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Codification of local methods of brittle fracture assessment such as the Beremin model or other similar models in order to have industrial methods.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-04

*Conclusion title:* Advanced mechanical assessment methods – warm pre-stress

*Description of conclusion:* The main ageing mechanism of the RPV from a lifetime point of view is the embrittlement of the ferritic steel core zone (core shells and their joining welds) due to irradiation. Embrittlement affects the strength of the material with respect to the fast fracture risk. The mechanical assessment of the fast fracture risk is usually based on conservative methodologies. Specifically, current methodologies in several countries do not consider the beneficial effect of the WPS on the actual toughness of the material despite the physical knowledge acquired through several R&D projects. Efforts are still needed to integrate relevant methodologies considering this phenomenon in the corpus of accepted methods.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* In addition to the mitigation strategy on nuclear power plant management such as neutron flux control for the RPV, several methodological *Proposals for dispositioning:* Integrating the WPS in the corpus of accepted methods may provide additional safety margins versus the conventional approach in the analysis of PTS transients and therefore promote LTO beyond 60 years.

Important up-to-date projects are the EU funded APAL and the WPS benchmark by WGIAGE. Advances in thermohydraulic methods bring new challenges in the application of the WPS effect. K-T curves are often less "smooth" and not strictly, monotonously decreasing after the global maximum.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-05

*Conclusion title:* Effectiveness of annealing of the RPV and re-irradiation behaviour of the materials

*Description of conclusion:* For some of the vessels, the irradiation-induced changes of material properties, of welds with high Ni+Mn content, are expected to be higher than predicted by the national regulations. Annealing of the beltline of the vessel is an effective mitigating measure to recover the FT of these materials. This was proven by a pilot application in Balakovo 1 Nuclear Power Plant.

Thermal annealing could be (again) an issue for the RPVs in reactors designs besides VVERs. Alternatively to the dry annealing, wet annealing can be applied, which means heating up the RPV to the maximum design temperature. It only provides a partial recovery of 30 to 40%, but is much easier to apply. The success and material properties would have to be confirmed by surveillance specimen.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Eventually, for some of the vessel materials with an unfavourable chemical composition the integrity of the RPV during PTS transients can no longer be proven until the end of the foreseen plant lifetime. Therefore, some mitigating measures will have to be taken.

#### *Proposals for dispositioning:*

- The effectiveness of vessel annealing as one of these measures should be investigated in more detail before its industrial application, i.e. the boundary conditions in terms of time at temperature, the expected recovery of FT, the reirradiation behaviour of the materials.
- A supplemental surveillance programme to follow up the FT and strength properties of the vessel materials after annealing until the end of the foreseen plant lifetime should be developed.
- The application of the master curve or similar procedures for direct determination of FT should be encouraged and supported by corresponding regulatory research and regulations.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-06

*Conclusion title:* Fracture toughness and strength data of RPV materials after long-time exposure to operating temperatures

*Description of conclusion:* So far, FT data after long-time exposure to operating temperatures are very scarce. Besides, physical understanding of the embrittlement mechanisms of thermal ageing could improve. Therefore, it could be useful to develop a more systematic approach to get more data after long-term thermal exposure and to gain a better understanding of the ageing mechanisms depending on the chemical composition and microstructure of the materials.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* While it appears that for many RPV materials thermal ageing is not significant and may be neglected for the integrity analyses of the vessel, there are some experimental results that show a significant embrittling effect after thermal exposure for much less than 40 years.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Beside mechanical testing, microstructural investigations should also be undertaken. Harvesting materials after long-term operation at a hot leg temperature or slightly higher (i.e. the pressuriser) might be the most promising way to get appropriate materials for these investigations. It needs to be considered that although temperatures are slightly higher for the pressuriser than for the RPV, it may make a big difference in terms of significance of thermal ageing.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel, 4.5 Safety Class 1 piping *Conclusion number:* E4.2-07

*Conclusion title:* Effect of long-term thermal ageing on the properties of nickel-based DMW

*Description of conclusion:* While all RPVs are made of ferritic low-alloy steel, the connected piping of many PWR designs is austenitic and most penetrations of the vessel closure head and vessel bottom are made of nickel-based alloys. Most of these piping and all these penetrations are welded to the vessel by nickel-based alloys that are susceptible to PWSCC of PWRs. Furthermore, these alloys tend to long range ordering after long-term thermal exposure that is accompanied by increased hardness and may decrease their toughness and increase their susceptibility to PWSCC. These effects may also apply to newer alloys such as alloy 690 or alloy 52 M that are less susceptible to SCC. However, there is still a lack of data regarding the long-term behaviour of such alloys.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Different aspects are important for LTO: An increased susceptibility to PWSCC may lead to an increasing number of cracks and leakages of the DMW that will have to be detected as early as possible by enhanced ISI. A higher probability of cracking eventually accompanied by decreasing toughness would have consequences for the reliability of DMW in general. The integrity analyses for the DMW of the MCLs to the RPV nozzles are questioned, if leak before break behaviour is claimed for these lines.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Therefore, the effect of long-term thermal ageing on the mechanical properties of DMW and their susceptibility to PWSCC should be investigated.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-08

*Conclusion title:* Improving non-destructive examination techniques of DMW

*Description of conclusion:* In some cases, there could be a lack of reliability in detecting and sizing flaws in DMW, especially in complicated geometries and in high radiation areas like RPV penetration welds. This concerns austenitic as well as nickel-based weld materials.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* The susceptibility of nickel-based alloys to PWSCC and austenitic welds to SCC in BWR coolant is well known. Regarding the long incubation times and eventually an increasing susceptibility to SCC with ageing (see E.4.2.2.3-01) an increasing probability of cracking can be expected during LTO. The likelihood of cracking is raised at welding repair spots at the inner surface causing disadvantageous residual stress profiles. As these repair spots are not always documented, it would help to focus on recurrent inspections if these spots could be identified by a nondestructive methodology.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Therefore, it appears that it could be useful to further enhance the ISI of DMW welds to timely detect any cracks, thus avoiding large cracks, leakage and failure of these welds. Furthermore, a nondestructive methodology should be developed to identify undocumented welding repair spots.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 4.2 Reactor pressure vessel/4.3 Reactor vessel internals/4.5 Safety Class 1 piping

*Conclusion number:* E4.2-09

*Conclusion title:* Fatigue lifetime assessment of welds with incomplete penetration (and other structural areas with complicated geometry)

*Description of the conclusion:* The fatigue life assessment should be performed for all significantly fatigue-loaded structural parts of the RPV, regardless of the complexity of the area being assessed for LTO beyond 60 years. An analysis based on a linear elastic approach and general fatigue life curves is not appropriate to provide the required fatigue life.
