Examples of design basis documentation reconstitution projects can be Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant in Sweden, Dukovany and Temelin Nuclear Power Plants in Czechia, Paks Nuclear Power Plant in Hungary and Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant in Bulgaria. Many other nuclear power plants are currently facing this challenge, for e.g. Armenian Nuclear Power Plant in Armenia, Atucha Nuclear Power Plant in Argentina, Angra Nuclear Power Plant in Brazil, and Koeberg Nuclear Power Plant in South Africa.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* With operating nuclear power plants ageing physically and affected by obsolescence, and with increasing requirements of the latest codes, standards and regulations, more SSCs important to safety will need to be modernised, refurbished or replaced. Up to date DBD is an important precondition for effective modification/ configuration management as well as a source of TLAAs which needs to be revalidated, to demonstrate safe LTO.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Each nuclear power plant needs to assess the availability of its original design basis documentation as it pertains to LTO. This involves several key actions:

- Inventory and assessment: Conduct a thorough inventory assessment of existing documentation to identify gaps and assess the current state of records.
- Digitisation and preservation: Digitise physical documents to ensure they are preserved and easily accessible. This also helps in protecting the documents from physical degradation.
- Centralised repository: If not already in place, establish a centralised digital repository where all design basis documents are stored. This ensures that all relevant personnel have access to the necessary documentation.
- Regular audits and updates: Implement a schedule for regular audits and updates of the documentation to ensure it remains current and accurate.
- Training and awareness: Train staff in the importance of maintaining and updating design basis documentation. This includes understanding how to properly store and retrieve design documents.
- Collaboration with regulatory bodies: Work closely with regulatory bodies to ensure compliance with all relevant standards and guidelines. This can also help in obtaining guidance on best practices for documentation management.

By taking these high-level steps, nuclear power plants can improve the availability and reliability of their original design basis documentation, ensuring it supports ongoing operations and regulatory compliance. For additional information on this issue and ways to address it, IAEA-TECDOC-2018 [421] can provide additional details.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.2. Development of codes, standards and regulations

*Conclusion number:* E5.2-01

*Conclusion title:* Harmonisation of nuclear codes, standards and regulations for LTO

*Description of conclusion:* Regarding design and construction codes, the ASME B&PV Code Section III has often been used as a reference or basis for the other international design and construction codes, with possible differences among them in terms of technical provisions and arrangements, while keeping common objectives and principles. However, the methodologies for the assessment of components for LTO may vary from country to country. For instance, some countries can use only deterministic methodology, but some countries can use probabilistic methodology. This comes from the difference of regulatory requirements of each country. On top of a harmonisation effort of the international regulatory requirements for LTO, the international industry should work together to develop more sophisticated methods and implement them in the appropriate codes & standards in a consistent, if not identical, way.

There should be a distinction between requirements coming from technical codes, like ASME Sections III/XI and RCC-M/RSE-M, and those coming from regulators. It seems it is more difficult to harmonise regulatory requirements between different countries than technical codes. The regulatory framework has often grown historically over a long period of time and considers country-specific constraints (political, economic, geographic/geological, cultural, etc.).

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Sophisticated methods to evaluate the components for LTO need to be developed. To achieve this, the co-operation at the international regulatory level is necessary.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* The international regulatory side should develop the harmonised requirements to evaluate the components for LTO. International industry also needs to co-operate to develop sophisticated methods and codes. Industry should seek regulatory approval of new methods and co-operate with the regulators to obtain a position in an amount of time that is compatible with the industrial needs.

Different working groups/SDOs should collaborate to harmonise the technical codes in a similar manner as the activities for new reactors. Such working groups include international SDO forums (e.g. SDO Convergence Board for mechanical components, ASME International Working Groups, CEN/WS 64 on AFCEN codes) and international initiatives addressing, among others, the harmonisation of codes and standards (e.g. WNA CORDEL, NEA MDEP, IAEA NHSI). Regulators should participate in such working groups.

Stronger harmonisation of regulatory requirements needs clear international guidelines, for e.g. in a manner comparable to an IAEA safety guide or the WENRA reference levels.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.3 Technological obsolescence

*Conclusion number:* E5.3-01

*Conclusion title:* Long lead time to procure obsolete spare parts

*Description of conclusion:* Understanding of the need for components and spare parts must be aligned with the lead time to acquire them from the market. Typically, the nuclear power plants' detailed planning for components and spare parts needed are handled in a 12- or 18 month cycle. These time frames are based on the nuclear supply chain decades ago, when the plants were constructed. Many suppliers invested in nuclear quality management and assurance programmes. Manufacturers were domestic and the spare and replacement items being ordered were for current equipment and technologies, some still in production. The current nuclear supply chain is quite different. Manufacturers are horizontally integrated, often sourcing raw materials and parts that comprise their equipment from locations all over the world. Fewer suppliers have invested in nuclear quality management and assurance programs, and the spare and replacement items being ordered are for equipment that is no longer in production, and increasingly obsolete. The current supply chain is also impacted by geopolitical issues, efforts to reduce toxic substances, the availability of raw materials, and competition from entities building data centres and other types of infrastructure improvements. Due to increasingly long and dynamic procedures to purchase items necessary to support operations and maintenance, detailed planning for at least 24 months is needed to develop obsolescence solutions.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Lead times and obsolescence are likely to increase with time. Timely handling of obsolescence will be important to maintain availability at the plant and reliable safe operation of systems, structures and components with safety impact.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* EPRI 3002023779, "Effective Refuelling Outage Preparation and Execution Guidance\_ Update to 1022952" [422] was published in 2022. This report suggests planning intervals consistent with the 12-18 month cycles mentioned above. Recent discussions at EPRI have suggested an earlier start, perhaps 24 months or more in advance, to minimise risk of unavailability. More discussion on advance identification of long-lead time items, and perhaps and update to the existing EPRI guidance may help industry achieve advances in a suitable proactive approach for obsolete spare parts management. Long-term supply contracts and bridging strategies must be in place, as well as a better collaboration with industry.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.3 Technological obsolescence

*Conclusion number:* E5.3-02

*Conclusion title:* Introduce alternative replacement strategically

*Description of conclusion:* To be in control of how and when introducing alternative replacements opens the opportunity to use operational experience that will have a positive impact on plant performance and equipment reliability.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* Common cause failures (CCFs) could affect many obsolete components at the same time, with potential severe impacts on redundancy and the safety of critical systems. However, introducing alternative replacements without taking into consideration the OPEX of different utilities could be an equally risky solution.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Establish and follow the key performance indicators due to the obsolescence programme to verify the programme efficiency. CCF risks should be minimised by using best practices for introducing alternative replacements.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.3 Technological obsolescence

*Conclusion number:* E-5.3-03

*Conclusion title:* Timely and gradual implementation of alternative replacements save O&M costs

*Description of conclusion:* On a component level, most of the obsolescence issues can be solved on a rather small budget because of efficient solution methods.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years:* The importance given to O&M cost is low compared to the life extension actions that must performed depending on lifetime for qualification and other major tasks, often identified in the ageing management programme. However, actions initiated by the obsolescence management programme must be performed in a timely manner to avoid postponed maintenance activities and a large backlog of obsolete items.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Establish and follow the key performance indicators due to the obsolescence programme to verify the programme efficiency.

*Relevant sub-section of the report:* 5.3 Technological obsolescence

*Conclusion number:* E5.3-04

*Conclusion title:* Industry and regulators to develop common working process and acceptance criteria

*Description of conclusion:* If both the regulators and nuclear power plants adopt a common approach due to COTS and commercial grade dedication, there will be more solutions available on the market to use as alternative replacements. This can be achieved by more international co-operation and the development of common working processes and understanding.

*Importance for LTO beyond 60 years*: This is important to solve obsolescence issues. A wider selection of possible solutions has the potential to increase the equipment reliability.

*Proposals for dispositioning:* Implement working processes as described in EPRI 3002002982, "Plant Engineering: Guideline for the Acceptance of Commercial-Grade Items in Nuclear Safety-Related Applications", [351].

### <span id="page-308-0"></span>**6.3. Summary of conclusions**

The main objective of this report is to identify AFEs which need to be resolved to ensure safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years, as described in Sub-section 6.2. It should be noticed that no technical issue of a generic nature linked to the effects of ageing has been identified as critical and liable to involve the systematic shutdown of nuclear power plants after 60 years of operation. The AFEs which need to be addressed in the frame of research activities aim at improving the knowledge of ageing phenomena and the performance of engineering methodologies for safe LTO beyond 60 years.

In addition to the AFEs, some important APAs were also identified and described in Subsection 6.1. The main objective of APAs is to provide the technical audience with information and advice on what is available, documented and can be used as a knowledge basis for assessment, justification and preparation for safe LTO beyond 60 years. APAs refer to previous sections of this report and to relevant reference documentation. A list of APAs should not be seen as a complete list of all areas/topics which are properly addressed for LTO beyond 60 years in all countries operating nuclear power plants as there are many other properly addressed areas/topics which can be more country or nuclear power plant specific.

### *6.3.1. Summary of areas properly addressed*

This report identifies 16 APAs. After discussion among the task team members, it was decided that the following three APAs are of the highest importance:

- Conclusion number A2.3-01, IAEA Guidance for LTO beyond 60 years.
  - The IAEA safety standards represent the fundamental guidance for most of the IAEA member states for demonstration of preparedness for LTO. They are applicable for the whole period of nuclear power plant operation, including LTO beyond 60 years. The IAEA safety standards are regularly updated to include the latest experience of the IAEA member states and reflect the recommended approach to ageing management and preparation for safe LTO, including LTO beyond 60 years.
- Conclusion number A2.3-02, Sharing operating feedback and proven practices in ageing management.
  - The IAEA IGALL programme has an essential role in collecting, monitoring and sharing the latest proven practices in ageing management. The IGALL programme maintains a continuously updated database of known ageing effects and degradation mechanisms and proven AMPs and TLAAs to manage them. With the increasing age of operating nuclear power plants, the probability of adverse ageing effects on SSCs also increases. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that the latest operating feedback and proven practices in ageing management are shared among all operating nuclear power plants.

• Conclusion number A2.5-01, Approaches to LTO Justification.

There are proven approaches to justify safe LTO based on IAEA safety standards that are applicable also for operations beyond 60 years. The various national approaches can be grouped into two main categories:

- the PSR-based approach, typically used in countries with unlimited or continuing licences (with a PSR for LTO being typically more rigorous, with a greater focus on ageing aspects and covering the whole intended period of LTO);
- the licence renewal-based approach, typically used in countries with a limited licence (typically for 30 or 40 years) and which usually allows 20 years of licence extension.

In addition to the above three APAs selected by the task team members, it is important to note that the report mentions several other properly addressed topics in the fields of scientific knowledge, assessment methods and maintenance technologies (inspection and diagnosis techniques, repair, refurbishment, mitigation and replacement solutions). For example, as concluded in AFE E4.5-09, the benefit and the efficiency of several mitigation solutions such as MSIP and FSWOL for piping has been proven, and the application of such methods could be done in more nuclear power plants and in a more proactive manner.

### *6.3.2. Summary of areas for enhancement*

This report identifies 68 AFEs. After discussion among the task team members, it was decided that the following 15 AFEs are of the highest importance:

• Conclusion number E2.3-03, Enhancement of equipment qualification programme.

Many SSCs of the nuclear power plants were designed and manufactured as seismically and environmentally qualified, typically for 30 or 40 years. Then the qualified life for most of the SSCs was successfully extended to 60 years of operation; further extensions of qualified life up to 80 years can be challenging for many SSCs. Qualified life should be revalidated prior to its exceedance, which is a complex and expensive task that can be properly performed only if a comprehensive EQ programme is fully implemented.

Without a comprehensive qualification programme, the only solution to demonstrate fulfilment of the intended function of qualified equipment during the period of LTO is replacement or refurbishment of this equipment, which can cause extended outages and significant costs.

• Conclusion number: E2.5-01, Clarity of regulatory authority expectations.

Many countries operating nuclear power plants facing LTO, particularly those with a smaller number of nuclear power plants and a smaller regulatory authority, have not yet developed a comprehensive set of national regulations for the preparation for safe LTO. They typically rely on IAEA safety standards and sometimes also on the US NRC regulatory framework or the regulatory framework from the designer's country as a practical reference. Lack of clarity of the expectations for safe LTO has been observed in ten out of 27 SALTO peer review missions the in last analysed period of 2015 to 2022 [409], [39].

Participation of regulatory authorities in sharing experience on LTO regulatory oversight practices (such as IGALL WG4), use of international guidance (such as IAEA SRS-109 [10] and WENRA Safety Reference Levels [369]), training activities, international workshops, regional forums and co-ordinated effort among regulatory authorities to develop clear regulatory expectations could improve clarity of regulatory authorities' expectations for safe LTO.

• Conclusion number E3.4-01, Supply chain strategic management and long-term planning.

Maintenance of nuclear power plant SSCs and major equipment replacement and refurbishment relies on a limited supply chain. The need for very specialised (niche) resources becomes increasingly critical to ensure safe and economical operations. Therefore, a sustainable and resilient supply chain needs to be maintained to support the extended LTO of nuclear power plants.

The supply chain for these resources requires strategic management and long-term planning to ensure their availability, when required. This involves fostering partnerships with suppliers, investing in training and development to build a skilled workforce, and promoting research and development into advanced robotics and other technologies relevant to equipment replacement and refurbishment.

• Conclusion number E3.5-02, Knowledge and competence management and its important role in LTO.

The concept of knowledge management is rarely fully integrated and embedded in the management system, leading to errors in long-term resource planning and an increased risk of loss of the critical knowledge. A crucial factor of successful implementation of LTO programme is the establishment of a management strategy and policy that effectively incorporates knowledge management as an important management component.

Another important factor is the need of systematic assessment and mapping of personnel competencies. This process helps identifying gaps in knowledge and skills, allowing for more efficient training planning. Well-established competence management ensures compliance with regulatory requirements, improves the plant operation efficiency, and ensures that staff are prepared to handle potential emergency risks.

• Conclusion number E4.2-02, Use of master curve direct fracture toughness technology.

At higher fluence levels and extended operating time, there is a possibility that nuclear power plants might not be able to meet RPV FT requirements using traditional means (Charpy-based technology). The master curve approach may provide a more accurate evaluation of RPV beltline toughness than the Charpybased approach and allow licensees to justify safe continued operation for 60 years and beyond.

Efforts are needed to describe more precisely the embrittlement of RPV low-alloy steels and incorporate such methodologies as the master curve approach in the corpus of accepted methods.

• Conclusion number E4.2-03, Advanced mechanical assessment methods – local versus global approach to brittle fracture assessment.

The main degradation mechanism of the RPV from a lifetime point of view is the embrittlement of the ferritic steel core zone (core shells and their joining welds) due to irradiation. Embrittlement affects the strength of the material with respect to the brittle fracture risk. The mechanical assessment of the brittle fracture risk is usually based on conservative methodologies such as the global approach of fracture. Compared to the global approach currently in use, the local approach provides a more precise description of loading variables which govern the fracture behaviour of the RPV, such as local plasticity effects at crack tips (constraint effects, such as in case of small defects) and scale effects.

Codification should be conducted of local methods of brittle fracture assessment, such as the Beremin model or other similar models in order to have industrial methods.

• Conclusion number E4.3-01, IASCC behaviour in LWR environments: data and models for LTO beyond 60 years.

There is a need to continue carrying out experimental tests and modelling developments to improve the prediction of SCC and IASCC affecting internals. This covers analytical and service conditions testing, OPEX analysis as well as the development of advanced physically based modelling.

IASCC testing (initiation and propagation) and microstructural characterisation of materials should be performed at high fluence levels using components harvested from decommissioned PWRs. Understanding should be improved of the role of He on the IASCC susceptibility and quantitative data should be generated for the extension of existing models and predictive tools for IASCC. The VVER specific research programme investigating the corrosion behaviour of irradiated Tistabilised austenitic stainless steel should be implemented.

• Conclusion number E4.3-02, Irradiation embrittlement of SS and SS welds of RPVIs.

Structural integrity verification of RPVIs can be challenging without data and models covering the full range of dose at the end of intended LTO, for e.g. 80 years of operation or more. This information should be used to develop or improve models predicting irradiation embrittlement in RPVIs beyond 60 years of operation.

FT testing, including detailed fractographic examination, and microstructural characterisation of irradiated wrought SS and SS welds harvested from decommissioned BWRs and PWRs, should be performed. Specimens fabricated from components harvested from decommissioned LWRs can potentially be further irradiated in a materials test reactor with a neutron spectrum representative of LWRs to doses corresponding to for example 80 years of operation. Following further irradiation, FT testing, microstructural characterisation, and development of a predictive model should be carried out.

• Conclusion number E4.3-04, Repair of highly irradiated materials of RPVIs.

In the perspective of continued operation of reactors beyond 60 years, the development of methods for repairing irradiated RPVIs s provides an alternative to replacement in cases where this operation would be too complex to carry out.

The development of repair methods applicable to highly irradiated materials of RPVIs covers research on welding of irradiated materials considering advanced welding processes. Helium accumulation in irradiated SSs makes welding of such components challenging. R&D is still required to qualify adapted repair methods. Other methods than welding should also be investigated.

• Conclusion number E4.5-01, Harmonisation of the numerous approaches for EAF existing in parallel.

Different methods have been developed to date to address the effects of the LWRs environment on the fatigue calculations of nuclear power plants. For instance, US NRC regulatory requirements that address EAF during licence renewal activities are well developed. In France, AFCEN RCC-M code [385] provided recently explicit rules for EAF influence, based on extensive experimental programmes and optimisation of US NRC rules (Rule in Probationary Phase #3).

Although the relationship between the magnitude and frequency of the cyclic loading in LWR environments and the life of a component is well understood, additional testing is recommended to further reduce uncertainties, especially for cases where data are limited.

Therefore, additional testing is recommended to reduce uncertainties of the environmental impact on fatigue calculations and harmonise different code requirements, to better serve as a model for nuclear power plants using different approaches to relicensing for LTO.

• Conclusion number E4.6-03, NDE methods for selective leaching of buried and underground piping.

Further testing and field demonstration of NDE techniques to detect and quantify wall loss that has occurred due to selective leaching in gray cast iron materials would provide additional insights and confidence in the techniques. Small electromagnetic NDE sensors may offer advantages to detecting wall loss due to selective leaching in more complexly shaped buried cast iron components, such as valve bodies; these have not previously been evaluated.

Additional research on supplemental techniques not previously evaluated by the referenced technical reports should be carried out.

• Conclusion number E4.7-03, Fluence impact on concrete biological shield.

Prolonged exposure to irradiation may cause a reduction in mechanical properties and load carrying capacity and can therefore impact the structural integrity of the biological shield. Currently, the effect of irradiation on concrete is understood but poorly evaluated because the accelerated tests are not perfectly representative and are probably penalising.

Therefore, further research into concrete's long-term exposure to neutron irradiation is necessary, considering the unfavourable effects of the accelerated tests on harvested samples exposed beyond the fluence threshold.

• Conclusion number E4.7-08, NDE methods for steel liner embedded in concrete.

For portions of metallic liner embedded in concrete, there are no available NDE methods that are able to detect degradation of the liner plate. To find different deviations in connection with the embedded liner is not possible with the current techniques. The degradation is not possible to detect until the liner is penetrated and affects the leak tightness of the containment.

NDE methods should be developed that can detect ongoing degradations in the metallic liner or find deviations in the constructions.

• Conclusion number E4.8-01, Condition monitoring techniques for low-voltage cables.

Currently, a combination of different characterisation techniques is used to manage the ageing of the low-voltage cables, including visual inspection and some destructive techniques such as EAB. EAB gives clear acceptance end-pointcriterion independent of the initial value (not known for older installations) but it is a destructive test. Therefore, modern non-destructive methods should be developed and put into practice.

Recent studies have identified some promising techniques, such as the lowfrequency dielectric spectroscopy. However, their effectiveness in monitoring the ageing of installed low-voltage cables remains to be precisely studied, and acceptance criteria for different types of insulation (XLPE, EPR) remain to be defined. Other important aspects to be addressed are the verification of cables' conditions compared with the predictions.

• Conclusion number E4.9-01, Obsolescence management of I&C systems.

One of the biggest challenges as I&C systems become obsolete is that the replacements are increasingly digital. These digital replacements perform the same functions but may require additional programs to be in place (i.e. cybersecurity). They also require additional safety evaluations and common cause failure analyses that would not be required for a like-for-like replacement. Additionally, as digital upgrades to I&C systems are implemented, there needs to be consideration for the digital lifespan being shorter than for the analogue systems. Plans must be in place for the digital lifecycle, including software changes and more frequent hardware upgrades as necessary.

A suitable obsolescence management plan for I&C systems is necessary so that I&C managers are aware of the obsolete parts in their systems and ensure timely resolution, which includes a procurement plan and system/component replacement in a timely manner. This also includes a risk assessment based on the obsolete components' functions and a bridging strategy to ensure system functionality until a permanent solution can be put in place.

### **7. Dissemination plan and possible future actions**

<span id="page-314-0"></span>The objective of the NEA project "Status Report on LTO beyond 60 Years" is to perform a survey to provide an overview of the current status of knowledge regarding LTO of nuclear power plants, and to determine the gaps in knowledge and technology that need to be addressed to enable safe LTO of nuclear power plants beyond 60 years. The outcome of the report is a snapshot of the areas already properly addressed and the areas that could be enhanced, in terms of regulatory aspects, safety assessments and technical and scientific knowledge.

Research task results were compiled in this report which was approved by the CSNI on 2 June 2024 and published as an NEA status report. Dissemination activities, like national and international workshops, international meetings and conferences to share the project results nationally and internationally are planned for Q3/4 of 2025.

The results of the research task have been shared with contributing partners and other nuclear industry stakeholders such as nuclear power plants' operating organisations, regulatory authorities, support organisations and international organisations.

The following dissemination activities have been organised:

- 1. Presentation on LTO beyond 60 years research task interim results in NIC2024
  - Event organiser: NRG
  - Level of detail: 30-minute presentation
  - Place: Amsterdam, the Netherlands
  - Dates: 5-6 June 2024
  - Participants: operating organisations, regulatory authorities, support organisations and international organisations
- 2. Presentation on LTO beyond 60 years research task results at NEA WGIAGE meeting
  - Event organiser: NEA
  - Level of detail: 30-45-minute presentation
  - Place: Paris, France
  - Dates: March 2025
  - Participants: operating organisations, regulatory authorities, support organisations and international organisations
- 3. SMiRT conference
  - Event organiser: SMiRT
  - Level of detail: 30-45-minute presentation
  - Place: Toronto, Canada
  - Dates: August 2025
  - Participants: operating organisations, regulatory authorities, support organisations and international organisations

- 4. National workshops on LTO beyond 60 years research task results
  - Event organiser: key contributor to the project from participating countries (e.g. NRG, UJV, EDF, US NRC, EPRI, Vattenfall)
  - Level of detail: one day (connected with other relevant topics)
  - Place: to be determined
  - Dates: to be determined
  - Participants: all national stakeholders
- 5. International workshop on LTO beyond 60 years research task results
  - Event organiser: NEA
  - Level of detail: two days (connected with other relevant topics)
  - Place: Paris, France
  - Dates: November 2025
  - Participants: operating organisations, regulatory authorities, support organisations and international organisations
- 6. IAEA IGALL Steering Committee
  - Event organiser: IAEA
  - Level of detail: 30-45-minute presentation
  - Place: Vienna, Austria
  - Dates: December 2025
  - Participants: IGALL Steering Committee members and IGALL Working Group chairpersons (representatives of IAEA member states and international organisations in IGALL)
